title: Tennessee opens state’s newly expanded post-disaster response fund to Polk County flood survivors
description: Applications are now open for state-level flood recovery assistance for Polk County residents and businesses, marking the first use of Tennessee’s expanded disaster recovery fund. Individuals and households affected by severe flash flooding on Nov. 5 can apply for funding for disaster-related expenses like debris cleanup and disposal, mold remediation and fa[...]
text:
Tennessee Emergency Management Authority Commissioner Patrick Sheehan announces on Nov. 20, 2026 the opening of applications for Governor's Response and Recovery Fund programs for individuals, businesses and local governments affected by severe flooding in Polk County on Nov. 5, 2026. (Photo: Courtesy of TEMA)Applications are now open for state-level flood recovery assistance for Polk County residents and businesses, marking the first use of Tennessee’s expanded disaster recovery fund.
Individuals and households affected by severe flash flooding on Nov. 5 can apply for funding for disaster-related expenses like debris cleanup and disposal, mold remediation and fans or dehumidifiers. Small businesses can apply for a $10,000 stabilization grant and further help covering additional expenses. Polk County and the City of Copperhill can apply for state assistance with debris removal, repairs to public facilities and more.
The Governor’s Response and Recovery Fund is Tennessee’s answer to Federal Emergency Management Agency limitations and federal calls for states to take on more responsibility around disasters. 
The fund mirrors FEMA’s disaster assistance model, but aims to make financial aid more accessible to communities that face steep recovery costs but do not qualify for a federal disaster declaration, or that need funding on a faster or more reliable timeline than FEMA can provide. While FEMA assistance is triggered by a presidential major disaster declaration, the Tennessee governor can authorize use of the Governor’s Response and Recovery Fund. Gov. Bill Lee declared a major disaster in Polk County following the Nov. 5 flood.
“No program, even this one, can replace what people have lost or make the recovery process easy,” TEMA Commissioner Patrick Sheehan said Friday. “But we want survivors to know that they are not alone, and that state and local partners are continuing to work together to help address the needs created by this disaster.”
The fund was first created in 2025 to provide a faster cash infusion than FEMA could offer for East Tennessee communities devastated by Hurricane Helene. State lawmakers approved $44.2 million for the fund in April after expanding its purpose to include pathways for local governments and individuals to seek state assistance when federal aid is unavailable, insufficient or untimely.
“The fund will not cover every loss,” Sheehan said. “It cannot be used for lost revenue, lost wages, or insurance deductibles. Awards depend on program requirements, documented needs, and available funding, and submitting an application does not guarantee an award. Even within those limits, the assistance can help people and communities address important recovery needs and get back on their feet.”
Eligible applicants must show their need is connected to the flooding, and each type of application has its own eligibility and documentation requirements. Applicants must register as a supplier on Edison, the state’s payment system, before TEMA can process payments. 
Details and instructions are available on TEMA’s website. 
The fund generally doesn’t cover expenses already covered by an insurance provider, expenses eligible for assistance from another government program or expenses paid or needs met through another source, according to TEMA’s website.
Governor’s Response and Recovery Fund applications include:

Disaster Survivor Assistance for individuals and households, with applications accepted from Nov. 20 through Dec. 31 at 11:59 p.m. (One application per household, renters may qualify)
Small Business $10,000 Stabilization Grants for small businesses, with applications accepted Nov. 20 through Dec. 4 at 11:59 p.m.
Additional Disaster-Related Expenses for Small Businesses, with applications accepted from Dec. 7 through Dec. 31 at 11:59 p.m.
Local Government Disaster Assistance, with applications open from Nov. 20 through Dec. 31.

Sheehan said the small business stabilization grants are aimed at helping business owners who have already incurred disaster-related expenses in Polk County’s business district.
“These businesses are vital to the community. We want to do everything we can to help them remain open and continue contributing to Copperhill’s economic success,” he said.
The U.S. Small Business Administration is also offering options for relief for Bradley, McMinn, Monroe and Polk counties, including physical disaster loans, economic injury disaster loans and home disaster loans.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Commentary: How will the West Virginia Auditor’s Office regain public trust?
description: Voters find political corruption a major problem, and after a week of news reports and a federal indictment, the West Virginia Auditor’s Office is going to have a hard time earning back the public’s trust.
text:
Mark Hunt has served as West Virginia State Auditor since January 2025. (Photo by Amelia Ferrell Knisely/West Virginia Watch)Voters find political corruption a major problem, and after a week of news reports and a federal indictment, the West Virginia Auditor’s Office is going to have a hard time earning back the public’s trust.
Auditor Mark Hunt has been indicted by federal prosecutors, accused of signing nine deeds for a personal friend, Robert Johns. Legally, the deputy land commissioner is supposed to sign deeds. Hunt has been charged with nine counts of theft of more than $5,000 by a public official, and one count of bank fraud.
But Hunt isn’t the only Auditor’s Office employee facing federal charges. The grand jury also indicted Deputy Chief of Staff David Cole for allegedly helping create the deeds. Cole — according to a West Virginia Watch investigation — is also running a used car lot with Hunt. That property on which the small lot sits is owned by Johns. Hunt told West Virginia Watch he isn’t sure how much he paid for the lot. 
Another member of the Auditor’s staff, Frederic Caudill, was also indicted for allegedly helping create those deeds. And a fourth member of the office, Marie Hoffman, is charged with bank fraud for working at Hunt’s private law office while on the clock for the state.
The purpose of the State Auditor’s Office is to make sure that public money is being spent lawfully. The office has 12 departments with over 200 employees. 
Lawmakers have been unhappy with the news.
After West Virginia Watch’s initial report on the deeds — and before the indictments — Democratic lawmakers requested that West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey issue an opinion on whether Hunt followed the law in executing deeds for delinquent tax properties.
House Speaker Roger Hanshaw said Hunt should resign immediately.
“If he resolves to do otherwise, the House of Delegates will take swift action in January to restore integrity to the Office of the West Virginia State Auditor.”
Hunt has not resigned, and when speaking with the media, he insists his actions were lawful.
Last week, he told our reporter, “Office running smoothly, up $23 million this year alone. Once again I checked with all appropriate officials before doing anything.” 
Just yesterday, Hunt posted on X that his office is hiring audit inspectors. It may be difficult to find applicants because of the recent indictments. But maybe there are some people living under a rock who might apply.
On social media, people have been complaining that the Legislature hasn’t taken action to remove Hunt from office. The Legislature can only begin impeachment proceedings while they are in session, which doesn’t begin until January. But a special session is possible if it’s called by the governor or 3/5 of either the House or Senate agrees to a special session. 
According to state code, the governor can impeach an elected official for “official misconduct, malfeasance in office, incompetence, neglect of duty, or gross immorality.” Hunt’s indictments should count for that.
Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced last week that an investigation into Hunt’s used car dealership will be forwarded to federal prosecutors, but he hasn’t made any comments about the possibility of impeachment, or even a special session to allow the Legislature to do so. 
As long as Hunt is in office, West Virginians will not have confidence in the auditor’s office. Who could trust the officials in charge of finding and stopping fraud when members of the office may have been committing fraud themselves?
Voters won’t be able to choose a new auditor until 2028. After Hunt resigns or is impeached, Morrisey will have the task to replace him. But whoever he chooses will have to start working on day 1 to regain West Virginian’s trust.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Specter of cuts to education draw ire, questions, calls for tax increases
description: A budget warning delivered to school systems across the state over the weekend, telling them to prepare budgets next year that are essentially flat from this year, is drawing the ire of some education advocates and questions from county leaders.
text:
Maryland schools systems were warned by state officials over the weekend to prepare budgets for next year that are essentially flat from this year, drawing the ire of some education advocates and questions from county leaders. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)A budget warning delivered to school systems across the state over the weekend is drawing the ire of some education advocates and questions from county leaders.
In a letter from Budget Secretary Yaakov “Jake” Weissmann this weekend, state school systems were asked to prepare budgets that are essentially flat compared to the current year. It comes as the state faces multibillion-dollar budget challenges, driven in part by historic education spending.
“We really do not know much about what this is going to mean for counties,” said Sarah Sample, associate policy director at the Maryland Association of Counties. “There’s still a lot of questions.”
State analysts project a nearly $3 billion budget shortfall in the coming year, the first of was is expected to be a shortfall up to $16 billion over five years.
Education spending is one of the drivers of that shortfall.
The letter sent to local school leaders contains no specifics about cuts or how counties will be affected. Instead, it appears to be more of a warning to locals to prepare for potential cuts by hewing the fiscal 2028 budget request as close to the current year as possible.
Budget secretary calls on school systems to prepare flat budgets for next year

In the current budget year, the state spent more than $10 billion on education.
Next year, the fund dedicated to paying for the Blueprint for Maryland’s Future, the state’s sweeping decade-long education reform plan, will be exhausted. Covering the costs will require Gov. Wes Moore (D) and state lawmakers to draw an estimated $1.8 billion from the general fund. Of that, only $500 million relates to new costs.
Senate Minority Leader Stephen S. Hershey (R-Upper Shore) said the letter “certainly appears to acknowledge that the looming shortfall is not simply a general revenue problem, but rather the state’s inability to sustain its existing Blueprint funding commitments.”
Cutting the Blueprint funding will not be easy. It passed after several years of hard-fought political battles and has vocal supporters.
Maryland State Education Association President Paul Lemle, in a statement, said cuts would “undermine progress” in student achievement, expanded technical career training, increased teacher pay, easing teacher shortages and adding support for high poverty schools.
“Its devastating consequences for our students are completely unacceptable,” Lemle said in his statement.
The teacher’s union estimates the cuts could result in a loss of $430 million in state aid. Another $270 million could come from county cuts, according to the union.
“This approach should be rejected,” said Lemle, who called for tax increases instead. “Our students deserve better. Make sure the ultra-wealthy and corporations are paying their fair share, rather than avoiding the contributions that the rest of us are making to fund the public schools and services we all depend on. Fund our schools—don’t set back their continued progress with these sweeping, across-the-board cuts.”
The letter was also criticized by the Public School Superintendent’s Association of Maryland.
“Maryland’s school systems have held up our end of the Blueprint bargain,” the association said in a statement. “The State must sustain its side of that partnership.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
The association called for increases for students with disabilities, and asked that one-year budget changes not result in ongoing reductions in per-pupil spending. And it asked for increased flexibility.
“Give local school systems meaningful flexibility to protect classroom instruction and direct staff and resources where students need them most,” the association said. “Districts will remain accountable for student outcomes and equitable access. State expectations for implementation should reflect what districts can realistically deliver with the funding provided.”
When the General Assembly returns in January, it will face some “very hard conversations” on the budget, Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City) told business leaders last week.
Constitutionally, the only task the legislature must complete is passage of a balanced budget. Within that, the state is required to fund one priority — education.
Ferguson said it will taker all-options approach to solve the problem.
“The idea that we just solve it all with cuts, solve it all with just looking at keeping everything the same, is not realistic,” Ferguson said. “It is going to be a balanced approach. It is going to be a four-year plan. That means for the next 10 months, it is going to be very, very challenging.”
Pressure is mounting on state lawmakers from bond rating agencies, who want to see more fiscal discipline from the state. Instead of an annual effort to paper over long-term problems with fund balances and one-time fixes, the agencies expressed an interest in seeing an alignment of revenues and spending.
Analysts urge action on four years of projected gaps to get ahead of recession scenario

Moore, Ferguson  and House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Prince George’s and Anne Arundel) have agreed, at least in principle, to craft a four-year budget solution, starting in January.
Other legislative leaders, meanwhile, warn that tax increases may be part of the solution.
“I’m expecting cuts and I’m expecting revenues,” said House Majority Leader Del. David Moon (D-Montgomery) during a Maryland Chamber of Commerce event last week.
The options range from increasing the sales tax or expanding it to include services — or both — as well as corporate tax changes and other proposals rejected in recent past sessions.
“They’re all the goodies and the oldies that have been floated in various things I’ve been reading,” Moon said. “I have no magic ball other than to say it seems like something has finally happened.”
Sample said many counties would likely see little to no relief if the state made changes to how it funds the Blueprint. She estimated maybe as many as six could potentially benefit.
A number of different scenarios each mean different outcomes for the counties. Some could result in additional costs shifted onto the counties, she cautioned.
In all, the state’s political subdivisions are paying $2.2 billion over anticipated costs for the education plan, according to the association.
“At most, this letter could signal an FY28 Blueprint cost reduction for, maybe, six or so of the poorest jurisdictions some of which have already raised taxes and fees to keep up with rising costs since implementation began, while absorbing millions in unrelated state cost shifts,” Sample said.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: After voters booted some top Republican lawmakers, will KY’s GOP supermajority stay on course?
description: After a handful of key GOP Kentucky lawmakers lost their reelection bids earlier this month, some saw the outcomes as a signal that voters want the majority party’s platform to change within the General Assembly.  But Democrats shouldn’t get too excited. Although Nine Republican incumbents were ousted from their seats in suburban areas of the […]
text:
The Kentucky House of Representatives chamber on Jan. 3, 2024 as Gov. Andy Beshear delivered the State of the Commonwealth address to a joint session of the legislature. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Arden Barnes)After a handful of key GOP Kentucky lawmakers lost their reelection bids earlier this month, some saw the outcomes as a signal that voters want the majority party’s platform to change within the General Assembly. 
But Democrats shouldn’t get too excited.
Although Nine Republican incumbents were ousted from their seats in suburban areas of the state, particularly around Louisville, Republicans will still have supermajorities in the House and Senate. 
And Senate Republican Floor Leader Max Wise, of Campbellsville, told the Kentucky Lantern that he did not anticipate any major changes for the GOP when lawmakers return to Frankfort in January for the 2027 legislative session. On the Senate side, two Republicans that lost were Licensing and Occupations Chair Sen. Julie Raque Adams, of Louisville, and Education Committee Vice Chair Sen. Lindsey Tichenor, of Smithfield. Wise commended both women for their “passion for policy.” 
Wise added that he saw those election losses as “a trickle down from federal policies that were being put forth at that level.” Nationwide, some attributed the November “blue tsunami” as a reaction to the economy and the state of democracy under the Trump administration. 
Wise said he did not expect Kentucky Republicans to shift away from priorities, like lowering the state income tax as they have done for the past few years. 
Senate Republican Floor Leader Max Wise, of Campbellsville, speaks to reporters on the Senate floor. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)
“I do not think there was anything that we have done as state policy that was a direct effect on those elections at all. I think it was a traditional presidential midterm election,” Wise said. “We’ve seen historically how those have been for the sitting party during a presidential election of the president.”
However, Lexington Rep. Lindsey Burke, the new Democratic floor leader in the House, said lawmakers could address some affordability issues, like passing laws to expand housing or support Medicaid access. 
“I’m hopeful that there will be some shifts within the majority party’s priorities, but all I am hearing is a dogged commitment to continuing the same policies that led us here,” Burke said. “So, that’s not good for Kentucky, and that’s going to set us back even further. I hope that maybe behind closed doors, cooler heads and more principled positions can be had.”
Issues on the table
There are a host of issues before the Kentucky General Assembly as lawmakers prepare for the 2027 session. Earlier this year, lawmakers did not pass an omnibus housing bill aimed at tackling the state’s housing shortage or a bill to protect ratepayers from bearing electricity costs for data centers within their communities. Both issues are expected to come up in the future, as well as legislation to curb unwarranted use of Flock cameras. Other perennial issues include health care, supporting children’s needs, education and more. 
Jason Bailey, executive director of the progressive Kentucky Center for Economic Policy, said that while 2027 is not a budget session, Kentucky has a revenue forecast showing a projected $1.7 billion more over the biennium than anticipated. That may put “on the General Assembly to to use available resources to do several things,” such as allocate more Medicaid funding. Over the summer, Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear used $255 million from taxes to block a 4% reimbursement cut for providers. Bailey noted that among those incumbent Republicans who lost, Adams and Rep. Ken Fleming, of Louisville, were top voices for Republicans on Medicaid policy. They co-chaired the Medicaid Oversight and Advisory Board. 
Bailey said he also saw the elections as a sign of how voters feel about data centers. House Republican Whip Jason Nemes of Middletown, sponsored a 2025 bill expanding a sales and use tax break for data center equipment to all Kentucky counties. His opponent Democrat Jennifer Hardin criticized him for it. That House District sits in Jefferson and Oldham counties, where residents have vocally opposed data center projects. 
Caleb Brown, the chief executive of the conservative Bluegrass Institute, said it may be possible for lawmakers to “try to devote more state resources to Medicaid,” but he did not “think it’ll go anywhere.” He, too, believed housing to be a major issue in the next legislative session, despite Rep. Susan Tyler Witten, R-Louisville, not being reelected. She co-chaired the housing task force and proposed legislation in the area. 
“I wondered briefly how that might affect the appetite for housing reform, but the issue hasn’t changed,” Brown said. “Young people are still being priced out of home ownership.” 
Brown also predicts the General Assembly will take on guardrails on surveillance technology following a recent U.S. Supreme Court decision that said police officers conducted a Fourth Amendment search when reviewing a person’s cell phone location information. 
“I think that there will be a serious effort among people who care about freedom in the Republican Party versus everybody else to try to claw back some of the surveillance powers that the General Assembly rolled out last year,” Brown said. 
House Minority Floor Leader Lindsey Burke, D-Lexington. (LRC Public Information)
Yet, where some advocates see opportunities, Terry Brooks, the executive vice president and ambassador of Sunrise Children’s Services, said “kids lost” in many races during the 2026 General Election. Several of the incumbents had worked on legislation for families and children, including a law to aid Kentuckians raising minor relatives — kinship caregivers.
“My regret at the changed line-up in Frankfort is not an indictment of those newly elected lawmakers. In several cases, I frankly have heard nothing but positives as to the intent of the winning candidates,” Brooks said. “But kid advocates have to be realists. Rookies from the minority party simply are not going to be players of influence come January. It does not matter about what substance those newcomers may bring; it’s an issue of power and not ideas. Therefore, we face a pivotal point of inflection.” 
The politics of it all
Burke leads a caucus with about seven new members. All of them are centered around the state’s urban areas in Lexington and Louisville. Democrats did have one seat in Eastern Kentucky, but Rep. Ashley Tackett Laferty, of Martin, did not seek reelection. Her seat will be filled by Republican Tanner Hesterberg. 
Burke told the Lantern the most notable change for Democrats will be having more committee assignments. 
“Because our numbers increased significantly enough, that has changed the proportion of committee membership, and so we are going to have a greater presence in the committee meetings where the policies are hashed out, and I think that’s going to lead to a greater impact on legislation,” she said. 
A few more votes may also give Democrats some strength when it comes to dissenting votes. In 2024, some Republicans that are part of the right-wing Liberty Caucus joined House Democrats in voting against chamber rules and called for more power for rank-and-file members. Burke said it would be interesting to see how adding a “true voice from the left” to that conversation with Robert Bell, a representative-elect from Louisville who is a democratic socialist, may change things. 
“I think most of us are progressives and not quite as extreme as Representative-elect Bell holds his viewpoints, so it’ll be interesting to see how much that moves the needle and whether or not there can be some alliances with the Liberty Caucus, who also prioritize individual liberties and freedoms,” Burke said. “Often we can agree that that’s a good thing. So it’ll be interesting to see if by having a member go even further left, if we start to meet some of those far-right members and have the opportunity to work with them.”
Lexington and Louisville, the largest cities in Kentucky, have less representation in the majority party now. As for if the make-up of parties furthers an urban-rural divide, Burke said her caucus wants to hear from rural areas. She noted that House Democrats held a Medicaid listening tour in the interim session with Prestonsburg and Morehead stops. 
“While at the moment it may look more like a stark rural-urban divide,” she said. “The House Democrats are committed to representing everyone in the state, and we’re going to continue to do the work regardless of the outcomes of elections.”
From his view, Wise said Republicans have had “a pretty fair balance” in terms of policy and budget when it comes to rural and urban areas. The most recent one-time spending bill, which totalled $1.7 billion for projects, had about $189 million allocated for Louisville initiatives. Urban areas are “economic engines” but it’s also important to invest in water lines and infrastructure in small cities and counties, he said. 
“I don’t think you’re going to see us take our foot off the gas as a supermajority of what we’re going to continue to do in terms of policy,” Wise said. 
Kentucky Lantern reporter Sarah Ladd contributed to this story.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: What’s on the horizon for Virginia’s healthcare landscape in 2027?
description: As Virginia’s state lawmakers prepare for their 2027 legislative session, they’re also eyeing possible federal shifts in healthcare affordability and access, issues that defined congressional midterm elections and stand to impact state spending plans in the coming year.    “I think the American people sent a pretty darn strong message,” said Sen. Barbara Fav[...]
text:
The Virginia State Capitol on Nov. 23, 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)As Virginia’s state lawmakers prepare for their 2027 legislative session, they’re also eyeing possible federal shifts in healthcare affordability and access, issues that defined congressional midterm elections and stand to impact state spending plans in the coming year.   
“I think the American people sent a pretty darn strong message,” said Sen. Barbara Favola, D-Arlington, who chairs the chamber’s Education and Health Committee. 
Healthcare leaders and researchers have predicted the nation’s uninsured population would surge after Congress passed the reconciliation bill called H.R. 1 last summer. The bill entails forthcoming changes to Medicaid eligibility. 
Starting January 2027, enrollees will be subject to an additional verification process each year and expected to meet work or volunteer hours criteria unless they have certain medical conditions. 
More than 5,000 lawful immigrants were pushed off of the insurance program this fall as part of the rollout of changes. 
A state report found 13 rural hospitals could be subject to closure or service cuts, and multiple Virginian hospitals have already trimmed services and cited H.R. 1 as a factor.
“The requirements were intended to kick people off the rolls,” Favola said. “The way you stop the bleed is by keeping more people insured, not less.”
Sen. Barbara Favola, D-Arlington, speaks with reporters in the Virginia General Assembly Building on Feb. 25, 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)
Democratic candidates in Virginia and across the country cemented their campaigns on addressing H.R. 1 and restoring expired Affordable Care Act subsidies, helping flip both chambers to the party’s control. 
But Favola — who also serves on the Senate’s finance committee and attended a briefing on the state of Medicaid in Virginia at the chamber’s recent retreat — still noted “uncertainty” of how soon Congress will be able to deliver, and if President Donald Trump will sign whatever they send to his desk. 
That means the state legislature has to forecast carefully as it enters its next budget cycle. 
Medicaid’s expenditure growth has continued to increase due to ballooning healthcare costs and the program’s expansion, according to a presentation at the retreat. 
Virginia’s total healthcare spending increased from $9.4 billion in fiscal year 2017 to $28.5 billion in 2026. 
The boost stems from the state’s 2018 vote to expand the Medicaid program, which widened eligibility criteria for thousands of Virginians. This enabled people without employer-provided insurance who made too little to comfortably purchase an ACA plan to qualify for Medicaid coverage. 
But over 300,000 of those in the Medicaid expansion population could be at risk of dropping out of the program next year due to H.R. 1. The program is the largest source of federal funds to states, prompting Trump and GOP majorities in Congress to cut spending for the program and boost it elsewhere. 
Medicaid spending in Virginia is also expected to reach 24% of the state’s general fund budget by 2028. The general fund is the bucket of the state budget that is filled through taxes from individuals, corporations and sales and use taxes. 
More than adjusting Medicaid insurance for patients, H.R. 1 will also change hospital funding mechanisms that can affect their revenue and ability to chip into the state’s funding responsibilities for the expanded Medicaid populations. 
As the state budget happens in two year cycles, lawmakers will begin work on earmarking spending allocations for the next two years this coming January. 
Though Trump could prove a sticking point if Congress tried to reverse H.R. 1’s impact on Medicaid, Favola noted Democratic gains in GOP-leaning states with rural populations that rely on Medicaid. 
Late this summer, U.S. Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Virginia, and U.S. Rep. Jennifer McClellan, D-Richmond, suggested that voters could compel more lawmakers to take action on healthcare access and possibly reverse the H.R. 1 changes. 
What seems more immediately likely, Favola said, is for Congress to restore expired ACA subsidies that had helped low-income families better afford health insurance. 
The debacle was the center of a government shutdown last October and spurred 17 Republicans nationwide to side with the Democratic colleagues on extending the subsidies. The votes were not enough to preserve the subsidies at the time, but Democrats have since clinched nearly 260 seats and their largest majority in over 30 years. 
For now, Virginia has invested $150 million in a state-level substitute for the ACA subsidies, allowing eligible families to utilize them as open enrollment is under way for the next year.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Albemarle families navigate closure of schools after employees weren’t screened for child abuse
description: Under pressure to do well on an exam, University of Virginia graduate student Kara Guyton was home taking a test last Thursday, joined by her three elementary school children, who made forts with blankets while students in other parts of the commonwealth were in class. In Albemarle County, Guyton’s kids and others were out of […]
text:
A student balances a bubble outside the Albemarle County Schools Building on Nov.  20, the second day of the division’s closure of schools. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)Under pressure to do well on an exam, University of Virginia graduate student Kara Guyton was home taking a test last Thursday, joined by her three elementary school children, who made forts with blankets while students in other parts of the commonwealth were in class.
In Albemarle County, Guyton’s kids and others were out of the classroom because school leaders discovered that over 500 employees had not undergone proper screening, forcing families to make daily arrangements for more than 14,000 children beginning last Thursday.
Guyton said the closure announcement was “gut-wrenching” because she knew it would affect her family, with four school days before Thanksgiving. The closure could stretch past the break, depending on how long the employee screenings take.
“If you are sitting around thinking this is not normal, you’re not alone,” said Guyton, as she gathered with several other parents and their children outside the school administration office on Friday to raise awareness of the issue.
The decision followed the school division’s review of employee Child Protective Services Central Registry screenings, which had never been submitted to the Virginia Department of Health, despite clearing initial criminal history checks. 
This follows a series of resignations and arrests involving school employees and leaders over the past six months.
The list includes the arrest of an elementary school instructional assistant charged with sexual abuse, a former superintendent resigning and multiple employees being placed on leave during reviews.
Three school board members also resigned amid claims of public mistrust and administrative collapse. Three school officials also faced misdemeanor counts for failure to report suspected child abuse.
A view from outside the Albemarle County Office Building. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)
On Oct. 15, leaders of the Albemarle County Board of Supervisors formally requested accountability measures from the school board and assistance and oversight from the Virginia Department of Education, which said in an Oct. 27 memo obtained by the Mercury that “meaningful state action is now necessary.”
The agency added it “remains committed to working collaboratively with the local school board and division leadership to navigate this crisis to ensure any gaps, deficiencies, and blind spots related to policies, protocols, and organizational culture are identified and addressed transparently so that student safety is prioritized, and trust is rebuilt with staff, families, and community members.”
Soon afterward, Acting Schools Superintendent Chandra Hayes initiated internal review and uncovered the three-year administrative failure to submit 524 staff members for CPS Central Registry screening.
Hayes confirmed that none of the individuals currently under active law enforcement investigation or criminally charged with abuse, neglect, or failure to report were part of the unsubmitted group.
 Legal and policy drivers

Hayes cited two state laws and a board policy as the reasons she closed the schools beginning Thursday, saying employees must be vetted before students return.
“Families should not have to accept any uncertainty about the adults working with their children, and I will not risk the safety of our students,” Hayes said in the announcement.
The laws she raised focus on requiring schools to thoroughly check an applicant’s criminal and child abuse history before hiring them. Anyone with a confirmed history of child abuse, or certain criminal convictions, cannot be employed by the school. 
Hayes also referenced the school board’s policy calling for the immediate termination of a school employee if they are officially found responsible for child abuse or neglect and all appeals have been completed. The school division is required to terminate their employment and may recommend that the state revoke their teaching license.
In the aftermath, Albemarle schools continued meal service at cafeterias last Thursday and Friday and offered asynchronous learning tasks to students. Child care before and after school was canceled.
The superintendent said the division set a target reopening date of Nov. 30, after Thanksgiving, subject to confirmation by Friday.
Guyton, like other parents who spoke with the Mercury, said she understands the need to close the schools completely, but the future is still concerning. 
“I think that my fear at this point is what’s next, and it seems like every month we are hearing about … a scandal, a personnel issue, or it’s our former principal getting arrested, and it just feels like this upheaval of this year is never ending,” Guyton said. 
 ‘I’m pretty furious’

Parents said the leadership departures, legal charges and unvetted employees have been frustrating, and finding child care has been challenging since all 25 schools were closed, especially for single parents and for students with special needs.
About a quarter of the students come from economically disadvantaged families during the 2025-2026 school year, and nearly 14% have some disability.
Christina Ra, a Family Council Officer for Albemarle County Schools, said ACPS serves a diverse range of families, so the division’s crisis plans should account for how closures affect different students and families — including access to food, childcare, transportation and school activities — rather than relying on each school to improvise. 
The Family Council hosted parents, some of whom were irritated by the division’s actions, along with ACPS Chief Communications Officer Jason Grant, on a call immediately following the announcement. 
The meeting was originally a monthly council meeting to discuss technology and AI use in classrooms.
“The frustration came because it was as though a lot of the implementation was quick and not as thoughtful and inclusive as it should have been,” Ra said. “Some reps expressed concerns about children being alone at home and not actually having food.” 
Parents and supporters gather on Nov. 20, 2026, the second day of Albemarle County school closures, to raise awareness of issues facing the school division. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)
Elise Clerkin, a parent who has older children, said it was important for her to rally with other parents outside of the school division’s offices on Friday because she is “really fed up” with being let down by Albemarle Schools, and so are her friends, some of whom are teachers.
“I have respect for the new superintendent who’s coming in and doing her best in a terrible situation, but I’m honestly pretty furious,” Clerkin said. “You want at the very least to feel safe sending your kids to school, and you want them to be able to thrive in the public school environment, and I feel like we’ve just been let down.” 
Ben Pearson-Nelson, president of the Virginia Parent Teacher Association, said the closure and allegations shocked families and raised fears about student safety, accountability, and trust in school leadership. 
“I have no doubt in my mind that every school board member in the commonwealth is keenly aware and getting questions about what happened and what it means,” Pearson-Nelson said. “I envision a … double-checking of what processes are already in place, what mechanisms schools are using, and then also what holes exist.”
Ra said Hayes has done an “incredible job” to improve things. However, she said accountability for rebuilding public trust must extend to the school board, not rest solely on the acting superintendent. 
Ra called for the school board to demonstrate the same transparency, communication, visibility, and commitment to improvement that it expects from Hayes.
“Why is it her job alone?” Ra said. “We want to see accountability from the school board.”
A sign reading “Honk if you support us” stands upright during a gathering of parents raising awareness about issues facing Albemarle County Public Schools, Nov. 20, 2026. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)
 What’s next

Albemarle schools said no make-up instructional days will be required because of the surplus hours built into the state-approved division calendar. 
The Secretary and Department of Education implemented expedited Central Registry screenings, established oversight of an independent investigation into systemic and organizational failures, and reinforced the Oct. 27 directive to ensure continued state-level coordination with ACPS interim leadership.
Gov. Abigail Spanberger said in a statement that the division’s prior leadership “failed” the children and families they served, and neglected to  follow the background-check law, and uphold the trust of the commonwealth’s citizens.
“My administration is committed to the education and safety of every child in Virginia, and we will use every available tool to rectify this failure and ensure accountability,” she said.
As of Sunday, all processed CPS Central Registry background check applications have been cleared, with 12 applications still awaiting processing.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Land conservation group permanently protects over 1,000 acres of historic Virginia farmland
description: Nestled between Hanover County and the New Kent County line, Retreat Farm’s family ownership dates back to the 1700’s. In the 1600’s, colonists were said to have patented over 1000 acres at the bend in the Pamunkey River where “early Indian Councils and colonialists met to confer peace.”  Now, 1,145 acres of the property’s farmland, […]
text:
Retreat Farm’s family ownership dates back to the 1700’s. (Photo courtesy Capital Region Land Conservancy) Nestled between Hanover County and the New Kent County line, Retreat Farm’s family ownership dates back to the 1700’s. In the 1600’s, colonists were said to have patented over 1000 acres at the bend in the Pamunkey River where “early Indian Councils and colonialists met to confer peace.” 
Now, 1,145 acres of the property’s farmland, wetlands and 4.5 acres of shoreline will be permanently conserved by the Capital Region Land Conservancy (CRLC), the group announced Monday. 
This is the largest conservation easement held by CRLC and was made possible in part through the United States Department of Agriculture’s Natural Resources Conservation Service.
“Protecting agricultural land is essential to sustaining farming and supporting our rural communities because thousands of acres of farmland are being converted to other uses every day,” Dr. Edwin Martinez of the Natural Resources Conservation Service said in a release.
Retreat Farm has been an active farm for over 375 years and still produces crops today on 452 acres of the land. The land contains large marl deposits, a calcium carbonate-rich clay that is used as fertilizer, that was able to revive tobacco fields that had been excessively farmed in prior years.
Retreat Farm is on Piping Tree Ferry Road, where the ferry ran from 1720 until the early 1900’s. CRPL reports that the Blackwell family owned the farm until 1772 when it was sold to Carter Braxton. Braxton lived across the river and notably “signed the Declaration of Independence, and financed a considerable sum in support of the Revolutionary War,” according to CRPL. 
Retreat Farm sits on the banks of the Pamunkey River. (Photo courtesy Capital Region Land Conservancy)
The land has been passed down through family ownership until now, when they have granted the conservation easement. 
The move blocks development in the future while allowing agricultural use to continue, which CRPL said would diminish the property value and local land use taxes in perpetuity.
This helps make it more affordable for the family to own the land and prevent its sale even if economic pressures mount in the future. 
“Keeping 450 acres of fertile farmland in production is so important to our business and Hanover’s cultural identity,” said Eric Randolph, who currently farms the land.
Part of the conservation easement also allows limited forestry activities in the area.
The Retreat Farm includes thriving habitats of plants and wildlife. The property connects to another 500 acres across the river that is also under a conservation easement.

title: Recount director aims to meet Dec. 20 deadline in Senate Republican leader’s tight race
description: The recount of a closely contested state Senate race involving one of Indiana’s most powerful Republicans will begin soon, as election workers have less than a month to verify results before the statutory recount deadline. The Indiana Recount Commission met Monday to appoint a recount director and consolidate petitions filed by Democrats and Republicans to [[...]
text:
Indiana Secretary of State Diego Morales, second from right, presides over an election commission meeting Monday, Nov. 23, 2026. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The recount of a closely contested state Senate race involving one of Indiana’s most powerful Republicans will begin soon, as election workers have less than a month to verify results before the statutory recount deadline.
The Indiana Recount Commission met Monday to appoint a recount director and consolidate petitions filed by Democrats and Republicans to initiate a recount of Senate District 45 — currently held by Republican Senate President Pro Tem Chris Garten.
Preliminary totals show Garten, whom Republicans selected as the Senate’s new leader last week, ahead by 297 votes in his race against Democrat Nick Marshall.
Democrats called for a recount and raised the possibility of seeking a special election amid questions about Election Day voting equipment problems, while Garten filed his own petition for a recount of the race.
The Recount Commission selected Evan Norris, an attorney from Zionsville, to act as recount director during a short procedural meeting Monday. 
Norris also oversaw the recount in the Republican primary contest between state Sen. Spencer Deery and Paula Copenhaver that wasn’t completed until three months after the May primary. The Recount Commission’s decision in that race was later overturned by the state Supreme Court.
after the Recount Commission attempted to throw out
Recount work is already underway for the Garten-Marshall race in the southern Indiana district.
Garten sworn in as Indiana Senate leader after court intervention, calls for recount of own election

Indiana State Police impounded ballots from Clark and Floyd counties last week, with officials set to begin sorting ballots Tuesday during a pre-recount inspection in Clark County.
A similar inspection will be held in Floyd County next Monday, with the formal recount expected to begin the following day.
Norris said all materials will be scanned and recounted, including absentee and Election Day ballots from each precinct and vote center in Clark and Floyd counties.
The recount will also include an inspection of voting machines.
State law sets a Dec. 20 deadline to complete the recount, though the Recount Commission can extend that deadline for good cause.
Norris said the State Board of Accounts is sending 20 to 30 auditors to assist with the recount, so he doesn’t anticipate needing an extension at this time.
Current Republican Secretary of State Diego Morales is, by state law, chair of the three-member Recount Commission, along with Republican member Paul Mullin and Democratic member Michael Claytor. It is up to the commission to approve recount results during a meeting that has not yet been scheduled.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: After another tough year for loons, one lake exemplifies their struggle
description: It was another difficult summer for New Hampshire’s loons. After some improvement last summer, this year the loons that nest, fish and make their voices heard on the state’s lakes saw a dip in their parenting success. Fewer than half of mated loons successfully raised a chick through the summer, with a final tally of […]
text:
A lone loon dives for fish in Great Bay Estuary, near Durham, on Aug. 10. Common loons are state-listed as "threatened" in New Hampshire by the state Fish and Game Department and protected by the New Hampshire Endangered Species Conservation Act. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)It was another difficult summer for New Hampshire’s loons.
After some improvement last summer, this year the loons that nest, fish and make their voices heard on the state’s lakes saw a dip in their parenting success. Fewer than half of mated loons successfully raised a chick through the summer, with a final tally of 0.43 surviving chicks per breeding pair, according to the Moultonborough-based Loon Preservation Committee.
That’s below the level of 0.48 needed for the loons to sustain a stable adult population, according to Tiffany Grade, Squam Lake biologist with the committee.
“It’s really disturbing,” she said. “… The loons are continuing to struggle.”
As biologists digest the season’s data, they are also absorbing the findings of a report from Grade and other Loon Preservation Committee biologists on the broad prevalence of dangerous pollution in loon eggs, published in a peer-reviewed journal this year. The report showed the near-ubiquitous presence of contaminants in egg samples from across the state. In particular, eggs from Squam Lake, a focus of the study, showed high levels of certain contaminants as well as thin, relatively weak shells and smaller overall size, raising a red flag for biologists.
The findings highlight what the species is up against, and why humans should pay attention, said Grade and Micah Miller, director of the loon and Arctic programs and co-director for the Center for Ecotoxicology at the Biodiversity Research Institute in Maine, who was not involved in the study.
“Across the board, we know that the environmental and human health risks of having contaminants in the environment, that alone is enough reason to try to reduce exposure,” Miller said. 
A challenging coexistence
Of the various threats loons must contend with in New Hampshire’s waters, most are human-caused. 
The birds’ need for clean, clear lakes and plentiful freshwater fish bring them to the same lakes that attract throngs of human visitors every summer.
Those visitors include the anglers and boaters who love New Hampshire’s lakes but who can also present unique hazards to loons. Ingestion of lead fishing tackle remains the “most immediate” threat to loon populations, according to Grade. And disturbance — whether from wakes washing over a nesting site, humans approaching too closely and spooking would-be parents, or deadly boat-loon collisions — is another problem.
In fact, considering last year’s relatively successful loon season, the cold, rainy start to summer may have been a beneficial factor, Grade said: Unfavorable weather could have reduced boat traffic on New Hampshire lakes during the most crucial window of early-season nest building.
But rain isn’t always helpful to loons. Particularly strong storms, like those increasing in severity with climate change, can harm their nests, too. And climate change has also contributed to the increasing incidence of certain illnesses, like avian malaria. 
There is also the matter of chemical pollution.
The Loon Preservation Committee has been privately funding the testing of loon eggs from different water bodies around New Hampshire, after high PCB levels were detected at Squam Lake. (Courtesy of the Loon Preservation Committee)
The Environmental Toxicology and Chemistry study, authored by Grade and fellow Loon Preservation Committee coauthors R. Wesley Flynn and Harry Vogel, assessed a range of major contaminants that affect loons and their habitats, from industrial chemicals to pesticides, PFAS, and metals like aluminum, lead and mercury. 
These pollutants are persistent in nature, said Miller, who was not involved in the study. Many remain in an ecosystem for years after they are released, making them a continual threat to wildlife. As top-of-the-food-chain predators, loons get a magnified dose.
For the study, over a period of nearly 30 years, the Loon Preservation Committee collected eggs that they determined were not going to hatch from 28 lakes across New Hampshire. They then tested 92 eggs for contaminants and measured their overall volume, as well as the thickness of their shells.
The results reveal the widespread presence of organic and metal pollutants in the loon eggs. While the Loon Preservation Committee has previously raised the alarm over these contaminants during the course of the study, the paper’s publication was the first peer-reviewed research to confirm the presence of PFAS “forever chemicals” and flame retardant chemicals known as BDE in common loon eggs, according to the committee.
In many cases, the chemicals were observed at levels that alarmed the biologists because of their documented ability to cause negative effects in other species. Even in the group of eggs that biologists believe most closely resembles the “baseline” egg for New Hampshire loons, about half contained a higher level of contaminants than that known to cause negative effects in other birds, Grade said. 
Other groups surpassed those levels. One of particular concern was the cluster of eggs from central New Hampshire’s Squam Lake, located just northwest of Lake Winnipesaukee.
Squam Lake as a mirror
In some ways, that wasn’t surprising, the researchers said. In fact, Grade said, concern over the loons in Squam Lake was what initially touched off the analysis that ultimately led to this paper. In the winter of 2004-2005, the population of loons on Squam Lake shrank to about half of what it had been the year before. For years after, loon pairs on Squam struggled to reproduce, Grade said. 
The Loon Preservation Committee initiated intensive monitoring and management of the Squam loons at that point, in an effort to help them thrive, Grade said. But despite their work, the loons on Squam have continued to struggle to some degree in the years since. Within the last eight years, the average success rate on Squam Lake has been 0.3 surviving chicks per mating pair, according to Loon Preservation Committee data. 
There are many reasons for this, Grade said. The July report shed light on one in particular: The eggs on Squam Lake were disproportionately affected by certain contaminants, including PCBs, PFAS, and the pesticide DDT.
High exposure levels also appear correlated to weaker eggshells and smaller egg volumes, Grade said. While eggs from other lakes across the state were typical on average, the eggs from Squam were both smaller and thinner-shelled than expected.
This has implications for the health of loons overall, as the quality of an egg is generally indicative of the health of a mother bird, Miller said. 
“If she has a high contaminant load that’s interfering with her ability to lay down nutrients into that developing egg at the right time, you’re going to get, you know, some sort of malformations and so forth,” he said. 
With clear indication that contaminants are widespread in New Hampshire’s loons, the study is a first step toward assessing what is happening to the birds as a result, Grade said. 
While Squam Lake is a “more extreme” example, concerning levels of contamination were found in eggs from all over the state, Grade said. 
“What we saw in this paper is the widespread nature of this contamination in loon eggs across the state,” she said.
Other water bodies were also singled out in the report for the high PFAS content in eggs from their shores, including Canobie Lake, Lake Winnipesaukee and Arlington Mill Reservoir. The report noted the relative proximity of Canobie Lake and the Arlington Mill Reservoir to the former Saint-Gobain Performance Plastics factory.
“The exposure patterns are vastly different depending on where you are looking and what the source might be,” Miller said. 
The study is limited to some degree by the fact that the eggs collected for analysis were, by study design, all eggs that had failed to hatch. 
While some eggs were prevented from hatching due to external factors, like human disruption, others may have stopped developing due to internal factors. Some of the contaminant levels observed in the study exceeded those known to cause embryo mortality in other bird species, according to the report. The result? The samples may be biased somewhat toward higher contaminant levels, since heavily contaminated eggs are more likely to be collected for research, Grade and Miller said. 
(Both said, however, that this way of conducting egg studies is much preferred by biologists, especially when a bird species is imperiled, as loons are. Grade said she believed the bias in the results was insubstantial.)
Also by virtue, in part, of the difficulty of collection, the egg samples were limited in number, with some geographic gaps in data, Miller noted. But he added that the study was a valuable and unique example of long-term monitoring effort. 
Loons as a mirror
Fortunately for loons, despite the headwinds they face, the species seems to be increasing — albeit slowly — in prevalence in northern New England, Miller said. But their continued improvement is not a given, and the presence of high contaminant levels in their eggs is still concerning, for loons and other wildlife, he said. 
Just as eggs can signal the health of parent birds, loons themselves can be a window into the wellbeing of an ecosystem as a whole, Grade said. The contamination of loon eggs has concerning implications for them and for New Hampshire’s waterways, she said. 
Grade called for more widespread testing, for the sake of both environmental and human health. Already, testing connected to the project has resulted in a fish consumption advisory for Squam Lake related to elevated PCB content. 
Grade added that action to reduce chemical emissions was crucial to prevent the plight of the loons on Squam Lake from becoming more widespread. 
“Squam is really kind of holding up a mirror to the rest of the state, and as far as we know, the loon population,” she said. “And in some ways, it may be almost an early warning signal, you know, to what could happen. But we’re working very hard to try to make sure it doesn’t happen throughout the rest of New Hampshire.”

name: Nevada Current
title: Democrats demand answers from Oz after delay in $50B rural health awards
authors: Sarah Jane Tribble / KFF Health News
description: Congressional Democrats are demanding answers and more transparency from the Trump administration after a nine-day delay of annual awards from a $50 billion fund meant to improve healthcare for rural Americans. Saying rural care is “in an acute state of crisis,” 18 members of Congress sent a letter to Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services […]
text:
Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, speaks at the Health Connect South conference in Atlanta on Sept. 17, 2025. (Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder)Congressional Democrats are demanding answers and more transparency from the Trump administration after a nine-day delay of annual awards from a $50 billion fund meant to improve healthcare for rural Americans.
Saying rural care is “in an acute state of crisis,” 18 members of Congress sent a letter to Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz late Thursday. The letter pointed to what it called “an alarming lack of public transparency” and said the fund “lacks sufficient guardrails to protect rural hospitals at greatest risk of closure.”
Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski said her state “got no explanation from CMS as to why” it got $3 million less in its second-year Rural Health Transformation Program allocation. It was a roughly 1.5% reduction from its $193.4 million first-year award. State leaders have not received information about an appeals process, she said.
Any delay in knowing how much they received and any reduction in their base funding is significant, Budzinski said, because states need to plan for an “acute impact” from the loss of other federal funding.
In the first year, states competed for their initial share of the $50 billion, which is handed out at $10 billion a year for five years. They won awards ranging from $147 million to $281 million. Most of the lawmakers who signed the letter were from states that lost funding this year. Rep. Terri Sewell of Alabama, which got $4.1 million less, along with Sen. Michael Bennet of Colorado, which saw a nearly $3 million drop, also spearheaded the letter along with Budzinski.

One concern, Budzinski said, is “making sure that the money isn’t going to consultants, that it’s actually getting to the rural providers that it is supposed to be getting to.” The lawmakers asked Oz for a response to detailed questions by Nov. 25. They also requested a briefing about the delays to the funding announcement, which was first reported by KFF Health News, and the impact on states.
The second-year awards were due to be announced by Oct. 31, but an Oct. 30 letter from CMS stated officials “discovered an additional administrative process requirement.” Instead, second-year funding was announced Nov. 9.
Those kinds of delays prevent state officials from being able to “fully prepare for what’s to come,” Budzinski said.
CMS oversees the fund and its newly formed Office of Rural Health Transformation. Agency officials did not respond to questions for this article before the given deadline.
Republicans passed the Rural Health Transformation Program last summer as a last-minute sweetener to offset other ramifications of President Donald Trump’s signature budget law, including an estimated $137 billion in Medicaid spending cuts for rural America over 10 years.
That rural money is “retail therapy for Congress,” said Cara James, president and chief executive of Grantmakers in Health, while speaking at a Milken Institute event this month.
Because the same tax law cut Medicaid spending, which rural hospitals and people disproportionately use, as well as supplemental food assistance and other government grants, the short-term money would not “help sustain people” in rural America, James said.
Then, she posed a persistent fear about the fund: “If it’s even getting to the communities.”
Five rural hospitals have closed or been converted into lower-level facilities since the rural fund was created, including one in Michigan that shuttered beds and switched to providing only emergency services to survive, according to a list curated by the Cecil G. Sheps Center for Health Services Research at the University of North Carolina.
The letter stated lawmakers’ concerns that too much of the rural fund “could flow to large consulting and technology firms rather than supporting providers and communities on the ground.”
After the law passed last year, state leaders had just over seven weeks to write applications as they competed for the first-year funds. All 50 states won funding with allocations determined by a federal scoring process. Each year, officials are to revisit the funding allotments.
Most states saw their funding change by less than 2%. North Dakota and Iowa won the largest gains; New Jersey, Florida, and Vermont saw the biggest reductions.
Although federal officials have created state data maps, released a slew of press announcements, and led sessions on the complicated scoring of state applications, it’s not enough, said Alan Morgan, CEO of the National Rural Health Association.
The association, which represents hospitals and community clinics nationwide, sent its own letter to federal officials Nov. 9. Morgan said that the way states win money needs “to be articulated in a way that success can be replicated by all states going forward.”
Morgan said his association’s analysis found that state leaders are sending the federal money to local hospitals and clinics because communities and individuals are “relying on rural hospitals to be there to deliver care.” But it’s unclear, he said, how much of the overall rural fund local hospitals are actually receiving versus how much is benefiting other entities, such as consultants.
In their letter, Budzinski and the other Democrats asked if CMS would establish a searchable database that tracks spending. They also asked for an explanation of how federal officials will evaluate state performance and allocate awards.
It was just the latest congressional letter to federal health officials on this issue.
In August 2025, a month after the law passed, Democrats sent a letter about the program’s rollout to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. And last November, Budzinski reached out to Oz on behalf of Illinois. Bennet, along with Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine and others, signed a letter in June asking that the funds be targeted to rescue rural hospitals and clinics.
“We haven’t gotten full responses to any of these inquiries,” said Budzinski, who will become chair of the House’s largest Democratic caucus, the New Democrat Coalition, as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress.

title: Commentary: Rolling the dice on prediction markets: North Carolina’s warning for Indiana
description: Are prediction markets financial forecasting tools, or simply gambling by another name? For Indiana lawmakers, the answer carries significant consequences. text:
Will Indiana lawmakers regulate prediction markets that allow trading on sports, politics and more? It's a key question for the 2027 General Assembly. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Are prediction markets financial forecasting tools, or simply gambling by another name?
For Indiana lawmakers, the answer carries significant consequences. As prediction markets expand into sports wagering, they threaten to undermine the gaming laws, consumer protections, and regulatory framework established by the Indiana General Assembly.
Indiana need only look to North Carolina to understand why this issue deserves attention.
Earlier this year, North Carolina lawmakers handed prediction markets a regulatory free pass. Through legislation signed into law by Gov. Josh Stein in July, the state expressly recognized federally regulated prediction markets as lawful without requiring state gaming licenses or compliance with the regulatory framework governing traditional sportsbooks.
The legislation imposed a modest 6% tax on prediction markets’ net trading fee revenue. Meanwhile, North Carolina increased the tax on licensed sportsbooks from 18% to 23% of gross wagering revenue.
Although the taxes apply to different revenue bases, the disparity is striking. North Carolina welcomed a new class of sports wagering competitors under a separate, less restrictive regulatory structure while increasing the burden on sportsbooks already operating under state law.
Rather than protecting its existing gaming framework, North Carolina created an alternative pathway for gambling-like products to reach consumers.
Indiana should pay attention, because much is at stake when it comes to protecting vulnerable residents.
Consider the most glaring inconsistency: age restrictions.
Election betting is booming as the midterms near. Do states have the power to curb it?

Indiana law requires individuals to be at least 21 years old to legally place a sports wager. Licensed sportsbooks must verify customers’ ages and comply with requirements enforced by the Indiana Gaming Commission.
Prediction market platforms such as Kalshi allow individuals as young as 18 to participate, including in sports-related contracts. That means an 18-, 19-, or 20-year-old Hoosier who cannot legally wager on a Colts game through an Indiana-licensed sportsbook can purchase a contract predicting the outcome of that same game through a prediction market.
The consumer risks money on the same sporting event, hoping for the same financial return. The only meaningful difference is what the company calls the transaction. In 2025 alone, individuals under the age of 21 exploited this loophole to wager an estimated $3.9 billion on sports and parlay-type “contracts,” as Kalshi calls them, on that platform.
The problem extends beyond age restrictions.
Indiana’s licensed sportsbooks operate under a regulatory system requiring state licensure, gaming taxes, responsible gaming safeguards, and ongoing oversight.
Prediction market operators, meanwhile, contend their products are federally regulated financial contracts under the jurisdiction of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, rather than state-regulated gambling.
Under that interpretation, companies offer sports-related contracts to Indiana residents without obtaining Indiana sports wagering licenses or complying with the same requirements imposed on licensed operators.
Even more concerning, established sports betting companies are entering the prediction market business themselves, creating the possibility of offering substantially similar products through two entirely different regulatory systems.
Why should one company follow Indiana’s gaming laws while another offers essentially the same product without doing so?
Indiana lawmakers have repeatedly considered, but declined to authorize, internet casino gaming, commonly known as iGaming. Whether one supports or opposes iGaming, that decision belongs to Indiana’s elected lawmakers.
But if companies can use federal commodities regulation to offer products functioning like sports wagers outside Indiana’s gaming laws, what prevents that same approach from eventually extending to casino-style gambling products?
Don’t just take our word for it. BetMGM CEO Adam Greenblatt recently warned that if prediction markets survive, “it’s a matter of time before casino-like products emerge in some other form.” In other words, the prospect of prediction markets becoming a backdoor to iGaming isn’t merely hypothetical — it’s a concern being actively raised by the gaming industry itself.
Prediction markets are not currently equivalent to full-scale online casinos. Nevertheless, their expansion raises the possibility of opening a back door to iGaming, allowing gambling-like products to enter Indiana without legislative authorization or the safeguards that would ordinarily accompany it.
That should concern anyone who believes Indiana, not private companies operating under a disputed interpretation of federal law, should determine the future of gambling within its borders.
The legal questions surrounding prediction markets remain unresolved. Courts are weighing competing claims of federal commodities regulators and state gaming authorities.
But Indiana lawmakers need not ignore the practical consequences while those disputes unfold.
North Carolina’s decision to grant prediction markets favorable treatment demonstrates the risks of creating exceptions to established gaming frameworks. Indiana has an opportunity to examine those consequences before following a similar path.
