title: Outcry over intended Medicaid cuts grabs lawmakers’ attention
description: LINCOLN — Uproar over changes coming to a broad spectrum of Nebraska Medicaid services swept through healthcare and low-income advocate circles Monday. The concern followed announcements late Friday afternoon by Gov. Jim Pillen’s administration. The Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services notified health care providers of a variety of changes and Me[...]
text:
A stir is created by the latest Medicaid-related changes announced by the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services. (Courtesy of  IronHeart/Getty Images)LINCOLN — Uproar over changes coming to a broad spectrum of Nebraska Medicaid services swept through healthcare and low-income advocate circles Monday.
The concern followed announcements late Friday afternoon by Gov. Jim Pillen’s administration. The Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services notified health care providers of a variety of changes and Medicaid reimbursement rate cuts in programs ranging from dental to at-home personal care to hospital operations.
Tony Green, director of the disability and aging services for Nebraska at a news conference in 2023. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Those who received emails expressed outrage and disappointment. By Monday, groups and individuals had contacted state lawmakers and efforts were underway to try to stop changes that DHHS officials say are necessary to sustain the Medicaid insurance programs in light of escalating healthcare costs.
“These changes represent difficult, but responsible decisions intended to preserve access to essential services over the long term, not simply to obtain short term savings or abandon the individuals who depend on Medicaid,” said a letter from Jeremy Brunssen, interim director of Medicaid and long-term care for DHHS.
Center of controversy 
At the center of the shifts, said a press release from the Nebraska Hospitals Association, is a proposed 3% reimbursement rate cut in 2027 to physicians, dentists and other providers who accept Medicaid. Another 3% cut is to follow the next fiscal year.
“These state cuts, combined with Medicaid cuts enacted by the federal government, will be a devastating blow to our already fragile rural healthcare infrastructure,” said Jeremy Nordquist, the association’s president and CEO. “Nebraska patients and Nebraska communities will feel the pain.”
Nebraska’s projected budget deficit set at $1.1 billion heading into 2027 legislative session

Kris Perkins is the co-owner of A Place At Home, a private agency that provides non-medical home care to hundreds of elderly and disabled Nebraskans, a portion of whom are Medicaid recipients. 
She said she opened an email sent to her at 4:12 p.m. Friday from Tony Green, director of DHHS’ Division of Disability and Aging, announcing what she called significant reductions in reimbursement rates effective Jan. 1.
“That gives agencies just 41 days to prepare for a decision that could fundamentally change the availability of home care services throughout Nebraska,” Perkins said.
She, Nordquist and others believe that public health aid for low-income and vulnerable populations is the brunt of the state’s financial woes. 
Said Perkins: “You can’t balance the budget on the backs of your most needy populations.”
State Sen. Victor Rountree of Bellevue said he and other lawmakers have been flooded with concerns from people including those representing Nebraskans with disabilities — ”many feeling they’re numbers on a spreadsheet.”
The state faces a newly revised projected shortfall of about $175 million for the current budget period ending June 30, 2027, and about $1.124 billion for the 2028-29 biennium that starts in July. Pillen has said the financial predicament means the state will need to find trims and make “tough decisions” over the next three years.
State tried to ‘minimize’ impact
A state DHHS spokesman said the agency researched rates in the region to come up with adjustments that would minimize the impact on both providers and beneficiaries while keeping Nebraska in line with neighboring states. 
Over the years, said Jeff Powell, the spokesman, Nebraska’s Medicaid costs have increased significantly and the state had to respond. He said that nationally, Medicaid expenses have risen more than 40% since 2020.
DHHS ‘error’ in case of Nebraskan with disabilities hits home with state lawmaker

“DHHS will still need to request approximately $500 million in additional funding from the Legislature during the upcoming session to address rising Medicaid and waiver costs,” Powell said. “Without these adjustments, the additional funding request could exceed $1 billion.”
Rountree, who found out about the additional cuts Friday night, said it was unfortunate especially as the holiday season approached. He said he had a busy weekend and Monday fielding concerns and lawmakers are deliberating next steps.
The Nebraska hospital association is among groups calling for the Legislature to curb the “devastating cuts.” The association said that in addition to the 3% cut in provider reimbursement rates, concerns include:

New copay requirements for people receiving certain Medicaid services
Cuts to mental health and substance use treatment reimbursement, and changes to certain behavioral health services 
Changes to inpatient and outpatient hospital reimbursement 
Changes to specialty drug reimbursement
New limits on adult dental coverage, capping Medicaid benefits at $2,000 annually
A 4% cut in in provider rates in 2027 and again in 2028 for those who receive services through the Developmental Disabilities Waiver

Nordquist said Nebraska has already seen some rural clinics close, and “underpaying providers” drives up financial pressures elsewhere.



Quotation







When a rural hospital closes its dialysis or labor and delivery unit or shuts down entirely, every resident in that community loses access to care, whether they are on Medicaid, Medicare or private insurance.


– Jeremy Nordquist, head of the Nebraska Hospital Association



“When a rural hospital closes its dialysis or labor and delivery unit or shuts down entirely, every resident in that community loses access to care, whether they are on Medicaid, Medicare or private insurance,” he said.
Powell, in response, said Nebraska hospitals and healthcare providers are important parts of a healthcare system the Pillen administration values. He cited the governor’s signing of the Hospital Quality Assurance and Access Assessment Act in 2024 that “generates nearly $1 billion annually in additional funding for hospitals statewide.”
A grandma and a business owner 
From Perkins’ vantage point, elderly and disabled Nebraskans are in jeopardy of losing access to essential care, as agencies like hers may not be able to employ caregivers. 
According to intended changes, Perkins said, Medicaid reimbursement to agencies such as hers that deliver personal care will be reduced to a flat rate of $26.32 per hour, down from her current rate of $31.69. She said reimbursement rates currently vary according to the provider.
Independent providers are to receive $17 an hour.
Sarah Maresh, director of health care access for Nebraska Appleseed. (Courtesy of Nebraska Appleseed)
Perkins recalled a study the state conducted five years ago, which identified about $43 as the hourly rate necessary to operate a home care agency while accounting for caregiver wages, payroll taxes, workers’ compensation, insurance, administrative costs and more.
“This isn’t just about business,” she said. Perkins said she wants to employ caregivers at a rate that lets them pay bills. She also is the grandmother of a profoundly autistic, nonverbal 7-year-old whose speech therapy, she said, is in jeopardy.
Green, in his email to A Place At Home, said the state recognizes the impact on providers, families and others. 
“Our responsibility is not only to maintain services today but also to ensure Nebraska can continue providing meaningful, quality services well into the future,” wrote Green, who recently announced his February retirement from DHHS, the state’s largest agency.



Quotation







Our responsibility is not only to maintain services today but also to ensure Nebraska can continue providing meaningful, quality services well into the future.


– Tony Green, Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services


Sarah Maresh of Nebraska Appleseed called Friday’s Medicaid-related announcements “mind-boggling and sweeping.” 
She pointed out as “extremely harmful” Nebraska’s accelerated implementation of copays for certain Medicaid services and recipients. Maresh said Nebraska is calling for the new copays 21 months earlier than what is required under the Big Beautiful Bill.  
According to a state notice, copays are between $4 and $35 for services ranging from vision-related treatments to inpatient hospital stays. Certain populations are exempt, including pregnant women and people in nursing homes or other medical institutions.
Anticipated savings to the state from the copays, Maresh said, is roughly $6,000, which she describes as more “punitive” to poor people than a monetary boost to the state.
Angie Lauritsen, director of Nebraska For Us, noted that Nebraska for two months has not released new data related to the impact of previously implemented  changes related to work requirements for certain recipients of Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. 
At last report, about 1,100 Nebraskans had been denied or lost Medicaid coverage since Nebraska launched the requirements in May — eight months ahead of the federal deadline.
“Now Nebraska wants to fast-track implementation of even more cuts,” Lauritsen said. “For a program based on financial need to force patients to come up with additional funds they do not have, this move makes it clear that the ‘Republican Tax Law’ hurts people in need to fund tax cuts for the wealthy.”
She noted a sign of how well the rollout is going: “The Trump administration is now giving the rest of the country an additional six months to execute changes that are well underway here. Nebraska has no plans to slow down.”
Not a ‘race worth winning’
State Sen. John Fredrickson of Lincoln, who is vice chair of the Legislature’s DHHS Committee, took to social media to challenge the state’s latest moves.
State Sen. John Fredrickson of Omaha. Dec. 6, 2023. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
“Being first to make it harder to see a doctor isn’t a race worth winning,” he wrote. 
He said his priority bill last session would have let Medicaid cover copays. “It passed 31-18 with support from both sides of the aisle. The Governor vetoed it. … Nebraska can do better.”
Maresh said advocacy agencies “won’t stop”; they plan to participate in public comment periods and hearings, and will urge action by state policymakers and lawmakers.
 “I’m guessing there is going to be a busy legislative session coming up to protect healthcare access for all Nebraskans,” she said.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming AG asks high court to rebuff ruling on 3 abortion laws
description:
Appeal asserts judge applied incorrect legal standard when striking down mandatory ultrasounds and other restrictions.  
The post Wyoming AG asks high court to rebuff ruling on 3 abortion laws appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
A Wyoming district judge erred when he struck down an ultrasound requirement and two other anti-abortion laws in June, lawyers for the state argue in a recently filed appeal.
Judge Thomas T.C. Campbell incorrectly applied a more strenuous legal standard to decide the constitutionality of two laws passed by legislators in 2025, state lawyers argue in their appeal to the Wyoming Supreme Court. One of those laws enacted a mandatory ultrasound requirement and 48-hour waiting period for patients seeking abortions. The second required abortion clinics in Wyoming to operate under a more stringent set of regulations — rules that reproductive rights advocates maintain are really intended to make running such a facility unfeasible.

Keith Kautz, photographed here toward the end of his tenure as a Wyoming Supreme Court justice, now serves as the state’s attorney general. (Ana Castro for WyoFile)

The appeal from Wyoming Attorney General Keith Kautz and two other lawyers in his office further asserts Campbell erred when he blocked a 2025 law governing the prescription of off-label medications, which critics say would indirectly ban common abortion medications. The state’s lawyers maintain the law does not “impose any restrictions at all” on abortion providers.
The appeal is the latest in a series of legal battles over abortion in Wyoming that began when the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, finding the U.S. Constitution did not protect the right to an abortion. 
In the years since, the Wyoming Legislature has repeatedly passed new restrictions on abortions, including attempts to ban the practice in most circumstances. The Wyoming courts, including the state’s high court, have repeatedly batted down those laws, concluding they violated a 2012 amendment to the state constitution that protects a competent adult’s “right to make his or her own health care decisions.” At the same time, it allows the Wyoming Legislature to set “reasonable and necessary restrictions” on that right in order to protect health and general welfare.
The amendment was enacted amid conservative backlash to the passage of the Affordable Care Act, also known as Obamacare.
In striking down the three abortion-related laws passed in 2025, Campbell used a legal standard called strict scrutiny, typically the most strenuous standard of review that courts employ when they weigh whether a law is constitutional. (A 2025 U.S. Supreme Court decision noted it was “the most demanding test known to constitutional law.”) The standard requires the government to clear a challenging hurdle: showing restrictions are “necessary to achieve a compelling state interest” and that less restrictive alternatives weren’t an option. 
In January, a divided Wyoming Supreme Court used the same strict scrutiny standard in State v. Johnson, when it struck down Wyoming’s two previously passed abortion bans as unconstitutional. “The majority determined the State did not present enough evidence to show the restrictions (and exceptions) on performing abortions and the ban on medications (and exceptions) are no more restrictive than necessary to serve the State’s interest in protecting prenatal life. Therefore, the majority held that those laws are unconstitutional,” the court explained in a summary released along with its decision.
Anti-abortion billboards can be seen along some Wyoming highways.  (Tennessee Watson/WyoFile)
Campbell’s ruling “illustrates the incongruity” of the Johnson case, Kautz and his attorneys wrote. The Johnson decision recognized that the same constitutional amendment that protected Wyomingites’ right to make their own healthcare decisions also provides the Legislature with the authority to restrict those rights in some circumstances.
However, “it effectively negated that authority by holding such laws are subject to strict scrutiny review,” the appeal states. “As a result, even modest regulations like those in the laws here cannot pass constitutional muster.”
Kautz, a former Wyoming Supreme Court Justice, asked the high court to require Campbell to reevaluate the ultrasound and surgical center laws based on the rational basis test, a lower hurdle for the government to overcome. As for the off-label medication law, Kautz argued it was constitutional regardless of what legal standard it was assessed under.
Abortion remains legal in Wyoming as this latest case winds through the system. The state is home to only one clinic that provides procedural abortions: Wellspring Health Access in Casper.
A University of Wyoming survey released last month found the state’s residents broadly divided on abortion access. About 36% of Wyomingites believe abortion should always be available as a matter of personal choice. The same percentage supported restricting abortion except for cases involving rape, incest or when a woman’s life is in danger. About 15% said it should be permitted for other reasons, but only after the need had been clearly established. Roughly 14% backed a total ban.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Commission rejects allegation that eavesdropping on closed meeting violated open-meetings law
description: PIERRE — The South Dakota Open Meetings Commission found no violation of law occurred when a person allegedly eavesdropped on the non-public portion of a city council meeting, but the commission decided to reprimand another city council for failing to adequately disclose its reasons for closed-door sessions. The Open Meetings Commission considered those and [...]
text:
Members of the South Dakota Open Meetings Commission, from left, Katelynn Hoffman, Michael Smith, Lance Russell and Austin Hoffman, listen to testimony from Stephanie Budihas during a meeting in Pierre, South Dakota, on Nov. 23, 2026. (Photo by Meghan O'Brien/South Dakota Searchlight)https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/112326-Open-Meeting-Commission-web.mp3
 Listen to an audio version of this story produced by reporter Meghan O’Brien. Broadcasters: See below for a downloadable version with a host intro script.
PIERRE — The South Dakota Open Meetings Commission found no violation of law occurred when a person allegedly eavesdropped on the non-public portion of a city council meeting, but the commission decided to reprimand another city council for failing to adequately disclose its reasons for closed-door sessions.
The Open Meetings Commission considered those and other cases Monday. The commission’s five members are county prosecutors, known as state’s attorneys, and are appointed to the commission by the state attorney general.
Eavesdropping not a violation
State law requires public bodies to conduct most of their business in public, but with a majority vote of their members, they can enter a non-public executive session to discuss legal matters, the performance of a public employee and a limited list of other topics.
A resident of Gary, a small town in northeastern South Dakota, accused the city council of a violation for not preventing the city finance officer from sitting close enough to the door of a closed-door meeting to overhear what was discussed.


For broadcasters

Produced 1 minute, 13 second audio story with host intro script



According to Rachel Hinsvark’s complaint, the finance officer “positioned herself directly outside the executive session room, in the hallway between the library and city office — close enough to hear the ongoing discussion.” Hinsvark also alleged city council members included city employees in executive session without voting to approve their presence in the meeting.
Hinsvark told commissioners “there must be procedures in place that do not rely solely on trust” for meeting attendees to vacate an executive session, and that the city council “has a responsibility to safeguard executive sessions.”
“This is not simply about an employee sitting at the door,” Hinsvark told commissioners. “It’s about public trust, accountability and ensuring the rules governing public bodies mean something.”
Commission members voted unanimously to dismiss the complaint after finding nothing in the state’s open-meetings laws addressing eavesdropping on a closed meeting.
“What statute would’ve she specifically violated?” Austin Hoffman, a commission member, said of the finance officer. “I’m not certain there’s anything directly pertaining to that situation.”
Commission members also found nothing in state law requiring a vote about who’s allowed to attend an executive session.
Tripp City Council violations
State law says a motion to enter executive session must state the specific law containing a justifiable reason for the executive session.
According to a complaint from resident Stephanie Budihas, Tripp City Council members went behind closed doors in July without stating a purpose.
Commission Chair Michael Smith said that was clearly improper.
“I don’t think there’s any way to defend the violation,” Smith said.
The commission voted unanimously to reprimand the city council for that.
During another meeting in August, Budihas said, council members entered an executive session while citing “general descriptions ‘personnel & legal,’” and minutes published afterward did not cite specific sections of state law used to justify the executive session.
The commission voted 4-1 to reprimand the city council for that instance.
Smith cast the sole no vote.
“I felt like it was improper, and I still do, that we’re asking laypeople to cite the statute,” Smith said. “I mean, while we as legal counsel need to ensure that what they’re going into executive session for is defensible legally, I don’t expect a farmer or a retired individual to have that state law recitable.”
Hoffman agreed with that sentiment but still voted for the reprimand based on what’s in the existing state law.
“I’m not saying I think it’s right. I think there needs to be broader language there,” Hoffman said. “But I think that’s what meets that statute.”



Other cases
In other cases Monday, the commission:

Voted to reprimand the city of Egan Board of Trustees for failing to provide notice of a public meeting.
Voted to reprimand New Effington’s Board of Trustees for conducting an executive session without adequately explaining the reason.
Voted to reprimand the Town of Hermosa Board of Trustees for gathering at a campaign meeting for a board member with a majority of members present, and with the possibility of discussing public policy, but without notifying the public.
Approved written reprimands arising from two hearings in April, including violations by the city of Gary for disallowing public participation in a public meeting and the Hermosa Town Board of Trustees for discussing city business an hour before the official start of meetings.

The remarks came hours after 14 Republican[...]
text: President Donald Trump and Republican state officials attacked California Gov. Gavin Newsom on Monday for moving to commute more than 500 death sentences as the prominent Democrat weighs a 2028 presidential campaign.Trump condemned Newsom during a speech at U.S. Department of Justice headquarters in Washington, D.C. The remarks came hours after 14 Republican state attorneys general also denounced the commutations, which changed the sentences to life in prison without the possibility of parole.“This afternoon, we come together to stand against the travesty and to wrap our arms around the families of victims who were so cruelly betrayed by bad government and our political system,” Trump said.Death penalty support faltersThe Republican onslaught against Newsom, one of Trump’s most high-profile critics, takes place amid falling public support for the death penalty. Forty-nine percent of Americans support the death penalty for people convicted of murder, according to a Gallup poll conducted in October — the first time since 1971 that support for the death penalty has fallen below 50%.Newsom announced the commutations on Nov. 5. In an open letter about the decision, the governor wrote that after nearly 30 years in public office, he had come to understand the limits “of what government can justly accomplish.” He said “state-sanctioned killing” was incompatible with California’s values and noted that he had opposed the death penalty for decades.On Monday, Newsom accused Trump of selling access to pardons. He pointed to Trump’s decisions to grant pardons to a man who attacked a police officer on Jan. 6, contractors convicted of killing Iraqi civilians and former Honduran President Juan Orlando Hernández, who was convicted of trafficking 400 tons of cocaine.“Donald Trump doesn't oppose mercy. He sells it,” Newsom said in a recorded address. “If you're poor, Black or brown, you get the needle. If you're rich and know Donald Trump, you get a pardon and a phone call.”Trump’s decision to highlight the death penalty also comes after Tennessee’s unsuccessful execution of Christa Pike, who survived a botched attempt at lethal injection. Twenty-seven states have the death penalty, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. In California, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Oregon, the death penalty has been paused by executive action.At the federal level, three individuals remain on death row after former President Joe Biden commuted 37 of 40 death sentences in December 2024. Biden exempted the Tree of Life Synagogue shooter, the shooter of nine parishioners in a South Carolina church and a man convicted for the Boston Marathon bombing.Of the 16 federal executions carried out during the modern era, 13 occurred during Trump’s first term, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.Attempt to speed up death penalty processTrump announced Monday that he would sign a presidential directive ordering the Justice Department to seek the death penalty for child murderers, rapists and human traffickers who kill their victims. He also said the directive aims to speed up the death penalty process.Details of the directive weren’t immediately available and it was unclear how much practical effect it would have. Trump has no power over state-level death penalty cases, for instance.Trump has long supported the death penalty. In 1989, he took out a full-page advertisement in New York newspapers calling for the restoration of the death penalty in response to the “Central Park Five” case in which five teens were accused of assaulting and raping a Central Park jogger. They were all eventually exonerated.State attorneys generalIn their letter to Newsom, the GOP state attorneys general wrote that those on death row in California are “not victims of a broken system.” They noted that California voters twice in the past two decades rejected abolishing the death penalty.“Some crimes are so heinous that the ultimate penalty is the only just penalty,” the letter, led by Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, said.The attorneys general of Alabama, Arkansas, Idaho, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Montana, Nebraska, North Dakota, Ohio, South Carolina, South Dakota and Texas also signed on to the letter. They include four states — Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas — where Democrats will soon control the office following the November election.Many of Newsom’s commutations are not yet final. California’s constitution requires the state Supreme Court to review clemency grants to those convicted twice of a felony. Of the 548 individuals on California’s death row, 382 fall into that category.In a notice to crime victims, the California Office of Victim and Survivor Rights and Services said that the commutations would not change convictions or restitution orders.“The commutation will not pardon, forgive, or minimize the crime that was committed,” the Nov. 5 notice says. “After commutation, the offender will remain in a California state prison under this new sentence and will not be eligible for release.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Democrats demand answers from Oz after delay in $50B Rural Health Awards
authors: Sarah Jane Tribble, KFF Health News
description: Congressional Democrats are demanding answers and more transparency from the Trump administration after a delay of annual awards from a $50 billion fund meant to improve healthcare for rural Americans. Saying rural care is “in an acute state of crisis,” 18 members of Congress sent a letter to Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator […]
text:
Eighteen members of Congress sent a letter to Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz late Thursday. The letter called out “an alarming lack of public transparency” and noted the rural health fund “lacks sufficient guardrails to protect rural hospitals at greatest risk of closure.” (Alex Wroblewski/Bloomberg via Getty Images)Congressional Democrats are demanding answers and more transparency from the Trump administration after a delay of annual awards from a $50 billion fund meant to improve healthcare for rural Americans.
Saying rural care is “in an acute state of crisis,” 18 members of Congress sent a letter to Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz late Thursday. The letter pointed to what it called “an alarming lack of public transparency” and said the fund “lacks sufficient guardrails to protect rural hospitals at greatest risk of closure.”
Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski said her state “got no explanation from CMS as to why” it got $3 million less in its second-year Rural Health Transformation Program allocation. It was a roughly 1.5% reduction from its $193.4 million first-year award. State leaders have not received information about an appeals process, she said.
Any delay in knowing how much they received and any reduction in their base funding is significant, Budzinski said, because states need to plan for an “acute impact” from the loss of other federal funding.
In the first year, states competed for their initial share of the $50 billion, which is handed out at $10 billion a year for five years. They won awards ranging from $147 million to $281 million. Most of the lawmakers who signed the letter were from states that lost funding this year. Rep. Terri Sewell of Alabama, which got $4.1 million less, along with Sen. Michael Bennet of Colorado, which saw a nearly $3 million drop, also spearheaded the letter along with Budzinski.
One concern, Budzinski said, is “making sure that the money isn’t going to consultants, that it’s actually getting to the rural providers that it is supposed to be getting to.” The lawmakers asked Oz for a response to detailed questions by Nov. 25. They also requested a briefing about the delays to the funding announcement, which was first reported by KFF Health News, and the impact on states.
The second-year awards were due to be announced by Oct. 31, but an Oct. 30 letter from CMS stated officials “discovered an additional administrative process requirement.” Instead, second-year funding was announced Nov. 9.
“Those kind of delays prevent a state to fully prepare for what’s to come,” Budzinski said.
CMS oversees the fund and its newly formed Office of Rural Health Transformation. Agency officials did not respond to questions for this article before the given deadline.
Republicans passed the Rural Health Transformation Program last summer as a last-minute sweetener to offset other ramifications of President Donald Trump’s signature budget law, including an estimated $137 billion in Medicaid spending cuts for rural America over 10 years.
That rural money is “retail therapy for Congress,” said Cara James, president and chief executive of Grantmakers in Health, while speaking at a Milken Institute event this month.
Because the same tax law cut Medicaid spending, which rural hospitals and people disproportionately use, as well as supplemental food assistance and other government grants, the short-term money would not “help sustain people” in rural America, James said.
Then, she posed a persistent fear about the fund: “If it’s even getting to the communities.”
Five rural hospitals have closed or been converted into lower-level facilities since the rural fund was created, including one in Michigan that shuttered beds and switched to providing only emergency services to survive, according to a list curated by the Cecil G. Sheps Center for Health Services Research at the University of North Carolina.
The letter stated lawmakers’ concerns that too much of the rural fund “could flow to large consulting and technology firms rather than supporting providers and communities on the ground.”
After the law passed last year, state leaders had just over seven weeks to write applications as they competed for the first-year funds. All 50 states won funding with allocations determined by a federal scoring process. Each year, officials are to revisit the funding allotments.
Most states saw their funding change by less than 2%. North Dakota and Iowa won the largest gains; New Jersey, Florida, and Vermont saw the biggest reductions.
Although federal officials have created state data maps, released a slew of press announcements, and led sessions on the complicated scoring of state applications, it’s not enough, said Alan Morgan, CEO of the National Rural Health Association.
The association, which represents hospitals and community clinics nationwide, sent its own letter to federal officials Nov. 9. Morgan said that the way states win money needs “to be articulated in a way that success can be replicated by all states going forward.”
Morgan said his association’s analysis found that state leaders are sending the federal money to local hospitals and clinics because communities and individuals are “relying on rural hospitals to be there to deliver care.” But it’s unclear, he said, how much of the overall rural fund local hospitals are actually receiving versus how much is benefiting other entities, such as consultants.
In their letter, Budzinski and the other Democrats asked if CMS would establish a searchable database that tracks spending. They also asked for an explanation of how federal officials will evaluate state performance and allocate awards.
It was just the latest congressional letter to federal health officials on this issue.
In August 2025, a month after the law passed, Democrats sent a letter about the program’s rollout to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. And last November, Budzinski reached out to Oz on behalf of Illinois. Bennet, along with Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine and others, signed a letter in June asking that the funds be targeted to rescue rural hospitals and clinics.
“We haven’t gotten full responses to any of these inquiries,” said Budzinski, who will become chair of the House’s largest Democratic caucus, the New Democrat Coalition, as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress.
This story was originally published by KFF Health News, a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF—an independent source of health policy research, polling, and journalism. Learn more about KFF.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska’s projected budget deficit set at $1.1 billion heading into 2027 legislative session
description: LINCOLN — Nebraska lawmakers will have a $1.1 billion math problem to solve when they convene for the 2027 legislative session in January. At a Monday meeting, Nebraska’s Tax Rate and Review Committee received an update from the Legislative Fiscal Office that set the state’s projected budget deficit at $1.124 billion for Nebraska’s upcoming two-year […]
text:
The Nebraska State Capitol Building in Lincoln. (Rebecca S. Gratz for the Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Nebraska lawmakers will have a $1.1 billion math problem to solve when they convene for the 2027 legislative session in January.
At a Monday meeting, Nebraska’s Tax Rate and Review Committee received an update from the Legislative Fiscal Office that set the state’s projected budget deficit at $1.124 billion for Nebraska’s upcoming two-year budget spanning from July 1, 2027 to June 30, 2029. Additionally, it set a $175 million deficit for the current budget period ending June 30, 2027.
Once lawmakers address the $175 million deficit, that will reduce the next budget’s deficit by roughly the same amount.
The latest numbers reflect changes from Nebraska’s Economic Forecasting Advisory Board meeting Oct. 30. The board predicted revenues for the current fiscal year would remain flat, but lowered expected revenues in the next cycle by about $355 million.
This solidified that 2027 will be the third consecutive legislative session to deal with a projected deficit. After several years of repeated spending cuts, State Budget Administrator Neil Sullivan said everything is on the table for Gov. Jim Pillen in his next approach for balancing the budget.
“I’d say there’s about a billion (dollars) to solve; we probably got $3 billion or more in ideas,” Sullivan said.
Legislative Fiscal Analyst Keisha Patent, who presented the report to the committee, said the report did not include several recent budget requests from state agencies.
Among these is about $38.9 million for the Nebraska Department of Education, which Patent said would be necessary to maintain the 80% reimbursement rate for special education costs that lawmakers first set in 2023.
Last session, in the midst of earlier budget-balancing debates, lawmakers agreed to hold special education funding flat for fiscal year 2027. Patent said changing that to add $38.9 million would require a vote by the new Legislature.
Patent said Nebraska’s Department of Health and Human Services has requested about $254 million more to cover cost increases in several programs, including Medicaid, developmental disability services and child welfare. She said those costs do not factor in the 3% Medicaid reimbursement rate cuts DHHS announced on Friday.
“I anticipate there’s going to have to be something that comes through on the deficit side,” Sullivan said of DHHS’ funding request. “But that’s going to have to … be offset as much as possible.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Patent’s report did note several areas of savings brought on by federal Medicaid changes under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. New work requirements are estimated to create about $1.8 million in savings for Nebraska in each of the next two fiscal years. Narrowed eligibility for noncitizens is estimated to create about $3.7 million in savings each year, and the new six-month eligibility requirement is estimated to save $2 million to $3 million per year.
State Sen. Ben Hansen of Blair, who chairs the committee and will not be returning for the 2027 session, said returning lawmakers may need to turn their attention to the large transfers coming out of Nebraska’s general fund every year. These transfers include the state’s two property tax credit programs, as well as the Education Future Fund and the Community College Future Fund, which altogether cost the state nearly $2 billion each year.
Hansen said it might not be a popular idea, but lawmakers may need to consider scaling back some of those funds, increasing income tax rates or revisiting state aid to schools. Otherwise, he said, lawmakers will have to continue to make cuts to a large collection of smaller funding pots, which has been the persisting strategy over the last several sessions.
Inside Nebraska’s budget: Why the state faces structural deficit after $1B surplus

“This is the part where I’m hoping people might actually have to come together and agree on something,” Hansen said. “Whether that means not transferring out as much to education as we did before, along with reviewing tax rates, stuff like that.”
Patent agreed that the general fund transfers are among the “big ticket” items within Nebraska’s budget, and said lawmakers will have some tough decisions to make in 2027.
“(Nebraska’s economy) is not that bad, but it’s also not great enough to produce a lot more revenue in light of the taxable base changes,” Patent said.
Sullivan said the governor’s office is examining the trends within the state’s property tax credit funds, along with other funding models, but declined to say if the governor was considering scaling back those funds.
“Property tax relief is hard. It’s hard to mess with,” Sullivan said. “We’re going to be looking at the trends on that and what’s projected for the future. I’d love to see where is our property tax relief going to, and then that all gets entangled into school funding models as well.”

name: VTDigger
title: Concerns emerge over Lyndon police chief’s credibility
description:
“I'm disclosing the following information out of an abundance of caution,” Caledonia County state's attorney wrote in the letter.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Concerns emerge over Lyndon police chief’s credibility.
text:
Lyndonville in Dec. 2025. Photo by Ascended Dreamer via Wikimedia Commons. Creative Commons Attribution ShareAlike 4.0 

A small-town police chief’s credibility is under question. 
Caledonia County State’s Attorney Claire Burns issued a letter challenging the reliability or truthfulness of Lyndon Police Chief Jack Harris on Friday. 
“There is credible information that Chief Jack Harris engaged in conduct that risks undermining his credibility,” the letter, obtained by VTDigger, reads. “I have concluded that the conduct in question creates a cognizable basis to challenge the credibility and accuracy of representations made by Chief Jack Harris.”
A “Brady” — or “Giglio” — letter is filed by prosecutors when a law enforcement officer’s credibility is called into question and can effectively end an officer’s career, as prosecutors can decline to take cases that officer had investigated. 
Following a Giglio letter, a state’s attorney or prosecutor must provide information about the reason an officer’s credibility is in question to relevant defendants, but is not required to provide that information to the public, according to the Vermont Department of State’s Attorneys and Sheriffs.
Burns did not include any specific information in her letter, and wrote in an email to VTDigger Monday that she cannot comment further. 
“I’m disclosing the following information out of an abundance of caution,” Burns wrote in the letter.
Selectboard member Chris Thompson said the town’s selectboard, which appoints the chief of police in Lyndon, is awaiting more information from the state’s attorney. 
“We don’t want to speculate,” he told VTDigger when reached by phone.
The police department in Lyndon’s six-square mile town employs four full-time officers, according to the Lyndon Fire Department’s website. Located in the Northeast Kingdom, about 5,628 residents live there, according to the 2025 Census. 
The Vermont Criminal Justice Council may conduct an investigation, and defense counsel may “initiate relevant litigation” for cases that were investigated by Harris, Burns told VTDigger. 
“Next steps are rather amorphous, as they differ for every situation,” she wrote.
Burns said she has not yet tabulated the number of cases which could be impacted by the challenge to Harris’ credibility.
Harris and Lyndon Municipal Administrator Justin Smith had not responded to requests for comment by the time of publication.

title: Less than 10% of Iowa corn left in the field with final 2026 crop report
description: Just 8% of Iowa corn acres remained in the field as of the last crop report of the 2026 season, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture.  Harvest has been behind the typical schedule this year due an incredibly rainy September that kept farmers from getting out in the field. According to the report for […]
text:
Mature corn on the edge of a partially harvested field in western Iowa in October 2025. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Just 8% of Iowa corn acres remained in the field as of the last crop report of the 2026 season, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. 
Harvest has been behind the typical schedule this year due an incredibly rainy September that kept farmers from getting out in the field. According to the report for the Nov. 16 through Nov. 22 reporting period, corn harvest in Iowa was 6 percentage points behind the five-year average as farmers head into Thanksgiving. 
Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig encouraged Iowans to pause on the holiday and “give thanks for our farm families who work year-round to produce the safe, healthy and nutritious food we enjoy on Thanksgiving and every day.”
“After a challenging fall marked by weather-related delays, harvest is nearing completion across much of Iowa,” Naig said in a statement Monday. “Despite the many difficulties facing agriculture, we still have much to be thankful for.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Iowa had  an unseasonably warm and “overall wet” reporting period, according to State Climatologist Justin Glisan. 
While the statewide average precipitation for the period, at 0.55 inch, was around one-tenth of an inch above the normal, Glisan said some weather stations in the state reported “more than a month’s worth of rain.”
Nearly all of the state had rain during the period, but southwest, central and north central Iowa had the most precipitation, with Guthrie Center recording the highest total of the period at 1.85 inches. 
Soil moisture continued to rate primarily adequate for the period. Topsoil moisture rated 82% adequate and 15% surplus for the period; subsoil moisture rated 81% adequate and 14% surplus.
Crop reports from the USDA are published weekly in April through November along with the growing and harvest seasons.

title: Physician surrenders Wisconsin license, accepts warning from Iowa board
description: The Iowa Board of Medicine has issued a warning to a physician who recently surrendered his license to practice in another state. Wisconsin state records indicate Dr. Bart Kneeland, 56, of Cedar Falls, was first licensed to practice medicine and surgery in Wisconsin in 1998. According to the Wisconsin Medical Examining Board, the board fielded […]
text:
The Iowa Board of Medicine regulates the state's medical profession as part of the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing. (Photo by Getty Images, board seal courtesy the State of Iowa) The Iowa Board of Medicine has issued a warning to a physician who recently surrendered his license to practice in another state.
Wisconsin state records indicate Dr. Bart Kneeland, 56, of Cedar Falls, was first licensed to practice medicine and surgery in Wisconsin in 1998. According to the Wisconsin Medical Examining Board, the board fielded a complaint from the staff at a family medicine clinic in Antigo, Wis., where Kneeland worked. The complaint alleged unsafe prescribing practices involving “multiple patients,” the records show.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
After reviewing the medical records of six patients, the Wisconsin board alleged Kneeland, among other things, had failed to advise one patient of the risks associated with taking opioids and benzodiazepines concurrently, failed to order drug screens after tests showed patients were taking unprescribed medications and failed to perform drug screens on a patient who had been prescribed morphine.
By the time the Wisconsin board filed its charges, Kneeland had already moved to Iowa and been issued a licensed to practice medicine in Iowa.
On May 4, 2026, Kneeland informed the Iowa board of the fact that he had surrendered his physician’s license in the state of Wisconsin where he had been investigated for alleged improper opioid prescribing practices.
As a result, the Iowa board charged Kneeland with violating the laws or rules governing the practice of medicine in another state, and with entering into a voluntary agreement restricting his practice in another state.
The Iowa board and Kneeland recently agreed to resolve the matter with a settlement that calls for Kneeland to accept a warning from the board. In addition, his Iowa license will be placed on probationary status for two years, during which time he will be subject to practice monitoring. As part of the agreement, Kneeland has also agreed to complete one educational course, of no specified duration, on the topic of prescribing controlled substances.
UnityPoint Health records indicate Kneeland currently works for UnityPoint Clinic Family Medicine in Cedar Falls. The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Kneeland for comment.

title: With no legal wins so far, Kalshi blocks operations in Utah
description: Amid multiple legal disputes between Utah leaders and Kalshi, the prediction market platform has paused operations in the state. A spokesperson for Kalshi attributed the action “to the adverse final judgment in federal court,” in a lawsuit the company filed challenging a 2026 state law that included proposition bets in the definition of the state’s […]
text:
Kalshi photo illustration, Tuesday, April 7, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Amid multiple legal disputes between Utah leaders and Kalshi, the prediction market platform has paused operations in the state.
A spokesperson for Kalshi attributed the action “to the adverse final judgment in federal court,” in a lawsuit the company filed challenging a 2026 state law that included proposition bets in the definition of the state’s constitutional gambling ban, which allowed state officials to prohibit prediction market companies’ operations within state limits.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The company is immediately putting residency restrictions in place based on information users provided when opening their accounts, the spokesperson said, and then will enforce the block with a GPS-based tool.
Utah files criminal charges against Kalshi over operations within the state

As the company geofenced Utah, the court hasn’t yet ruled on a Commodity Futures Trading Commission emergency request for a relief “holding that Utah gambling laws are preempted and unenforceable,” since, the commission argues, derivatives markets are governed by federal law, according to the complaint.
“This is an unfortunate outcome for the more than 177,000 Utahns who use Kalshi. We will continue to fight this in court, and we look forward to returning to Utah once our legal position is vindicated,” Jacki McGavick, spokesperson for Kalshi said in a statement.
At the same time, Kalshi is also facing criminal charges in Utah — 12 online gambling promotion felony charges, one felony count of pattern of unlawful activity, and a misdemeanor charge for general gambling promotion according to charging documents filed by Utah Attorney General Derek Brown in October.
On Monday, Brown told reporters he was “thrilled” about Kalshi blocking operations in the state.
Utah sues Kalshi for ‘brazen pattern’ of violating state’s gambling ban

“We’ve asked them to follow the law. We’ve asked them that, ultimately, gambling products are illegal in Utah. It’s illegal under our state constitution, and we’re thrilled that they have made that decision,” Brown said. “And we’ll now look at what options we take at this point. But I’ll be meeting with my prosecutor shortly to figure out where we go at this point.”
While the state has secured a substantial legal victory in court, Kalshi has avoided criminal charges — similar to those filed in Utah — in Arizona courts.
Utah’s Attorney General also filed a civil lawsuit against Kalshi in October, accusing the company of a “brazen pattern of unlawful conduct.” Now that Kalshi has blocked its operations in the state, Brown said his office will review how that will affect that challenge.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Rhode Island joins growing list of states to sue TikTok
description: Attorney General Peter Neronha is alleging in a new lawsuit that TikTok knowingly exploited Rhode Island’s youth for their time, attention and money by pitting them “against some of the most powerful and manipulative design features in the world.” That’s according to a 78-page suit filed Monday against the giant, short-form video platform in Providence […]
text:
TikTok star Charli D’Amelio is cited in Rhode Island’s lawsuit against the social media company as an example of its alleged selective enforcement of age restrictions. According to the complaint, D’Amelio was allowed to livestream and receive virtual gifts at age 15, despite minimum ages of 16 for livestreaming and 18 for receiving gifts at the time. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)Attorney General Peter Neronha is alleging in a new lawsuit that TikTok knowingly exploited Rhode Island’s youth for their time, attention and money by pitting them “against some of the most powerful and manipulative design features in the world.” 
That’s according to a 78-page suit filed Monday against the giant, short-form video platform in Providence County Superior Court, making Rhode Island the latest entry on a list of nearly three dozen jurisdictions to sue TikTok.
Neronha may have only a few weeks left in his term-limited office, but the lawsuit against another tech goliath follows his participation in a successful multistate suit against Facebook parent company Meta earlier this year. The lawsuit argues that TikTok “has been exploiting and deceiving Rhode Island’s children and their parents for the sake of its own profits in violation of Rhode Island law.”
“Rhode Island’s children are not a product to be optimized, and this Office intends to hold TikTok accountable for its alleged actions,” Neronha said in a statement Monday.
The complaint, which formally names TikTok Inc. and TikTok USDS Joint Venture LLC as defendants, argues that the company identified faults in its content moderation practices as well as other dangers with the app, but never addressed — and even downplayed — these problems in favor of profit and maintaining the size of its young user base.
Rhode Island to receive at least $49.4 million in landmark Meta settlement over addictive features

“TikTok has never warned users about the many dangers of its App,” reads the lawsuit signed by Assistant Attorney General Sarah Rice and Special Assistant Attorney General Alex M. Carnevale. “Instead, it falsely portrays the App as a safe place where users and parents can control their engagement, their spending, and their data. None of this is true.”
The partially redacted complaint cites five facets of the platform comprising “a sophisticated mix of design features” that prompt children to return again and again, including:

Recommendation algorithms, which rely on users’ interests, usage patterns and other data to push more relevant content to users. The lawsuit claims that TikTok analyzes user behavior to curate and push to users eight-video batches of content, which then produce further recommendations based on users’ reactions and interactions with the content. 
Infinite scroll and autoplaying videos, which can facilitate easy and often lengthy consumption of content.
The app’s frequency of push notifications, which the lawsuit compares to “a salesman constantly knocking on your door for your business.” 
Filters and video effects which promote unreal and unachievable appearances, such as filters that can smooth skin, bleach teeth, fatten lips, slim noses, apply digital makeup and generally sculpt fresh facial features for users. 
TikTok LIVE and its attendant coin-based economy used for gifts given to creators during livestreams — gifts which cost users real money to purchase.

“Before TikTok, few tech companies had monopolized children’s online time for profit as quickly and effectively,” the lawsuit reads.
TikTok did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday.
The state is asking the court for civil penalties against TikTok, as well as restitution for affected consumers, the disgorgement of allegedly unlawful profits, and a permanent injunction against the practices the complaint describes.
Screenshots included in Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha’s Nov. 23, 2026, lawsuit against TikTok show virtual gifts that users can purchase with the platform’s Coins currency and send to livestreamers. (Screenshots from Providence Superior Court complaint)
The ‘coveted’ lion 
The lawsuit reserves particular scrutiny for TikTok LIVE, which lets users broadcast themselves doing a wide range of activities — playing video games, eating dinner, answering questions, performing music, opening trading cards and so on — and receive virtual gifts purchased by viewers using an in-app currency called coins.
Clicking on a top video on the LIVE page late Monday afternoon, for instance, produced a stream of a woman in Cap’n Crunch cosplay playing Fortnite.
“Welcome to TikTok LIVE!” the live chat reads when a user enters a new livestream. “Have fun interacting with others in real time.”
The disclaimer also reminds users that they must be 18 or older to send gifts.
Neronha’s lawsuit argues that TikTok’s present safeguards to enforce age limitations, also known as age-gating, are largely powerless.
“The process relies on the user, whether a child or adult, to accurately input their actual age [when creating an account],” the lawsuit reads. “But this age-gating process has the opposite effect: it incentivizes children to input a false date of birth when registering.”
The platform then “knowingly harms its users monetarily and psychologically for its own financial gain,” the lawsuit alleges, suggesting children are particularly susceptible to spending money in hopes of attention from content creators.
The opacity of TikTok’s in-app currency served as a special point of concern for the AG’s office. 
Gifts for streamers are purchased with coins, which are themselves purchased with real money. The conversion rate can vary and depends on factors like the amount of coins purchased as well as the location and platform of the purchase, but one coin generally costs around 1 cent. On Monday, 30 coins could be purchased on TikTok’s website for 31 cents.
Gifts users can purchase range from a humble ice cream cone — worth 1 coin — to more extravagant affirmations, like what the lawsuit describes as the “coveted” lion animation, which, when gifted during a livestream, runs across the bottom of the screen and roars. It costs 29,999 coins, or nearly $300. 
The lucrativeness of receiving gifts can also incentivize young users to perform acts for money, the AG’s office argues, citing national reportage of young users “being sexually exploited over LIVE” by older adults exploiting them to perform on camera in exchange for gifts.
TikTok’s gift economy, Neronha’s office concludes, operates “in part like a virtual strip club.” 
Received gifts can be converted into another virtual currency called Diamonds, which livestreamers can then exchange for real money.
But, the lawsuit argues, “TikTok buries its 50% commission in a short article published on its website” and obfuscates how much of users’ money actually goes to creators when they purchase coins.
The AG’s office also points to Rhode Island’s own Youth Risk Behavior Survey, which found that, in 2025, 30% of high school students reported persistent sadness or hopelessness, up from 25.8% a little over a decade ago in 2013.
The lawsuit argues that TikTok is “contributing to a mental health crisis in the state.”
The lawsuit notes that “Rhode Island teenagers’ use of social media remains nearly universal and constant,” with 78.9% of Rhode Island teens in 2025 reporting social media use several times a day — slightly more than the 74% who reported getting fewer than eight hours of sleep on an average school night.
Rhode Island is the latest state to sue TikTok over alleged harm to children, following similar suits recently filed by South Dakota, North Dakota, Idaho, Wisconsin and West Virginia. South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley announced Nov. 19 that his office had coordinated with the AGs in those four states.
Alabama has already been successful in its legal challenges against TikTok. The state reached a settlement in September that required $116 million in restitution to the state, a $183 million fund for contingency payments and other stipulations.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas lawmakers hear about efforts to secure utilities as national systems face outages
description: TOPEKA — In the midst of computer, aviation and banking outages across the country, a Kansas legislative committee learned Monday what utilities do to ensure their systems are secure.  Utility organizations and others briefed the Joint Committee on Kansas Security about what it takes to keep systems secure in a time of constantly changing challenges […]
text:
Brad Mears, executive director of the Kansas Municipal Utilities, tells the Kansas Security Committee on Nov. 23, 2026, that utilities are taking multiple steps to protect their operations from online security threats. (Kansas Reflector screen capture from Kansas Legislature video)TOPEKA — In the midst of computer, aviation and banking outages across the country, a Kansas legislative committee learned Monday what utilities do to ensure their systems are secure. 
Utility organizations and others briefed the Joint Committee on Kansas Security about what it takes to keep systems secure in a time of constantly changing challenges in cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. 
Brad Mears, executive director of the Kansas Municipal Utilities in McPherson, said his organization considers “security resilience” to be about not just operational issues but about public safety. 
Kansas Municipal Utilities is a state association for cities that own and operate electric, natural gas, water and wastewater operations. Mears pointed to recent Microsoft outages as an example of how organizations can be affected. 
“Cybersecurity is not a hypothetical thing, and it’s not limited to large systems either that might be open to an attack,” he said. “Many Kansas cities run small utilities. They have limited staff, and a single incident could be dramatically detrimental to the entire community that they serve.”
Arkansas City’s water utility in September 2024 experienced a ransomware attack, which is when an outside entity takes control of internal computer operations and asks for ransom to return that control, said Randy Frazer, city manager. 
Although water services weren’t affected, the city was affected financially and had no immediate access to control its system “in any way,” he said.
“A ransom note appeared on multiple of our monitors,” Frazer said. “Our SCADA, our supervisory control and data acquisition system, basically a dashboard that we use to control our plants and monitor everything, it initially turned black.”
Frazer said even dealing with an attack that didn’t cause any customer impact is expensive. The forensic and legal consults were $60,000 and infrastructure costs to replace services were $105,000, and then there were overtime costs and other staffing costs, he said.
Matt Metzinger, Arkansas City information technology director, said the city initially took the plant off the internet, closing all active connections. As he is the only person on the IT team, he said the city consulted legal counsel and cybersecurity experts, as well as vendors. 
“We found out that they had been in our plant about three or four days prior, because anytime you have a cybersecurity incident, obviously they’re going to go in and scout your system,” he said. “They’re going to see where and what they can exploit.”
The cybersecurity attack was ultimately about accessing personal customer information, such as credit card and Social Security numbers, Metzinger said. 
The city took all processes offline to manually operate the water system, which was never affected, he said. 
It’s this type of situation, though, that has led Mears’ organization to work on cybersecurity issues with its member organizations over the last few years. 
Each utility needs to understand how to operate its system if it has to go offline and run manually, among other issues, he said. 
“We want to make sure that everybody can take their systems, remove them from the interconnections that the automation requires,” Mears said. “Just as an example for electric, what if we lose control of our generation, distribution, or substations, or there’s malicious activity that can actually damage the physical assets that we have out there, as well? In each case, the goal is to be able to provide a potential manual operation in order to keep things going.”
Through training and support from national organizations, Mears said, agencies have developed operational plans to prepare for a variety of circumstances. 
Basic steps include strengthening sign-in capabilities to the system, determining a leader who can make quick decisions when an incident occurs, understanding critical systems, and making sure only vendors who need access are granted access, he said. 
Jeremy Ash, general manager at the Kansas City Board of Public Utilities, which operates in Wyandotte County, is one of the larger utility organizations in the state and has 43 people in its IT department. The board serves 67,000 electric customers and 55,000 water customers, he said. 
Over a seven-day period, its system experienced 2.4 million attempts to gain access or to infiltrate it in some way, Ash said. 
“The threats, they’re everywhere, and Brad (Mears) talked a little bit about the different kinds of vulnerabilities that we have, the adoption of artificial intelligence, and really how that’s causing all of our security teams to have some new challenges to what we do,” he said.
The company has about 500 employees, and all are trained to watch for anything that “just doesn’t look right” and to notify the IT department immediately, he said. 
Vendor relationships and security are critical, too, he said. 
“With the adoption of everything being digitized and all of the commerce that we transact over the web, all of our third-party partners need to be playing on the same security field that we’re playing on,” Ash said. “The information has to be protected, the systems have to be protected, and so the third-party exposure … all of that has to be at the top of the security game, or there’s real exposure for us.”
Ash said the security employees who protect the company operate under regulations set by various authorities, such as the Federal Energy Regulation Commission and the Southwest Power Pool. 
“The people that are interfacing with the energy markets, the people that are running our generators, the people that are pushing the protections onto the electric system to protect our employees and to protect the public, it’s a separate set of eight security professionals that run that run that, and they’re separated for a reason, so that we don’t have cross pollination,” Ash said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Former Jackson Public Schools employee arrested for embezzling
description: Jackson Public Schools administrative building
text:
A former Jackson Public Schools employee is facing multiple charges for allegedly altering records and embezzlement.
Sonji Smith-Sims, a former payroll supervisor for the district, allegedly reactivated inactive employee accounts, replaced their direct deposit information with her own and issued to herself payouts totaling more than $220,000 between Sept. 15, 2023 and May 15, 2025, according to a statement State Auditor Shad White’s office released Monday on social media. 
Special agents from the state auditor’s office arrested Smith-Sims, 54, on Nov. 12 on charges of alteration of records, embezzlement, tax evasion and identity fraud, according to Jack Tannehill, a spokesperson for the auditor’s office. 
The state Department of Revenue also charged Smith-Sims on Oct. 27 with tax evasion and identity theft.
School district officials asked the JPS police department to investigate Smith-Sims, according to the statement. It is not immediately clear when officials made that request. JPS officials could not immediately be reached for comment.
Smith-Sims is not currently detained, according to Tannehill. The agency’s investigation did not find anyone other than Smith-Sims in the alleged crime, he said. Smith-Sims could not immediately be reached for comment. It is unclear if she is represented by an attorney.
“Anybody caught stealing tax dollars, especially tax dollars meant to educate young students, should face mandatory prison time,” White told Mississippi Today. “I’ll always support public schools and my office will continue to do everything in our power to make sure that education dollars are actually spent educating students.”
Chris Graham, commissioner for the Mississippi Department of Revenue, said the agency worked alongside the auditor’s office by “combining our investigative resources and expertise.”

title: SC state park reopens refurbished golf course, with new villas in the works
description: The golfing greens at Cheraw State Park are open again for golfers, with plans underway to add more cabins for overnight stays. The golf course in Chesterfield County reopened Nov. 3 after an eight-month refurbishment. That followed the Sept. 21 re-opening of the golf course at Hickory Knob State Park in rural McCormick after a […]
text:
The golf course at Cheraw State Park in Chesterfield County reopened with refurbishments on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Perry Baker, courtesy of the Department of Parks, Recreation and Tourism)The golfing greens at Cheraw State Park are open again for golfers, with plans underway to add more cabins for overnight stays.
The golf course in Chesterfield County reopened Nov. 3 after an eight-month refurbishment. That followed the Sept. 21 re-opening of the golf course at Hickory Knob State Park in rural McCormick after a four-month renovation. Those are South Carolina’s only golf courses inside state parks.
Together, the improvements cost $1.5 million, “reflecting South Carolina’s continued investment in enhancing these valuable recreational destinations,” parks director Joy Raintree said in a statement.


Cost to play
For 18 holes at Cheraw State Park:

$55 with a cart Mondays through Thursdays
$30 without a cart Mondays through Thursdays
$65 with a cart Fridays through Sundays
$40 without a cart Fridays through Sundays
Seniors, veterans and law enforcement officers can play for discounted rates

For 18 holes at Hickory Knob State Park:

$50 weekdays with a cart
$30 weekdays without a cart
$60 weekends with a cart
$35 weekends without a cart
Seniors, veterans and law enforcement officers can play for discounted rates

Source: Department of Parks, Recreation and Tourism


Both state-owned, 18-hole golf courses got new turf, removing grain in the previous greens that could affect how fast and how far a ball traveled.
“There’s no grain right now, so, in my opinion, they roll a little bit more true,” Joshua Slawiak, the park’s head golf professional, told the SC Daily Gazette.
The courses also got new sand in their bunkers, plus drainage upgrades to make maintenance easier, according to the parks department. Tee boxes got new sod, and the agency aerified the fairways, which helps keep the greens healthy, according to the agency.
At Cheraw, the agency installed an irrigation system and replaced the decking on bridges throughout the course to make golf cart rides smoother.
“All of these improvements serve to provide an enhanced golfing experience for our visitors,” agency director Duane Parrish said during the reopening ceremony. “I want to ensure that the quality of play matches the beautiful natural surroundings here on the course.”
The course spent eight months closed for renovations. Along with the planned refurbishments, the closure gave the grass time to regrow, Slawiak said.
This was the first major renovation project on the course in 30 years, and three decades of playing golf can wear away much of the land, Slawiak said.
“Simply put, I’m watching grass grow in spots I’ve never seen it grow before,” he said. “It’s amazing how grass will grow when nobody’s walking on it.”
The work at Cheraw, the first state-owned park in South Carolina, isn’t over yet. Construction is underway on five villas with easy access to the golf course and views of nearby 360-acre Lake Juniper and the park’s forests.
Each of the properties will have four bedrooms, two bathrooms and a covered back porch, according to the parks department. They are expected to open for the first visitors in 2028.
The state received a $3.5 million federal grant to help pay for the villas. Parrish didn’t give a total cost for the project.
Cheraw State Park has nine cabins and 17 campsites. Each comes with a discount on a round of golf, Slawiak said.
Eight of the cabins have one bedroom and fit up to three people each. One cabin has four bedrooms and two bathrooms, with a maximum capacity of seven people.
The new villas are meant to draw more people into the area, allowing larger groups to stay at the park, Parrish said.
“The golf course improvements in the future villas are helping us to write the next chapter, attracting more visitors and more tourism dollars while continuing to serve as a treasured resource for the local community,” Parrish said.
Having a golf course at Cheraw is a big draw for the area, Slawiak said. The park does around 28,000 rounds of golf per year, he said.
The park also offers kayaking, walking trails and fishing. Cheraw State Park was one of 16 in the state built by the Civilian Conservation Corps, a federal work program created to give young men jobs during the Great Depression.
Both of the state-owned golf courses were designed by Tom Jackson, a renowned golf course architect originally from Taylors. People often make trips out of playing the Cheraw course, which takes reservations for tee times days to months in advance, Slawiak said.
People enjoy the tranquil nature of the lakefront course, and the reception to the refurbishment has been very positive, he said.
“It just enhances the community,” Slawiak said. “People have a reason to travel into Cheraw and then spend time here and realize just how nice of an area it actually is.”
