name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: A mayor, a 19-year-old and a ‘Bachelorette’ alum: Beacon Hill’s incoming class
authors: Ella Adams | State House News Service
description: When the House and Senate gavel into the first sessions of the 195th General Court on Jan. 6, there will be at least 21 lawmakers new to their chambers, about a tenth of the 200-person legislative roster.
text:
MEET THE INCOMING CLASS of 2027.
When the House and Senate gavel into the first sessions of the 195th General Court on January 6, there will be at least 21 lawmakers new to their chambers, about a tenth of the 200-person legislative roster. 
Every freshman but one is a Democrat. While a handful cruised through the general election without challenge, at least four flipped seats in some tight races on November 3 by ousting Republican incumbents and turning the seats of two longtime, outgoing Republicans blue – including the House minority leader’s seat, which has been red for three decades. A South Coast seat held by a Democrat flipped red, in what was the MassGOP’s lone pickup.
New faces trudging up the hill come January include the Legislature’s new youngest member – a 19-year-old from Billerica – two 23-year-olds, a “Bachelorette” contestant and HGTV host, two Somerville city councilors, and the sitting mayor of Gardner. The classmates’ priorities mirrored each other in many ways, regardless of where they hail from. Addressing affordability, increasing government transparency, bringing in local aid, and easing the housing crisis were among their most promoted campaign issues. 
The 2nd Plymouth House race remains uncalled between Republican Rep. John Gaskey and Democratic challenger Sarah Hewins. Recounts were scheduled for Wareham on Friday, November 20, and in Carver on Monday, November 23. If Hewins, who was ahead of Gaskey by a small margin based on preliminary counts, beats Gaskey, she will be the 22nd newcomer in January and shrink the House’s minority caucus by another member.
Take a look at the three new senators-elect and 18 confirmed representatives-elect:
SENATE
Kate Lipper-Garabedian (D), Melrose
A former public school teacher, judicial clerk, legal counsel for the state’s education secretariat, and at-large Melrose city councilor, Lipper-Garabedian is one of two representatives moving down the hall. She has been in the House since winning a 2020 special election and will now fill outgoing Sen. Jason Lewis’s Fifth Middlesex seat in the Senate after cruising to election without challenge.
Erika Uyterhoeven (D), Somerville 
In a hard-fought primary against a fellow Somerville state rep, Uyterhoeven’s progressive agenda won over voters in retiring Sen. Pat Jehlen’s Second Middlesex District. A three-term lawmaker and self-described “antitrust economist,” she’ll be moving down the hall with a perspective that was not always highlighted in the House – Uyterhoeven has taken votes against House leadership and ran a campaign that included addressing issues with Beacon Hill’s transparency.
Persis Yu (D), Hyde Park 
The Hyde Park social worker and attorney beat Sen. Mike Rush in the Democratic primary in September for his Norfolk and Suffolk seat, and faced no challenger in the general election with a campaign based on a Massachusetts “where families – not corporations or billionaires – come first.” Yu, the daughter of an immigrant who fled fascism, went to college in Washington state, spent a decade at the National Consumer Law Center, and has worked five years at a nonprofit that aims to protect people from predatory lenders.
HOUSE
Lorena Betts (D), Chelmsford 
Betts says “Beacon Hill is broken” and “disconnected from the real struggles families face every day” and told voters she’s not a career politician. An interpreter, civic educator, and community organizer, she will take over former Rep. Rodney Elliott’s 16th Middlesex seat, returning to the State House where she used to work as a legislative aide and where she now plans to promote affordable housing, accessible care, and clean energy.
Daniel Darris-O’Connor (D), Billerica
The 19-year-old Billerica Select Board member defeated 16-year incumbent Republican Rep. Marc Lombardo for his 22nd Middlesex House seat with a campaign focused on his town government record and on the fact that “Billerica deserves a rep who shows up and gets things done.” Now a college student at the University of Massachusetts Lowell, Darris-O’Connor was also a student representative to the Billerica School Committee while in high school. He’ll be the youngest lawmaker on Beacon Hill in January, and one of the youngest in the state’s history.
John Drinkwater (D), Lowell
The former Lowell city councilor has lived his entire life in Tewksbury and Lowell and spent almost 17 years working at the Massachusetts AFL-CIO, five of them as the federation’s legislative director. Drinkwater has since worked as director of governmental affairs for the Union of Painters & Allied Trades District Council 35 and will assume the 17th Middlesex seat that now-Sen. Vanna Howard left vacant. He campaigned on helping working families and on his background as the son of a public school teacher and a pipefitter. Drinkwater first ran for state office in 2018, when he finished second in the primary for the First Middlesex Senate District to the late Sen. Ed Kennedy.
Ben Ewen-Campen (D), Somerville
The Harvard Medical School biologist whose research has taken him from studying birds in Alaska to beetles in Montana has spent almost nine years as Somerville Ward 3 city councilor. Ewen-Campen told 27th Middlesex voters – whose current representative, Uyterhoeven, is heading to the Senate – that he’ll fight on Beacon Hill to stabilize rents, for workers’ rights and green jobs, and against invasive surveillance technologies, pointing to his work on the city council passing progressive policies. 
Krista Ferrante (D), Princeton
Ferrante beat out her Republican opponent to flip the First Worcester District seat that’s been held by outgoing Republican Rep. Kim Ferguson of Holden for 16 years. A corporate archivist who has been working in tech as a records manager and data governance lead for over 12 years, she campaigned on regulating AI and protecting data privacy, supporting local agriculture, and improving government transparency. 
Chris Lambton (D), Dennis
The “Bachelorette” contestant, HGTV home and landscaping show personality, and former New York City public high school teacher and coach will assume outgoing Rep. Chris Flanagan’s First Barnstable seat. The longtime Dennis resident ran a campaign with priorities like affordable housing, the blue economy, and mental health awareness and assistance. He has also been chair of the Dennis Select Board and operated his family’s landscaping business and an oyster farm.
Lisa Lopez (D), Canton
Lopez told voters that she is “Retired. Ready. All in.” The Canton Select Board member has retired from her work at a medical device company. In the years since President Donald Trump’s first election, she has worked as a pro bono immigration attorney. She has sat on the town’s community preservation committee and is Canton Housing Authority chair. Housing, health care, and education are among her priorities alongside climate and clean energy, which she’ll push in outgoing Rep. William Galvin’s Sixth Norfolk seat.
Joe Markey (D), Lynnfield
Markey is a civil service commissioner, workers’ compensation attorney, former chair of the Lynnfield Housing Authority and six-term Lynnfield town moderator. He flipped outgoing House Minority Leader Brad Jones’s 20th Middlesex seat, beating out his Republican opponent in a district that has been red for three decades. Markey’s campaign focused on affordability, housing, local aid, and government transparency. 
Will Mbah (D), Somerville
The Cameroon native who studied in Sweden and then received a visa to work in the US is moving from his four terms on the Somerville City Council to outgoing Rep. Christine Barber’s 34th Middlesex seat. After working in city government for so long, he told voters that he “has seen just how many progressive policies require state-level approval to implement at the local level.” His campaign issues included immigrant rights, equitable public safety, and worker protections. 
Leila Migliorelli (D), Melrose
Migliorelli was a Melrose city councilor for six years and has spent two decades working in donor relations at Tufts University. She also created the Melrose Housing Trust and focused her campaign on affordability, expanding health care access and strengthening public schools in the 32nd Middlesex District, which Lipper-Garabedian vacated for her successful Senate bid.
Connor Murray (D), Andover 
The 23-year-old has advocated to reduce gun violence, lobbied for climate issues, and worked as an intern for now-Sen. Vanna Howard and as a field director for Rep. Tara Hong’s successful 2024 campaign. Murray will fill the open 18th Essex seat left by outgoing Rep. Tram Nguyen. He spent time at a DC think tank, graduated from college in New York in 2025, worked as a freelance actor and political consultant, and wants to “make sure that people who grow up here can afford to stay, build their lives, and succeed in the communities they love.”
Mike Nicholson (D), Gardner 
In his second term as mayor of Gardner, the city’s first Hispanic/Latin American elected official is heading to Beacon Hill – but not for the first time. Earlier in his career, Nicholson was a legislative intern for then-Sen. Jennifer Flanagan and outgoing Rep. Jonathan Zlotnik (whose Second Worcester seat he’s filling). Nicholson’s list of local government roles ranges from Rutland town administrator to mayoral aide, and the former UMass Minuteman Marching Band trumpet player and drum major’s priorities include economic development, housing, and education.
Ed Pacheco (D), Dartmouth 
Pacheco says he’s heading to Beacon Hill “to be a moderate, balanced voice who puts results over rhetoric,” and to focus on issues surrounding Dartmouth’s wastewater system, educator retention and recruiting, and “rising pressure” of 40B affordable housing developments. Pacheco has lived in Dartmouth for over two decades and will assume outgoing Rep. Chris Markey’s Ninth Bristol seat. The former night security officer at Dartmouth High School and nonprofit worker also opposes the development of large-scale data centers in the district.
Celina Reyes (D), Lawrence
Reyes is a Lawrence city councilor who was also the first president of SEIU 509’s Family Child Care Chapter, after she started her own family-run child care business. Her major campaign issues included housing and seniors, education and good government, and public health and safety. She cruised to election in the general after ousting Rep. Francisco Paulino in the September 1 primary for his 16th Essex seat following his indictment for alleged fraud. Paulino has pleaded not guilty.
Jack Richardson (D), Falmouth 
The 23-year-old, third-generation Falmouth resident ousted Republican Rep. David Vieira for the Third Barnstable House seat, campaigning on reducing housing and energy costs, cleaning Cape waters, and protecting people from federal immigration enforcement while not taking corporate PAC money. The former district director for Sen. Dylan Fernandes was also campaign manager for now-Rep. Thomas Moakley’s 2024 campaign and worked on former Sen. Susan Moran’s campaign. He went to American University, sat on the Falmouth Select Board, Housing Authority and town meeting, and is a longtime soccer referee. 
Ravi Simon (D), Sudbury
Outgoing Rep. Carmine Gentile’s sole staffer of almost five years will become his successor in the 13th Middlesex District with a priority list that includes quality education, climate action, and standing up for “Massachusetts values.” Simon’s resume features three years on the Lincoln-Sudbury School Committee, working as a speech and debate coach at Amherst College, and being a field organizer in 2018 for the committee to elect former Boston City Councilor Josh Zakim as secretary of state.
Jesse St. Gelais (R), Acushnet 
The GOP’s only flip came in the Eighth Bristol House District, where St. Gelais ousted Democratic Rep. Steven Ouellette with campaign priorities that included demanding the audit, supporting local aid and stopping “the climate agenda.” He has spent more than two decades in the insurance business, is a lifelong South Coast resident and ran on “common sense solutions” for the district.
Lora Wondolowski (D), Greenfield 
The founding executive director of the Massachusetts League of Environmental Voters campaigned on rural school funding, available and affordable housing, and farms and climate to win former Rep. Natalie Blais’s open First Franklin seat. After a close Democratic primary, Wondolowski beat an unenrolled candidate to secure the seat. A single parent, Wondolowski has raised money for progressive grassroots organizations at the Peace Development Fund in Amherst for more than four years.

Patrick Morrisey)The state of West Virginia will give $3.4 million of its federal Rural Health Transformation Program funds to Telostrand Laboratory to expand access to diagnostic testing, and to five initiatives at Boone Memorial Hospital, Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced Monday.
“West Virginians deserve access to quality healthcare regardless of where they live,” Morrisey said in a news release. “These investments will help doctors catch health problems earlier, give patients better access to specialists, and make it easier for families to get the care they need closer to home. It’s about improving healthcare outcomes, keeping people healthy, and helping more West Virginians remain in or return to the workforce.”
According to the news release, the awards include: 

     $1,686,716 to Telostrand Laboratory to expand access to non-invasive diagnostic testing and shared laboratory services for rural healthcare providers. 
     $338,705 to Boone Memorial Hospital to expand inpatient remote patient monitoring across inpatient and observation beds, helping providers identify signs of deterioration sooner and reduce avoidable transfers and readmissions.
     $597,184 to Boone Memorial Hospital to expand at-home remote patient monitoring for high-risk patients managing diabetes, hypertension or complex needs following a hospital or emergency department discharge.
     $420,200 to Boone Memorial Hospital for artificial intelligence-enabled documentation and revenue cycle tools, helping reduce administrative burden and give healthcare professionals more time to focus on patients.
     $219,184 to Boone Memorial Hospital to improve Type 2 diabetes outcomes through nurse-led care coordination, nutrition and diabetes education, and glucose monitoring. Boone Memorial is adding its own funds for weekly food boxes and fitness classes for participants.
     $190,571 to Boone Memorial Hospital to expand specialty care in Boone County through two telehealth pods at the Comfort and Nellis clinics. The project will expand access to services including behavioral health, cardiology, podiatry, and pulmonary care.

The five-year federal Rural Health Transformation aims to “empower states to transform the existing rural healthcare infrastructure and build sustainable healthcare systems that expand access, enhance quality of care and improve outcomes for patients,” according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.
West Virginia received $199 million in federal dollars from the program for 2026 and $202 million for 2027. The program was part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which made historic cuts to healthcare and food assistance spending.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: ‘Dummymander’ helps propel Rep.-elect Smith to Congress in NC-03 victory
description: Four years ago, Smith lost his N.C. House seat to redistricting. This year, a new round of redistricting sent him to Congress.
text:
Raymond Smith seated at the far end of the table on the left, poses for a picture with the newest members of North Carolina's Congressional delegation. Democrats flipped seven U.S. House seats in North Carolina in the 2026 midterms. (Photo: Raymond Smith on X) GOLDSBORO, N.C. — Democrat Raymond Smith had a nine-hour heads up that he needed to get to Washington. He had become the representative-elect for North Carolina’s 3rd Congressional District. 
Smith trailed Republican U.S. House Rep. Greg Murphy by a slim lead of 233 votes at the end of Election Day. A week later on Nov. 10, provisional and absentee ballots were tabulated. They put Smith ahead by 293 votes, according to unofficial results from the State Board of Elections. 
The following morning, Murphy conceded. 
Smith received a call around 9 p.m. on Nov. 11 saying he needed to be in Washington first thing in the morning. Orientation for newly-elected members of Congress had begun at the start of the week, but Smith said he wasn’t invited until his race was called. 
Virginia Foxx concedes long-held seat in NC’s closely watched 5th Congressional District

“I caught the first flight out of Raleigh, which was 6 a.m. I threw some stuff in a bag and got to Washington,” Smith said. “I lived that life while I was in the military, so I’m used to moving fast and packing quickly and packing light.”
Smith met the other new members of North Carolina’s congressional delegation at the U.S. Capitol, sharing a photo on social media. Each of the seven were Democrats who flipped seats in the Tar Heel State. 
Last year, North Carolina Republican state lawmakers tried to unseat Democratic U.S. Rep. Don Davis in the 1st Congressional District by making the district more Republican-leaning. They did so by moving some Democratic voters out of Davis’ 1st District and into Murphy’s 3rd District.
“Republicans were trying to grab one more seat, and in doing so, you have to do one of two things,” said Adam Newmark, a political science professor at Appalachian State University. “You either pack more Democrats into those three or four districts that you’ve crafted out as Democratic districts, or you have to shave off in some Republican districts from the sizable Republican advantage to try to create another district that’s for Republicans.”
U.S. Rep.-elect Raymond Smith (Photo: Campaign website)
The move made Murphy, who has held office since 2019, vulnerable to the blue wave. Some are calling the mid-decade gerrymander a “dummymander”: Davis won reelection, and Smith unseated Murphy.
Smith, who spent the week after the election raising funds for a potential recount, said it took a few days in Washington for his new reality to sink in.
“I started looking at the Capitol. I started looking at the Library of Congress. I started looking around at all of this history, and then it hit me,” Smith said. “I said, ‘Whoa, wait a minute. You’re a congressman now,’ and it became pretty emotional at that point.” 
Smith, 65, is an Army veteran who was born and raised in Goldsboro. He’s a former educator who served on the Wayne County school board before becoming a state legislator. 
In Raleigh, Smith represented Wayne and Sampson counties in the North Carolina House for two terms. North Carolina Sen. Gale Adcock, a Democrat from Wake County, was his mentor. 
“I just found him to be a delightful person,” Adcock said. “He’s very easy to talk to. He’s very approachable, very knowledgeable, well-spoken, friendly, willing to ask tough questions.”
NC Republicans eye 2028 comeback as two US House races move to recount

During his time at the legislature, Smith advocated for more funding for public schools, educators, and North Carolina’s HBCUs. He lost his seat in the 2022 election after a round of redistricting. 
Smith said education is one of his top priorities for Washington, but he also wants a voice in decisions related to transportation, agriculture, appropriations, healthcare, and the military.
His district contains the nation’s largest pork producer in Duplin County, as well as Eastern North Carolina’s only Level I trauma center in Greenville. There’s also Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune and Seymour Johnson Air Force Base. 
“I always tell people that the 3rd is the most eclectic district in the entire state of North Carolina,” Smith said. “As I look around the various committees and things of that nature, I’m struck by the need for more attention to armed services.”
If appointed to the U.S. House Committee on Armed Services, Smith would join Davis and Republican U.S. Rep. Pat Harrigan from North Carolina’s 10th Congressional District.

text:
Rep.-elect Stacy Heidenreich, left, and Rep.-elect Chris Tiongson, both Democrats from Fargo, smile for a photo at KFGO studios during the 2026 campaign. (Photo courtesy of Stacy Heidenreich)North Dakota legislative elections are officially final after a third-place finisher in a Fargo district declined to demand a recount by Saturday’s deadline.
Democrats Chris Tiongson and Stacy Heidenreich were the top two vote-getters in District 41 House, ahead of Republicans Jennifer Benson and Rich Slagle. 
Benson trailed Heidenreich by 36 votes, which fell within the margin for a demand recount. If requested, Benson’s campaign would have been required to fund a demand recount.
The secretary of state did not receive a request for a demand recount, Deputy Secretary of State Sandy McMerty said in an email Monday. That means the election results certified by the State Canvassing Board last week will stand, she said.
“I’ve been kind of waiting on pins and needles this whole week,” Rep.-elect Heidenreich said in an interview Monday. “I can just breathe a sigh of relief that it’s official.”
Benson did not return calls seeking comment.
North Dakota certifies 2026 election with 1 possible recount, court challenge looming

Heidenreich said District 41 is “very purple” after Republican Sen. Kyle Davison won reelection to the Senate in the same district that will send two freshmen Democrats to the state House. District 41 Republican Reps. Karen Grindberg and Jorin Johnson did not seek reelection.
The two Democrats have already visited with Davison about working together, Heidenreich said.
“Even though we are from different parties, we all have the same thing in mind,” she said.
Heidenreich is a 30-year veteran of the banking industry and an assistant vice president at Gate City Bank. 
Orientation for new state lawmakers and the organizational session are next week.
“I’m just really excited to get to Bismarck and work on the priorities that I heard from the community while I was doorknocking, which is daycare costs, general affordability, and protecting teachers and public education,” Heidenreich said.

name: VTDigger
title: The best intentions often do more harm than good
description:
Truckloads of unrequested clothing and goods can bury relief workers after a disaster. This holiday season, the most useful gift is cash.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  The best intentions often do more harm than good.
text:
This commentary is by Tessa Simson, an honors student at the University of Rhode Island majoring in political science.
Vermonters take pride in helping their neighbors. Whether it’s responding to floods that devastated our own community in 2023 and 2024 or donating to relief efforts across the world, we believe in helping others. But what if our values, expressed through well-intentioned donations, end up doing more harm than good? 
Take Hurricane Mitch, for example. In 1998, Hondurans were hit by a disastrous hurricane, which left millions homeless and claimed thousands of lives. For months following this tragedy, the affected community members were desperate for relief and the necessities that could save lives. However, when a plane full of necessary aid attempted to land on a runway in Honduras, the air crew found donated clothes — items that were neither requested by Hondurans nor needed at the time — blocking the runway, meaning the plane full of crucial aid was unable to land.
This situation is not unique to Hurricane Mitch. Disaster strikes, people and places are in shambles, often with no way to recover independently. Then the second disaster strikes. Unsolicited material donations arrive in large quantities, overwhelming storage units and airplane cargo capacity. Volunteers and relief workers have to deal with the donations instead of prioritizing essential aid distribution, and communities are left with huge amounts of unwanted items.

READ MORE

Vermont has a strong culture of giving and community service and is famous for its “neighbors helping neighbors” mindset, with a long-standing tradition of volunteerism and civic involvement. Its response is to donate to countries and people in need, which feeds directly into the second disaster.
When I was a student at Camels Hump Middle School, our art class was given blank shoes and asked to decorate them however we wanted. We were told they would be donated to communities affected by Hurricane Sandy, the 2012 storm that devastated the coasts of New Jersey and New York. As I painted the shoes, I imagined the people who might receive them, hoping that they would appreciate the thoughtful designs and bright colors I had used. Looking back, however, it’s clear we were focusing on how good it felt to give rather than thinking critically about making a noticeable impact in a devastated community. 
So what should we do instead? In scenarios like these, where communities did not request material donations, cash donations are the best option. They help communities and humanitarian organizations center their spending on the community’s actual needs. Relief organizations can purchase specific aid items and allocate cash to specific local businesses. This also reduces waste, since cash will not be discarded the way a material donation often is. 
Vermonters’ generosity and urge to help their own communities and others are beautiful traits of our small state. But we have to be mindful with our actions. With the holidays around the corner, I encourage all Vermonters to reflect on the unintended harm a physical donation may cause to a community or country that did not ask for it. Instead, take time to research the location and community you would like to help, and send money through a trusted source. As the saying goes, cash is king.

Lynn BreckenridgeFebruary 6, 1941 – November 15, 2026Rock Springs, WyomingShared by: Vase Funeral Home
Lynn Breckenridge, a beloved resident of Rock Springs, Wyoming, passed away peacefully on Sunday, November 15th, 2026, at the age of 85. He was listening to his favorite songs and surrounded by his loving family. Born on Thursday, February 6th, 1941, in Loveland, Colorado, Lynn was the cherished son of Elmer Breckenridge and Beulah Helen Cogdell and was lovingly raised by his grandparents, Arthur and Emma Breckenridge.
Lynn spent his early years in Colorado, attending local schools and graduating from Cache La Poudre in 1960. Following graduation, he married the love of his life, Jo, the mother of his four daughters. Although they later divorced, they remained lifelong friends. They moved to California where he had an adventurous job cleaning pools in Beverly Hills and met multiple famous people. He then went on to a rewarding career as a truck driver, traveling far and wide across the United States for various companies.
In addition to his professional pursuits, Lynn held a wide range of interests that brought joy and enrichment to his life. He had a deep passion for music, playing guitar at an early age, yodeling, attending concerts, Honky Tonkin’ and most of all singing and DJing karaoke. He was known for his storytelling, sense of humor, smoking a pipe with sweet cherry tobacco, and driving his ’56 Chevy Belair. He was a big reader and history buff. He also loved nature and animals, reveling in the beauty of the great outdoors which included finding hot springs, places to fish, and mountainous areas where he could view wildlife. His adventurous spirit took him on many memorable journeys, most notably Alaska and Costa Rica. Above all, he cherished spending time with his family.
Lynn’s kind and generous heart extended beyond his immediate circle. He was compassionate and loved helping animals and those in need. As a lasting tribute, his family requests donations in his memory be made to local animal shelters or homeless shelters, continuing his legacy of generosity.
Lynn completed his memoirs three weeks before he passed, which is now available on Amazon, titled “Happy Trails and Tears: Sentimental Memories” authored by Lynn Breckenridge.
Lynn is survived by his four devoted daughters: Tamela Lynn Moreno and her husband Rodolfo “Rudy” of Rock Springs, WY; Teresa “Roxan” Powell and her husband Frank of Erda, UT; Heidi Darlene Pamplin and her husband Shaun of Whitewright, TX; and Heather Jolyn Breckenridge and her spouse Teri Girtsman of Gaithersburg, MD. Lynn is also survived by five nephews: John Breckenridge, Brett Breckenridge, Tom Breckenridge, Hoby Breckenridge, and Dale Breckenridge; and one niece, Brenda Maile.
Preceding Lynn in death were his paternal grandparents, Arthur Breckenridge and Emma Harlow; maternal grandparents, David Cogdell and Nellie Turknett; parents Elmer Breckenridge and Beulah Helen Cogdell and her husband Harold “Pappy” Hedke; two brothers, John Breckenridge and David Breckenridge; a sister, Helen Florence Breckenridge; and a grandson, Riley Bunnell.
Cremation has taken place and a Celebration of Life in Northern Colorado will take place next summer. Details will be posted on Facebook.
Friends and family are welcome to express condolences and share memories at Vase Funeral Homes.
Lynn Breckenridge will be profoundly missed, but his spirit and kindness will continue to resonate through the many lives he touched.

Marilyn Jo GroesbeckMarch 28, 1947 – November 16, 2026Shared by: Davis Funeral HomeMarilyn Jo Groesbeck, 79, passed away peacefully on Monday, November 16, 2026, at the Help for Health Hospice Home in Riverton, Wyoming, with her family by her side.
Marilyn was born on March 28, 1947, in Onamia, Minnesota, to Ira and Cynthia Howard Ablard. When she was just one year old, her family moved to the Hidden Valley area, where her father, following his honorable discharge from World War II, farmed the land and built their family home. Marilyn grew up in the area, graduated from Riverton High School, and went on to pursue her passion for education.
She attended Northwest College in Cody, Wyoming, where she earned her bachelor’s degree in Education. Continuing her educational journey, she attended the University of Wyoming, where she received her master’s degree in Education, Business, and Fine Arts.
Marilyn was a longtime resident of the Wind River Indian Reservation, where she dedicated much of her life to education and serving her community. She began her teaching career at Wyoming Indian High School as a Home Economics teacher. Her commitment to education and the community led her to serve on the school board for 20 years.
She later joined the University of Wyoming as an outreach coordinator, a position she held for 15 years. Wanting to be closer to home, Marilyn began another chapter in her career, serving as the Middle School and Elementary Principal for 12 years. She continued her dedication to education and her community by serving on the St. Stephens Indian School Board for another 10 years.
After a lifetime devoted to education, leadership, and helping others, Marilyn retired. She treasured the opportunity to spend more time with her lifelong friends, enjoying their weekly lunches, sharing stories, reminiscing about old times, and simply enjoying one another’s company.
While Marilyn accomplished so much throughout her career, her greatest joy and one of her proudest blessings was her family. She loved her children deeply, and being their mother was a role she held close to her heart. Her love only continued to grow with each grandchild and great-grandchild who came into her life. She treasured her time with them and found happiness in the everyday moments they shared. Whether reading stories, working on arts and crafts, sharing her love of art, or simply being together, she cherished every opportunity to create memories with them. She loved watching her family grow and took great pride in each generation. Her children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren were a special part of her world, and the love she had for them was something she carried with her every day.
Marilyn also found joy in creativity and the simple pleasures of life. She loved working on art projects, watercolor painting, calligraphy, reading, and exploring arts and crafts.
Marilyn was of the Episcopal faith. Her family remembers her as a kind, loving, and compassionate woman who gave so much of herself to others. She was a devoted mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother, a cherished friend, and a dedicated educator who touched countless lives throughout her years.
Marilyn’s legacy is much greater than her many years of service and accomplishments. It lives on in the lessons she taught, the friendships she nurtured, the memories she created, and, most importantly, in the generations of family she loved so dearly. The love she gave her children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren will continue to live on through them. She will be deeply missed, forever loved, and always remembered.
Marilyn is survived by her brother, Butch Ablard; her sons, Nathan (Karlee) Groesbeck and Keenan (Michelle) Groesbeck; Shawn (Sacheen) Brown; and her daughter, Kayla Seminole.

Peggy Ann Temple KoeppMay 9, 1938 – November 16, 2026Big Piney, WyomingShared by: Covill Funeral Home & CrematoryPeggy Ann Temple Koepp, 88, of Coatesville, Pennsylvania, passed away peacefully on Monday, November 16, 2026, at the home of her daughter, surrounded by the love and comfort of her family.
Peggy lived a life filled with love, faith, family, and adventure. She was a woman of strength and independence, with a caring heart and a deep love for those closest to her. Whether she was spending time with family, enjoying the outdoors, or working on one of her beautiful quilts, Peggy found happiness in the simple things that made life meaningful.
Born in Denver, Colorado, Peggy was the daughter of the late Robert P. Pierce and Lois Nell Vickrey Pierce. Throughout her life, she carried with her a love for the outdoors and an adventurous spirit. She especially enjoyed hunting and fishing, activities that brought her happiness and many treasured memories.
Peggy shared 30 wonderful years of marriage with her beloved husband, David R. Koepp, before his passing in 2015. Their years together were an important and cherished chapter of her life.
Above all else, Peggy loved her family. She was a loving mother to her son, Skip Durbin and his wife, Lisa, and her daughter, Robin Olson and her wife, Rose DeRosa. She also carried in her heart the memory of her beloved son, Paul Durbin, who preceded her in death.
Peggy is also survived by her brother, Robert Pierce, and her sister, Lynn Dean. She was preceded in death by her beloved sisters, Carol Marsh, Sally Reed, and Lana Roche.
Being a grandmother brought Peggy tremendous joy. She was blessed with three grandsons and two granddaughters, and her family continued to grow through generations of grandchildren, great-grandchildren, and great-great-grandchildren. Peggy’s love for family extended beyond bloodlines, embracing those who became part of her family along the way. Each held a special place in her family’s story, and the love she shared will continue to be felt for generations to come.
Peggy had a special talent for quilting. Each quilt was more than a beautiful piece of handiwork; it was a reflection of her patience, creativity, and the love she put into everything she made. Those who were fortunate enough to receive one of her quilts have something truly special to remember her by.
Her faith was also an important part of her life. As a devoted member of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, Peggy found comfort, strength, and friendship through her church family. Her faith helped guide the way she lived and the love she showed to others.
Peggy will be remembered not only for the life she lived, but for the love she gave so freely. Her independent spirit, kindness, and devotion to family leave behind a legacy that will live on in the hearts of everyone who knew her.
Although she will be deeply missed, her family takes comfort in the memories they shared, the lessons she taught, and the love that will always connect them.

title: Who leads Delaware’s legislature in 2027, and what they’re paid
description: Democrats will hold the two top jobs and can pass most bills alone, but some spending still needs Republican votes. DOVER, Del. — After the holidays, state lawmakers will settle into their seats at Legislative Hall for the 2027 session of the Delaware General Assembly. text:
Democrats will hold the two top jobs and can pass most bills alone, but some spending still needs Republican votes.
DOVER, Del. — After the holidays, state lawmakers will settle into their seats at Legislative Hall for the 2027 session of the Delaware General Assembly. Each party chose its leaders for both chambers earlier this month. Here are three things Delawareans should know:

After the Nov. 3 election, Democrats have enough votes to fill the top leadership job in each chamber. Both jobs are filled by a vote of the full Senate or House. Senate Democrats chose Sen. Bryan Townsend for president pro tempore. He was Senate majority leader for the past six years. House Democrats picked Rep. Melissa Minor‑Brown to stay on as speaker.
Democrats can pass most bills on their own, except some yearly money bills, such as the Bond Bill for roads, schools and other building projects, and the Grants‑in‑Aid bill for fire companies, senior centers and other nonprofits.
They can also give final approval to eight proposed changes to the state constitution, as Delaware LIVE reported Nov. 4.

These two top jobs come with more power and more pay. For example, the Senate president pro tempore and the speaker of the House pick the committee chairs and decide which committee each bill goes to in their own chambers. All lawmakers are paid $54,308 a year, and leaders get more. The two top leaders get the most, $74,599 a year.
Tables 1 and 2 show the leaders of both chambers and what they are paid, plus how many votes key decisions take and whether Democrats can pass them on their own if they all vote together.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Coffia, Grand Traverse Democrats urge Benson to remove utility-linked members from transition team
description: The presence of three members on Democratic Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson’s transition team — who are closely associated with the state’s regulated utilities — has raised concerns from some Democrats over the impact they could have on Benson politically when she takes office in January. Over the weekend, the Grand Traverse Democratic Party and one of […]
text:
Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson spoke to reporters the morning after winning the gubernatorial election, telling reporters that her agenda for the first 100 days would be rolled out soon. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)The presence of three members on Democratic Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson’s transition team — who are closely associated with the state’s regulated utilities — has raised concerns from some Democrats over the impact they could have on Benson politically when she takes office in January.
Over the weekend, the Grand Traverse Democratic Party and one of its leaders, state Rep. Betsy Coffia (D-Traverse City), both called on Benson to immediately remove Gary Torgow, Fadwa Hammoud and Mel Brown from her transition team. 
The party noted that Torgow sits on DTE Energy’s corporate board, and that Hammoud and Brown both work for Miller Johnson, the law firm that represents both DTE and Consumers Energy. Miller Johnson is currently engaged in a federal lawsuit, representing the utilities, in a bid to stop Proposal 2 of 2026, known as the Michiganders for Money out of Politics, from taking effect. 
The ballot proposal passed by a wide margin on Nov. 3. It seeks to prevent DTE and Consumers Energy from using corporate money to make political contributions and to prevent the utilities, or any other large corporation that holds contracts with the state, from influencing politics in Michigan.
A message seeking comment from Benson’s transition team was not returned at the time of publication. A comment or statement from the team will be added to this story when one is received.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Hammoud also previously worked with the Department of Attorney General under Attorney General Dana Nessel, as she was one of two special prosecutors tasked with investigating the Flint Water Crisis.
Still, the Grand Traverse Democratic Party said Benson’s decision to place them on the transition team was disappointing, and that removing them would help Benson avoid corporate influence on her decisions as governor — especially as it concerns Proposal 2.
“Michigan voters passed that proposal with 81 percent of the vote,” the party wrote in a statement issued Sunday. “Michigan voted to take money out of politics, not to give it to a seat on a transition team. It was our honor to have you launch your campaign for governor in Grand Traverse County, and we are asking you to stay committed to the will of Michigan voters.”
At its most recent convention, the Grand Traverse Democrats said, it passed a resolution to send Benson a letter calling on Torgow, Hammoud and Brown to be taken off the team.
Their members also urged Benson to support bills to regulate corporate spending power in Michigan elections currently allowed by the Citizens United court precedent, as well as the Bringing Reforms in Integrity, Transparency and Ethics or BRITE Act, which would improve government accountability standards.
“Voters delivered an overwhelming mandate, and we need action,” the Grand Traverse Democrats wrote in a letter to Benson. “We stand ready to help you deliver it.”
Rep. Betsy Coffia (D-Traverse City) speaks at a news conference in Lansing to unveil government transparency legislation on March 13, 2024. (Photo: Anna Liz Nichols)
Coffia sponsored the House version of the Citizens United bills, and she similarly called for Benson to remove Torgow, Hammoud and Brown.
“I have a lot of respect for Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson and believe there is much good we can accomplish in the coming legislative term. That is why I must state publicly, with all due respect to the Governor-elect, it is inappropriate and a clear conflict of interest to put DTE board members and lawyers connected to the lawsuit to block MMOP on the Governor elect’s transition team,” Coffia said in a Facebook post. “This is especially glaring given the brazen bad faith actions by the utilities trying to stop the will of over 80% of Michigan voters who just weeks ago overwhelmingly approved the MMOP ballot initiative to stop the utilities and government contractors from giving political donations. Michiganders have spoken. They don’t want big money players steering Michigan’s politics any longer.”
Coffia continued by saying that Michigan’s government needs to be receptive to its constituents and set a clear foundation for Benson’s earliest days as governor.
“All transition team members with ties to the utilities, government contractors and the lawsuit against MMOP need to be removed from this important PUBLIC INTEREST role,” Coffia wrote. “The people of Michigan have high expectations of us and a great need for their leaders to bring our A Game. Let’s give it to them.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico sues FEMA over refusing to pay $68M for post-fire reforestation costs
description: New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham’s office last week sued the Federal Emergency Management Agency over denying the state’s request for $68 million that is intended to help reforest the burn scar of the Hermits Peak-Calf Canyon Fire.
text:
New Mexico officials on Nov. 17, 2026, sued the Federal Emergency Management Agency, alleging federal officials wrongly denied the state’s request for funds to grow millions of seedlings at the John T. Harrington Reforestation Center, pictured above in 2024, for the Hermits Peak-Calf Canyon Fire burn scar. (Photo by Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham’s office last week sued the Federal Emergency Management Agency over denying the state’s request for $68 million that is intended to help reforest the burn scar of the Hermits Peak-Calf Canyon Fire. 
FEMA is overseeing a $5.45 billion fund aimed at compensating victims of the 2022 wildfire in northern New Mexico that resulted from two botched prescribed burns on federal land. The fire destroyed millions of trees and caused widespread damage of other types, primarily in Mora and San Miguel counties.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The state — which is eligible for compensation along with individuals, businesses and local governments — sought funding from the agency that New Mexico leaders hoped would help provide the roughly 17.6 million seedlings they estimate are needed to reforest much of the 534-square-mile area the wildfire impacted. 
The funding would go to the John T. Harrington Reforestation Center, which sits at the base of fire-scarred mountains in Mora. State and federal Agriculture Department officials have laid out an ambitious plan for the center, which they hope will ultimately produce 390 million drought-resistant seedlings to reforest burned areas across the Southwest.  
State officials wrote in the lawsuit Nov. 17 that they held multiple meetings with FEMA and other federal officials before submitting a claim for the reforestation funds in April 2024. The lawsuit also notes that an independent actuarial report a firm produced for the compensation fund later that year listed the reforestation center as a project for which FEMA anticipated paying $70 million. 
However, FEMA officials denied the state’s claim in June 2025, prompting the state to appeal the ruling. FEMA denied that appeal in September of this year, according to the lawsuit, which prompted the state to sue.
FEMA denied the initial claim and the appeal on several grounds, including that the reforestation center was not damaged in the fire; that the reforestation center has been in the works since 2020; and that the federal law governing compensation for fire victims does not allow payments for “prospective expansion of operational capacity intended to meet future reforestation needs.”
Dianne Segura, an external affairs officer for the Hermits Peak-Calf Canyon Fire Claims Office, declined to comment on the lawsuit Monday, saying the office does not comment on pending litigation.
Spokespersons for the governor’s office did not immediately respond to Source NM’s emailed request for comment Monday. 
New Mexico governor preparing FEMA lawsuit over outstanding $445M wildfire claim 

In the lawsuit, the New Mexico plaintiffs said FEMA ignored a section of the Hermits Peak Fire Assistance Act that dealt separately with reforestation, including a provision that enables FEMA to pay “a cost of reforestation or revegetation on Tribal or non-Federal land,” as well as a section that authorizes the claims office administration to pay for “any other loss” office leaders determine to be appropriate. 
They also argue that the funding would go specifically to seedlings for the Hermits Peak-Calf Canyon Fire, even though the center has broader goals of helping reforest much of the Southwest. A General Obligation Bond approved by New Mexico voters in the Nov. 3 general election includes $17.65 million for the center.
“The fact that the State recognized a pre-Fire reforestation need does not eliminate the distinct Fire-caused surge,” New Mexico Chief General Counsel Holly Agajanian wrote. “The Fire created a site-specific need of extraordinary scale, requiring production dedicated to restoration of the burn scar in addition to ordinary regional demand.”
The lawsuit is the second New Mexico has filed against FEMA for denials in the claims process. In September, the state alleged FEMA wrongfully denied its $61 million reimbursement request for costs the New Mexico National Guard incurred in 2022 helping people safely flee the fire, remove debris and prevent flood damage.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: West Virginia Attorney General backs down from environmental groups investigation
description: The West Virginia Attorney General’s Office is retreating from its investigation into at least six environmental groups.
text:
West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey
speaks to the Legislative Oversight Committee on Health & Human Resources Administration during legislative interims on Aug. 11, 2026 in Charleston, West Virginia.
(Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)The West Virginia Attorney General’s Office is retreating from its investigation into at least six environmental groups. 
The reversal comes less than a month after a U.S. District Judge Joseph R. Goodwin issued a temporary restraining order against the Attorney General’s Office on grounds that the subpoenas violated the groups’ First Amendment Rights. 
“Following Judge Goodwin’s ruling, my office has permanently withdrawn all of the investigative subpoenas. We believe in the rule of law, and we respect the Court’s decision,” Attorney General JB McCuskey said a statement issued Monday. 
On Nov. 20, McCuskey sent the West Virginia Rivers Coalition and 350.org, a group dedicated to reducing fossil fuel use, stating that it was rescinding subpoenas it issued in September for a decade’s worth of records. 
“I have directed my attorneys and staff to take no further investigative action of any kind in either matter,” McCuskey wrote. 
McCuskey had opened the investigation into the groups on the basis that their activities could potentially harm West Virginia’s coal and natural gas industries. However, in court, attorneys for his office shifted the argument to be that the groups were raising money from concerned citizens based on an outdated study. 
McCuskey said in his statement that he was “acting on information that certain groups had made false and misleading statements to raise money.” 
“We issued investigative subpoenas — a well-established process regularly used when there are potential violations of the state’s consumer protection laws,” McCuskey said. “The subpoenas were an investigative step, and my office did not file suit against anyone.” 
Goodwin, appointed to the bench by President Bill Clinton in 1995, found the subpoenas to be overly broad, calling it a “fishing expedition.” 
“But even on a fishing expedition, hoping to just get one bite in the vast and quiet water, a person brings a fishing pole. And in other cases, perhaps, a net,” Goodwin wrote, “Here, AG McCuskey has abandoned both the fishing pole and the net. Instead, he has brought dynamite to the lake. Tossing a couple in, he hopes to catch something.”  
In the letter, McCuskey also wrote that he would ensure no new future investigations into the work these groups do in educating the public about climate change and effects from greenhouse gas emissions. 
“This commitment is an act of the Office, not a personal undertaking. It binds the Office and all of its current and future officers, employees and agents acting on its behalf. The policy has been entered in the Office’s official records and distributed to relevant attorneys and staff,” McCuskey wrote. 
The West Virginia Citizens Action Education Fund, a sister organization of the West Virginia Citizens Action Group, released a statement Sunday regarding its subpoenas being rescinded. 
“Nonprofit organizations must be able to educate, engage communities, participate in matters of public concern and speak freely with partners without fear of becoming targets of government investigation for exercising constitutional rights,” said Dani Parent, Executive Director of West Virginia Citizens Action Education Fund and Citizens Action Group. “Free speech and the right to associate with others are fundamental to a healthy democracy. They must be protected, and a diversity of voices in the advocacy space is critical to a functioning democracy.”
In his letter, McCuskey said he was trying to uphold the West Virginia Consumer and Credit Protection Act, but he recognized it had limits. 
“But in a contest between even the most essential statutory protection and the Constitution, the Constitution must always prevail,” he wrote.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: State officials describe acts of animal abuse at Orlando halal butcher shop
description: State prosecutors spoke in graphic and explicit terms Monday morning to describe alleged acts of animal abuse and cruelty in a halal slaughterhouse in Orlando. The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services (FDACS) began its investigation after receiving 19 videos from an animal advocacy group recorded during a public slaughter event at Ali Meat[...]
text:
Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins speaks during a news conference on Capitol Hill on Oct. 31, 2025, in Washington, D.C. The House speaker's office held the news conference on the 31st day of the government shutdown to discuss food stamp programs running out of funding. (Photo by Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)State prosecutors spoke in graphic and explicit terms Monday morning to describe alleged acts of animal abuse and cruelty in a halal slaughterhouse in Orlando.
The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services (FDACS) began its investigation after receiving 19 videos from an animal advocacy group recorded during a public slaughter event at Ali Meat International on June 6 and 7, 2025, officials said.
Customers could buy an animal and take part in slaughtering it.
Six individuals associated with the market were arrested Friday and were being held at the Orange County jail on a range of felony charges. Four of them are undocumented immigrants and ICE has placed detainers on those men, Attorney General James Uthmeier said during a press conference in Orlando.
The manager of the meat market, Nadeem Shakeel, 44, has been charged with six felonies, including conspiracy to commit aggravated abuse or killing of cattle, conspiracy to commit aggravated animal cruelty with intent to torture, and aggravated animal cruelty with intent to torture.
Senior Assistant Statewide Prosecutor Lauryn Day said what has taken place at Ali Meat International — going back to 2021 — went “far beyond any human religious slaughter practices.”
“We reviewed video and eyewitness accounts of workers who were forcefully kicking, stomping, twisting, shocking, tossing, and sawing back and forth the necks of multiple animals. Which is not only unsuccessfully meeting the Halal meat requirements, but also subjecting these animals to extreme acts of cruelty,” she said.
“We reviewed reports of workers tossing live baby lambs into metal fences, stunning the animals in their eyes, mouths, ears. And then again, the admission from workers that meat was taken from these animals while they were still alive and conscious at the facility.”
U.S. Department of Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins announced Friday that the USDA had revoked Ali Meat International’s permission to slaughter livestock without federal inspectors’ present “to prevent future violations and ensure humane treatment of livestock.”
State officials said they’d been alerted to the incident by Animal Outlook, an animal advocacy organization. The group said video footage of the public slaughter took place during the 2025 Eid al-Adha holiday and was sent to them by an individual who attended the event and openly recorded it. Officials with Animal Outlook contacted FDACS Agriculture’s Office of Agriculture Law Enforcement with a complaint detailing the alleged abuse with those videos on Aug.  26, 2025.
Halal refers to foods and drinks permitted under Islamic dietary law. Day said that members of the community who purchased the meat at the slaughterhouse have been under the “false impression” that what they were consuming was Halal meat and that those animals were treated with the “epitome of humane slaughter methods,” when in fact it was “the exact opposite of any sort of humane treatment.”
“Let me be clear: This case is not about religion,” she said. “This is about enforcing the law and protecting animals from cruelty. Religious beliefs do not provide a license to disregard animal welfare laws or subject animals to unnecessary suffering. Faith should never be used as a shield for cruelty, whether it is towards children, animals, the elderly, or any living being in our great state of Florida.”

title: Marshall Health to operate The Greenbrier Clinic next year
description: Marshall Health plans to operate The Greenbrier Clinic beginning next year under an agreement between the two organizations.  The entities have signed a letter of intent to take operational responsibilities of the clinic effective Jan. 4, 2027, according to a news release Friday from Marshall Health Network.  The Greenbrier Clinic includes a diagnostic clini[...]
text:
Beginning next year, Marshall Health will operate The Greenbrier Clinic, located in White Sulphur Springs, West Virginia. (Photo courtesy of The Greenbrier Clinic)Marshall Health plans to operate The Greenbrier Clinic beginning next year under an agreement between the two organizations. 
The entities have signed a letter of intent to take operational responsibilities of the clinic effective Jan. 4, 2027, according to a news release Friday from Marshall Health Network. 
The Greenbrier Clinic includes a diagnostic clinic, ambulatory surgery center, family care practice and medspa. It’s located within The Greenbrier resort, in White Sulphur Springs, West Virginia, which has been owned by the family of U.S. Sen. Jim Justice since 2009. Earlier this year, the Justice family announced that they and Kennedy Lewis Investment Management agreed to a joint venture for the hotel. 
Under the letter of intent, Marshall Health and The Greenbrier Clinic will “explore opportunities to expand primary and specialty care, enhance diagnostic imaging capabilities, modernize clinical operations and strengthen existing executive health and concierge medicine programs to better serve the Greenbrier Valley,” the news release says. 
“This partnership represents an opportunity to build on The Greenbrier Clinic’s longstanding reputation while bringing the resources and expertise of an academic health system to the region,” Scott Raynes, president and CEO of Marshall Health Network, said in the news release. “In the coming months, we look forward to exploring how we can work together to strengthen existing services, expand access to care and reimagine a delivery model that meets the changing needs of the community, employees and visitors.”
“Since 1948, The Greenbrier Clinic has been an integral part of the resort, providing generations of patients with personalized, preventive healthcare,” Jill Justice, president of The Greenbrier Clinic, said in the release. “We take great pride in its history and the impact it has had on our guests, employees and surrounding community. This proposed partnership with Marshall Health Network offers an opportunity to build on that legacy, combining the personalized care for which the Clinic is known with expanded resources and expertise to serve future generations.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: In Jackson, Transgender Day of Remembrance honors the dead and ‘gives flowers’ to the living
description: Maria Willis, left, and Sammara Ricks toasts the night's festivities at the 2nd Annual Transgender Day of Remembrance held at Fondren Hall, Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, in Jackson.
text:
Drag performers in Jackson swirled in shimmering dresses to the “Dreamgirls” soundtrack as audience members drew out dollar bills from their wallets Friday to celebrate Transgender Day of Remembrance. The next night in a separate venue, attendees cheered a young transgender woman, Lana Brown, who spoke fiercely about refusing to allow another transgender person’s name “become a forgotten headline.”
The annual tradition honors members of the transgender and gender nonconforming communities who lost their lives to anti-trans violence. Since last year’s remembrance day, groups tracking the community recorded the deaths of 62 people across the United States. In Jackson, their names were read aloud with the addition of Alexis Santee, a Mississippian who died a few weeks earlier after a medical emergency not directly tied to violence.  
A photo of Mississippian Alexis Santee, who was deeply connected to her transgender community, is displayed at the TRANS Program’s Transgender Day of Remembrance in Jackson on November 21, 2026. Credit: Anna Hu/Mississippi Today
This year, one event was hosted by Awakening Love, the first trans-led drop-in center in Mississippi, and the other came from the Transgender Resources, Advocacy, Networking and Services Program, which provides resources and social connection to transgender Mississippians. They join the international tradition started in 1999 to remember Boston entertainer Rita Hester, a Black transgender woman whose 1998 murder was never solved. 
The groups have celebrated separately for the past two years, after what TRANS Program Director Jensen Matar described as a “tiff” led them to follow different visions for the celebration. He also emphasized that the groups have love for each other, and are working towards the same goals. At both events, celebration came alongside somber moments reflecting on the historical and continuing violence transgender people face.
The Awakening Love event, hosted at Fondren Hall on Nov. 20, was centered around the Black transgender community. 
Attendees at the 2nd Annual Transgender Day of Remembrance held at Fondren Hall, Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Laney Henderson, a Black transgender woman and recent nursing school graduate, grew up with Alexis Santee. They attended Provine High School together in Jackson and bonded over their shared identities. Henderson remembers her friend as an ambitious woman who did not mince words. But when she gave compliments, Henderson said, “it really meant something.”
Hendersen initially planned to wear a conservative outfit for the event, but she then imagined hearing her friend respond, “No, ma’am.” Instead, she showed up to the event in a form-fitting, sky-blue sequined dress.
“I can’t really just grieve her, because she wouldn’t want me to,” Henderson said. “I would have to really celebrate her.”
At the Friday night event, drag performances interspersed a reading of the names of those who died, a keynote speech by Canton-raised transgender-rights advocate Sybastian Smith, and awards given to advocates for and allies of the Mississippi community. 
Information offered by various vendors at the 2nd Annual Transgender Day of Remembrance held at Fondren Hall, Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
During a group performance, Awakening Love founder Love Latonia and a cast of veteran performers stomped and strutted across the stage as the assembled audience walked up from their seats to toss tips. They culminated the performance by waving the striped blue, white and pink transgender flag while Latonia threw her head back, her whole body vibrating with emotion as she lip-synced the final notes of the Jennifer Hudson classic, “And I Am Telling You I’m Not Going.” By that point, the crowd was on their feet.
The group chose a powerful song to send a message, Latonia said: “We’re here and we’re not going anywhere.” 
It was also important for organizers to honor transgender people and give them “their flowers” while alive, she said. The celebration included an award given in memory of Alexis Santee to organizer at the People’s Advocacy Institute Natt Offiah. Additional honorees included Robin Webb, Jensen Matar and Sybastian Smith. 
The Jackson Gay Men’s Chorus performs at TRANS Program’s Transgender Day of Remembrance celebration in Jackson on November 21, 2026. Credit: Anna Hu/Mississippi Today
Mahogany Toney, a Black transgender woman from Birmingham, Alabama, who represented her mutual aid nonprofit organization, spoke about feeling loved and welcomed in the event, while honoring the histories of the ancestors and peers who came before her.
“It feels so transcendent, because we’ve come so far in just generations,” she said. 
The next night at Broadmeadow United Methodist Church, the TRANS program held its vigil of remembrance and resilience. Announcers read the 62 names of community members taken in acts of violence nationally, and seated attendees repeated the names as their photos flashed across a television screen that had been wheeled into the room. Listed under the photos were causes of death, if known. Three words showed up most commonly: shot, stabbed and suicide. 
A report from Advocates for Trans Equality shows that of the transgender people who died by violence, over half were Black women. As the slideshow progressed, some attendees wiped away tears. Others, such as Eddie Sharp-Johnson from Gulfport, expressed a sense of anger that so many names were listed. Coming from a family where some don’t approve of his transgender identity, he said seeing the lives lost hit home. 
“That could have been me up there,” he said. 
Janea Hunter works the room during the 2nd Annual Transgender Day of Remembrance held at Fondren Hall, Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
TRANS Program members shared their mental health struggles throughout the night. Ellie King, outreach leader of the program in north Mississippi, talked about her own experiences with suicidality, emphasizing that many in the transgender community endured similar situations. 
“It’s scary and it’s frustrating, and it’s viscerally terrifying,” she said. “But we’re not alone in all of this. We are here as a community to stand up against the systems, stand up against the bias that we face.”
In the night and with this audience, King said, she felt understood.
Music and an open mic portion counterbalanced the emotionally heavy moments. The Jackson Gay Men’s Chorus performed three songs, including a lilting rendition of “Somewhere Over the Rainbow.”
Jensen Matar, left, and Malaysia Walker, right, pose after Walker receives the TRANS Program’s Transgender Pioneer Award. November 21, 2026.  Credit: Anna Hu/Mississippi Today
Malaysia Walker, a Black transgender woman who grew up in Jackson and now lives in New Orleans, gave the program’s keynote speech. Standing in a glittering sequined dress she designed and sewed herself, Walker encouraged her audience to strive against the naysayers  that want them to fail, who say, “‘it’s not your time.’”
“We all have to take the time and look within ourselves and see, deeply, who we are as people and what we can do not only to advance our own lives but advance those behind or beside us,” she said.
Before letting her off the stage, Matar shared that if it weren’t for seeing Walker’s advocacy, TRANS program might not exist. He thanked Walker for her inspiration and presented her with the program’s Transgender Pioneer Award. 
Before closing out the evening at the Methodist church, the leaders of Awakening Love and TRANS Program announced that next year, the groups will host a joint celebration for Transgender Day of Remembrance. 
“I hope we do not have TDOR next year,” Matar said, referencing the hope that eventually, there will be no lives of people lost to transphobic violence to commemorate. “But in the event that we do, it will be together, and it’s going to be very beautiful.”

title: Mining company seeking to revive defunct Interior Alaska silver mine plans new 27-mile road
description: Alaska Silver USA Corp., a mining company seeking to reopen the troubled Illinois Creek mine southwest of Galena, has asked the state of Alaska for permission to construct a 27-mile gravel road on state land between the Yukon River and the mine site. “The purpose of the proposed private access easement is to facilitate mine […]
text:
This map, published by the Alaska Department of Natural Resources, shows the route of a proposed road supplying the Illinois Creek Mine southwest of Galena, in Interior Alaska. (Screenshot)Alaska Silver USA Corp., a mining company seeking to reopen the troubled Illinois Creek mine southwest of Galena, has asked the state of Alaska for permission to construct a 27-mile gravel road on state land between the Yukon River and the mine site.
“The purpose of the proposed private access easement is to facilitate mine development and transportation between the Yukon River barge and the Illinois Creek Mine,” wrote the Alaska Department of Natural Resources in a public notice published Friday.
Public comments are being accepted on the proposed use of state land through Dec. 21, the department wrote.
Illinois Creek, about 60 miles southwest of Galena, was owned by USMX of Alaska Inc. when it was permitted in 1996. It started producing gold the following year, but construction delays and the then-falling price of gold caused USMX to declare bankruptcy.
The mine passed to other owners who failed to resume operations, and the state of Alaska was left to clean up vast quantities of cyanide-contaminated water and other toxic debris.
The mine was reclaimed by 2005 and since then, the site has been owned by other firms with plans to revive it.
Its current owner, Alaska Silver USA, is headed by Aaron Schutt, the former CEO of Doyon Ltd., the regional Native corporation for Interior Alaska. Last month, the firm completed a season of exploratory drilling at the site.
Information published by the company through January 2026 indicated approximately 260,000 ounces of gold and 8.3 million ounces of silver in the area, plus large quantities of lead and zinc.
An additional site nearby is believed to contain significant amounts of gallium, a rare mineral used in modern electronics.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: A mother’s plea: Think about those who won’t be at the holiday table before you drink and drive
description: TOPEKA — Thousands of Kansans are involved in alcohol-related crashes every year, either because they made the poor choice to drive while intoxicated or had the misfortune of being in the path of someone who did. Those crashes kill about 80 people annually in Kansas. And Christina Branson, of Topeka, understands this painful reality all […]
text:
Christina Branson appears for a Nov. 17, 2026, recording of the Kansas Reflector podcast in Topeka. She advocates to remember those like her daughter who were killed by drunk drivers. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Thousands of Kansans are involved in alcohol-related crashes every year, either because they made the poor choice to drive while intoxicated or had the misfortune of being in the path of someone who did.
Those crashes kill about 80 people annually in Kansas.
And Christina Branson, of Topeka, understands this painful reality all too well.
Four years ago, a drunk driver killed her daughter, Cheyanne Branson, in a head-on crash on U.S. Highway 24 east of Topeka in Jefferson County. Christina turned to advocacy following her daughter’s death, which includes convincing the governor in 2024 to sign a proclamation that made Dec. 16 an annual day of remembrance for drunk driving victims.
On the Kansas Reflector podcast, Christina said it has gotten easier to talk about her daughter’s death, “because the memories don’t make you cry as much.”



“They make you smile. The videos make you smile,” she said. “It’s just, the holidays are harder because you got that unopened present or, you know, Thanksgiving was the next holiday we were going to spend together. We were going to do green bean casserole and deviled eggs, which were her favorite. And I spent Thanksgiving waiting for the funeral. That was the day after.”
Cheyanne was a staff sergeant in the Kansas Air National Guard’s 190th Air Refueling Wing, stationed at Forbes Field in Topeka. She was 23 when she died.
She loved the service and the “new family” she gained there, her mom said. After she died, Kansas Guard members created a commemorative patch for her that reads, “Ad Nuggets Per Aspera,” a reference to her fondness for chicken nuggets and a play on the state’s motto.
She also loved animals and had a “hobby zoo” with pygmy goats, her mom said.
“She’d laugh and snort and she’d get everybody going,” Christina said. “No matter what mood you were in, you’d talk to her and you were just smiling. And she just had a way of making things positive in a very dreary situation.”
Christina Branson wears a patch honoring Cheyanne Branson’s love of chicken nuggets. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)
Cheyanne had just gotten back from a trip to California and was on her way to her boyfriend’s house on Nov. 12, 2022. They planned to go to the Kansas City Chiefs game the next day. Her boyfriend checked her GPS tracker and noticed her vehicle had stopped moving, and she wasn’t answering her phone. He drove to her and found she had been killed.
Manuel Enriquez, according to court records, had startled others that day with his reckless driving. He admittedly had smoked marijuana, and his blood alcohol level was 0.21, more than twice the legal limit of 0.08. He killed Cheyanne while attempting to pass another vehicle at a high speed.
After the crash, court records show, he got out of his truck and, with minor injuries, sat down in the ditch. He never checked on Cheyanne.
A judge found him guilty of second-degree murder at a bench trial in 2024 and sentenced him to 11 years and 11 months in prison. On appeal, he has argued that the judge should have found him guilty of involuntary manslaughter.
Cheyanne was one of 96 people who died in alcohol-related crashes that year in Kansas, according to Kansas Department of Transportation statistics. For 2024, the most recent year of available data from KDOT, there were 2,169 alcohol-related crashes involving 3,889 people. There were 81 deaths and 1,195 injuries in those crashes.
Over a 10-year period, KDOT recorded 817 deaths from alcohol-related crashes. The data show male drivers were responsible for 80% of the deaths and 70% of the crashes.
A memorial along U.S. Highway 24 for Cheyanne Branson, who was killed in a drunk driving crash in 2022. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)
Christina said she could have turned to chemical substances to numb the pain of Cheyanne’s death, but it wouldn’t bring her back. She joined Mothers Against Drunk Driving instead. Through the organization, she has helped educate people who have been charged with driving while intoxicated, with the goal of getting them to change their “whole thought process,” she said.
“I call it generational domino effect, where you sit and watch Mom and Dad drink and drive,” she said. “Then you start doing it, then your kids start doing it, and it’s got to break because all you’re doing is showing the next generation it’s OK.”
She said two of her own family members have had DUIs since her daughter’s crash. She tells them what happened to Cheyanne, shows them pictures from the crash. Her approach has worked, she said.
Christina also has lobbied legislators for stronger laws around drunk driving, especially for repeat offenders.
“People are going to make mistakes. We’re human,” she said. “It’s whether anybody does anything different after that to change it. Are they going to continue with that path, or are they going to change?”
She said she wants people to remember that an Uber ride is only $40.
“Take a few minutes to think about that and those that made the sacrifice they didn’t ask for, and remember them, that they’re not going to be at the table during the holidays,” she said.
Cheyanne Branson was killed by a drunk driver on Nov. 12, 2022, along U.S. Highway 24 in Jefferson County. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)

title: Iowa Western Community College’s EMT program receives Workforce Pell approval
description: Another Iowa community college has received federal approval to classify a short-term credential pathway as Workforce Pell-eligible. Iowa Western Community College announced in a news release its emergency medical technician program has received Workforce Pell approval from the U.S. Department of Education, allowing students enrolled in the program to eventu[...]
text:
Iowa Western Community College has received Workforce Pell approval for its emergency medical technician program. (Photo courtesy of Iowa Western Community College)Another Iowa community college has received federal approval to classify a short-term credential pathway as Workforce Pell-eligible.
Iowa Western Community College announced in a news release its emergency medical technician program has received Workforce Pell approval from the U.S. Department of Education, allowing students enrolled in the program to eventually receive federal financial aid.
“We are proud that Iowa Western is among the first colleges in the country to receive approval for a Workforce Pell program,” said Iowa Western Community College President Dan Kinney in the release. “This is about more than being an early adopter. It is about opening doors for students who want to quickly gain valuable skills and enter careers our communities need.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Iowa Western, based in Council Bluffs, was one of 11 Iowa community colleges selected to participate in Iowa STRONG, or Systems, Training, and Resources for Opportunity, Navigation, and Growth, a Workforce Pell expansion initiative led by Hawkeye Community College and supported with a $10.8 million grant.
Unlike traditional Pell grants, which go to students in need who are pursuing a degree, Workforce Pell will provide funding to students enrolled in 8- to 15-week programs.
According to the release, Iowa Western is working through the implementation process for Workforce Pell and “hopes to make Pell Grant assistance available to eligible students in the EMT program soon.” The college plans to submit more programs for eligibility in the future.
Iowa Central Community College’s emergency medical technician pathway was the first program in the U.S. to receive Workforce Pell approval in August. Receiving approval for its first Workforce Pell program helps the community college take further steps in expanding access to noncredit and workforce-oriented education, the release stated.
“Short-term workforce programs allow us to respond quickly and directly to needs we see in our communities,” said Matt Mancuso, Iowa Western vice president of business and community education, in the release. “Students can gain specific, high-value skills and employers gain trained professionals in areas where they need them most. Workforce Pell can make these opportunities accessible to individuals who might otherwise be unable to afford the training.”
