name: Source New Mexico
title: Democrats demand answers from Oz after delay in $50B rural health awards
authors: Sarah Jane Tribble, KFF Health News
description: Congressional Democrats are demanding answers and more transparency from the Trump administration after a nine-day delay of annual awards from a $50 billion fund meant to improve healthcare for rural Americans.
text:
New federal rules likely will force three dozen states to reduce their annual Medicaid payments to healthcare providers by a total of more than $50 billion. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo / New Jersey Monitor)Congressional Democrats are demanding answers and more transparency from the Trump administration after a nine-day delay of annual awards from a $50 billion fund meant to improve healthcare for rural Americans.
Saying rural care is “in an acute state of crisis,” 18 members of Congress sent a letter to Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz late Thursday. The letter pointed to what it called “an alarming lack of public transparency” and said the fund “lacks sufficient guardrails to protect rural hospitals at greatest risk of closure.”
Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski said her state “got no explanation from CMS as to why” it got $3 million less in its second-year Rural Health Transformation Program allocation. It was a roughly 1.5% reduction from its $193.4 million first-year award. State leaders have not received information about an appeals process, she said.
Any delay in knowing how much they received and any reduction in their base funding is significant, Budzinski said, because states need to plan for an “acute impact” from the loss of other federal funding.
In the first year, states competed for their initial share of the $50 billion, which is handed out at $10 billion a year for five years. They won awards ranging from $147 million to $281 million. Most of the lawmakers who signed the letter were from states that lost funding this year. Rep. Terri Sewell of Alabama, which got $4.1 million less, along with Sen. Michael Bennet of Colorado, which saw a nearly $3 million drop, also spearheaded the letter along with Budzinski.



New Mexico receives another $211M in funding
The New Mexico Health Care Authority announced on Nov. 18 that the state had received another $211.04 million in funding through the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services’ Rural Health Transformation Program for the second year of funding. The state received approximately the same amount in the first year of the program.
According to an HCA news release, in the program’s second year, New Mexico will continue “working with rural communities to improve access to health care” including by providing help to rural hospitals and health care workers.
“With this funding we can build on the work already underway across rural New Mexico,” HCA rural health director said in a statement. “Our focus is on making lasting improvements in health care, close to home.”  — Source NM



One concern, Budzinski said, is “making sure that the money isn’t going to consultants, that it’s actually getting to the rural providers that it is supposed to be getting to.” The lawmakers asked Oz for a response to detailed questions by Nov. 25. They also requested a briefing about the delays to the funding announcement, which was first reported by KFF Health News, and the impact on states.
The second-year awards were due to be announced by Oct. 31, but an Oct. 30 letter from CMS stated officials “discovered an additional administrative process requirement.” Instead, second-year funding was announced Nov. 9.
Those kinds of delays prevent state officials from being able to “fully prepare for what’s to come,” Budzinski said.
CMS oversees the fund and its newly formed Office of Rural Health Transformation. Agency officials did not respond to questions for this article before the given deadline.
Republicans passed the Rural Health Transformation Program last summer as a last-minute sweetener to offset other ramifications of President Donald Trump’s signature budget law, including an estimated $137 billion in Medicaid spending cuts for rural America over 10 years.
That rural money is “retail therapy for Congress,” said Cara James, president and chief executive of Grantmakers in Health, while speaking at a Milken Institute event this month.
Because the same tax law cut Medicaid spending, which rural hospitals and people disproportionately use, as well as supplemental food assistance and other government grants, the short-term money would not “help sustain people” in rural America, James said.
Then, she posed a persistent fear about the fund: “If it’s even getting to the communities.”
Five rural hospitals have closed or been converted into lower-level facilities since the rural fund was created, including one in Michigan that shuttered beds and switched to providing only emergency services to survive, according to a list curated by the Cecil G. Sheps Center for Health Services Research at the University of North Carolina.
The letter stated lawmakers’ concerns that too much of the rural fund “could flow to large consulting and technology firms rather than supporting providers and communities on the ground.”
After the law passed last year, state leaders had just over seven weeks to write applications as they competed for the first-year funds. All 50 states won funding with allocations determined by a federal scoring process. Each year, officials are to revisit the funding allotments.
Most states saw their funding change by less than 2%. North Dakota and Iowa won the largest gains; New Jersey, Florida, and Vermont saw the biggest reductions.
Although federal officials have created state data maps, released a slew of press announcements, and led sessions on the complicated scoring of state applications, it’s not enough, said Alan Morgan, CEO of the National Rural Health Association.
The association, which represents hospitals and community clinics nationwide, sent its own letter to federal officials Nov. 9. Morgan said that the way states win money needs “to be articulated in a way that success can be replicated by all states going forward.”
Morgan said his association’s analysis found that state leaders are sending the federal money to local hospitals and clinics because communities and individuals are “relying on rural hospitals to be there to deliver care.” But it’s unclear, he said, how much of the overall rural fund local hospitals are actually receiving versus how much is benefiting other entities, such as consultants.
In their letter, Budzinski and the other Democrats asked if CMS would establish a searchable database that tracks spending. They also asked for an explanation of how federal officials will evaluate state performance and allocate awards.
It was just the latest congressional letter to federal health officials on this issue.
In August 2025, a month after the law passed, Democrats sent a letter about the program’s rollout to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. And last November, Budzinski reached out to Oz on behalf of Illinois. Bennet, along with Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine and others, signed a letter in June asking that the funds be targeted to rescue rural hospitals and clinics.
“We haven’t gotten full responses to any of these inquiries,” said Budzinski, who will become chair of the House’s largest Democratic caucus, the New Democrat Coalition, as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress.

title: Virginia sues SpaceX, Grok for AI-generated, nonconsensual sexualized images
description: On Tuesday, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones announced that the state was suing SpaceX, the parent company of X and its AI tool Grok, over claims the platform generated sexualized images of people, including children, without consent, contrary to the company’s pledges to protect users’ content and privacy.  “With a single existing photograph, Grok could, [...]
text:
On Nov. 23, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones announced a lawsuit against SpaceX, parent company of X and its AI tool Grok, for generating and displaying nonconsensual sexualized images of people on the platform, including children. (Photo by Getty Images)On Tuesday, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones announced that the state was suing SpaceX, the parent company of X and its AI tool Grok, over claims the platform generated sexualized images of people, including children, without consent, contrary to the company’s pledges to protect users’ content and privacy. 
“With a single existing photograph, Grok could, and did, fabricate a realistic image or video of a person nude, or partially nude, or engaged in sexual activity, all without the individual’s knowledge or consent. This violation is not acceptable,” Jones said in a statement, calling the suit a “first step towards holding this company accountable.”
Jones referenced a study by the Center for Countering Digital Harm that reported that between Dec. 29, 2025, and Jan. 8, 2026, Grok created and posted about three million sexualized images on X, including “23,000 images that appeared to depict children.” 
The study found that a week or more after being identified, nearly 30% of the sexualized images of children were still visible in X posts, and ones that had been marked “removed” by the platform were still accessible through separate URLs. 
Virginia’s lawsuit was filed in coordination with Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield, who lodged a separate but similar suit in his state. 
“It’s no surprise that Grok and X became a haven for perpetrators using AI to create and share child sexual abuse material,” Rayfield said Tuesday. “The lack of needed safety measures was considered a feature, not a bug, which they promoted as ‘spicy mode.’”
The lawsuit seeks relief for X users and victims in Virginia, and civil penalties of up to $2,500 per violation for each willful violation of the Virginia Consumer Protection Act. It alleges SpaceX “derived substantial revenues and other commercial benefits, including benefits in the form of data collected from consumers, via Grok’s use in the Commonwealth.”
Filed Nov. 23 in Richmond City Circuit Court, a hearing for the suit has not yet been set. 
In January, European Union regulators representing 27 nations began investigating X for Grok’s sexualized images of people, including content that “may amount to child sexual abuse material,” PBS News reported.  
Malaysia and Indonesia briefly blocked access to Grok earlier this year over concerns about sexualized deepfake pictures. 
“Companies that deploy powerful tools don’t get to ignore consumer safety and call it innovation. The law applies to everyone, and this office will hold big tech accountable when they break the law,” Jones added.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming GOP selects five priorities for 2027 legislative session
description:
Delegates agree to a narrow set of priorities out of a laundry list of topics, including hyperscale data centers, election integrity initiatives and introducing runoff elections.
The post Wyoming GOP selects five priorities for 2027 legislative session appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
GILLETTE—The Wyoming GOP solidified its legislative priorities for the upcoming session when delegates met this month in Gillette. There was little discussion about the shellacking that some of the party’s endorsed candidates received during the primary.
Delegates agreed to a narrowed set of priorities out of a laundry list of topics, including hyperscale data centers, election integrity initiatives and introducing runoff elections to Wyoming.
Many attendees remarked that the Nov. 14 meeting was relatively uneventful with some entertaining remarks from David Holland, the vice chair of the party and interim chair of the meeting. He kept the delegates awake with jokes and remarks, some said, as he managed the meeting more like a preacher to his congregation than a vice chairman.
The room full of delegates from all over Wyoming seemed hesitant to discuss the election after just two of the six endorsed candidates — Chuck Gray for U.S. House of Representatives and Rep. Harriet Hageman for U.S. Senate — won their primaries. 
Many delegates seemed particularly disgruntled by the results of the governor’s race in the primary, in which the state GOP-endorsed candidate, Brent Bien, received less than 24% of the vote behind eventual winner Eric Barlow, and Trump-endorsed Megan Degenfelder.
“Does anybody know the cost estimate for runoff elections? The additional cost to the counties?”Joe Martinez, Hot Springs County Delegate 
The group passed its runoff election resolution almost unanimously and with little discussion.
A runoff election would take place when none of the candidates in a race receive more than 50% of the vote. Barlow received 45% of the vote in the Republican primary, and Gray received just 24.9% of the vote in the crowded primary for U.S. House.
“Does anybody know the cost estimate for runoff elections?” Hot Springs County Delegate Joe Martinez asked the chair. “The additional cost to the counties?”
Holland gave a tongue-in-cheek response to the question.
“Does anybody know the cost of having people elected to office who do not represent a majority of the voting public?” Holland said to some chuckles.
“The cost is we don’t have a duly elected governor for a majority of Wyoming,” said Janet Mader, a Campbell County delegate.
Martinez and fellow delegate and Hot Springs County Commissioner-elect Phillip Scheel shook their heads at the response from their fellow delegates.
Other delegates remarked that Rep. Chip Neiman, R-Hulett, had sponsored a bill that would have appropriated $2 million from the state general fund to facilitate a runoff election.
Scheel responded once again that counties foot the bill for elections. The chair responded with another joke.
“I wonder what we could do with that 50% property tax exemption we didn’t get,” Holland said to a bigger laugh.
Ultimately, the delegates from 23 counties agreed on the following five priorities:

Corralling data center development into accountability under the Industrial Siting Act
Barring legalized marijuana or THC products
Barring Medicaid expansion
Combining a variety of election integrity bills and requiring runoff elections
Protecting life

The meeting concluded as Holland and his delegates discussed an existential threat to the Republican Party nationally: losing young people. Holland asked delegates not to neglect instilling everlasting conservative values into their children well before their teenage years. 
Young people also need to be taught about money, Holland said. One of his biggest disappointments in President Donald Trump was the national debt surpassing $40 trillion. He tried to rationalize the scale of that number.
“If I told you I’d pay you back in a trillion seconds — that is 37,000 years,” Holland shouted. “It is older than the history of the world.”
The rest of Holland’s speech was interrupted by an A/V system glitch. Static boomed through the room like a thunderclap, causing some delegates to flinch.
Despite the technical difficulties, Holland still sent off the “big family” of the Wyoming GOP with a message as he asked them to promote unshakeable conservative values.
“Young people are looking for something that we can offer them as a rock, and we can start in our lives, in our churches, in our parties. We got a challenge ahead of us for the next two years, four years, 10 years. Go out and do it!” he shouted.

title: Franklin state rep seat flips after recount; Democrat Hall wins by one vote
description: After a recount, Democrat Vivian Marie Hall has won a seat in the state House of Representatives, beating out Republican Michael Visconti by a single vote. The initial count immediately after Election Day showed Visconti defeating Hall, 1,358 to 1,355. New Hampshire state law allows candidates to request a recount if they lose by 20% […]
text:
New Hampshire Secretary of State's Office staff and volunteers count ballots during an official election recount on Nov. 9, 2026, at the State Archives building in Concord. There were 16 recounts called for state House races after the 2026 midterm elections. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)After a recount, Democrat Vivian Marie Hall has won a seat in the state House of Representatives, beating out Republican Michael Visconti by a single vote.
The initial count immediately after Election Day showed Visconti defeating Hall, 1,358 to 1,355. New Hampshire state law allows candidates to request a recount if they lose by 20% or less of the total votes. A recount was called and the subsequent count found Hall winning 1,358 votes to Visconti’s 1,357.
The district encompasses all of Franklin. She’ll be one of three representing the city in the House. Democrat Scott Burns and Republican James Thibault also won elections there. Thibault’s district also includes Northfield.
The race was one of 16 that saw recounts over the past few weeks. It was the only recount to produce a new winner.
However, Republican Pam Brown is still pursuing her case even after a recount reaffirmed her narrow loss in Kingston. Brown was defeated by Democrat Paul Paone, 2,084 to 2,086, just two votes, in the initial count. A recount narrowed that to one vote, 2,084 to 2,085. Brown has appealed to the state Ballot Law Commission, which is weighing in on Monday.
Democrats made big gains this month as a “blue wave” swept across the country. Hall’s victory brings Democrats’ new supermajority in the state House to 292-107, with one independent. Democrats will also hold a 15-9 majority in the state Senate and a 5-0 majority on the Executive Council. Republicans have held majorities in all three of those chambers since the 2020 elections.
The new state representatives and senators will be sworn in Dec. 2.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Some Oklahomans could be getting a fresh area code as 580 runs out of phone numbers
description: Oklahomans with a 580 phone number could soon be sharing their part of the state with a new area code. Telephone companies expect to run out of phone numbers that start with 580 in early 2029. Last week, the North American Numbering Plan Administrator (NANPA) filed a request with the Oklahoma Corporation Commission (OCC) to […]
text:
A cellphone with a phone number is pictured. (Photo by Graycen Wheeler/KOSU)Oklahomans with a 580 phone number could soon be sharing their part of the state with a new area code.


Telephone companies expect to run out of phone numbers that start with 580 in early 2029. Last week, the North American Numbering Plan Administrator (NANPA) filed a request with the Oklahoma Corporation Commission (OCC) to implement a fix before that happens.
The agency is recommending an overlay—a second three-digit code for the area that currently uses 580. This is the same solution that introduced central Oklahoma’s 572 area code in 2021 and eastern Oklahoma’s 539 area code in 2011.
This is the first time this group of corporation commissioners will consider such a request. Kelsey Schwartz, a public information officer with the OCC, said commissioners will consider all the possible options to address this issue.
“They look at the lifespan of those relief options, the burden on the public and come to a decision on if they agree with the fact that the recommendation is the best move forward or not,” Schwartz said.
If corporation commissioners approve the request, new phone customers in western and southern Oklahoma may be assigned numbers starting with the new, yet-to-be-determined area code starting in 2028.
According to NANPA’s filing, the idea is to give people living in the 580 area code time to adjust and prepare.
Existing customers wouldn’t feel many effects from the overlay; they’ll keep the 580 area code for phone numbers they already have.
But people with 580 area codes will need to start dialing the full ten-digit number for local calls, because two locals could have the same seven-digit number. The overlay will not affect service numbers like 911 or 411.
NANPA filed the request on behalf of telecom providers in Oklahoma after projections showed they would run out of 580 numbers a year earlier than expected. Across the country, only two other area codes are expected to exhaust their available phone numbers before 580.
The Oklahoma telecommunications industry and NANPA determined an overlay would be the best option.
Another option, which NANPA considered but is not requesting, would split the 580 area and assign part of it a new area code. That’s how the 580 area code was created in 1997, carved out from an area formerly covered by 405.
The OCC is not scheduled to consider this request on its published upcoming meeting agendas. Schwartz said it may take commissioners a few weeks to review the filing on their own.
“As it comes closer to the commissioners making a decision, we will be pushing out information about it,” she said. “And once they make a decision, we’ll push out information about that as well, reminding people that you’re going to have to do the ten-digit dialing or you can keep your phone number.”

(Photo by Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)A panel of the Atomic Safety and Licensing Board recently approved a New Mexico Department of Justice petition to intervene on a mining company’s federal license renewal to restart uranium mining and processing in McKinley County. 
The company, NuFuels, Inc., a subsidiary of Laramide Resources, seeks a license renewal from the federal Nuclear Regulatory Commission for its Crownpoint Uranium Project that would allow it to extract up to three millions pounds of “yellowcake” uranium annually for up to 20 years, according to the NMDOJ.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Atomic Safety and Licensing Board’s approval of New Mexico’s intervention means now a public hearing will be held to address potential deficiencies in NuFuels’ renewal application, including its claims that it can restore groundwater quality to pre-mining levels, Attorney General Raúl Torrez said in a news release Friday.
“This is a significant and unprecedented step forward in holding uranium mining companies accountable for the risks their projects pose to New Mexico communities,” Torrez said. “The applicant’s own disclosures raise serious questions about its ability to protect New Mexico’s water, and the panel recognized that those questions deserve answers in a public hearing.”
NuFuels’ officials hope to use a mining method known as in situ recovery to access uranium, including on 175 acres of private land in Church Rock. In situ recovery entails the injection of lixiviant — a chemical solution composed of water, oxygen and either carbon dioxide or sodium bicarbonate — to dissolve the uranium underground. 
From there, pumps extract the uranium liquid into recovery wells, where the uranium is separated. The leftover water is then discharged back into the aquifer. When fully operational, the company would discharge roughly 4,000 gallons of leftover water a minute back into the aquifer at the Church Rock site. 
The NMDOJ in August weighed in on the company’s application, noting that state officials are dubious the in situ recovery process can restore groundwater. It also said the company is relying on outdated baseline data and that it is ignoring Navajo Nation laws related to uranium transport and production. 
The panel granting the NMDOJ’s petition agreed the state raised multiple “material” or otherwise important issues regarding the company’s license renewal that deserve further inquiry and explanation at a public hearing. 
In a statement to Source NM, Laramide Vice President Josh Leftwich noted that the Atomic Safety and Licensing Board’s decision only determined which of the NMDOJ’s “contentions warrant further consideration.”
“It does not constitute a finding that those allegations are substantiated, that the project is unsafe, or that NuFuels has failed to satisfy the requirements for license renewal,” he said.
He said the company respects New Mexico’s right to participate in the process “and will address the issues raised with supporting technical and scientific evidence.”
The 61-page ruling from the licensing board does not determine a date for the public hearing, but it asks the state and the company to submit scheduling proposals in the coming weeks. 
The company also needs approval from the New Mexico Environment Department before it can discharge leftover water back into the aquifer. 
Anti-uranium advocates wrest control of public hearing on proposed mine near Navajo Nation

In August, the company held a public hearing on that discharge permit request in a Gallup-area casino regarding that pending permit. Indigenous community members and advocates expressed frustration that NuFuels would pursue a uranium mine in an area still contending with the biggest uranium spill in the nation’s history, the 1979 Church Rock mine spill, as well as numerous other public health and environmental harms from decades of uranium mining.
Leftwich told Source NM that the company is reviewing public comments it received at the meeting and in the two months afterward as it completes an assessment of the mine’s impacts on surrounding communities. The company will hold another public meeting to discuss that assessment once it’s drafted, he said. 
“Laramide remains committed to working constructively with communities and regulatory authorities, meeting applicable environmental and regulatory requirements, and advancing the Churchrock–Crownpoint project through a transparent and responsible development process,” he said.

title: A deer at a Shelby County deer farm tests positive for a ‘zombie’ deer disease
description: Kentucky wildlife officials say a dead deer at a Shelby County deer farm has tested positive for a fatal, incurable brain disease known as chronic wasting disease.  On Nov. 19, the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s National Veterinary Services Laboratory informed the Kentucky Department of Agriculture and the state veterinarian that a five-and-a-half-year-old[...]
text:
Deer inside a fenced enclosure on a Kentucky deer farm. (Provided)Kentucky wildlife officials say a dead deer at a Shelby County deer farm has tested positive for a fatal, incurable brain disease known as chronic wasting disease. 
On Nov. 19, the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s National Veterinary Services Laboratory informed the Kentucky Department of Agriculture and the state veterinarian that a five-and-a-half-year-old deer inside the deer farm tested positive, according to a Monday release. 
Chronic wasting disease, about which much is unknown, is sometimes called the “zombie deer disease” because it causes deer to have significant weight loss, listlessness and eventually leads to death. A deer can have chronic wasting disease for months or years before symptoms appear. 
The Kentucky Department of Agriculture release states the department has established a 15-mile “surveillance zone” around the deer farm, and it is monitoring and restricting deer movement within other deer farms in the zone as part of a state plan to address chronic wasting disease. 
Deer farms, also known as “captive cervid facilities,” are places where people raise deer on fenced-in properties as livestock, regulated by the Kentucky Department of Agriculture. Last year, state and federal agencies killed more than 100 deer at a Breckinridge County deer farm after multiple deer inside the fenced-in site had tested positive for chronic wasting disease. 
Deer farm herd killed to stem spread of ‘zombie’ deer disease in Kentucky. Now what?

An effort by a Republican state lawmaker to put more restrictions on deer farms failed to gain traction last year. The proposed regulations would have incentivized deer farms to add a second fence around the farms to prevent captive deer from interacting with wild deer and potentially spreading the disease. Debates over how to control chronic wasting disease, the threat it poses to the deer population and the role of deer farms have also been contentious in other states. 
In a Monday release, the Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources stated the positive test in Shelby County will not affect the current deer hunting season, but a state commission that crafts hunting regulations will discuss the positive test at an early December meeting. 
Only three other wild deer in Kentucky outside of deer farms have ever tested positive for chronic wasting disease.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Commentary: Kentucky cut recidivism. Fragmentation could stall the progress.
description: Kentucky has done something worth celebrating. Over two decades, bipartisan efforts from both the legislative and executive branches have methodically built a criminal justice reentry system with programs to prepare incarcerated people to rejoin society. The results — reported in new research from KYFREE — show the investment is paying off. The share of peop[...]
text:
Kentucky has made progress in helping formerly incarcerated people rebuild their lives, but there's still work to do. (Getty Images)Kentucky has done something worth celebrating. Over two decades, bipartisan efforts from both the legislative and executive branches have methodically built a criminal justice reentry system with programs to prepare incarcerated people to rejoin society.
The results — reported in new research from KYFREE — show the investment is paying off. The share of people returning to prison within two years of release has fallen by nearly one-third.
Celeste Gander, a criminal justice consultant and our report’s author, pointed out there’s still work to be done: “Successful reentry depends on many systems working together, and the next stage of reform in Kentucky is making the system work as one.”
Reentry runs through corrections, probation and parole, workforce programs, health care, housing, local jails and dozens of community groups. Each does its part. However, coordination is fragmented across agencies, and no reliable feedback loop exists between the Department of Corrections and the community partners who see what happens after release.
Returning people to prison is expensive. The Council of State Governments Justice Center projects that reincarcerating Kentuckians released from state custody in 2022 will ultimately cost $149 million.
One problem is hiding in plain sight. Our report found about 60% of returns to custody among people released in 2023 were for technical violations of supervision rules, not new crimes.
Accountability matters. Supervision rules exist for a reason and breaking them should carry consequences. But sending someone back to prison who is working, housed and not committing new crimes rarely makes anyone safer. It can cost a job, an apartment and a family’s stability. And taxpayers get the bill.
The report offers a road map of 20 recommendations, including making reentry a statutory priority of the Justice and Public Safety Cabinet, codifying the Governor’s Office of Reentry Services into law, limiting incarceration as a response to technical violations, and letting people request a state ID earlier than 90 days before release. Something as simple as an ID can decide whether a person starts a job the week they come home.
Another important finding came from a focus group with people who were previously incarcerated in Kentucky prisons. They said peer support, specifically from others who had been incarcerated, was often the single most important factor in their successful transition home.
Yet a standard supervision condition bars contact with people who have felony convictions unless approved in advance. Seeking out that support can lead to a violation, or even revocation of supervision. Adjusting policies like this to reflect reality and support people trying to do the right thing is a no-brainer.
I believe conservatives should champion strengthening reentry.
A steady paycheck brings structure, purpose and responsibility. And Kentucky’s economy needs people who are ready and willing to work.
Children need their parents to be active in their lives. A mother or father who comes home, finds a job and stays out of trouble can begin to heal the wounds incarceration inflicts on families.
Fewer people returning to prison means fewer victims and safer communities for all Kentuckians.
People who have served their time and done the hard work of turning their lives around have earned a second chance.
Government’s job is to make sure that chance is real, and that the money spent on it delivers results. Bureaucracy should never be a barrier to an individual’s redemption.

name: Mississippi Today
title: They voted for Donald Trump in 2024 and Scott Colom in 2026. Here’s why
description: Still image of Mark Vines from Scott Colom's “Lost Her Way” ad.
text:
In early September, as the nation turned its attention to Mississippi’s surprisingly competitive U.S. Senate race, Scott Colom walked into AC’s Steakhouse in Hernando and sat down at a table with a group of Trump supporters. 
The Democrat was locked in a tight battle with incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith in a state that President Donald Trump won by 23 points less than two years earlier. Colom wanted to ramp up his outreach to the president’s voters, so his campaign organized a small, in-person roundtable with Trump-supporting Republicans. 
Over Cajun chicken tenders and fries, the group peppered Colom with questions about his views of capitalism, transgender participation in women’s sports and government spending. By the end of the meal, Colom had won them over.
As the dust settles from Mississippi’s historic Senate race, a Democratic victory in the heart of Trump country, many political observers have noted a massive Democratic turnout. Another factor that contributed to Colom’s victory was his ability to win over a small but potentially significant number of skeptical Republicans.
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom greets people in line at a President Donald Trump rally for Colom’s opponent, Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026 in Corinth. Credit: Special to Mississippi Today
The lunch meeting took place in DeSoto County, a Republican stronghold that Trump won by about 24 points in 2024 and where Colom pulled off a stunning turnaround for Democrats in November, winning the county by about seven points.
Beyond DeSoto County, U.S. House results across the state suggest there were tens of thousands of voters who voted for Republican House members but not Hyde-Smith. GOP House candidates collectively won more than 20,000 more votes than Hyde-Smith.
In interviews with Mississippi Today, voters who supported Trump in 2024 and Colom in 2026, including some at that lunch meeting, cited Trump’s war in Iran, his failure to release the Epstein files and Hyde-Smith’s uninspired campaign as reasons they crossed over to support Colom. 
A few weeks before the roundtable in Hernando, Colom’s campaign filmed an ad with Mark Vines, 50,  a Southaven businessman who said he voted Republican for 20 years and supported Trump in 2024. 
The ad, titled “Lost Her Way,” featured Vines explaining that he wouldn’t vote for Hyde-Smith because she voted to block the release of the Epstein files. Colom and Vines made strange bedfellows. In addition to Vines’ longtime Republican voting record, he had even criticized Colom on X shortly after the Democrat entered the race for “quoting platitudes.” 
But Vines grew more and more dismayed over the push by Trump and his allies, Hyde-Smith among them, to conceal the Epstein files. He called Hyde-Smith’s office and wrote letters urging her to support the release of the files. He said he never got a response, not even a robo-email. 
“The first thing they did was make a farce of the whole Epstein thing, which was probably the biggest piece of corruption. So that kind of set the tone that OK, this is not going to be the change that we voted for,” Vines said. “So we felt betrayed.”
Some elected Republicans in Mississippi have said that sentiment might be widespread. Rep. Jansen Owen, a Republican state lawmaker from Poplarville, wrote on X that Republicans should be clear-eyed about the political cost that came with congressional votes to block the release of the Epstein files.
“I’ve heard from a lot of constituents in my very Republican district who cite the Epstein file vote as their reasoning for going left, voting third party, or skipping the Senate race altogether,” Owen wrote. 
Feeling alienated from the party he had supported for decades and the president he supported less than two years before, Vines decided to attend one of Colom’s town halls in Horn Lake. He was immediately struck by Colom’s work ethic and the way he made himself accessible to voters, even those who disagreed with him about various issues. He believed that stood in stark contrast to Hyde-Smith’s cloistered approach. 
“She’s a nepotism hire, she was appointed,” Vines said. “And then I looked at the history, and that’s kind of been our history in the state. It’s not really merit based, and that kind of flies against the whole fundamental principle of being a conservative.”
For some Republicans, Colom’s personal work ethic as a candidate and willingness to offer ideas beyond increasing spending on government programs seemed to embody an embrace of meritocracy they felt Democrats had abandoned in recent years. That’s how Chris Cook felt.
“You make your own way with meritocracy,” Cook said. “I’m more in line with that, which I know is less traditional, or at least in the past 5-10 years or so, less associated with the Democratic Party. But that’s where I started to see a little bit of a moderate in him, and not just that extreme left sort of perspective.”
Cook, 60, who works for a financial advisory firm in Hernando, had been invited to the roundtable at AC’s Steakhouse by Vines. After filming the ad with Vines, Colom’s campaign asked him to help put together a group of Republicans who could meet with Colom and tell him what issues mattered to them.
Cook came to the lunch and said the attendees didn’t hold back on questioning Colom. He was struck by Colom’s overtures to Republicans and his willingness to incorporate their concerns into his campaign rather than dismissing them. 
Cook voted for Trump because he doesn’t like career politicians. He grew frustrated with political stagnation and had a sense that nothing substantive ever changed despite the grandiose promises of establishment politicians. Trump’s promise to “drain the swamp” of entrenched government bureaucrats appealed to him.
Cook also believed the Democratic Party swung too far left on some cultural issues under former President Joe Biden. Cook coaches youth soccer and was concerned about the prospect of trans girls competing against biological girls. 
On the campaign trail, Hyde-Smith called Colom a “transgender defender” and attempted to cast the Democrat as an out-of-touch radical. But after Cook met Colom, those attacks fell flat. 
He was open to pivoting away from Trump and the Republicans because he believed the president had shown himself to be unrestrained in his thirst for raw power, focusing on pet priorities such as renaming buildings while using the economic strain on Americans caused by his policies as a “bargaining chip” in his political battles.  
Hyde-Smith refused to acknowledge those issues, and as a result seemed to be a creature of the same political machine Cook had initially supported Trump to dismantle, Cook said.
“I really chose Scott more so because it went back to the career politician thing with the senator that had been in place for so long, and stuff just wasn’t really changing. And I didn’t see anybody really doing anything to try to get my vote,” Cook said. “And I did see him.”
Cook believes he’s far from alone among voters on both sides of the aisle who will refuse to prioritize party loyalty over everything else.  
“Myself personally, and I feel like a large part of the country are no longer just going to support a party because I’m a Republican and my father was a Republican, or I was a Democrat and my father was a Democrat,” Cook said. “I think people are now paying a lot closer attention to what’s really going on.” 
The demographic perhaps most likely to swing back and forth is younger voters. 
Mississippi Today spoke with a 23-year-old Brandon woman who voted for Trump in 2024 and Colom in 2026. The woman, who works in marketing, asked for her name not to be used so she could discuss her political beliefs without professional consequences. 
The woman, who was not at the lunch meeting in Hernando, was raised by Republican parents. She was a loyal Trump supporter and even attended his inauguration in 2024. But one of Trump’s campaign promises that appealed to her most was the president’s promise to limit America’s interventions in foreign conflicts.
“These are topics that Trump ran on and then Cindy Hyde-Smith ran on, no more forever wars,” the Brandon woman said. “Not only did he not get out of the wars but he continues to perpetrate the wars, and it’s American citizens’ tax dollars that are going to the Middle East, to Israel.”
By contrast, Colom relentlessly criticized the war in Iran and vowed not to take money from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. Some researchers have said support for Israel has become a generational chasm within the Republican Party.
A 2026 analysis by the Brookings Institution citing Pew data noted that unfavorable views of Israel among Republicans aged 18 to 49 shifted from 35% in 2022 to 50%, compared with a shift from 19% to 23% among Republicans aged 50 and older.  
As the war in Iran dragged on and Hyde-Smith seemed to be a rubber stamp for Trump’s agenda, the Brandon woman decided that she could not vote for her. But she didn’t immediately decide to vote for Colom. Her mind was made up just days before the election, when she saw Colom strolling through the line outside Trump’s rally in Corinth, talking to the president’s supporters. To her, that displayed a level of respect for voters and for the office that Hyde-Smith refused to muster. 
“She wouldn’t have a debate with Scott Colom,” the Brandon woman said. “She basically just assumed that because she was the Republican candidate and had an R next to her name that the Mississippi Senate race was hers.” 
As Colom continues to receive national attention and plaudits from his historic win, he seems not to have shifted away from his decision to keep speaking with Republicans and voters who might disagree with him. 
On Thursday, he announced that he would host a community conversation in Itawamba County next week, the county where he received his lowest percentage of the vote on election day. 
“No matter where you live or how you voted, your voice matters, and I’ll always show up for you,” Colom said. “That’s what Mississippi deserves because Mississippi Matters.”

name: Nevada Current
title: Commentary: Hello from the bright side, where we’re always looking
description: Back in the spring of 2018, I was offered a part-time reporter job at a newsroom with no name, set up by some upstart nonprofit organization nobody had ever heard of. At the time, I was working a full-time PR job to pay my bills and licking my wounds after being downsized by another media […]
text:
A Nevada Current selfie. Clockwise from bottom left: Editor April Corbin Girnus, Reporter Dana Gentry, now-retired Editor Hugh Jackson, national editor Sean Scully, reporter Michael Lyle, and reporter Jeniffer Solis.Back in the spring of 2018, I was offered a part-time reporter job at a newsroom with no name, set up by some upstart nonprofit organization nobody had ever heard of. At the time, I was working a full-time PR job to pay my bills and licking my wounds after being downsized by another media outlet a few months earlier.
It seemed like a risky endeavor, but it turned out to be the best decision I’ve made in my professional career.
Eight (and a half!) years later, States Newsroom is the largest state-focused nonprofit news organization in the nation; the Nevada Current is an indelible part of the state’s media landscape; and I am taking over as its editor.
Before I can talk about our future, I have to talk about how we got to today. I follow in the footsteps of inaugural editor Hugh Jackson, who retired last week. Hugh is best known for his political commentaries, which are infused with a wit and acidity unmatched by anyone else in the state. But to the staff of the Current, he is a lot more than that.
Hugh is the reason some of us were able to stay in journalism after being written off (and/or laid off) by legacy publications. He had a vision for what a small and scrappy news outlet could be, and he had a commitment to hiring a diverse staff that reflects the state. He told us to swing for the fences with our stories and broke us of the ingrained habit of chasing the same stories everyone else was. He prioritized context and clarity over quickness or clicks.
He would tell us that sometimes our audience is tens of thousands of readers, and sometimes it’s 63 state legislators in a Reno exurb with the power to right systemic wrongs. And while it never happened, I suspect that if we’d ever published a story that absolutely nobody read, he would have reminded us that some things need to be said aloud even if nobody at all is listening.
Underpinning everything at the Current has been the same question: What is making Nevadans’ lives harder than it needs to be, and who is responsible?
That guiding spirit will live on, even as some things evolve.
I am not coming into this role with plans to demolish our existing infrastructure and replace it with a gaudy ballroom. A hostile takeover this is not. But I do believe we can sharpen our coverage, expand our reach, and better meet this moment in our state, our nation and our industry.
I welcome our loyal readers–and new ones-to help shape this next chapter.
Dana Gentry, Michael Lyle, and Jeniffer Solis will continue the incisive enterprise reporting they are known for. Each of them has built their own beat, broken news, and changed narratives. I’m honored to lead them and support them in doing more of that.
Still, I’m interested in hearing what areas and issues you think warrant further scrutiny and attention in the state.
Hugh’s voice is irreplaceable, but I hope we can elevate new voices. (Interested in writing commentary for us? Let’s talk!)
We also remain committed to collaborating with, and being a resource for, other newsrooms. We love the outlets that republish our content via a creative commons license. We also love those newsrooms that don’t republish us but shape their own coverage after seeing ours. (We see y’all.)
So, Hugh may be gone, but to remix a phrase he probably wrote dozens of times since our 2018 launch, there’s a bright side, and it’s where we’re looking now.

name: Source New Mexico
title: University of Michigan regents approve $785 million Los Alamos computing center project
description: The University of Michigan Board of Regents voted Thursday to proceed with work on the computing center — which opponents refer to as a data center — the university is developing with Los Alamos National Laboratory.
text:
Rendering of the University of Michigan and Los Alamos National Laboratory computing center. (Image courtesy of the university).
The University of Michigan Board of Regents voted Thursday to proceed with work on the computing center — which opponents refer to as a data center — the university is developing with Los Alamos National Laboratory.
The project is planned for a site on Textile Road in Ypsilanti Township despite across-the-board opposition from the community’s elected officials. As a state university, Michigan does not require local zoning approval for the project to move forward.
The vote was 7-1, with Regent Paul Brown voting no.
Regent Carl Myers said he’s excited about the scientific work that will be conducted at the facility, which he said will include cancer, clean energy, and extreme weather research.
“We worked very hard to find the right balance between the project and the community, and I think we’ve been successful,” he said.
The university says it will commit $5 million to projects in the greater Ypsilanti area over the next five years.
The Michigan and Los Alamos project has attracted significant community pushback. Residents and local leaders say the Ann Arbor university is targeting a neighboring community with more low-income areas and communities of color for a project that will add costs for Ypsilanti Township residents without providing substantial benefits.
Community members have also raised concerns about noise, generator emissions, and other environmental impacts from the 100 megawatt project.
The Textile Road site is located on the Huron River.
“We will not have any negative impact on the Huron River,” outgoing Michigan President Domenico Grasso said in a Thursday statement.
Phase one of the project includes the development of 150,000 gross square feet. Phases one and two are not expected to exceed 300,000 gross square feet, according to the memo Robert Hewlett, university chief financial officer and executive vice president, submitted to the regents seeking project approval.
The project’s first phase will cost an estimated $450 million, with the cost of phase one and two not to exceed $785 million, Hewlett said.
A State of Michigan grant and university bond proceeds with debt service from a combination of rental payments and general fund resources will fund the project’s first phase, according to Hewlett.
Thursday’s vote authorizes the issuing of bids and awarding of contracts for the project.
The project received a $100 million grant in 2024 from the Michigan Strategic Fund and Michigan Economic Development Corp., a taxpayer-funded agency providing business incentives.
A community partnership and investment resolution attached to Hewlett’s request for action says the university should build on successful programs in the Ypsilanti area like those at the University of Michigan Health Ypsilanti Health Center. The facility provides care for residents who might otherwise need to travel to Ann Arbor, and brings patients and workers to downtown Ypsilanti, according to the document.
Michigan said it will develop and enact a comprehensive community partnership program for Ypsilanti Township focused on education, parks and recreation, partnerships with community organizations, and identifying and funding public safety initiatives, environmental enhancements and other projects to improve residents’ quality of life.

name: WyoFile
title: Controversial railroad ties set to be removed from Laramie’s West Side
description:
Rep. Karlee Provenza says Omaha Track will move the ties out of state starting Monday. 
The post Controversial railroad ties set to be removed from Laramie’s West Side appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
LARAMIE—The piles of creosote-soaked railroad ties that raised public health and safety concerns among West Side residents and local officials starting this summer will soon be moved elsewhere, according to Democratic Rep. Karlee Provenza. 
“I got a phone call from the legal counsel for Omaha Track, who oversees the storage of the ties, and they told me last night that they were moving the tracks out of the area starting on Monday,” Provenza told WyoFile on Friday. 
Union Pacific began stacking the ties this summer on its property adjacent to the Laramie River and the West Side, a historic, working-class neighborhood sandwiched between the train tracks and Interstate 80. 
As WyoFile previously reported, neighboring residents say the pungent smell of the creosote — a preservative long used to protect wooden ties from natural decay and pests — quickly fouled up the area. 
The preservative is a mixture of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons “derived from the distillation of tar from wood or coal,” according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Depending on exposure levels, it poses health risks, including cancer, and can linger in soils and pollute water. 
Provenza, whose House district encompasses the West Side, said it’s her understanding that the ties are being moved out of state, but those details remain unclear. Omaha Track and its legal counsel did not respond to WyoFile’s request by publishing time. 
“I won’t celebrate until the ties are gone, and I hope they’re not being sent to someone else’s backyard,” she said. “But it’s a big deal that the people that live at the end of Cedar Street and near that area aren’t going to be breathing in creosote and aren’t going to have to worry about their homes burning down.”
Martha Jenkins sits on her front porch in Laramie’s West Side. (Maggie Mullen/WyoFile)
Soon after the ties appeared, a handful of West Side residents formed a nonprofit, Healthy Neighborhoods, and threatened to sue Union Pacific and Omaha Track if the companies didn’t remove the ties. They felt legal action might be necessary after initial responses from local and state authorities were tepid. 
Martha and Mark Jenkins, two of the nonprofit’s founders, told WyoFile on Friday they were “delighted” at the news. 
“To prevail in this kind of local battle, I think it’s very meaningful,” Mark said. “I think it shows that people can pull together if they feel like something is actually wrong and make a difference for each other.”
The post Controversial railroad ties set to be removed from Laramie’s West Side appeared first on WyoFile .

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT’s transportation program needs funds, but tolls aren’t in the mix
description: CT’s transportation program needs funding soon, according to state analysts, but no one is pitching tolls. Options include more borrowing.
text:
While Gov. Ned Lamont is trying to salvage most of a planned ramp-up in Connecticut’s transportation rebuild, analysts warned Friday that isn’t sustainable for long without more revenue.
Analysts never suggested tolls, and neither the governor nor legislative leaders are calling for them. But finding more dollars for transportation is the latest item on a long to-do list awaiting state officials in the new year.
Lamont’s budget staff and the legislature’s nonpartisan Office of Fiscal Analysis both projected Friday that the state’s $2.4 billion Special Transportation Fund would slip anywhere from $132 million to $400 million in deficit — a gap ranging from 5% to 14% — between next fiscal year and 2030.
Those projections were included in the analysts’ fiscal accountability reports — omnibus analyses of spending, borrowing and revenue trends delivered yearly to legislators in preparation for the next General Assembly session.
“We know it’s out there, and it’s going to be a major conversation” in 2027, House Speaker Matt Ritter, D-Hartford, said, adding that legislators share Lamont’s desire to rebuild Connecticut’s highways and bridges.
“If we are serious about investing in Connecticut’s transportation infrastructure, we need to have a serious conversation about how we fund it,” said Sen. Christine Cohen, D-Guilford, co-chairwoman of the Transportation Committee. “That means getting creative about establishing sustainable revenue streams.”
But while the transportation fund faces challenges soon, it’s less than 10% of an overall state budget that has enjoyed historic surpluses for nearly a decade, averaging almost $1.9 billion per year in black ink. Lamont and lawmakers have used most of that to reduce pension debt and build reserves but could redirect some toward transportation.
But Ritter conceded that legislators are being asked to address many other major funding needs in the next two years, including K-12 schools and special education in particular, along with Medicaid, affordable childcare and social services.
House Minority Leader Vincent J. Candelora, R-North Branford, said Democrats — who now hold a 116-35 advantage in the House and 33-3 in the Senate — would have more options to fund transportation had they embraced GOP proposals to scale back state employee raises, eliminate unfilled positions, reduce Medicaid benefits for undocumented residents and seek greater efficiencies at public colleges and universities.
“They’re going to have to figure their way out of this,” he said.
Ritter predicted legislators, including Candelora and other Republicans, would find a solution to bolster transportation and other key programs while keeping state finances in the black.
“I know he [Candelora] will be part of the conversation,” the speaker added.
That conversation will be centered on the transportation fund, even though it doesn’t pay directly for the rebuild of Connecticut’s infrastructure. That’s covered through a combination of annual state borrowing and federal grants.
The STF, which gets most of its revenue from the sales and fuel taxes, covers the annual principal and interest payments on that borrowing. It also pays the operating costs for the Departments of Transportation and Motor Vehicles, including bus and rail public transit programs.
And at first glance, the fund appears to be flush.
The STF finished with robust surpluses between 2023 and 2025, enough to increase the fund reserve by more than $700 million. State officials have since used much of those surpluses to pay down transportation debt early.
The STF also is on pace for a healthy 10% surplus, about $240 million, this fiscal year.
But critics say a big factor behind those increases is Connecticut isn’t rebuilding its infrastructure fast enough. Sufficient work is being done to ensure safety but not to ease congestion, they say.
Lamont won praise from transportation advocates two years ago when he recommended boosting annual construction borrowing by 40%, from $1 billion to $1.4 billion by 2028.
But he reversed himself last November over concerns about the STF’s long-term stability, settling on $1.2 billion in borrowing this year and then $1.1 billion annually through 2030.
Lamont, who tried to convince legislators in 2019 and 2020 to install electronic tolling on state highways to finance an unprecedented construction program, said during a gubernatorial debate last month he wasn’t reviving that idea.
“Nobody wanted to do that,” he said. “We’re not going to do that.”
But the Democratic governor said he did want to invest more in transportation.
The administration’s fiscal accountability report called Friday for an increase in borrowing, albeit slightly slower than it planned two years ago.
It would maintain this fiscal year’s $1.2 billion borrowing in 2027-28 cycle then grow to $1.3 billion two and three fiscal years from now.
Legislators could consider shifting more sales tax receipts to the transportation fund, or raising fuel tax rates, if future deficits develop as analysts warn.
Even the largest STF deficit projected down the road, about $400 million by 2030, is well shy of the $800 million to $1 billion analysts say highway tolls on all traffic would generate. In other words, it’s a problem state officials could solve for now without turning to tolls.
Don Shubert, president of the Connecticut Construction Industry Association and a tolls supporter, said he recognizes the political will for that isn’t strong right now and praised Lamont for prioritizing transportation borrowing.
“I think we need to stay focused on maintaining the momentum and avoid cutting projects,” he said. “The entire construction industry is going to be looking [for] leadership, real leadership on this issue,” Shubert said, adding he hopes state officials are “looking at all options.”
But between 2016 and 2020, Connecticut included hundreds of millions of dollars in the state budget for construction, to complement the billions obtained via borrowing and federal grants. That eventually stopped as Lamont and legislators struggled to keep overall budgetary spending under a constitutional spending cap.
But legislatures and governors have carved out cap exceptions in the past, and Shubert said they should consider a new one for construction spending.
The president of the Connecticut State Building Trades Council, Keith Brothers, could not be reached for comment.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: HMSA Creates New Obstacle To Mainland Care For 17k Patients
description: Starting next year, 17,000 patients who buy HMSA insurance through the Affordable Care Act will have limited access to out-of-state care.
text:
When Akemi Hiatt was diagnosed with colorectal cancer in 2022, she and her husband researched treatment options in Hawaiʻi. 
Local doctors told her that she would need chemotherapy and radiation to shrink the tumor before getting surgery. Those treatments could be debilitating and carry a long list of potential side effects she hoped to avoid, including infertility.
Seeking a second opinion, the couple flew to a top cancer treatment center located in Texas – a provider in the Blue Cross Blue Shield Network covered by their HMSA insurance – where the doctor told them chemotherapy wasn’t necessary. He felt confident that he could remove the tumor with surgery alone. 
Hiatt underwent a two-part surgery, after which her tests came back negative. She is now in remission. 
“It’s not to say the doctors here aren’t great,” her husband Paolo Vidali said. “But when you go to the continent, there can be a doctor who sees 10 times as many patients and just has a deeper level of expertise.” 
Under the 2027 Affordable Care Act plans offered by Hawaiʻi’s largest private insurer, HMSA, the path that Hiatt and Vidali took to her recovery would no longer be covered.
Under the 2027 Affordable Care Act plans offered by HMSA, the path that Hiatt and Vidali took to her recovery would no longer be covered. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
Beginning Jan. 1, HMSA will limit out-of-state coverage, including telehealth, for the roughly 17,000 people who buy individual plans through the Affordable Care Act marketplace. The change will impact a population of people who don’t have employer-sponsored health insurance: those who are self-employed; earn too much to qualify for MedQuest, Hawaiʻi’s Medicaid program; or are too young for Medicare. It will also affect the dependents of these policyholders, such as college students attending schools on the mainland. 
Patients will still be able to visit emergency rooms and urgent care centers on the continent. But services not available in Hawaiʻi will have to be approved by HMSA in advance, on a case-by-case basis. If a doctor in Hawaiʻi can provide the “medically necessary service,” even if that doctor has less experience or expertise, patients will be expected to be treated here. 
While HMSA says that this change will only affect a small number of members, the impact on those members could be significant, requiring self-advocacy of people already ill or possibly forcing them into treatments they would rather approach differently through mainland care. Ultimately, the change grants greater discretion over healthcare decisions to a health insurance nonprofit whose financial incentives may or may not align with what patients feel is in their own best interest. 
It also raises a particular concern in a state with a chronic physician shortage, which can often lead to long wait times and delays in care.
The change applies only to ACA individual plans, not to HMSA’s other PPO plans, according to the company. 
Latest From Civil Beat
HMSA says the change is a response to fraudulent enrollments by people who do not live in Hawaiʻi. Kehau Giles, assistant vice president of commercial products at HMSA, said “potential fraud,” including potentially high-cost or repeated out-of-state claims, cost the company an estimated $25 million last year. 
Giles emphasized that ACA plans are intended for people who live in the state where they enroll.
She said the affected patients make up about 2% of HMSA’s members, and that currently, 90% of individual ACA members do not use mainland services at all. 
“The list of things we cannot handle here in Hawaiʻi is a very short, short list,” she said, adding, “I think you’re kind of touching on something that is very, very rare.”

Scott Saiki, the state insurance commissioner, said there’s nothing the state can do about health insurers limiting their benefits.  (Blaze Lovell/Civil Beat/2024)

Scott Saiki, Hawaiʻi’s insurance commissioner, said that the state Insurance Division has no jurisdiction over changes to benefits by private insurers, though it accepts and investigates complaints from consumers whose services are denied. 
Hiatt acknowledged that going out of state is not an option for everyone, but having the backing of your insurance company to do so is crucial. 
“I wasn’t questioning the skills or the recommendations” of doctors in Hawaiʻi, she said. “I just thought, this is my life. So maybe it’s worth seeking that second opinion.”
Higher Costs, Less Coverage
Across the country health insurers are hiking up rates and canceling plans in the face of rising healthcare costs and decreasing federal support for the Affordable Care Act, also known as Obamacare, and Medicaid, said Timothy Halliday, a research fellow at the University of Hawaiʻi Economic Research Organization, or UHERO. 
“It’s not good, but I’m not surprised,” he said of the changes. “I think it’s just a case of simple math.” 
HMSA recorded an $88.3 million operating loss last year, ending 2025 with a $3.1 million net loss. In addition to exploring a major merger with Hawaiʻi Pacific Health, the nonprofit is making several changes to its plans next year, and it notified affected patients shortly before the start of the annual open enrollment period.
Last month, HMSA notified 16,000 kūpuna that their Akamai Advantage plans would be discontinued. Those patients will have to choose between paying more or cutting their coverage back. 
Mark Mugiishi is the CEO of the Hawaii Medical Service Association, better known as HMSA. Cory Lum/Civil Beat/2022
Employer-sponsored plans are also growing more expensive by double digits, prompting some employers to shift more of the burden to employees. HMSA also announced that it would eliminate its catastrophic plan, in which 500 people are enrolled this year. That plan has a high deductible but a lower monthly fee. HMSA will migrate those patients onto its Bronze PPO I plan. For the average 40-year-old, that would raise the monthly premium from roughly $296 to $563. 
Catastrophic plans are common and available all over the U.S. In Hawaiʻi, HMSA is the only insurer to offer one.
Dr. Scott McMurry, a family physician on the Big Island, called the catastrophic plan a “better than nothing” plan that allows families that cannot afford other plans to maintain some form of coverage.
“With a relatively small enrollment in catastrophic coverage, consolidating our plan offerings helps create a more sustainable ACA portfolio while continuing to provide members with meaningful coverage choices,” Jennifer Diesman, HMSA’s senior vice president of external affairs, wrote in a statement.
‘It Can Often Be Life Or Death’
Civil Beat spoke with patients in a range of circumstances who will be affected by the new limits on out-of-state coverage.
One patient is weighing whether to end therapy after 13 years, because HMSA will no longer cover his Oregon-based therapist, whom he sees virtually. A Maui resident said he routinely receives care in California because the waits to see a physician on Oʻahu are so long. A woman who suffers from severe migraines said that once every few years she must fly to California for a ketamine treatment that is difficult to obtain in Hawaiʻi. She said she fears the preapproval process under the new rules could delay and obstruct her care.
The change will also affect dependents under 26 who are covered by their parents’ plans, because routine and elective care outside Hawaiʻi will no longer be covered. Under federal law, children can generally stay on a parent’s ACA plan until they turn 26.
HMSA’s new policy could prevent college students on the mainland from getting coverage for preventative care where they live.  Craig Fujii/Civil Beat/2026
Robert Hiltner, a retired Honolulu resident, said he is worried about his 20-year-old daughter, a student at Scripps College in California, who will lose coverage under his plan in January. 
“I’m disappointed and shocked,” he said, adding that he wants to make sure his daughter is insured. “But if we can’t find something, what do we do?”
Giles, the HMSA representative, said dependents attending college on the mainland who need broader access to routine care “may want to explore other options.” 
Ashley Lukens Wilder, a Honolulu resident and single parent, was diagnosed with brain cancer a decade ago at the age of 36. At the time, she couldn’t find any neuro-oncologists practicing in Hawaiʻi. 
Then, her insurer, University Health Alliance or UHA, declined to cover the cost of surgery in California with a more experienced surgeon, reasoning that a general brain and spine surgeon at Queen’s Medical Center could technically perform the operation. It held to that position even after Wilder submitted a letter from her Hawaiʻi doctor. 
“You’re sitting here telling people you have to accept a subpar, unspecialized surgeon to operate on their tumor,” she said, “knowing that surgeon is going to have the greatest impact on how long they live.” 
“Would you rather have a surgeon who has maybe done the procedure three or four times in their life, or three or four times a week?”Dr. Scott Miscovich
Her employer ultimately helped her move to a different insurance plan, which partially covered the cost of surgery in California. 
“This new decision by HMSA to require pre-approval for patients to go out of state,” Wilder said, “will result in people dying.” 
Dr. Scott Miscovich, president of Premier Medical Group, said the changes affect a small share of the population but can carry serious consequences, particularly for patients with complex conditions. 
“Would you rather have a surgeon who has maybe done the procedure three or four times in their life, or three or four times a week?” Dr. Miscovich said. “It can often be life or death.” 
Hiatt, the colorectal cancer survivor, said that she could have gotten her surgery in Hawaiʻi and survived, but her day-to-day life would be much more challenging. 
“Being in Hawaiʻi, we already know there’s a shortage of doctors,” she said. 
“You need to have the option to travel,” she continued. “It shouldn’t be something you have to argue for.” 
Ashley Lukens Wilder is a fundraising consultant for Civil Beat.
