name: California
title: Why California’s universities are setting up their own AI data centers
description: Some colleges are setting up their own data centers and designing AI products to rival ChatGPT. The community colleges and the UC systems are both discussing expanding these AI alternatives, even as they continue to work with commercial providers.
text:
In summary
Some colleges are setting up their own data centers and designing AI products to rival ChatGPT. The community colleges and the UC systems are both discussing expanding these AI alternatives, even as they continue to work with commercial providers.  


On Thursday, the University of California announced another deal with OpenAI to give ChatGPT to students. At the same time, California’s higher education systems are considering building their own data centers and creating in-house alternatives to ChatGPT, Claude, and other commercial AI products.
College administrators say they want to explore all options without limiting themselves to just one vendor. Some tech leaders say these alternatives to ChatGPT are not only possible but would save money and avoid data security risks. The California Community Colleges system — the largest higher education system in the country — is  asking the state for $21 million next year to develop a more independent AI network that would, according to the proposal, be a “fraction of the cost of commercial solutions.” 
The University of California is considering doing something similar, though the system has yet to put forward a formal proposal. California State University spokesperson Amy Bentley-Smith said the 22-campus system is having “initial conversations” with the UC and community colleges about collaboration on AI but did not share other details. 
While they discuss designing their own AI, the UC, Cal State and community college systems continue to use commercial providers. 
UC spokesperson Stett Holbrook told CalMatters the purchasing amendment of the new OpenAI agreement isn’t finalized yet, even though the university has already announced the deal. That disclosure emerged after reporters for CalMatters repeatedly asked for a copy of the purchase agreement. The previous OpenAI contract requires the UC to pay a minimum of $10 per user per month for ChatGPT EDU licenses and a minimum of $30 per user per month for another advanced ChatGPT platform. The Cal State system signed contracts with OpenAI that extend through 2029 for roughly $56 million. The community colleges’ chancellor’s office has AI cooperation agreements with Google, Microsoft, Adobe and IBM but no systemwide financial arrangement with any AI company.
University-designed AI models are cheaper and ensure more privacy, but they’re “not quite necessarily as intuitive,” said Craig Hayward, a strategic advisor to the community college chancellor’s office on AI. “Your prompting game needs to be more on point to get the value out of them.” 
Locally, individual universities are already moving forward with their own AI plans. This month, Cal Poly San Luis Obispo announced the creation of its AI data center, which is intended to serve the whole campus, according to Chris Lupo, the director of the university’s school of applied computing. 
The most advanced, university-controlled AI platform is at UC San Diego, where university IT services collaborated with its supercomputing center to create TritonGPT, a nod to the campus mascot and OpenAI’s ChatGPT. The San Diego platform has licensed or shared aspects of its AI development with other UC campuses to help them develop their own chatbots, including BearGPT at Berkeley and SCOUT at Merced. UCSD was also cited as a partner in the community college system’s AI proposal. 
“This is the model that the higher education system in the state of  California is trying to expand,” said Zachary Johnson, the senior director of AI strategy for UCSD.
Why sovereign AI is gaining popularity
For the community college system, developing an independent or sovereign AI system comes with three main benefits, Hayward said.
The first is cost. While tools such as Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini are the most popular examples of AI, they’re expensive, with individual plans reaching $200 per month and incurring further costs to go beyond usage limits. 
To develop their own AI systems, colleges don’t work from scratch — they use other AI tools, known as open-weight models, including Chinese products such as Kimi or DeepSeek or American ones such as Llama and Gemma. Getting these products up and running can be costly, but once operational, they are often not only cheaper than ChatGPT or Claude but also give schools more control. The code behind these low-cost models is typically free to use or change, allowing colleges to rename and rebrand the AI or even repurpose it entirely.
The second benefit is control. The Cal State contract with OpenAI specifically says that the company cannot use student data to train its models, but Hayward said these kinds of agreements still have risks and unknowns. “There’s just this concern that somehow it’s going to leak,” he said, adding that internally developed AI tools give colleges “end-to-end control” over the data. 
That control is helpful for research and for operations. Campuses can develop AI uses that are tailored to help with other projects that commercial models like ChatGPT or Claude aren’t necessarily built for, such as using AI to help with admissions or course enrollment. Lupo at Cal Poly San Luis Obispo said these more independent AI models also allow computer science professors and students to design their own AI experiments without having to worry that a third-party might change its model in the middle of an experiment. 
The San Diego Supercomputer Center at UC San Diego in San Diego on Nov. 18, 2026. Photo by McKenzie Patterson for CalMatters
Hayward said the last benefit is environmental. The community college system has lofty climate goals, including reducing potable water usage by 50%. He said that by adapting open-access or open-weight AI models, colleges take on more of the burden of AI computing internally, which means they can more closely track the power and water demands of these systems. “We can better monitor and know our AI footprint,” Hayward said. “It’s somewhat obscured when you use big vendors like Anthropic and Google.” 
Pushback to OpenAI
For many UC and Cal State leaders, however, big vendors still hold a lot of sway. 
“OpenAI models are more advanced than open-weight models,” said Holbrook, with the UC. He said these commercial models can more easily integrate into sophisticated university systems without requiring schools to build their own large data centers. 
In September, an AI committee formed by the UC President’s Office sent a proposal to the UC Board of Regents, recommending that the UC develop its own AI systems along with commercial products. Late last month, the UC Academic Council, which oversees academic matters, sent a letter to UC President James Milliken, saying the council was not properly consulted about the new agreement with OpenAI.
Cal State faculty have also pushed back. In January, San Francisco State professor Matha Kenney circulated an independent petition calling on Cal State Chancellor Mildred García to terminate the system’s contract with OpenAI. “ChatGPT Edu does not use reliable peer-reviewed sources to answer students’ questions and is indifferent to whether its answers are correct,” the petition says. It has about 4,000 signatures. 
Even UC San Diego, the leading model for university-controlled AI, has integrated commercial products from Anthropic and OpenAI into its AI platform.
Students walk through the UC San Diego campus on July 29, 2026. Photo by Zoë Meyers for CalMatters
When the university first started developing TritonGPT about three years ago, it was a student project, designed to help the IT department’s help desk, said Johnson, the AI senior director of the university. Over time, users started bringing other questions to the chatbot, realizing how effective it was. Now UCSD operates TritonAI, which includes TritonGPT plus many other university and commercial AI products. Users can choose which model they prefer. 
Johnson said that the open-weight AI platforms are adequate for the “vast majority of users” but that some computer science or “heavy AI users” may need commercial models. “We’re a university doing really innovative things so we need to have the full range of capabilities available.”
8,000 miles of shared power
To compete with the most advanced commercial products, California’s community colleges want campuses not only to develop their own AI but to work together, too.
Underneath California’s schools, libraries and universities is a massive, 8,000-mile network of fiber cables that helps power the state’s educational technology. That infrastructure, known as the California Research and Education Network, dates back to the 1990s dot-com boom, when the federal government worked with states to purchase fiber optic cables for education. Thousands of institutions across the state still use the network today.
The data center at the San Diego Supercomputer Center at UC San Diego in San Diego on Nov. 18, 2026. Photo by McKenzie Patterson for CalMatters
As campuses purchase their own hardware for AI computing, the California community college chancellor’s office wants to connect each campus through this existing fiber network. The goal is to create an interconnected AI and computing platform that’s more powerful than anything a single campus can build. 
And that project is already underway, said Tom DeFanti, a special advisor for the organization that runs the research and education network. He said a total of about 20 community college districts, UC and Cal State campuses already have access to AI computing power through the shared network. 
The largest data center is at UCSD, which uses its supercomputer center to run AI models, but other campuses are slowly adding new hardware and joining the network. Cal Poly San Luis Obispo built its AI data center after receiving a $3 million donation from the estate of Robert N. Noyce, a co-founder of Intel. Lupo said the campus has yet to attach its AI technology to the broader network but is “discussing” it. 
At the moment, California’s shared AI network is dwarfed only by Texas, which has an even larger system with more processing power, said Frank Wuerthwein, the director of the San Diego Supercomputer Center. 
But he said compared to the processing power of commercial companies, both states pale in comparison. 
Reporter Mikhail Zinshteyn contributed to this story.

name: California
title: California confirmed 60 measles cases this year, more than the past two years combined
description: California has confirmed more measles cases this year than in the previous two years combined, and its biggest outbreak spread through the unvaccinated pockets of one of the state’s most vaccinated counties. Just days ago, the U.S. lost its status as a measles-free nation, but Californians shouldn’t panic, public health officials said. Most Californians are [...]
text:
California has confirmed more measles cases this year than in the previous two years combined, and its biggest outbreak spread through the unvaccinated pockets of one of the state’s most vaccinated counties.
Just days ago, the U.S. lost its status as a measles-free nation, but Californians shouldn’t panic, public health officials said. Most Californians are likely protected, but people who are unsure of their vaccination status should check.
Pockets of unvaccinated communities have driven local outbreaks in the state, including two earlier this year in Shasta and Riverside counties as well as a regional outbreak in Sacramento and Placer counties.
The Sacramento-Placer outbreak, this year’s largest, sickened 21 people. The outbreak began when a family member of a Placer County resident traveled to South Carolina. More than 98% of prekindergarten kids have been vaccinated in Placer County, said Dr. Rob Oldham, the county’s health officer, but health officials estimate fewer than half of the people in the communities where the virus spread were vaccinated. All of the cases occurred among unvaccinated individuals or people with unknown vaccination status, said Oldham, who added that it could have easily turned into a much larger outbreak.
Dr. Phuong Luu, Sacramento County’s health officer, said 450 people were exposed in her county alone. The health department temporarily reassigned people across seven divisions to contact and monitor people who had been exposed. 
She called the measles elimination status loss “a sad day for public health” and said it is more critical than ever that Californians stay up to date on vaccinations.
“People in California don’t stay in California, and people from other states come to visit,” Luu said. “And so the best way to protect yourself is to be fully vaccinated and ensure that your loved ones are fully vaccinated.”
Measles elimination status loss
Last week, international health officials with the Pan American Health Organization stripped the U.S. of its measles elimination status, a designation indicating that the highly infectious disease had stopped circulating in the country. The U.S. held this status for more than two decades.
The U.S. first eliminated measles in 2000 primarily through vaccination efforts, but anti-vaccine sentiment grew over time and vaulted to national prominence with Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s appointment as secretary of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. Uncontrolled outbreaks in Pennsylvania, Texas, South Carolina, Arizona and Utah sickened more than 8,000 people and killed more than a dozen since 2025.
Dr. Sanchi Malhotra, a pediatric infectious disease specialist at UCLA Health, called the status loss “embarrassing.” 
“Children are getting sick and dying from something we have a very good vaccine against,” Malhotra said.
Unvaccinated communities fuel California outbreaks
The state has confirmed 60 measles cases this year, a sharp jump from the 25 documented last year and 15 the year prior. Yet California has one of the highest immunization rates in the nation. 
Nearly 96% of incoming kindergartners were vaccinated for measles, mumps and rubella at the start of the 2025-26 school year, according to data sent by the state health department to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That’s higher than the 95% target that prevents measles from spreading unchecked in a community.
State Public Health Officer Dr. Erica Pan said in a statement last week that high vaccination rates prevented larger outbreaks in California. Pan noted that in September a person with measles traveled by bus and train from Los Angeles to the Bay Area, potentially exposing hundreds of people, but there were no additional cases.
Vaccination rates have remained high and steady in California since the state implemented strict laws governing school enrollment and vaccine requirements in 2015, but experts still urge caution.
Measles vaccination rates dropped in recent years among California’s immediate neighboring states to levels well below the threshold needed to prevent widespread transmission.
“We have to be more vigilant,” Oldham said. “We’ve had these pockets that have always existed, but if they reach a critical mass it will make things more difficult.”
Dr. Peter Chin-Hong, an infectious disease specialist at UCSF, also said Californians cannot become complacent about vaccination.
“Infectious diseases are not limited to borders,” Chin-Hong said. “What we have in California is a big force field, but that force field could be weakened.”
People who are unsure about their vaccination status should talk to their primary care doctor to check whether they need to be tested for measles immunity or receive an updated shot, Chin-Hong said.
Expert medical groups and public health organizations recommend two doses of the MMR vaccine, which is 97% effective against measles and additional protection against mumps and rubella. No vaccine ever provides 100% protection, Malhotra said, but in the rare instances when a vaccinated person contracts measles the vaccine also protects against severe complications and hospitalization.
“The biggest myth is it’s just another childhood illness,” Malhotra said. Measles can cause pneumonia, inflammation of the brain, pregnancy complications and death. 
“Measles is the most infectious disease we have. It’s a canary in the coal mine,” Malhotra said. “If we’re seeing measles outbreaks, it makes us worry what other vaccine-preventable diseases are on the horizon.”

name: California
title: California politicians decide how quickly high-speed rail gets done. It’s their job to move faster
description: Construction crews are doing their jobs to build high-speed rail in California. The politicians in Sacramento aren't. The next wave of Capitol leaders can fix that.
text:
Guest Commentary written by

Carter Lavin
Carter Lavin is the co-founder of the Bay Area transit rider group Transbay Coalition and part of the Move California network.


Avery Barrett
Avery Barrett is a high-speed rail advocate with the Transbay Coalition and Move California.


Construction crews have already electrified and upgraded the train corridor from San Francisco to San Jose, upgraded rail capacity in Los Angeles and are finishing 119 miles of high-speed rail guideway in the Central Valley, where track-laying is imminent.
But while the hard-working union members moving earth and pouring concrete in California’s heartland are doing their jobs, the politicians in Sacramento aren’t. The next governor and state Legislature can fix that. 
The high-speed rail project has made it through an obstacle course of red tape to get this far. Lawsuits over bond requirements and CEQA delayed the project by years and added billions to its cost. 
Fortunately, those fights have largely been won. In 2017, the California High-Speed Rail Authority was finally able to spend the construction funds approved by voters in 2008. Two years ago, the project gained environmental clearance for every section of rail between San Francisco and L.A.
But there are three big hurdles still in the way that could be fixed by lawmakers and Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra: lack of collaboration from PG&E, the Authority being forced to do work that falls under Caltrans’s responsibility and a block on outside investors helping fund key infrastructure. 
PG&E and other utilities have a lot of infrastructure in the path of high-speed rail. The Authority needs the utility’s cooperation to move equipment, and these companies have no incentive to move quickly. A single utility relocation can take years while the work around it stalls. 
While the Authority has resolved many of these, there are 103 relocations that still need to happen just for the initial 119 miles — and thousands more to go before Los Angeles, the Central Valley and the Bay can be connected by high-speed rail. 
The Legislature must step in and set reasonable deadlines for PG&E and others to complete necessary work.
For speed, reliability and safety reasons, a train moving at 220 mph cannot intersect with roads. The Authority has spent hundreds of millions of dollars rebuilding streets at dozens of locations, creating overpasses and other structures to ensure traffic flows safely. In the process, they often separate existing freight rail from roads as well  — making communities less congested and safer.
The improvements made so far are expected to prevent thousands of crashes in the next three decades. This is critical road infrastructure, and 100% of the cost is coming out of the budget for high-speed rail. 
Getting the High-Speed Rail Authority and Caltrans to collaborate more will speed the project along and save taxpayers billions.
Lastly, many deep-pocketed investors with an eye toward long-term projects — like pension funds — have expressed interest in working on tunnel infrastructure. The Legislature’s strict limits on the project’s activities outside the Central Valley have blocked the kind of planning that would make this work possible, creating unnecessary delay and preventing access to key resources. 
Legislation that makes it easier for investors and the Authority to collaborate on the tunnels needed to connect the Central Valley to the Bay and Southern California would drastically speed up the project.
Californians deserve to be connected to each other, and we deserve transportation that’s fast and sustainable. In the next two decades, California is estimated to grow by 1 million people. Accommodating their needs through freeway widening and airport expansions would be incredibly costly, time consuming and an environmental disaster.
High-speed rail moves at the speed of politics. It’s on lawmakers to do their job and create laws that will help get the project done sooner, better and at a lower cost.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT Mobile ID: Here’s how to get one, what to know
description: CT launched a mobile ID last week. Here’s what residents should know about how to access it and how it works.
text:
The Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles launched a Mobile ID app on Wednesday. 
While it won’t replace a physical identification card in many instances, it will be accepted at travel security checkpoints, including in the state’s largest airports in Hartford and New Haven. State officials said they expect more places will accept the mobile ID in the future as well.
“Our administration has made it a priority to make state government more accessible and convenient to access by putting more services online and available through mobile devices,” Gov. Ned Lamont said in a press release.
Here’s what residents should know to get started.
How do I get a Mobile ID?
To enroll in mobile ID residents must download the free Connecticut Mobile ID app from the Apple App Store or Google Play Store and will need the following:

A smartphone.
A valid, physical ID, with no major wear, damage, or scratch marks on either side. 
A dark, flat surface with good lighting for pictures.

The physical DMV-issued identification cards that are eligible are: Non-Driver identification cards, Driver’s License, Learner’s Permit, Adult Learner’s Permit, Commercial Driver’s License.
To set up, residents must register their phone number in the app. They must take pictures of their physical ID, along with a selfie to verify identity. The app then checks if the information is accurate to the state’s system of record. 
Where can I use my mobile ID?
Residents can use their mobile ID at participating Transportation Security Administration, or TSA, airport security checkpoints nationwide. In Connecticut, these include Bradley International Airport and Tweed New Haven Airport. The mobile ID, like the physical one, must be REAL ID compliant.
It can also be used at participating businesses, such as bars, restaurants, dispensaries, and retailers, and may also be used online. The state has not provided a master list for users.
There are still places where the app will not work. State and local police will not accept Mobile ID at launch, which includes during traffic stops. Mobile ID also will not work at polling stations for voting.
Mobile ID is an optional companion to a physical driver’s license or state ID but is not a replacement so residents must still carry their physical ID with them as always.
How does the mobile ID work? 
To open the app, users must always authenticate using Face ID, a fingerprint, or a PIN to ensure if your phone is lost or stolen, a stranger won’t have easy access to it. The mobile ID app also automatically times out after inactivity. 
To share a mobile ID, the user’s phone generates an encrypted QR code, which is scanned by the verifier’s device. Users choose to accept or deny the verifier’s request after scanning. 
The data users share is encrypted, meaning the verifier will not have any of the user’s information stored on their device. The app developer, IDEMIA, said they do not permanently collect, store or hold onto personal data themselves. 
If I have questions, who do I contact?
For trouble with scanning the physical ID, receiving text verification codes, or accessing the Mobile ID app, visit the get support page on IDEMIA’s website.
If the app is displaying incorrect address information, the physical license data needs updating, or the user encounters revoked status, contact the DMV through the CT DMV Contact Form, or by calling 1-860-263-5700.
If the physical driver’s license or state ID is lost, stolen, or damaged, residents cannot set up a mobile ID until they’ve received another card. For more information, visit the CT DMV Replacement License Portal or visit a local DMV for a replacement.

title: Utah lawmakers face major Medicaid forecast problem that ‘smashed a hole’ in the state budget
description: Utah lawmakers have a big budget problem they’ll have to deal with next year.  A nasty combination of higher healthcare costs, faulty forecasting models, accounting errors and other complex issues have compounded into a major, $175 million Medicaid budget deficit and about $242 million in additional future ongoing costs that Utah lawmakers will need to […]
text:
If lawmakers don’t find revenue to pay for higher Medicaid costs in the 2027 legislative session, they’ll need to consider cuts to services. (Illustration by Alex Cochran for Utah News Dispatch) 


Key points

Utah is facing a major blow to its budget due to a $175 million deficit of Medicaid funds in the past year and higher-than-projected ongoing costs totaling more than $242 million.
The financial hole was caused by a series of compounding issues, including faulty forecasting, accounting errors partly due to a transition to a new online system, and rising healthcare costs all while the federal government imposes complicated new eligibility requirements on Medicaid.
Legislators must find a way to address the shortfall in the coming legislative session, which could mean painful cuts to social services.




Utah lawmakers have a big budget problem they’ll have to deal with next year. 
A nasty combination of higher healthcare costs, faulty forecasting models, accounting errors and other complex issues have compounded into a major, $175 million Medicaid budget deficit and about $242 million in additional future ongoing costs that Utah lawmakers will need to confront during their upcoming session set to start in January. 
The Legislature can dip into rainy day funds specifically set aside for Medicaid, but that will only make up a portion of last year’s $175 million shortfall and close out the current year’s costs. And it’s not enough to fully account for higher ongoing costs expected for not only the upcoming 2027 fiscal year, but also future years. 
So lawmakers are expecting a “brutal” year for social services budget requests. And if they don’t find revenue to pay for the higher costs, they’ll need to consider cuts to services. 
The budget problem also comes as state officials in Utah — and across the country — are grappling with implementing tighter federal Medicaid eligibility requirements included in HR1, the major federal spending legislation passed by Congress last year known as the “one big, beautiful” bill. 
States struggle to impose new Medicaid work rules, even with 6-month reprieve

Already, because of HR1, state officials estimate somewhere between 32,700 to 44,700 Utahns may lose Medicaid coverage. 
But now, on top of that, state leaders must also deal with hundreds of millions of dollars in budget issues that could lead to more cuts. 
Medicaid advocates including Nate Crippes with the Disability Law Center hope lawmakers find ways to address the issue without slashing services. 
“Let’s not jump to cuts,” he said in an interview with Utah News Dispatch. “Given we’re already facing work requirements and people losing coverage because of HR1, I think further cuts at the state level are going to be really harmful and impactful.” 
‘Smashed a hole’ in the state budget
After lawmakers on the Health and Human Services Interim Committee were first briefed on the issue in August, last week the powerful budgetary Executive Appropriations Committee heard more about what went wrong and how legislative fiscal analysts, the Department of Health and Human Services and the Governor’s Office of Planning and Budget are working to fix it. 
During Wednesday’s hearing, House Majority Whip Candice Pierucci, R-Herriman, said that while she understood part of the problem was rising healthcare costs, what was most “concerning” is that it was also due to “egregious” accounting errors. 
“As you know, this has smashed a hole in the budget for our next year, and (we’re) just trying to understand how this actually happened,” she said. 
Pierucci also said as lawmakers have discussed the issue, “a lot of people have felt like that was a pretty big mistake” and they’re wondering how to prevent it from “ever happening again.” 
“I mean, it feels like in the private sector, if something had happened like that, there’d be a change in personnel potentially,” she said. 
Rep. Candice Pierucci, R-Herriman, speaks on the House floor during a special session of the legislature at the Capitol in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Dec. 9, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
Senate Minority Leader Luz Escamilla, D-Salt Lake City, expressed concerns about potential cuts to Medicaid services due to the problem. 
“I look at the people that are (involved) in social services appropriations, and that is going to be a brutal committee to be serving next year,” Escamilla said. 
Pierucci asked Utah Department of Health and Human Services Commissioner Tracy Gruber about the department’s plan to fix the issue. 
“We’re doing a deep dive in all of our Medicaid finance procedures and operations,” Gruber said, “and also ensuring that the team that we have in place have the right skills and competencies to manage arguably one of the more complex government programs that the state’s currently operating.”
What went wrong?
Utah Medicaid Director Julie Ewing briefed lawmakers on four main reasons why Utah’s Medicaid budget projections were so far off. 
The first problem, she said, was the post-COVID-19 Medicaid “unwinding” coupled with rising healthcare costs. 
During the COVID-19 pandemic, people enrolled in Medicaid could not be removed from the program, resulting in high enrollment numbers. When that public emergency ended, the state was then required to unwind that continuous eligibility requirement, which led to about 200,000 people being removed.
But even though enrollment went down during that unwinding, the people who stayed on had more acute — and therefore more expensive — medical needs, she said. Projections didn’t anticipate the needs of that population or their costs. 
“So consequently we have a new Medicaid population that’s actually of a higher acuity, even though it’s smaller,” Ewing said. “And if you couple this with the nationwide healthcare inflation, cost per member per month went up, faster than the projected per-member, per-month costs that were in the forecast.”

Second, Utah’s health department implemented a new system called PRISM which acts as the “backbone of the Medicaid program.” It enrolls providers, pays claims, processes prior authorizations — “it does everything for Medicaid,” she said. 
“The changeover to the new system temporarily disrupted many of those functions, which led to muddled data, and so DHHS was unable to see the emerging cost patterns,” Ewing said. “And additionally, without the data, proxies had to be used and assumptions had to be used. And these assumptions and proxies led to significant differentials between what actually came in.” 
Third, Ewing said the state’s Medicaid program had “outgrown our legacy forecasting tools, which led to inaccuracies.” 
The health department isn’t the only agency that forecasts the state’s Medicaid budget. It’s developed in coordination with the Legislative Fiscal Analyst’s Office and the Governor’s Office of Planning and Budget. All of those agencies were relying on a “very complex spreadsheet,” Ewing said, “which was not built to handle this level of program volatility that we experienced.” 
The model also didn’t have the capability to adjust for “radical federal policy shifts, complex eligibility churn,” and it did not anticipate the higher acuity needs of the existing Medicaid members after the public health emergency unwinding, she said.
All these issues compounded, creating faulty forecasts for the real costs of Utah’s Medicaid program. 
The fourth driver, Ewing said, was “several accounting errors that obscured both the final deficit amount and failed to account for ongoing” costs and accruals from previous years. 
Legislative Fiscal Analyst Jonathan Ball said the bulk of the issue boiled down to “data quality and modeling quality.” He said to fix the problem, fiscal staff have “totally rewritten how we do the estimates.” 
A supporter wears an “I love Medicaid” button during a news conference held at Pioneer Park in Salt Lake City on May 6, 2025. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
The budget hole
In total, Ball said fiscal analysts estimate Utah lawmakers will need to set aside about $346 million in one-time money to address last year’s $175 million deficit, as well as set aside enough money to finish off the current fiscal year and include a “buffer” in case costs overrun the new projections. Additionally, they estimate lawmakers will need to find $242 million in ongoing money to address future costs.
Where will that money come from? Ball noted the Legislature has rainy day funds set aside specifically for Medicaid totaling about $107 million, plus some other funds lawmakers deposited into an account after the state expanded Medicaid. Ball also noted lawmakers already set aside about $30 million in buffer funds for Medicaid that they can use to put toward last year’s deficit.
“So we can cover all of last year’s deficit with these rainy day funds and buffers, (and) we can cover a little bit more than half of the current year costs with those,” he said. “And then what you all will be left with is finding that other half of one-time (needs) and either reducing the future costs or finding revenue to cover that $242 million in future costs.” 
Gruber said it’s “obviously a very challenging deficit in Utah’s Medicaid program.” But she added the deficit is “unfortunately, not unique to Utah.” 
“About two-thirds of the nation’s states have a similar deficit in the Medicaid program,” she said, though she acknowledged Utah is also facing its own unique issues due to budget forecasting issues. 
Utah’s Medicaid program has more than 300,000 enrollees, and the program is a “significant driver of the healthcare economy,” she said. 
“We understand the importance of getting the Medicaid forecasting and accounting under control,” Gruber said. 
What is being done to fix the problem?
Health department leaders have put together a plan to ensure Utah’s Medicaid budget problem doesn’t happen again. 
That includes “modernizing” the Medicaid program’s forecasting, which Gruber said has already been implemented for the next fiscal year after working with the Governor’s Office of Planning and Budget and legislative fiscal analysts to come up with new methods. 
Second, the plan calls for an “independent operational review” of major cost drivers in the Medicaid program to generate several policy recommendations for lawmakers to consider. 
Third, they’re working on rebuilding the Medicaid program’s finance operations, including “ensuring that we have the right staff capacity and the right competency and the right technology to manage a very sizeable budget,” Gruber said. 


Let us know what you think...


 

As part of those efforts, DHHS leaders are requesting an additional $2.1 million and 21 full-time employees “to expand cost-containment competencies and anti-fraud IT tools,” according to their plan. 
“We understand the challenge that this deficit is placing on the department and on the state,” she said. “We’re doing all that we can to prevent it from happening in the future.”
Rep. Ray Ward, R-Bountiful, is also working on a bill aimed at finding efficiencies within Utah’s Medicaid program, including ensuring the program isn’t overpaying on certain services. 
“If there’s a service that we can still give people what they need in some way but not be overpaying for it, that would be much better than just cutting out a needed service,” he told Utah News Dispatch in an interview earlier this month. “That’s what we’re looking for.” 
Ward said he doesn’t expect his bill will be able to take care of the full budget dent, but he’s hoping it will “add up to some significant portion of that.”  
“I’m (working) to find as many things as I can that I think will still let people get the services they need,” he said. 
Potential cuts
Ewing told Utah News Dispatch in an interview last week that DHHS is working with a consultant to do an “end-to-end review” of Utah’s Medicaid program, and they’ve offered up options for lawmakers as potential cuts.” 
Lawmakers have also asked DHHS staff to make some specific recommendations, “and we’re currently working on that,” she said, but details of those recommendations aren’t ready to share yet.
However, Ewing noted that it’s important to remember that Utah’s Medicaid program also heavily relies on federal matching dollars, so if the state cuts funds, that could forgo an even bigger amount in federal funding. 
“So, if you cut a dollar in state (funds), you’re not only cutting that dollar, you’re also leaving anywhere from $1.61 to $9 on the table in federal matching dollars that flows into the state,” she said. 
If lawmakers want to do drastic cuts, like $200 million from the state Medicaid budget, it would actually cut much more. 
“It’s really important that we convey that so that there’s not sticker shock at the end when providers are getting paid less and different things, in significant ways,” she said. 
She also noted that any cuts could not happen quickly because federal law requires time before any cuts are implemented. 
“Of course, we don’t want to see people lose access to care,” Ewing said. “But having said that, too, I think we also owe an obligation to lawmakers and taxpayers to come up with an idea of how we bend this cost curve.” 
Editor’s note: The key points for this article were written by a Utah News Dispatch journalist.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Commentary: New gang task force should remind us of the infamous Metro Gang Strike Force
description: State and local law enforcement officials recently announced a coordinated effort to combat gang violence, particularly among groups of Somali American youth. Let’s hope they learned from the fiasco known as the Metro Gang Strike Force, a multijurisdictional unit that was abruptly shut down in 2009 amid a series of scandals, including beatings, thefts and […[...]
text:
Minneapolis Police Department squad cars parked downtown. (Photo by Chad Davis/Minnesota Reformer)State and local law enforcement officials recently announced a coordinated effort to combat gang violence, particularly among groups of Somali American youth.
Let’s hope they learned from the fiasco known as the Metro Gang Strike Force, a multijurisdictional unit that was abruptly shut down in 2009 amid a series of scandals, including beatings, thefts and mishandled evidence. I’ve not been reassured, however, by recent comments from by law enforcement leaders. 
The new initiative calls for collecting and sharing intelligence through the state’s Crime Gun Intelligence Center, led by the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension, the FBI and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. 
Information will be shared among dozens of agencies, with each case assigned to a participating agency, according to BCA Superintendent Drew Evans.
Unlike the Metro Gang Strike Force, which was a stand alone unit comprising officers from law enforcement agencies across the Twin Cities, the new initiative appears to be coordinated but decentralized, at least for now. Yet the announcement left unanswered questions about oversight and accountability.
The new initiative is aimed, in part, at young Somali Americans whom law enforcement officials have deemed gang members. “Somali American gang and group violence is a problem, and not the Somali community,” Evans said. 
Not a single Somali American law enforcement officer or official spoke at the news conference. Their absence was striking, given that Somali American police officers had gathered with community members around the same time to discuss youth violence, prevention and the dangers of racial stereotyping. Their voices should have been part of the announcement.
The history of the Metro Gang Strike Force shows why those voices matter. One of the unit’s worst offenses was the targeting of people of color, particularly Black and Latino young people, often without probable cause. Strike Force members seized property without justification, often without making arrests. Some officers took the property home for personal use, even driving cars they had seized. If you were a young person of color, you were a suspect.
What safeguards will protect the civil rights of Somali Americans and other communities of color under this latest anti-gang initiative?
Given the Metro Gang Strike Force’s record of misconduct, the question demands an answer.
Yet law enforcement officials offered no explanation for how they would prevent similar abuses.
To avoid repeating that history, every officer and official involved in the new program should get intensive training on civil rights protections and the racist practices that became a hallmark of the Metro Gang Strike Force. Training, however, must be backed by meaningful oversight and accountability.
Evans of the BCA announced that an attorney from the Minnesota attorney general’s office would serve as an adviser to the new coordinated anti-gang effort. But an adviser alone is insufficient. The Metro Gang Strike Force operated without adequate legal oversight, including a designated prosecutor responsible for reviewing the Strike Force’s day-to-day operations. To prevent similar abuses, the new initiative needs an attorney with meaningful oversight authority, actively reviewing cases and protecting the rights of those under scrutiny.
Things got so bad that after the Strike Force was dismantled, the League of Minnesota Cities Insurance Trust paid $3 million to settle claims arising from the misconduct of the officers. A special master appointed by a federal judge oversaw payments to victims. By the time it was over, the Strike Force had undergone a special review by the Minnesota Legislative Auditor and an independent investigation, commissioned by the state’s public safety commissioner. Legislators also scrutinized the unit during hearings after it was dismantled.
Equally troubling in last week’s announcement was the emphasis on coordinating a law enforcement crackdown, with little discussion of prevention. Gangs don’t emerge from nowhere. Young people need culturally responsive mentorship, family support and meaningful alternatives to violence. Rather than relying primarily on enforcement, officials should develop a broader strategy that addresses the conditions contributing to youth violence. A law enforcement approach alone is not going to solve these problems.
Then there’s the elephant in the room: Federal law enforcement. The same authorities from the U.S. Attorney’s Office and FBI who have joined the effort to combat gang violence, including shootings involving Somali American youth, have failed to provide meaningful cooperation with state investigations into the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti. 
Somali American youth would be right to see a double standard: 46 law enforcement agencies mobilizing to investigate violence that officials say was perpetrated by “Somali gangs,” while federal authorities have obstructed investigations into the killings of Good and Pretti, shielding federal agents from prosecution.
Nor can we ignore the political climate surrounding the anti-gang initiative. President Donald Trump has repeatedly targeted Somali Americans with inflammatory and racist rhetoric, supported by other politicians including Minnesota U.S. Rep. Tom Emmer, the House majority whip. Such rhetoric undermines community trust in law enforcement’s motives.
Standing behind Evans at the news conference was a familiar figure: Ramsey County Sheriff Bob Fletcher. Fletcher was voted out of office in 2010 amid criticism of his oversight of the Metro Gang Strike Force. The Ramsey County Sheriff’s Office served as the unit’s fiscal agent, although Fletcher was never implicated in wrongdoing. He maintained that he had no involvement. Yet questions about his oversight persisted as the scandals unfolded. Now, he’s back at a news conference discussing another coordinated anti gang initiative.
This latest anti-gang effort is being overseen by the BCA, a state agency within the Minnesota Department of Public Safety. But oversight cannot stop there. The governor, attorney general and Minnesota Legislature must closely watch this initiative, push for a broader approach that includes violence prevention and be prepared to intervene if necessary. 
The news media must remain vigilant, too. Minnesota needs an effective response to gun violence, but one grounded in accountability, community trust and respect for civil rights. 
Our state cannot afford another Metro Gang Strike Force scandal.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Toxic chemicals, customer service and a toaster oven: Elon Musk’s SpaceX disputes WA state fine
description: Elon Musk’s multitrillion-dollar company is fighting with Washington state over a $6,000 labor fine, fending off allegations of an unsafe workplace. In November 2024, the Washington Department of Labor and Industries opened a chemical exposure investigation at the Redmond headquarters of Starlink, the division of SpaceX that makes satellites.  The state had [...]
text:
SpaceX is disputing safety violations alleged by the Washington Department of Labor and Industries after its Redmond Starlink facility was the subject of a chemical exposure investigation. (Photo by Aspen Ford/InvestigateWest) 
This report was produced in a collaboration between Washington State Standard and InvestigateWest.

Elon Musk’s multitrillion-dollar company is fighting with Washington state over a $6,000 labor fine, fending off allegations of an unsafe workplace.
In November 2024, the Washington Department of Labor and Industries opened a chemical exposure investigation at the Redmond headquarters of Starlink, the division of SpaceX that makes satellites. 
The state had received complaints stating the customer service department was connected to an engineering lab that didn’t have proper ventilations. Workers were experiencing eye irritation and headaches and dust was accumulating on their desks. 
Unlike the lab workers, the customer service department didn’t wear protective equipment, according to a complaint. The two teams shared a breakroom. 
The complaints weren’t news to SpaceX management. Customer service workers had filed dozens of internal complaints alleging chemical exposure symptoms that stemmed from an adjacent production lab. Management did not act until Labor and Industries opened its investigation, InvestigateWest reported.
The agency’s inspection took place in an unassuming office complex in Seattle-area suburbia. Tenants of the building included a pediatric clinic, a pediatric dentistry office, a “holistic” medical clinic, a mortgage lender and the Starlink customer service department, which adjoined two small Starlink labs.
After detecting a high level of lead on a work bench, the state issued SpaceX a violation and the $6,000 fine. 
The department issued a second violation because SpaceX had not evaluated their employees’ potential exposure to chemicals. For that, there was no fine.
The third violation was unexpected. 
In the middle of the investigation, a state compliance officer received multiple photos of a toaster oven. Cooking inside of it was a small piece of metal laying on top of aluminum foil. Workers feared anyone who used the toaster oven might have been exposed to harmful chemicals.
The officer issued a third violation for not keeping eating areas “safe and healthy.” No fine. 
SpaceX is contesting all three violations. After Labor and Industries rejected the initial appeal, SpaceX appealed again. 
The matter is now before a judge with the Board of Industrial Insurance Appeals, a quasi-judicial agency independent of Labor and Industries. Potential outcomes range from affirming the fine and the three violations to vacating them, with numerous variations in between.
On Nov. 18 and 19, during a trial-like hearing conducted over Zoom, SpaceX attorney Skylar Sherwood and Assistant Attorney General Diane Cornell examined witnesses familiar with the investigation. Judge Magda Baker presided.
Haley Laing, former SpaceX environmental health and safety manager who was subpoenaed for testimony, described the layout of the customer service department as a “very open space” with two labs conducting lead-based work adjoining one side. 
A map drawn by Washington Department of Labor and Industries compliance officer Richard Caldwell depicts, on the left, the Redmond office where customer support employees worked and adjacent rooms in the commercial building where technicians used leaded solder and hazardous chemicals that require special equipment to protect workers from fumes.
The labs were former conference rooms. They had windows and the doors were not airtight. SpaceX did not post signage to caution workers that toxic substances were used inside, Laing said.
The state compliance officer, Richard Caldwell, was not permitted to photograph inside the labs; SpaceX had a contract with “DARPA,” the federal government’s Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, he said during testimony. To some employees, the labs were known as ‘Starshield,’ a type of satellite made for national security, InvestigateWest reported.
The labs’ proximity to the customer support department was supposed to be temporary; the compliance officer said he was told they would be moved to another site in 2025. It’s not clear whether that happened. 
One lab was about the size of a storage closet, “probably 80 to 100 square feet,” Laing said. The other, “probably 250 square feet.” Inside, lab technicians cured parts in industrial ovens and assembled hardware onto circuit boards. 
In December 2023, a year before the state investigated and prior to Laing’s employment, SpaceX safety employees reported a lab in the customer service building did not have “proper ventilation” for lead soldering and that lab workers had to “keep the door open.” They recommended ordering a fume extractor.
It didn’t happen immediately. During testimony, Laing said SpaceX installed the fume extractor fix in late 2024 “in direct response to” the state’s inspection, after the compliance officer alerted her to ventilation concerns.
The lab worker and the toaster oven
Melissa Kiss worked as a customer support representative at Starlink from 2023 to 2025. Appearing via Zoom and under questioning from Cornell, the state’s attorney, she recalled the moment she witnessed something odd inside the employee breakroom.  
A small metal part – described as a ‘connector’ in inspection files – was cooking in a toaster oven shared by more than 200 workers in the building, according to InvestigateWest.
“So, when you were in the break room, when you observed this, there was someone from the lab?” Cornell asked.
“Yes,” Kiss said.
“And in speaking with an employee from the lab, what’s your understanding of what’s in the (oven)?” 
“It was my understanding that it was some part from the lab and they were drying the part and that they did this often.” 
A toaster oven at the Starlink customer service department was used to “cook” a metal part, alarming employees who feared chemical exposure. (Hearing exhibit)
Laing, the SpaceX manager, sent an email to all employees in the building months after the breakroom incident. She said the lab technician was drying off water and that the temperature of the toaster oven wasn’t high enough to “off-gas” or “volatilize” parts of the connector, according to an email obtained in a public records request. 
One lab worker told Caldwell, the compliance officer, that his team was under a mandate to “triple production.”
Sherwood, who is a partnering attorney with Fox Rothschild, one of the highest grossing law firms in the country, tried to underline Laing’s argument during the Wednesday hearing. 
“You never saw or handled that part that was pictured in the toaster oven, correct?” Sherwood asked Caldwell. 
“I did not.”
“And you don’t know whether the part had contacted any solvent or chemical?” 
“You can’t put work parts in the employee break room toaster oven at all.”
“That’s not my question, Mr. Caldwell.”
“Uh, because the material,” Caldwell said, stammering. “We don’t know what’s on – the material is made of, the part is made of, I don’t know —”
“Your honor,” Sherwood interrupted. “He’s going way off script.”
Testifying the next day, Laing, the former safety manager, said the lab worker used the toaster oven because the industrial oven in the lab was occupied. 
Washington’s ‘regulatory gap’ for lead
SpaceX is relying on the state’s vague description of how free of lead surfaces should be to argue against the first violation.
Labor and Industries argues that the lead found on a work bench in the small soldering lab was 18 times greater than the allowable limit. 
According to state rules, surfaces should be kept “as free as practicable of accumulations of lead.” There’s no hard number, no scientific unit of measurement. 
Instead, Caldwell said in testimony, the state relies on “industry leading standards” from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.  
“When there’s a small regulatory gap like this, you are supposed to go to industrial standards, industry leading standards,” the compliance officer said. 
He went on to explain that lead is especially harmful for children, but also for anyone. 
“Lead attacks the brain, the central nervous system, the kidneys and the reproductive system,” Caldwell said. 
“Were employees exposed to lead?” asked Cornell, the state attorney.
“Yes they were.”
“And how many employees were exposed to lead based on your inspection?”
“Two directly in the lab, but depending on how that dust migrates, it could be the entire customer service area.”
“Does it matter if the exposure is direct or indirect?”
“No,” Caldwell said. “Because you haven’t controlled the dust, and again, we don’t know where that dust is migrating.”
Attorneys for the two sides have until January 15 to submit briefs. After that, the judge will decide whether SpaceX kept areas as free as practicable of lead, whether SpaceX conducted an employee exposure evaluation and whether SpaceX kept eating areas “safe and healthy.”
If SpaceX ends up paying the fine, the money will go into a Labor and Industries account that supports families whose loved ones died at work. 
Judge Baker said the ruling would take time.
“It’s gonna be a complicated decision to write,” Baker said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: PODCAST: Poor conditions raise questions about future of CT’s oldest prison
description: WSHU’s Ebong Udoma spoke with CT Mirror’s Katy Golvala to discuss her article, “Calls mount to shutter Osborn Correctional, one of CT’s oldest prisons,” as part of the collaborative podcast Long Story Short.
text:
Discolored water, extreme heat, delayed medical care: these are just some of the conditions described by people incarcerated at Connecticut’s oldest prison.
WSHU’s Ebong Udoma spoke with CT Mirror’s Katy Golvala to discuss her article, “Calls mount to shutter Osborn Correctional, one of CT’s oldest prisons,” as part of the collaborative podcast Long Story Short. Read the story here.
WSHU: Hi, Katy. You say you first got into this story after hearing complaints about the water quality at Osborn Correctional Institution. You say people incarcerated there thought the water didn’t smell or look right, and was giving them skin rashes and stomach issues. Could you just tell us a little bit about what was going on then?
KG: Yeah. So I got in touch with a gentleman who was incarcerated at Osborne at the time, Dallas Bailey. He complained to the corrections ombudsman at the time, DeVaughn Ward, who was put in place by the state to oversee DOC. So they go into facilities, visit, and often talk to the people who are incarcerated there about how things are going. Dallas complained to DeVaughn about the water. He said that it was giving him severe gastrointestinal distress. You know, in the morning before you ran it, it would come out with a brown tint like tea, and then, you know, it had a fuzzy quality to it, he said. And this issue was actually litigated. So a group of current and formerly incarcerated people at Osborne had sued the state about the water issues, among other issues, and in there as well, you know, you had many men saying that showering in the water was giving them skin rashes. People like Dallas were saying that drinking the water was giving them digestive issues, and both Dallas and several men in the lawsuit were diagnosed with a stomach infection called H. pylori, which results in gastrointestinal distress. And experts hired for the plaintiffs in that case found that there’s actually no way to test water for H. pylori, and that the water actually does meet all federal and state standards.
WSHU: There still was a settlement of some sort with the men.
KG: Correct, correct. There was a settlement with those men. Each plaintiff got $5,000, so they settled the case in 2024.
WSHU: Okay. Now you talked about the corrections ombudsman, the State Corrections Ombudsman, and this past summer he’s left now. But while he was there, he called the prison a facility beyond its useful life because of a lack of central air conditioning during the summer heat wave. Could you tell us about that and his report?
KG: Yes, he said that because of a lack of AC and other reasons. Osborne is one of three correctional facilities in Connecticut without facility-wide AC, but the state has a plan in place for the other two. They have projects underway to bring facility-wide AC to those places, but Osborne is so old that bringing facility-wide AC to that prison would have cost the state around $ 120 million. So instead, what they’re doing is they have brought in portable air conditioning units that can go into the windows of the prison and bring in cool air, but when Ombuds Ward visited Osborne in the middle of a heat wave, he was still clocking temperatures of 85 degrees, 89 degrees. So, you know, he basically said, are we really sure that this temporary solution is working? For that reason, and others, he said he thinks it is a facility beyond its useful life, and I think that is when the story started clicking for me.
WSHU: Now this is a prison that’s been around since 1963.
KG: That’s right.
WSHU: And it was the maximum security prison for the state before it was converted to a medium security facility.
KG: That’s right.
WSHU: But there’s also an issue with the fact that they have prison production going on at Osborne. Could you just tell us a little bit about that and how that ties into the coalition that has been formed to try and close this prison?
KG: So the state of Connecticut has something called the Correction Enterprises of Connecticut. These are factories in certain prisons. They make mattresses used in the prisons. They’re making uniforms that the people incarcerated wear. They’re making and refurbishing furniture that government agencies can buy; they’re making license plates, and they do not get paid a minimum wage, right? So the most recent report I could find, from 2018, was that they’re paid anywhere from 90 cents to $1.80 an hour.WSHU: You also spoke with Mike Lawlor, criminal justice expert, and what was his take on what is going on? And he’s been involved in a lot of the restructuring of the prison population in Connecticut and criminal justice in general. What was his take?
KG: Yeah, that’s right. And I should say the organizers are calling for a phased-in closure. They also realize that this can’t be an immediate closure. So, but what Mike Lawlor said is, you know, should Osborne close based on the facility? Yes. Is it possible? Maybe. He does expect some proposals that have come up before to come up again this session that could just help reduce the correctional population, such that there might be a place to put the people who are currently incarcerated at Osborne. So, one bill he expects to come up is parole eligibility for people who were sentenced when they were very young and are now much older, and another is, you know, ways to reduce the pre-trial population through bail reform. Those are ways in which, you know, you don’t necessarily need to build a new prison or reopen an old prison. Perhaps you can just reduce the population and use the facilities that are currently in service.
WSHU: But whichever way we look at it, this is going to be an issue that the legislature is going to have to try and start to grapple with in the next legislative session.
KG: That is what organizers say they will be demanding, and that type of organizing effort takes a lot of persistence; it remains to be seen whether this coalition can and will do that work.
WSHU: Well, we’ll see how it unfolds.
KG: That’s right.
WSHU: Thank you so much, Katy.
KG: Thank you.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippians can see how often health insurers deny requests for prior authorization
description: Sherri Reeves reviews a medical bill at her home in Lexington on Friday, July 17, 2026. Reeves dropped her health insurance coverage after Congress declined to renew the enhanced premium tax credits, resulting in a dramatic increase in her premiums.
text:
Mississippians shopping for health insurance plans can compare monthly premiums, deductibles, provider networks and covered benefits. But another number can shape whether they can actually get the care their doctor prescribes: the rate at which insurers deny requests for prior authorization.
Prior authorization is a process used by insurance companies to review certain medical procedures, prescriptions or other services before agreeing to cover them. As a result of the 2024 state law that made changes to prior authorization, the Mississippi Insurance Department published a dataset this year showing insurer-level rates of prior authorization requests, denials and appeals.
House Public Health Committee Chairman Sam Creekmore, a Republican from New Albany, said that the data is worth considering when shopping for plans. 
“You really don’t think about it ‘til you need it,” he said. Then, when a health event occurs, Creekmore said people may find themselves thinking, “Well, I got the wrong insurance, or I’ve got insurance that denies everybody.”
The data, which contains prior authorization requests from 2025, shows a wide range in denial rates across 26 insurers. The highest volume of requests went to ProtectRx, a pharmacy-benefit and utilization-review company that denied 30% of the nearly 290,000 requests it received from Mississippi health providers last year. 
Health insurance company Centene, which operates Affordable Care Act marketplace plans and Medicaid plans, had the second-highest volume of requests. The company’s Ambetter marketplace insurance denied a quarter of the over 166,000 requests it received. Among the state’s largest insurers, Molina Healthcare of Mississippi had the lowest denial rate of 6% and OptumRx had the highest rate, denying nearly half of all requests. 
While the total number of prior authorizations remained about the same between 2024 and 2025, the number of denials doubled to over 200,000, Bob Williams, a health insurance regulator at the Mississippi Insurance Department said at a Senate hearing in October. He added that appeals for denied requests jumped from 9,000 in a year to over 50,000, possibly because providers realized after the law was enacted that they needed to submit more appeals.
Dr. Lucius Lampton, president of the Mississippi State Medical Association and a family physician in Magnolia, said navigating prior authorization poses a significant burden on both medical providers and patients. 
“Prior authorization, if it exists at all, should be rare and have extraordinary justification for necessity,” he said, adding that no insurance company in Mississippi should require 166,000 prior authorizations in a year. He sees the process as a hurdle insurance companies have set to prevent patients from accessing services, where if there are enough hurdles, medical providers won’t have time to fill out all the paperwork.  
“I don’t understand ethically how that’s acceptable to our system,” Lampton said.
Mississippi figures cannot be directly compared to national averages due to differences in reporting guidelines, but high denial rates are not unique to the state. KFF, a health policy research organization, found that the largest marketplace insurers denied between 3% and 25% of prior authorization requests nationally in 2025.


The prior authorization process
The data also shows that while appeals for denied prior authorization requests can be uncommon, nearly half of appeals were successful. The high rate of reversed denials also calls into question why the prior authorizations were necessary in the first place, Lampton said. At the same time, doctors and nurses may not have enough time to handle those appeals, especially if they have limited staff. 
At Lampton’s practice, Timothe Monceret handles prior authorization requests. She said gathering all the necessary patient documentation can take her 30 minutes on the fast end. Other times, she’s on the phone for an hour with the insurance company before she can move forward with a request. 
Monceret said she often submits requests for diabetes medicines, and that insurers can be “nitpicky” about how the forms are filled out. One request for Wegovy was denied because the provider didn’t specify a plan to gradually increase dosage, even though Wegovy’s FDA-approved dosing schedule already requires gradual dose increases. When Monceret added in the word “titration,” which means a gradual change in the dose of a drug, the request was approved. 
Among the hundreds of thousands of prior authorizations Mississippi healthcare providers submitted to ProtectRx, one the largest categories of denied prescriptions were GLP-1 based drugs used to treat diabetes and obesity, including Wegovy and Ozempic. The company also frequently denied drugs used to treat autoimmune diseases and a glucose monitor used to manage diabetes. 


The high number of required prior authorizations signals that insurance companies are controlling what drugs patients have access to, said Chad Netterville, executive director of the Mississippi Rural Hospital Alliance. 
“I think what’s clear is that they are trying to control the cost for these employers around prescriptions,” he said. 
Getting to the data
Sen. Walter Michel, a Republican from Ridgeland, sponsored the 2024 legislation that tightened timelines for insurers to respond to prior authorization submissions and established reporting requirements. The law also states that after receiving all the necessary information, insurers must respond to non-urgent prior authorization requests within seven calendar days, and to urgent requests within 48 hours.


Michel said he’s proud of the law. The National Council of Insurance Legislators adopted a version of it of as a model for how other states could regulate prior authorization. The state changes come as insurance companies are taking voluntary steps to reduce the burden of prior authorization. 
UnitedHealthcare eliminated about 30% of its prior authorization requirements from Oct. 1, and operates a national “Gold Card” program that exempts some providers from certain prior authorizations. Providers gain gold card status based on a track record of approved prior authorization requests. Centene, which provides coverage to over 25 million Americans, announced a similar national program in November for “invited” providers, including through its Mississippi Magnolia Health plan. 
“These latest actions … are designed to reduce unnecessary paperwork, make information easier to understand and help patients and care providers spend more time focused on care,” a spokesperson from UnitedHealthcare said in a written statement. 
Michel said that after a few years of reporting, it will be easier for the insurance department and legislators to identify outliers with high denial rates. Currently, the law does not set target denial rates or caps on allowable denial rates. Instead, said Mississippi Insurance Commissioner Mike Chaney, “We’ve set our focus on transparency, timelines and reporting.” 
The Mississippi law came amid increased reporting of prior authorization statistics nationally. The state is among several that require more specific numbers than CMS’s 2024 Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule. However, the numbers in the Mississippi report are not comparable to national averages, said Michelle Long, a senior policy manager at KFF. That’s because Mississippi’s data combines individual and some group, or employer-sponsored, health plans. In contrast, federal data for private insurance covers ACA Marketplace plans but not employer-sponsored coverage. 
Creekmore said he is open to the idea of breaking out individual and group plans in future reports. Breaking out the market types could show if denial rates were higher in one or the other and driving changes in statewide numbers. He also said he wants more detail on types of denied drugs, particularly GLP-1 medications. Having more specific reporting, he said, could help lawmakers decide whether certain policies deserve more scrutiny.
“I think it’d be helpful to have it more detailed,” he said. 
This story was produced with support from the Sarah Yelena Haselhorst Fund for Health Journalism.
