name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri’s budget crisis didn’t come out of nowhere
description: Nearly a decade ago, then-Auditor Nicole Galloway issued a stark warning. Her February 2018 budget stress test found Missouri increasingly dependent on individual income taxes and ill-equipped to weather an economic downturn. “If there are economic bumps in the road ahead,” she said, “our state is not prepared.” The report got a round of news […]
text:
Missouri Gov. Mike Parson during his State of the State address on Jan. 19, 2022 (Tim Bommel/Missouri House Communications).Nearly a decade ago, then-Auditor Nicole Galloway issued a stark warning.
Her February 2018 budget stress test found Missouri increasingly dependent on individual income taxes and ill-equipped to weather an economic downturn.
“If there are economic bumps in the road ahead,” she said, “our state is not prepared.”
The report got a round of news stories. Then everyone moved on. Five months later, Gov. Mike Parson signed legislation touted as the largest single-year income tax cut in Missouri history.
Flash forward to last week, when a task force studying Missouri’s public school funding formula was told the legislature will likely need to cut $1.5 billion to $3.5 billion from what state agencies want to spend next year.
Missouri faces nearly $3 billion gap between spending requests and tax revenue

So what happened between the warnings and public discussion of a multibillion-dollar budget hole?
Federal pandemic assistance and unexpectedly strong tax collections helped Missouri build a massive surplus. By June 2023, the state’s general revenue fund held approximately $5.8 billion.
That gave lawmakers room to invest, increase spending and cut taxes.
So they did all three.
In 2022, Parson signed another income tax cut he called the largest in state history, estimated to reduce annual revenue by $764 million. A year later, lawmakers eliminated state income taxes on Social Security and public pension payments, at an estimated cost of $309 million a year.
Then, in 2025, Gov. Mike Kehoe signed legislation eliminating the state income tax on capital gains — profits from selling investments.
Originally estimated to cost $111 million annually, the exemption proved considerably more expensive. Its impact on fiscal 2026 revenue was later estimated at more than $500 million.
Meanwhile, spending grew.
Galloway’s successor, State Auditor Scott Fitzpatrick, documented just how quickly. From fiscal 2020 to 2025, general revenue grew 45.8%, while spending increased 53.4%. Inflation over that period was 24.5%.
Not all that spending growth was discretionary. Medicaid costs increased, pandemic assistance expired and maintaining existing programs became more expensive.
Nor is every appropriated dollar spent. Agencies leave money unused because of vacancies and project delays.
Still, Missouri was authorizing more spending than it collected annually and relying on the surplus to cover the difference. Now the money that made those budgets possible is nearly gone.
In December 2025, Fitzpatrick warned that continued deficit spending could exhaust the general revenue fund by fiscal year 2028. He repeated the warning in June, after lawmakers approved another budget exceeding projected revenue.
Missouri auditor warns deep budget cuts loom as surplus nears end

The Kehoe administration’s own budget instructions acknowledged that ongoing spending is projected to exceed recurring revenue by more than $1 billion.
As The Independent’s Rudi Keller reported last week, agencies are requesting approximately $16.5 billion in general revenue next fiscal year — nearly $3 billion more than the state expects to collect in the current fiscal year.
The governor’s budget office has projected that the once-enormous general revenue balance will shrink to $265 million by June 2027.
And much of the pressure comes from costs lawmakers can’t easily avoid.
Agency requests include more than $640 million in additional Medicaid expenses and $182 million for schools merely to maintain current funding. Hundreds of millions more in anticipated Medicaid and school costs aren’t included.
Nearly two-thirds of general revenue operating spending goes to education, social services and mental health. Shield those departments, and finding $2 billion elsewhere becomes extraordinarily difficult.
Further tax reductions remain on the agenda.
Kehoe — who vetoed or froze nearly $500 million in the budget this year, arguing “we have a spending problem” — recently identified income and property tax policy among his economic development priorities, emphasizing helping Missourians keep more of their money.
Meanwhile, incoming House Budget Chairman Bill Owen appears focused on the other side of the ledger.
The Springfield Republican says his party has put its energy into cutting taxes without adequately scrutinizing spending. He plans to examine agency budgets line by line.
That might uncover savings. But much of the budget, like Medicaid, is driven by enrollment and federal rules lawmakers don’t control.
Lawmakers could also redirect money set aside for highways and Capitol renovations. That might provide temporary relief, but it wouldn’t fix the recurring imbalance.
Which brings us back to Galloway. She worried about what a recession would do. Missouri got here without one.
Years of tax cuts, increased spending and the depletion of a historic surplus have reshaped its finances.
The state’s new revenue forecast arrives next month. Lawmakers return in January. The warnings have been on file for years.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Commentary: Ayoub: Trusting science, remembering DOGE, crying uncle
description: Three thoughts … Among endless political ads, one debate and a months-long campaign for Nebraska’s U.S. Senate seat, I recall hearing no one ask Sen. Pete Ricketts to explain his vote confirming Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as Health and Human Services secretary or ask challenger Dan Osborn what his vote would have been. The secretary’s […]
text:
A nurse vaccinates a child at the Latino Community Development Agency on July 9, 2026, in Oklahoma City. As vaccination rates decline nationwide, measles cases have surpassed 2025 to the highest since the disease was declared eliminated in the U.S. in 2000. (Photo by Courtney Bell/Oklahoma Voice)Three thoughts …
Among endless political ads, one debate and a months-long campaign for Nebraska’s U.S. Senate seat, I recall hearing no one ask Sen. Pete Ricketts to explain his vote confirming Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as Health and Human Services secretary or ask challenger Dan Osborn what his vote would have been.
The secretary’s confirmation came to mind last week when the country lost its measles elimination status, joining neighbors Mexico and Canada, the U.K. and such public health stalwarts as Armenia, Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan in giving the virus endemic standing in the U.S. The elimination status, which we had for over a quarter of a century, is defined as a country having no persistent transmission of the virus for more than 12 months. 
If you’re keeping score at home, Kennedy was given the keys to the office that safeguards the nation’s health on a 52-48 vote. 
Although she was not on the ballot this go-round, we could ask the same question of Nebraska’s other senator, Deb Fischer, also a “yea” on the Kennedy nomination.
Measles is making a comeback in the U.S. According to the CDC, since 2024 nearly 8,000 new cases have been reported, with 10 resulting in death. The American Hospital Association said nearly all those with the virus were either unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination histories.
Despite his public professing of support for the measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine, Kennedy has long been associated with anti-vaccination movements and, more critically, has done little as the nation’s top healthcare advocate to put teeth into vaccination campaigns. He also supported a presidential executive order in August that recommended splitting the vaccine into three separate shots, one per disease. No medical evidence exists that dividing the regimen increases efficacy, nor were any single doses actually available when the order came down, two arguments made by the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American Academy of Family Physicians and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists.
In fairness to Ricketts and Fischer, they were joined by four doctors (“Politican, heal thyself!”) in the Senate voting for Kennedy. One of them, Sen. Bill Cassidy, is now openly critical of the HHS secretary. In the larger view, Kennedy — whose work on the nation eating better is on the mark — represents this administration’s ongoing lack of respect for science, a view that trickles down to individuals making medical decisions … such as whether to vaccinate their children. 
Despite hundreds of millions of doses and continued effectiveness rates at about 97%, the measles vaccine, like many others, comes with a paradox. Getting children inoculated against the virus is a personal, parental decision, which, ironically, affects anyone with whom their child comes in contact, potentially passing measles along in classrooms, grocery stories and churches. Touting healthy diets is to be applauded, but stop playing footsie with the world’s most contagious disease, one that kills children. Or step aside and let someone who actually believes in science take the reins.
* * *
As their counterparts in larger cities did, airports in Omaha, Lincoln and outstate Nebraska took a couple of days to return to regular service after a three-hour ground stop was ordered on Nov. 13, canceling over 13,000 flights nationwide and delaying another nearly 28,000. The ground stop was one of a number of “outages” roiling the country over a couple of days.
True to form, the current stewards of our nation’s transportation infrastructure blamed the ground stop on Joe Biden, who hasn’t been in office for over 670 days. If you’re in the for-the-love-of-Mike-give-it-a-rest camp, I recommend continued breathing, as a hallmark of this administration is to pin its stumbles on previous White House occupants. 
Meanwhile, drawing a straight line from the recent halt of air travel and DOGE is speculative at best. You remember DOGE: All chain saw, no substantial savings. If, however, this administration and Congress decide they will indeed commit to upgrading our seemingly capricious aviation system, thanks to DOGE the FAA will be down nearly 1,700 workers, part of DOGE’s brief but brutal paring.   
* * *
Whether you have recently purchased Anthropic stock or don’t know a wysiwyg from a dongle, you can’t deny the impact AI has on our lives. We should also recognize the outsized role tech giant Nvidia’s superchips and its CEO Jensen Huang have had in the “race” to build out AI. 
That said, I’m full up on the Huang saga. Uncle! I’ve heard, read and seen enough. Not that the tech-bro chip genius doesn’t deserve props for making such a desirable doohickey. He does. But please, make it a “he did.”
Curiously though, neither Huang, the president nor even a chatbot has told us just how we will know if we’ve won the AI race.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Who is running for Nebraska Legislature leadership in 2027? Here’s the list so far.
description: LINCOLN — More than half of the Nebraska Legislature’s leadership spots will be vacant come the start of 2027 legislative session, and 25 senators have so far said they’ll run for the 19 roles. The Cornhusker State’s 49 lawmakers will vote by secret ballot on the first day of the 110th Legislature, Jan. 6, for the […]
text:
The returning state senators and senators-elect who will serve in the 110th Nebraska Legislature in the 2027-28 biennium. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns from 2024 and 2026 | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — More than half of the Nebraska Legislature’s leadership spots will be vacant come the start of 2027 legislative session, and 25 senators have so far said they’ll run for the 19 roles.
The Cornhusker State’s 49 lawmakers will vote by secret ballot on the first day of the 110th Legislature, Jan. 6, for the next speaker of the Legislature and chairs of nearly 20 committees. The speaker sets the daily agenda and decides time limits for bills during floor debate.
By the time the session begins, 29 of the 49 lawmakers will have served two years or less.
The Nebraska Examiner asked all 34 returning state lawmakers, as well as one senator returning after a four-year absence, whether they are planning to run for leadership in 2027. By publication, the Examiner had confirmed plans for all but two senators.
Fourteen first-time lawmakers can also run for leadership positions, but this is rarer. 
The last time that occurred was in 2017, when freshman state Sens. Joni Albrecht of Thurston and Justin Wayne of Omaha defeated returning chairs to lead the Business and Labor and Urban Affairs committees, respectively.
What does a committee chair do?
Committee chairs decide when to schedule bills for hearings, how to run hearings and whether the committee will vote on possibly advancing bills (if at all). Leaders in the past have been more spontaneous in scheduling closed-door sessions to vote out bills or have been more antagonistic in doing so if they themselves do not like the bill.
In Nebraska, all bills receive a public hearing, but typically just 100 or so will see the light of day each year due to limited time. Many are combined before passage.
The timing of hearings or executive session votes can also determine a bill’s chances of becoming law, given the 90-day or 60-day session limit.


Related articles
Ibach, Kauth detail runs for 2027-28 speaker of the Nebraska Legislature
‘Process over policy’: Arch reflects on qualities of a good speaker of Nebraska Legislature
Lawmakers detail what they want in next speaker of Nebraska Legislature
Government Committee chair won’t seek same role in 2027-28 Nebraska Legislature


Some chairs serve on other committees by virtue of their role, too, such as the chairs of the Executive Board, Appropriations, Health and Human Services and Judiciary committees on the new Legislative Oversight Committee. The group directs a reorganized oversight system to monitor the Nebraska departments of Correctional Services and Health and Human Services, separate from individual committee work.
Gov. Jim Pillen and Lt. Gov. Joe Kelly will again lead the executive branch, and Kelly will preside over the Legislature for the next four years. The speaker is in the line of succession, followed by an ordered list of committee chairs.
12 vacant positions
Due to term limits, or because a senator did not seek reelection or win reelection, the following chairships will automatically be open positions in the 2027-28 biennium:

Speaker of the Legislature.
Committee on Committees (which determines committee assignments).
Executive Board (which directs the day-to-day activity of the legislative branch).
Appropriations Committee.
Education Committee.
Natural Resources Committee.
Revenue Committee.
Transportation and Telecommunications Committee.

The order of positions elected is speaker, Committee on Committees and Exec Board before committee chairs are selected alphabetically. The Rules Committee is chosen last, also out of order.
State Sens. Brad von Gillern of Elkhorn, Jen Day of Gretna and Ben Hansen of Blair, from left, tally votes on the first day of the 2023 Nebraska legislative session on Jan. 5, 2023, in Lincoln, Nebraska, for the contested Education Committee chair position. Day left the Legislature in 2025 while Hansen and von Gillern will leave at the start of 2027. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska News Service)
This order means three more committees will come open because current chairs are seeking other roles, for the Agriculture; Banking, Commerce and Insurance; and Nebraska Retirement Systems committees.
State Sen. Rita Sanders of Bellevue, chair of the Government, Military and Veterans Affairs Committee, plans to leave her committee altogether in pursuit of a seat on the Natural Resources Committee, though not the chairship. 
Sanders said some lawmakers have encouraged her to consider the Committee on Committees chair. That committee divvies out committee membership for all but the speaker in the new year.
State Sens. Rick Holdcroft of Bellevue, Brian Hardin of Gering, Carolyn Bosn of Lincoln and Terrell McKinney of Omaha will again seek to chair the same committees they do now: General Affairs (Holdcroft), Health and Human Services (Hardin), Judiciary (Bosn) and Urban Affairs (McKinney). 
Just one of them has a challenger so far. State Sen. Stan Clouse of Kearney, the Urban Affairs vice chair, has said he’ll seek the top role.


Line of succession in Nebraska
Under the Nebraska Constitution, the speaker of the Legislature would cover for the governor if Pillen and Kelly are unable. If all three are incapable of performing the duties, the power flows to the following chairs until filled:

Executive Board
Committee on Committees
Judiciary
Government, Military and Veterans Affairs
Appropriations
Revenue
Education
Banking, Commerce and Insurance
Natural Resources
Agriculture
Health and Human Services
General Affairs
Urban Affairs
Business and Labor
Transportation and Telecommunications

Sources: Nebraska Constitution Article IV, Section 16; Nebraska Revised Statutes 84-120


‘We’ll have to see’
So far, just one seat has three contenders: the Appropriations Committee, between state Sens. Rob Dover of Norfolk, Loren Lippincott of Central City and Paul Strommen of Sidney.
State Sen. Jason Prokop of Lincoln said he’s been encouraged to consider the budget-writing chairship, too, but hasn’t decided. State Sen. Ashlei Spivey of Omaha, the fifth and final returning Appropriations member, didn’t respond to multiple requests for comment on her plans.
Finally, in three other leadership posts, current lawmakers are seeking other roles, but because of the order in which those positions are decided, they could still run for their current positions.
State Sen. Teresa Ibach of Sumner, current Exec Board vice chair, and state Sen. Kathleen Kauth of Omaha, current chair of the Business and Labor Committee, are running for speaker of the Legislature.
A majority of returning lawmakers told the Examiner they’re looking for someone who can bring people together and reach across the aisle for their next speaker.
State Sens. Eliot Bostar of Lincoln and Tanya Storer of Whitman have said they’ll seek the vice chair seat on the Exec Board held by Ibach. It’s the only vice chair position selected by the Legislature, and the board also serves as the Legislature’s human resources division. All other vice chairs are selected within committee membership.
If Kauth doesn’t become speaker, she has said she would try to return to the Business and Labor chair. State Sen. Dan Quick of Grand Island has said he’ll run for that spot.
Lippincott is currently Rules Committee chair but could run for that position again if he doesn’t get the Appropriations position. No one else has yet said they’ll run for Rules chair.
“We’ll have to see,” Lippincott said of his plans if he does not get Appropriations.
‘We need serious leaders’
Multiple lawmakers, all Democrats, have said they have been approached about different leadership roles but have not decided.
State Sen. John Fredrickson of Omaha said he’s keeping his “options open.”
“We have serious issues to tackle next session, and we need serious leaders,” Fredrickson said in a text.
Lawmakers detail what they want in next speaker of Nebraska Legislature

State Sen. Danielle Conrad of Lincoln, the Legislature’s longest-tenured member, now heading into her 13th year, said she’s looking at a few spots but hasn’t decided either.
State Sen. Margo Juarez of Omaha, a former school board member for Omaha Public Schools who serves on the Education Committee, said she’s thought about pursuing leadership and is still thinking about it. She also serves on the Natural Resources Committee but isn’t sure what committees she’ll land on. 
“A lot’s still up in the air,” Juarez said.
State Sen. John Cavanaugh of Omaha did not respond to multiple requests for comments on his plans in his final two years. He ran for the Business and Labor Committee chair in 2025 and currently serves as vice chair of the General Affairs Committee under Holdcroft.
‘Capitol cleaner’?
Former state Sen. Patty Pansing Brooks of Lincoln is the one senator-elect with previous service. She served six years as vice chair of the Judiciary Committee in her first eight years of service, between 2015 and 2023, but she said she’s heard she would be “lucky if she gets Capitol cleaner,” or any sway in her committee positions.
State lawmakers term-limited or not seeking reelection gather on the final day of Nebraska’s 2026 legislative session on April 17, 2026, in Lincoln, Nebraska. They are, from left, state Sens. Ben Hansen, Myron Dorn, Christy Armendariz, Tom Brandt, Wendy DeBoer, Megan Hunt, John Arch, Rob Clements, Jane Raybould, Dave Murman, Machaela Cavanaugh, Mike Moser and Fred Meyer. Two more lawmakers, state Sens. Brad von Gillern and Merv Riepe, were not reelected in the November 2026 election. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examine)
Pansing Brooks, like Conrad, returned after being term-limited. They’re part of a small group of just seven lawmakers to return after being term-limited. Lawmakers were first forced out in the 2006 and 2008 elections. Only one state senator has been term-limited twice: Ernie Chambers of Omaha. Conrad was just reelected and could follow Chambers’ lead after 2030.
One more chair position will be decided at the start of 2027: the Enrollment and Review Committee. This largely honorific role has traditionally gone to the youngest freshman. That chairperson reports bills between stages of debate after they’ve gone through grammar and technical review.
The role is expected to transfer from state Sen. Dunixi Guereca of Omaha, who is now 38, to state Sen.-elect Dawson Brunswick of Columbus, who is 28. The oldest freshman is 70.
The legislative session begins Jan. 6.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: ‘Sort of a nothing burger’: Oklahoma City mayor pans new law targeting cities that have homeless
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – The mayor of Oklahoma’s largest city called moot a new law aimed at penalizing certain cities for failing to enforce ordinances and laws targeting homelessness in their communities. Oklahoma City Mayor David Holt said House Bill 3985, dubbed the “Oklahoma Safe Neighborhoods Act of 2026,” will do little to address the root […]
text:
Crews use a front loader to clean up a former homeless camp on state property in Tulsa. (Screenshot of Operation SAFE video footage)OKLAHOMA CITY – The mayor of Oklahoma’s largest city called moot a new law aimed at penalizing certain cities for failing to enforce ordinances and laws targeting homelessness in their communities.
Oklahoma City Mayor David Holt said House Bill 3985, dubbed the “Oklahoma Safe Neighborhoods Act of 2026,” will do little to address the root cause of homelessness in the state’s largest cities that it targets and will likely be unenforceable. 
The law, which took effect Nov. 1, would let property owners seek monetary damages from cities with populations greater than 130,000 if those municipalities adopt a policy and follow a pattern of not enforcing ordinances or laws prohibiting public camping, obstructing public thoroughfares, loitering and panhandling, among other infractions.
Oklahoma City and Tulsa are among the cities with a population larger than 130,000. 
Oklahoma City Mayor David Holt speaks at a remembrance ceremony on April 19, 2025 on the 30th anniversary of the Murrah Building bombing in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
“We recognized it as just being a political bill, just a bill that has no actual effect, but makes somebody feel good,” said Oklahoma City Mayor David Holt, who also serves as dean of the Oklahoma City University School of Law. Holt is also a former state Republican senator.
In order to utilize the new law, a property owner would have to incur expenses to mitigate the damages caused by the failure to enforce or have seen a reduction in property value.
Holt said the way the law is written, there must be a papertrail that the police chief or city issued a directive to not follow the law or ordinance. The requirement that a city adopt a policy not to enforce laws and ordinances makes it “sort of a nothing burger,” Holt said.
“There’s simply no way in the world that the city of Oklahoma City is ever going to adopt a policy that says we are not going to enforce our laws,” Holt said.
Oklahoma City does enforce those laws and ordinances and still has homelessness, which is a complicated issue to resolve, he said.
“There’s 1,000 people right now speeding in Oklahoma City, right?” he said. “We’re doing the best to enforce the speeding laws, but nonetheless, people will get around it.”
House Appropriations and Budget Committee Chairman Trey Caldwell, R-Faxon, is the author.
From left, Rep. Trey Caldwell, R-Faxon, and Sen. Grant Green, R-Wellston, listen to Gov. Kevin Stitt’s State of the State Address on Feb. 5, 2024, in the House chamber of the Oklahoma State Capitol. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)
Caldwell said he strongly disagreed with Holt’s characterization of the law.
For companies considering where to locate, employee safety is a major consideration, he said.
“We have heard concerns from major businesses that have left Oklahoma City or reconsidered their presence here because they do not believe the city is adequately addressing these concerns,” Caldwell said. “Those concerns have real economic consequences for our community.”
In a statement, the City of Tulsa said it complies with all applicable state laws and ordinances and will continue to do so.
Meghan Mueller is president and CEO of the Homeless Alliance, which serves people experiencing homelessness in Oklahoma City.
Mueller said she has no problem with government accountability, but some methods don’t work, such as broad encampment sweeps.
“If we’re moving someone from one street corner to the next, it’s still a person on the street corner,” she said. “That’s not actually solving a problem.”
Senators spent about an hour discussing the measure before passing it by a vote of 30-16. The House passed it by a vote of 77-16.
Sen. Mary Boren, D-Norman, said lawmakers are targeting local governments instead of solving problems.
The Goldwater Institute, a conservative policy group based in Phoenix, said Oklahoma’s new law is based on model policy it developed.

title: Federal agents arrested the wrong Black woman in pursuit of Nekima Levy Armstrong for church protest
description: Before federal agents filmed themselves arresting Nekima Levy Armstrong for leading a protest in a church last winter — and the White House doctored the footage to make her appear to be crying — agents tackled and detained the wrong Black woman. Satara Strong-Allen, who is about 6 inches shorter and 15 years younger than […]
text:
Lawyer and activist Nekima Levy Armstrong, left, poses for a portrait with Satara Strong-Allen, right Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026 at the Aloft Minneapolis hotel. Strong-Allen was violently arrested at the hotel by federal agents who mistook her for Levy Armstrong in January. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Before federal agents filmed themselves arresting Nekima Levy Armstrong for leading a protest in a church last winter — and the White House doctored the footage to make her appear to be crying — agents tackled and detained the wrong Black woman.
Satara Strong-Allen, who is about 6 inches shorter and 15 years younger than Levy Armstrong, suffered a concussion at the hands of federal immigration agents and was detained for hours even after she explained she was not the widely known civil rights activist.
The error, which has not previously been reported in detail, underscores the fervor with which the Trump administration sought a public and forceful response to the activists involved in the anti-ICE demonstration — and the journalists who observed it — that disrupted Sunday service at a St. Paul church in January.
“They were targeting me, so they wanted to attack and assault me,” Levy Armstrong said in an interview.
Strong-Allen’s account of mistaken identity was hardly an aberration during the Trump administration’s Operation Metro Surge, which brought thousands of federal immigration agents to Minnesota.
Federal agents arrested ChongLy Scott Thao, a 56-year-old Hmong man and U.S. citizen, saying he matched the description of two wanted Asian men, one of whom had been in prison since 2024. Agents took him from his home in St. Paul in 10-degree weather while he was wearing only shorts and Crocs.
ICE agent Christian Castro shot a Venezuelan man in the leg in north Minneapolis in January after initiating a car pursuit of a driver he mistook for another Latino man. The man the agent shot, Julio Sosa-Celis, was neither the man driving nor the target for arrest.
And U.S. citizen Rogelio Jimenez said when federal agents arrested him in Brooklyn Park in January, they told him they were looking for someone else with the same name.
The Jan. 18 protest at Cities Church — where one of the pastors, David Easterwood, also works as a local ICE official — drew swift condemnation from the Trump administration as an assault on religious liberty.
Hours after the demonstration, the White House Press Office posted on social media that the Justice Department had opened an investigation, writing, “President Trump will not tolerate the intimidation and harassment of Christians in their sacred places of worship.”
Strong-Allen, who also helped organize the protest, would later be indicted as one of the 39 defendants in the Cities Church case, but she wasn’t wanted by federal authorities at the time she was tackled and detained by agents pursuing Levy Armstrong.
She was arrested around 2 a.m. on Jan. 22 in a downtown Minneapolis hotel, where she was staying with her wife, Chauntyll Allen, and Levy Armstrong out of concern for their safety.
Allen, a St. Paul School Board member, and Levy Armstrong were receiving threats and wanted to be able to turn themselves in to avoid a raid on their homes.
Strong-Allen had just stepped out of Levy Armstrong’s room to go to her own when the door across the hall opened and a federal agent came out, Levy Armstrong said. The agent chased after Strong-Allen.
“There was no ‘Freeze.’ There was no ‘You’re under arrest.’ There was none of that. It was literally just tackle,” Strong-Allen said in an interview.
She hit her head on a wall, and then agents were on her back, pushing her head into the floor while she asked to see a warrant, she said.
They put handcuffs on her and led her to their vehicle, slamming her foot in the door. On the way to the Whipple Federal Building, which served as the headquarters of Operation Metro Surge, she said an agent showed her an arrest warrant on his phone for Nekima Levy Armstrong.
“I was like, ‘Y’all are just incompetent,’” Strong-Allen recalled thinking. “I told them that was not my name.”
Nevertheless, they took her to Whipple, where they held her for hours and took her photograph and fingerprints. The authorities released her in the early morning hours. She had agents drop her off at a gas station because she didn’t trust them to take her home.
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement declined to comment.
Satara Strong-Allen shows scars Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026, which have stayed on her wrist from tight handcuffs since January, when she was violently arrested by federal agents who mistook her for lawyer and activist Nekima Levy Armstrong. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
For days, Strong-Allen said she felt foggy and saw spots. It took weeks to recover full movement in her hands, which were injured by the handcuffs. She still has small but visible scars from the handcuffing and where the agents slammed the car door on her foot. Medical records reviewed by the Reformer show Strong-Allen was diagnosed with a concussion, nerve injury in both hands, bruising in her foot and emotional distress.
The aggressive arrest led her to believe that the agents wanted to hurt Levy Armstrong, whom the White House had cast as a dangerous political enemy.
The botched arrest could have been avoided had federal authorities allowed Levy Armstrong to turn herself in as she was trying to do. Her attorney, Jordan Kushner, said U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen called him and indicated Levy Armstrong would be able to turn herself in but then called back and said she would have to be arrested.
“Obviously, he was getting instructions from D.C.,” Kushner said in an interview.
The U.S. Attorney’s Office declined to comment.
Federal agents returned to the hotel later that day to arrest Levy Armstrong. Video footage taken by her husband and one of the federal agents shows Levy Armstrong asking the agents to treat her with respect, telling them she has a brain tumor.
She also asked why the agent was filming her on a phone. He said because he wanted there to be a record of the arrest. Levy Armstrong asked him to stop — she was thinking about ICE officer Jonathan Ross filming himself before shooting and killing Renee Good just two weeks earlier.
“I don’t want to be a trophy for MAGA,” Levy Armstrong told the agents.
“It’s not going to be on Twitter,” the agent filming replied.
Soon after, then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem posted a still image from the footage on X, which the White House then doctored for a post that makes Levy Armstrong appear to be crying. A Trump administration official defended altering the image, saying “the memes will continue.”
The federal agents’ mistake is particularly striking given the level of surveillance they conducted. Agents trailed Levy Armstrong the day before her arrest, watching her run errands and move bags into her hotel room. Levy Armstrong suspects the Aloft hotel told federal agents which room she was staying in so they could be across the hall. The hotel declined to comment.
Federal prosecutors pointed to Levy Armstrong and Allen’s hotel stay as evidence they were flight risks and shouldn’t be released from jail pending trial. U.S. District Judge Laura Provinzino ruled against the government, calling the prosecutors’ assertions “simply speculative.”
Levy Armstrong and the other defendants — including the journalists Don Lemon and Georgia Fort — are charged with two felonies: conspiracy against the right of religious freedom at a place of worship and injuring, intimidating and interfering with the exercise of the right of religious freedom at a place of worship.
They are seeking to have the charges dismissed, arguing in part that they are being subjected to a vindictive prosecution by the Trump administration. The defendants also argue the government has failed to allege their conduct violated the 1994 federal law aimed at protecting access to abortion clinics and places of worship and that the law is unconstitutional.
“We did not commit a crime. We were at the church to inform parishioners about the immorality of their pastoral leadership,” Strong-Allen said.
A judge is weighing their arguments.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Commentary: Oklahoma lawmakers mandated more recess at school, but now it has cut into learning time
description: As the parent of two elementary school-aged kids, I have found myself having a love-hate relationship with Oklahoma’s new recess law. The law, which for all practical purposes took effect in August, requires public elementary schools to provide 40 minutes of daily recess. I love that it gives my children more time to play. Social […]
text:
A student plays on a playground in Oklahoma City on Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)As the parent of two elementary school-aged kids, I have found myself having a love-hate relationship with Oklahoma’s new recess law.
The law, which for all practical purposes took effect in August, requires public elementary schools to provide 40 minutes of daily recess. I love that it gives my children more time to play. Social interactions are important, and there’s a lot to be learned from them. And for one of my kids, recess is a favorite time of day.
But I also hate how the Republican-led Legislature usurped local control and forced this law upon schools without any clear acknowledgement that it would upend the school day.
To accommodate about 15-20ish more minutes of recess, my kids’ district has had to overhaul schedules. Thanks to lawmakers, my kids now have around five fewer minutes to eat lunch. School also starts five minutes earlier, which means I have almost 850 minutes a year – or over half a day – less to spend with them in the mornings before they leave home.
And I hate how lawmakers stripped teachers of one of the few remaining tools that they have long used to hold children accountable for their behavior: missing recess. Under the new law, teachers are forbidden from taking away recess as punishment.
So now if a child throws food in the lunchroom or refuses to do their school work, they are no longer required to take accountability, clean it up or face immediate consequences.
What message does that send to our children? And is a lack of consequences for bad behavior a school lesson that will set them up for success as an adult?
But mostly, I fear that this law puts elementary schools between a rock and a hard place. They’re already under enormous pressure to increase academic outcomes. Next year, if third graders aren’t reading at grade level, they will be held back.
Yet, our Legislature seems equally obsessed with requiring play time.
Wouldn’t it be better if we left it to the local districts to decide what is the best use of the school day? Aren’t they supposed to be the experts here?
For some reason we have a bunch of elected leaders, most with no education background, that feel like they’re in a position to tell schools how to best use their time. They’re not.
It turns out many elementary school teachers agree with my assessment.
The law has made it difficult for them to discipline children. Rather than quietly handling matters as they have in the past with a few minutes less recess, now teachers report having to waste time calling parents about minor disciplinary incidents and disrupt the days of everyone but the kids who got in trouble.
Plus, anyone who has ever had to get a kid out the door knows it’s never a quick process. It’s a transition. You have to get coats on and off. If you’re at school, you have to line up both inside and outside and wait for the kids who are meandering along. 
So as some teachers have pointed out, this extra recess time is actually eating into instructional time that would normally be used for academics.
In Edmond – traditionally one of the state’s highest performing districts – the law has educators pondering an existential question, according to Edmond Classroom Teachers Association President Simora Davis: “What is the point?”
In addition to longer school days, teachers there lost a professional development day to help the district add 15 minutes of daily recess. Professional development days, by the way, are designed to make teachers more effective.
“I get a lot of, ‘When are they going to change this?’ I get a lot of, ‘Why do we have to do this?’” Davis told Oklahoma Voice recently. “I also get a lot of, ‘Do you know what I could be teaching right now? Do you know how much I could get done in 20 minutes of class time?’”
Supporters in the Legislature argue this law allows students to burn pent-up energy and increase their focus.
Maybe it does, but to lengthen a school day just to accommodate recess seems counterintuitive to that logic. So we have more recess, but now proportionally we have a longer school day with less learning.
There are only so many minutes a child has in school each day. Do we want our elementary schools to be playgrounds or places where our children learn their ABCs and 123s?
As a parent, I want my kids’ schools to be academic meccas that set them up for success in the years to come.
Recess has a role to play in that, and maybe some schools will want to keep 40 minutes of recess if given the option. 
But our Legislature should not commandeer recess and dictate how it must happen.
It’s clear that this law is failing our elementary schools.
I appreciate that lawmakers aren’t afraid to try new things. Sometimes, like with our statewide cellphone ban, it works wonderfully.
But they also need to admit when their ideas backfire and make things worse.
The question is how long is it going to take for our Legislature to acknowledge this is a failed experiment, repeal it, and restore power back to local school boards and teachers?
With the myriad issues plaguing our schools, the last thing we need to be distracted by right now is recess.

name: WyoFile
title: Armed men, locked doors and a governor who couldn’t wait
description:
WyoHistory.org editors Leslie Waggener and Kylie L. McCormick recount the month in 1892 when two rivals claimed Wyoming’s governorship, with stakes of rightful party rule extending all the way to Washington.
The post Armed men, locked doors and a governor who couldn’t wait appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
On the morning of Dec. 2, 1892, a notary public swore in Democrat John E. Osborne as governor of Wyoming in the Capitol library. Osborne then entered the governor’s suite. How he got there depended on whom you asked. The Cheyenne Daily Leader, which backed Osborne, said he “took peaceable possession.” 
Amos Barber, a Republican who also claimed the governor’s office, issued a proclamation that day charging that Osborne had entered the Capitol “by stealth and force.” The Republican-leaning Cheyenne Daily Sun supplied alleged details to back him up: A carpenter had forced open a window, and Osborne had edged along an outside ledge to climb in. 

John E. Osborne spent his first night as Wyoming governor locked inside the governor’s suite with his rival’s private secretary. (Wikimedia Commons)

Soon after Osborne settled in, Richard Repath, Barber’s private secretary, came rushing up, “breathless with haste,” as the Leader put it. Repath locked the doors and put the keys in his pocket. Osborne was free to leave, the Sun noted, but then he would have to force his way back in. So, he stayed. For a while, Osborne and Repath “conversed at intervals,” the Sun reported, “and neither appeared to particularly object to the company of the other.”
At dusk, two men brought candles to a window. Osborne pushed up on the window. Repath shoved down. After a short struggle, Osborne won. The window went up and the candles came in, the Leader reported. Supper came in the same way, and so did bedding for what the paper called Osborne’s “first sleep as governor of Wyoming.”
Things got worse that night, according to the Sun. When Repath refused to let two of Osborne’s allies in, Osborne threatened to throw him “through the glass.” Repath “only laughed.” Democrats slipped notes under the door all night, while Osborne tried to fit a key to the lock with the file blade of his pocketknife. Repath eventually withdrew to the governor’s inner office, keeping the keys and leaving Osborne alone in the anteroom.
The next day, Osborne’s allies opened a side door with skeleton keys. For the rest of December, Osborne held the reception room of the governor’s suite, while Repath held the governor’s private office and its keys.
Two governors, one Senate seat
For a month, Wyoming had two rival governors. What was at stake reached well beyond the governor’s office.
Barber, the secretary of state, had been acting governor since Republican Francis E. Warren resigned in 1890 to go to the U.S. Senate. Barber had never been elected governor. Barber and Warren’s apparent support and protection of the invaders during the Johnson County War in April 1892 turned Wyoming voters against the Republican Party the following fall. While Republicans held onto a majority in the Wyoming Senate, initial vote counts showed they lost the House and governor’s office to the Democrats in a landslide. Osborne, a Rawlins physician, won the governor’s race on Nov. 8, 1892, 9,290 votes to 7,509.
The law said the winner would take office “within thirty days after” the state canvassing board counted the vote and declared him elected. Osborne’s side found a loophole: The law directing what the board could count named races for Congress and the Legislature, not governor. So, Osborne argued, the county returns were enough, and they showed he had been “unquestionably elected.”
Who held the governor’s office mattered because of the U.S. Senate. Until the 17th Amendment in 1913, state legislatures, not voters, chose U.S. senators, and Warren’s Senate term was ending. Several races for the Legislature were in dispute, and the governor signed the certificates of election for the winners. Those seats could decide which party controlled the Legislature, and with it, who went to the Senate. Democrats feared Republicans would use the count to send Warren back to Washington.
Armed men in the hallway





The Republican-leaning Cheyenne Daily Sun called Osborne the “pseudo governor,” Barber the “acting governor” and blamed “Democratic disturbers” for the armed men at the Capitol. (Cheyenne Daily Sun, Dec. 6, 1892.)

The fight dragged on. Claiming the governor’s authority, Osborne had called the canvassing board to meet on Dec. 5 and count the November returns. “The members did not heed his call,” the Sun reported. When Osborne went to the secretary of state’s office, where the board met, the chief clerk refused to let him in, citing “a plot to take the office by force.” Two of the board members, the auditor and the treasurer, said they “knew but one governor and his name was Barber.”
The next day, the Sun reported “armed men on both sides of the big hallway at the statehouse.” The paper blamed “Democratic disturbers” for the guns, then assured readers: “No trouble. No sign of trouble.”
Barber’s all-Republican board met on Dec. 8. It refused to count one Carbon County precinct, Hanna, because of flaws in its paperwork. Those votes would decide two seats in the state House. The Democrats went to the Wyoming Supreme Court, which ordered the Hanna votes counted on Dec. 31. Both seats went to Democrats.
A second oath
The standoff ended on Jan. 2, 1893. By then, the state board had finished its count and declared Osborne the winner. In his proclamation, Barber had promised to “cheerfully” step aside for “whoever may have been legally declared the choice of the people.” He kept his word.
Osborne took the oath a second time, reportedly wearing shoes he had made from the skin of outlaw “Big Nose” George Parrott. This time it was administered not by a notary but by Wyoming Supreme Court Chief Justice Herman V.S. Groesbeck. Osborne attached a note to the new oath. He was taking it, he wrote, only so that Barber “may no longer have such pretense for usurping the powers and duties of governor.” His first oath, he insisted, remained “of full force and validity.” That afternoon, Barber and Repath visited Osborne to formally hand over the governor’s office, and Osborne got the keys. 
Two weeks later, the Supreme Court ruled that the December oath was not valid. Osborne had taken that oath before the state board counted the vote and declared a winner, the court said, which made it “premature and invalid.” A candidate could not simply declare himself elected. “If one person may do this, another may.” The ruling did not touch the January oath. Groesbeck, who had administered it, joined the decision.
A senator short
As for the Senate seat behind it all, nobody got it. When the Legislature finally settled who belonged in it, there were 22 Republicans, 21 Democrats and five Populists. Lawmakers voted 31 times without agreeing on anyone.

Francis E. Warren had the last laugh. Two years after Democrats fought to keep him out of the Senate, he was back, and he held the seat for the rest of his life. (Wyoming State Archives)

For two years, Wyoming had only one senator, Joseph M. Carey. Once again, the governor had a say. Osborne appointed a Democrat, A.C. Beckwith, to the empty seat, but the U.S. Senate questioned whether a governor could fill a seat the Legislature had failed to fill, and Beckwith withdrew in July.
It was a bad time to be short a senator. That year, the U.S. Senate’s session ran through the summer as members debated a national depression and whether silver should remain a basis of the nation’s money. In 1895, Wyoming lawmakers finally filled the seat — with Francis E. Warren. He held it until his death in 1929.
Osborne went on to serve in Congress and in Woodrow Wilson’s State Department. In 1918, he ran for the Senate himself, against Warren, then 75. Warren won by more than 6,400 votes.

description: Through the first four months of fiscal year 2027, total Idaho state revenue collections are $82.5 million ahead of forecast, a new state report released last week shows. According to the October results posted in the new Fiscal Year 2027 Budget Monitor, the state is projected to end fiscal year 2027 in June with a […]
text:
The Idaho State Capitol Building in Boise as seen on Jan. 14, 2026. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Through the first four months of fiscal year 2027, total Idaho state revenue collections are $82.5 million ahead of forecast, a new state report released last week shows.
Idaho officials request raise for disability caregivers and restoring cuts to mental health services

According to the October results posted in the new Fiscal Year 2027 Budget Monitor, the state is projected to end fiscal year 2027 in June with a positive ending balance of $688.3 million. 
For the month of October itself, state revenues collections came in 1.9% below forecast. But year-to-date, state revenues are ahead of the forecast by 4.8%, the report shows.
The projected $688.3 million ending balance is an increase of almost $540 million compared to the ending balance Idaho state legislators estimated at the end of the 2026 legislative session. 
“Things are looking positive,” said Sen. Scott Grow, a Republican from Eagle who serves as co-chair of the Idaho Legislature’s Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee. “I’m happy to see we are running a little ahead.”
Idaho runs on a fiscal year calendar that begins July 1 and ends June 30 each year. That means the October revenue report includes data from the first four months of fiscal year 2027. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 What do Idaho’s increased revenues mean for budget setting next year?

Idaho state legislators will begin working on setting the fiscal year 2028 budget once the new legislative session begins in January. 
So far, this year’s revenue increases are a change compared to last year, when state legislators approved across-the-board budget cuts for almost all state agencies and departments to pay for tax changes included in the federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act. 
Grow’s committee, the Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee, or JFAC, is responsible for setting the state budget, which is then sent to the full Idaho House of Representatives and Idaho Senate for approval.
Grow said increased revenues could create new challenges for legislators during the upcoming legislative session. 
“The challenge we have is when revenues look a little stronger, some may want to go back and undo the cuts, refill or replace the cuts that were made last session,” Grow said. 
“I’ve been told before that when things are tight, it is more a little more understandable by departments and agencies that things are tight,” Grow said. “But when revenue seems to be strong, then we get a lot of (funding) requests.”
Grow said he doesn’t think the JFAC and the Idaho Legislature will reverse or backfill all of last year’s budget cuts this year. 
Sen. Scott Grow, R-Eagle, makes a comment during the Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee meeting on Jan. 14, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
Personally, Grow outlined three priorities where he favors investing any available increased funding:

Pay increases for state employees. 
Pre-funding the state’s wildfire suppression fund to pay next year’s wildfire bills.
Providing transportation funding to adequately maintain Idaho’s highway system.

Grow said funding a change in employee compensation, or CEC, plan is his No. 1 priority after Idaho’s more than 20,000 state employees did not receive a pay increase this year. 
“No. 1, we have got to have some sort of CEC, some compensation for our state employees,” Grow said. “We were flat this last year (on pay for state employees). Some of the departments have struggled with that and some agencies have lost some folks.” 
On Thursday, the Citizens Committee on Legislative Compensation voted to freeze the pay for Idaho state legislators in place for one year, in line with state employees who did not receive a pay increase, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. 
During Thursday’s meeting of the Citizens Committee on Legislative Compensation, House Speaker Mike Moyle, R-Star, said the Idaho Legislature will increase pay for  state employees next year.

title: Mule deer buck tests positive for CWD in Idaho near Oregon border
description: A mule deer buck that was killed by a hunter in Idaho along the Snake River near the border with Oregon has tested positive for chronic wasting disease, Idaho Department of Fish and Game officials said. The positive test marked the first time chronic wasting disease has been detected in Unit 13, which is located […]
text:
Chronic wasting disease, or CWD, is a contagious, incurable and fatal neurological disease that can be transmitted between hooved mammals such as elk, moose and deer. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)A mule deer buck that was killed by a hunter in Idaho along the Snake River near the border with Oregon has tested positive for chronic wasting disease, Idaho Department of Fish and Game officials said.
The positive test marked the first time chronic wasting disease has been detected in Unit 13, which is located in Idaho County and is bordered by the Snake River on the west and the Salmon River on the east. 
The location is about a half mile from the Oregon border, Idaho state officials said in a Wednesday press release.
Chronic wasting disease, or CWD, is a contagious, incurable and fatal neurological disease that can be transmitted between hooved mammals such as elk, moose and deer. 
The disease was first detected in Idaho in 2021.
In announcing the positive CWD test, Idaho Department of Fish and Game officials said tissue samples provided by hunters help give state officials important insight into where the disease is occurring and how common it is.
“With the hunting season now concluded in Unit 13, we encourage the public to continue supporting CWD surveillance by reporting road-killed deer and elk, animals found dead, and animals exhibiting unusual behavior,” said Stacey Dauwalter, IDFG Wildlife Health Program coordinator. “These reports and samples are essential to helping us monitor the disease.”
Idaho Department of Fish and Game officials said they have tested more than 3,500 elk and deer for chronic wasting disease so far this year. 
The recent positive test for the mule deer buck killed near the Oregon border marked the first CWD detection outside units that have previously had elk and deer test positive for CWD, Idaho Department of Fish and Game officials said. 
State officials said their priority is to keep the percentage of animals infected low so that big game populations will remain healthy. However, they said CWD cannot be eliminated because it remains in the environment for decades. 
More information about chronic wasting disease is available on the Idaho Department of Fish and Game’s website.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: How will Tommy Tuberville’s administration address public health?
description: During his time in the U.S. Senate, Tommy Tuberville supported the nomination of now-Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., who has falsely challenged the efficacy of vaccines, and the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) agenda.  During Kennedy’s confirmation hearing, Tuberville said that his granddaughter would “not be a pincushion.”  [...]
text:
U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville gives an acceptance speech after he wins the Republican nomination for Alabama's governor at his primary election victory tailgate at the Vulcan Park in Birmingham, Alabama, on May 19, 2026. Tuberville largely supported the MAHA agenda during his term in the U.S. Senate, but it is unclear how that will translate to his governance of Alabama. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector) 


Key points

Gov.-elect Tommy Tuberville’s policy agenda has focused on rural healthcare and reforming the state’s certificate of need process.
In the U.S. Senate, Tuberville supported the nomination of Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., who has falsely challenged the efficacy of vaccines, and expressed anti-vaccine sentiments.
The state continues to see issues with healthcare access in rural areas and infant mortality.




During his time in the U.S. Senate, Tommy Tuberville supported the nomination of now-Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., who has falsely challenged the efficacy of vaccines, and the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) agenda. 
During Kennedy’s confirmation hearing, Tuberville said that his granddaughter would “not be a pincushion.” 
How his support of the agenda will translate to his governance of Alabama is unclear. 
Tuberville’s policy plan, known as the playbook, does not address public health policies like vaccines, maternal and infant health outcomes or artificial food additives in the healthcare section. It does address Alabama’s lack of rural healthcare access and a goal to reform the state’s certificate of need law – a system that 35 states use that require proof of need to fund major capital improvements at health care facilities.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Stan McDonald, a former Alabama Ethics Commissioner, was appointed as the leader of Tuberville’s health policy transition team. Hannah Eddins, Tuberville’s communications director, said the transition team would participate in interviews later, but the playbook addresses the incoming governor’s initial plans. 
Currently, the State Committee on Public Health and the State Health Officer are not political appointees by nature, but have shifted in that direction in recent years. 
Prior to 2024, the committee members chose the State Health Officer with no input from the legislative or executive branches of Alabama’s government. But SB 128, sponsored by Sen. Tim Melson, R-Florence, changed the appointment to require final approval from the governor.
State Health Officer Dr. Scott Harris, who has held the position since 2017, is generally supportive of vaccines. In meetings of the committee since the resurgence of measles in the United States, Harris has emphasized that vaccination is the best way to prevent contraction of the highly contagious disease. 
“This is the best job I’ve ever had. I love being here. I hope I can stay here as long as I’m useful,” Harris said in a recent interview.
The State Committee on Public Health sets environmental standards, rules for healthcare facilities and vaccine schedules for children. Martha Wingate, a public health researcher on maternal and infant health outcomes and public health policies, said in an interview Monday that the limited politics in Alabama’s public health allows for more consistency in public health policy.
“I feel like we’ve got such a strong presence of physicians, nurses, (on the committee),” Wingate said. “How does this make sense from a clinical and from a public health perspective, and that taking care of our neighbors is really the biggest piece of that.”
Vaccine mandates
Gov. DeSantis’ push to change Florida’s vaccine requirements for school children failed during the 2026 session, but the governor promises to keep working to pass it before being term-limited out of office. Will the Legislature go along? (Photo by Scott Housley/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)
Tuberville has opposed vaccine mandates and introduced federal legislation this summer to withhold federal funding from public schools that do not recognize religious exemptions for vaccines.  
“This is a free country, and parents have every right to make personal decisions about what vaccines they choose to give their children,” he said in a July press release. “Taxpayer-funded K-12 schools have no right to turn students away at the door because of their vaccination status – especially if they have a religious exemption.”
Religious vaccine exemptions, and no-excuse exemptions, have growing support in the Alabama Legislature. Sen. Arthur Orr, R-Decatur, and Rep. Mack Butler, R-Rainbow City, to allow religious vaccine exemptions over the last three legislative sessions. Rep. Danielle Duggar, R-Spanish Fort, a new lawmaker, hopes to pass legislation prohibiting discrimination based on vaccine choices. 
ADPH encourages vaccination after measles case; no new cases immediately reported

As of Nov. 13, the CDC has confirmed more than 5,400 cases of measles in 2026 across the country. About 96% of the confirmed cases were not vaccinated against the disease. There were almost 2,300 confirmed cases in 2025, where about 93% were unvaccinated. The outbreak, which cost the country its measles elimination status, has been blamed in part on Kennedy’s hostility to vaccination.
According to the CDC, 94.3% of Alabama kindergarteners are vaccinated against the disease for the 2025-26 school year. In the 2024-25 school year, 95.2% of kindergarteners were vaccinated. Herd immunity can be reached with a 95% vaccination rate. 
In February, Harris said the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is not “one of the controversial ones, or shouldn’t be.”
In a recent interview, Harris said the committee likely would not change its vaccine recommendations for school-age children.
“We don’t have requirements for any other group of people. So ultimately, the state committee is going to make those decisions,” he said. “They’ve not seen fit to change any of those so far.”
Wingate said that even though there is a growing conversation on “medical freedom,” Alabama has a culture of “loving our neighbor.”
“Yes, there are individual rights, but there’s also this idea of how do we make sure that our neighbors’ children stay healthy, our neighbors’ grandparents stay healthy,” she said. 
Wingate said it is important to remember amid the measles outbreak that most physicians are being forced to treat a disease they have never seen before. Members of the committee have pointed that out as well.
Three Alabamians have tested positive for the disease since the onset of the outbreak last year. 
“The things that we can prevent from this ouchie, from this thing that hurts for just a minute, the stuff that we can prevent is a lot more scary than that little stick,” Wingate said.
Rural hospitals and infant health outcomes
Vaughan Regional Medical Center in Selma, AL, on Tuesday, Sep. 3, 2024 in Selma, Ala. Vaughn, like many of Alabama’s rural hospitals, is struggling with a low Medicare reimbursement rate. (Will McLelland for Alabama Reflector)
In his playbook, Tuberville promises to not let any rural hospitals close and to use his connections in Washington to strategically allocate funds from the Rural Health Transformation Program. 
“Alabama has more than $203 million coming this year from the rural health program, and every dollar goes to care, not consultants, with results published for every community,” the playbook says.
The program, funded through President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), is aimed to partially offset cuts to Medicaid. Experts say it might not be enough.
Wingate said that the funds should, and are, be used to train providers and increase resources for rural facilities. Part of the program’s grant application process required sustainability.
“I think that whole idea of instead of bringing people to the larger places, really saying, how can we get things out to people in the best way that we possibly can to at least get them to a point to where we can move them to that higher level care or to a place where they can get care,” Wingate said.
Alabama rural hospitals caught in ‘vicious cycle’ on Medicare wage index

Alabama’s infant mortality rate worsened slightly in 2025 and remains above the national average, according to data released earlier this month by the Alabama Department of Public Health. 
Many of the determinants are social, and are harder for the department to address, according to Harris. Wingate agreed that the bigger picture issues like race, socioeconomic status and education level are more difficult to address from the public health perspective.
“I think that the sleep related stuff I think you still can fix, but there but some of these other bigger picture things are a little more tricky,” she said. “All of it’s very tricky.”
However, addressing access to care through something like the Rural Health Transformation Program could help the state make improvements in maternal and infant health outcomes, Wingate said.
She said she wished figuring out how to manage public health and politics was easy, but it never has been.
“When we really take the immunizations, the access to care, all those things, and kind of put it in that space, it gets tricky, and it kind of goes against the grain a little bit,” she said. “That basic tenet that we want to take care of our neighbors, in my mind that’s a lot of what public health is. How do we do that in a way that’s meaningful? The politics aside, that’s really what’s important. Hopefully, any new administration would agree with that.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Blackburn taps child welfare advisory group to review Tennessee Department of Children’s Services
description: Incoming Tennessee Gov. Marsha Blackburn has formed a four-person advisory committee to “gather insights, input, and data to assess the current state” of the Department of Children’s Services agency, her transition committee announced.  The announcement came amid a series of new or renewed cabinet appointments made public last week by the governor-elect, who[...]
text:
Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn has formed a DCS advisory group to examine the future of Tennessee's troubled child welfare agency. Pictured: Margie Quin, DCS's current leader.(Photo: John Partipilo)Incoming Tennessee Gov. Marsha Blackburn has formed a four-person advisory committee to “gather insights, input, and data to assess the current state” of the Department of Children’s Services agency, her transition committee announced. 
The announcement came amid a series of new or renewed cabinet appointments made public last week by the governor-elect, whose term in office begins January 16. Blackburn has not said whether she will retain current Department of Children’s Services Commissioner Margie Quin.
One of the responsibilities of the advisory group will be to “provide recommendations regarding the department’s future direction and leadership,” the announcement said.
Since 2011, no DCS chief has held the job for more than four years. 
Quin has led the $1.6 billion agency since 2022, tapped by Gov. Bill Lee to bring reforms as the agency faced intense scrutiny over public reports of mistreatment of foster children in state custody, internal dysfunction, including staffing shortages and news reports of children taken from their families on suspicion of abuse or neglect then being forced to sleep on office floors, in some instances for months at a time. 
Despite improvements, DCS continues to fail Tennessee children, audit finds

Quin successfully sought hundreds of millions of dollars in state funding to build more transition homes, hire staff and raise salaries. The agency, which is also responsible for youth involved in the juvenile justice system, has also opened more detention space. 
Criticism, however, has continued to dog the agency. 
A 2022 audit found the agency failed to meet the needs of abused and neglected children, delayed child abuse investigations, including reports of sexual abuse of children inside its own facilities, and and lacked oversight in juvenile detention facilities.   
Among the findings in a 2025 audit, were poor conditions for children placed in transition facilities DCS established to avoid housing kids in state offices.  In addition, the agency has been the subject of at least two class-action lawsuits during Quin’s tenure. Child advocates have also criticized Quin’s emphasis on expanding institutional settings to house children and teens over home settings.
Former DCS leader Jim Henry will chair Blackburn’s advisory group. The other members are: Maggie McNally Kimball, executive director of Safe Harbor Child Advocacy Center in East Tennessee; Cleo Griffin, COO for membership and philanthropy at the YMCA of Memphis & the Mid-South; and Cameron Smith, a contributing columnist to the Tennessean newspaper who has been outspoken in his criticism of the treatment of children in DCS care. 
The group will examine the department’s operations, structure, and existing challenges, with an emphasis on identifying opportunities to strengthen its work, the announcement said. “The committee’s findings will help inform the incoming administration’s decisions and priorities for DCS moving forward,” it said.

title: Colorado submits proposal to host permanent US Space Academy
description: Colorado could become the home of two federal academies as the state pitches itself as the ideal site for the new United States Space Academy. A recently-submitted proposal envisions the approximately $8.2 billion academy campus being developed at the Banning Lewis Ranch in eastern Colorado Springs, roughly 20 miles from the U.S. Air Force Academy. […]
text:
The Space Academy would train graduates for U.S. Space Force but also work at NASA and the private sector. (U.S. Air Force photo by Eric Dietrich)Colorado could become the home of two federal academies as the state pitches itself as the ideal site for the new United States Space Academy.
A recently-submitted proposal envisions the approximately $8.2 billion academy campus being developed at the Banning Lewis Ranch in eastern Colorado Springs, roughly 20 miles from the U.S. Air Force Academy. Colorado leaders say the area is ripe for the new academy as the state’s aerospace industry continues to grow.
“Colorado is a national leader in aerospace, and our ecosystem grows stronger every year across the full spectrum of civil, commercial, and national security space,” Lt. Gov. Dianne Primavera, who chaired the proposal’s advisory committee, said in a statement. “Throughout our state, industry, institutions of higher education, federal laboratories, and military installations are carrying out critical missions while leading innovation for the future. The U.S. Space Academy would give young people from across the country a direct path into that future, and nowhere else offers the depth of opportunity Colorado does.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
At least 25 states have submitted proposals for the new NASA-led academy, following an August executive order from President Donald Trump to begin the process of establishing the institution and a request for proposals by NASA, the country’s space agency. The executive order imagines the academy as a school “combining rigorous technical education with leadership development, discipline and a durable commitment to public service.” The federal commission in charge is expected to issue a report of its recommendations to Trump by the end of the year.
The academy is not a purely military institution like West Point. It would prepare graduates to serve in the U.S. Space Force, but also to work at places like NASA and in the private space flight sector. The federal commission will recommend final service obligations for graduates.
Sen. Tony Exum, a Colorado Springs Democrat on the advisory committee, is confident about Colorado’s pitch.
“We’re primed and ready because of the infrastructure we have, the collaboration we have with higher education. We have world-class institutions to prepare these young folks as leaders in aerospace,” he said.
The proposal comes one year after Trump announced that U.S. Space Command would move from Colorado Springs to Huntsville, Alabama, which Colorado leaders called a politically-motivated decision to reward a Republican-aligned state.
“That decision (didn’t) have anything to do with the resources Colorado Springs and the state has to offer,” Exum said. “Those things are all still in place.”



Quotation







If the administration is determined to build a U.S. Space Academy, there is no question it should be based in Colorado. Other states would be starting from scratch. We’re not.


– U.S. Sen. John Hickenlooper


But Colorado is still making the case that a Space Academy in the state would thrive in proximity to existing military installations, federal laboratories and hundreds of aerospace and defense businesses.
“With the U.S. Air Force Academy, major Space Force installations, a deep concentration of aerospace expertise and access to Colorado’s nation-leading academic and research institutions, Colorado Springs offers an unmatched combination of military leadership, educational excellence, cutting-edge research, industry partnerships and space operations experience,” Paul Lundeen, a former state Senate minority leader and member of the advisory committee, said in a text message to Colorado Newsline.
Colorado leaders proposed the Banning Lewis Ranch site in Colorado Springs for a new U.S. Space Academy, as depicted in this rendering. (Rendering reproduced from proposal documents)
The 100-page proposal from Colorado suggests the development of a 321-acre campus and 187-acre “innovation district” for research and industry offices. The initial groundbreaking would be in 2027, and about 1,200 students could move to the campus in fall 2031. Eventually, the campus would allow for about 4,000 students, about the same population as other military academies.
The land is owned by Norwood Development Group, a major El Paso County developer, and the company would lease academy grounds to NASA.
Before completed construction, there would be interim operations at the University of Colorado Colorado Springs for 300 students beginning in fall 2028. That’s similar to what happened with the Air Force academy when it launched in 1955: The first class was sworn in at a temporary site before the campus was built.
“Colorado universities are poised to serve NASA and the U.S. Space Academy by launching a statewide educational partnership that develops our nation’s next generation of elite students to explore, operate and lead in space,” CU President Todd Saliman said in a statement.
A proposed new financing tool, which would need to make it through the state Legislature, would let the state use sales tax increases in the area around the academy for investment in the development. Expected sales tax revenue could support around $181 million in bonds, according to the proposal. Gov. Jared Polis has also contributed up to $50 million in state income tax credits in his recent budget proposal.
“Just as we do for major other initiatives like Sundance (Film Festival) or the quantum accelerator, the state would would provide some match to this through a tax credit. But obviously, this would be billions of dollars of federal investment,” he said earlier this month when outlining his budget request.
In total, Colorado outlines $320 million in possible public support.
The bid also has support from Colorado’s congressional delegation, though the makeup of the delegation changed with the midterm elections. Nearly every member supported the proposal in a Nov. 5 press release.
“If the administration is determined to build a U.S. Space Academy, there is no question it should be based in Colorado. Other states would be starting from scratch. We’re not,” U.S. Sen. John Hickenlooper, a Democrat who was reelected, said in a statement. “We’re home to leading universities, the nation’s largest space economy per capita, and more Space Force Deltas than any other state. When it comes to training tomorrow’s space leaders, Colorado has already shown there’s nowhere better.”
