title: Applications sought for higher education board seats
description: A member of the North Dakota State Board of Higher Education will resign to take a seat in the Legislature, opening up a short-term spot on the board.  That board seat and another spot on the eight-member board will expire next year, creating two more opportunities to serve on the body that governs the North […]
text:
Tim Mihalick, a member of the State Board of Higher Education, speaks during a board retreat at Bismarck State College on Aug. 27, 2026. Mihalick is leaving the board to serve in the Legislature. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)A member of the North Dakota State Board of Higher Education will resign to take a seat in the Legislature, opening up a short-term spot on the board. 
That board seat and another spot on the eight-member board will expire next year, creating two more opportunities to serve on the body that governs the North Dakota University System. 
Tim Mihalick will resign from the board Dec. 1 to represent a Minot district in the North Dakota House. 
Applications to complete the remainder of Mihalick’s term are due by noon Dec. 18.
That term and one held by Curtis Biller will end June 30, 2027. 
Applications for the two full four-year terms, beginning July 1, are due by noon Jan. 15. All three appointments will need to be confirmed by the North Dakota Senate during the 2027 legislative session. 
Candidates may apply for both the seven-month term and a four-year term but the applications will be considered separately. Applicants must complete a one-page application form and submit a resume and up to six reference letters. Applicants must have lived in North Dakota for the past five years and must not have been employed or paid by the North Dakota University System during the past two years.
The State Board of Higher Education sets policy for the North Dakota University System and governs the state’s 11 public colleges and universities.
Gov. Kelly Armstrong appoints members of the Board of Higher Education. State Superintendent of Schools Levi Bachmeier chairs a five-member committee that screens applicants. The committee forwards a list of three suggested appointees to the governor for each opening.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idahoans should know about the brazen new plan to sell our public lands
description: This election season, public lands were on the ballot. The issue showed up in campaigns across the country, including here in Idaho where we reelected leaders who have made this position clear: Public lands are not for sale. One recent poll showed 96% of Idahoans oppose selling public land, so it turns out these positions […]
text:
The Lewis Clark National Historic Trail, as seen near the Lemhi Pass in Idaho. Today the pass is traversed by a 35-mile long graded unpaved Backcountry Byway through public lands where colorful wildflowers like arrowleaf balsam-root, lupine and delphinium rival the sunset. (Photo by Bob Wick/Bureau of Land Management)This election season, public lands were on the ballot. The issue showed up in campaigns across the country, including here in Idaho where we reelected leaders who have made this position clear: Public lands are not for sale.
One recent poll showed 96% of Idahoans oppose selling public land, so it turns out these positions are also smart politics. It’s not everyday that you see an issue with such broad bipartisan support all across the state.
New poll finds 96% Idaho voters say public lands should remain in public hands

We’re fortunate to have U.S. Congressman Mike Simpson and U.S. Sens. Jim Risch and Mike Crapo on our side as advocates for keeping public lands in public hands, because unfortunately the attacks on our outdoor heritage just don’t seem to be going away.
The latest example sadly comes directly from the U.S. Department of Interior, which just released a strategic plan that, for the first time ever, prioritizes selling public land under its control. Here in Idaho, that most likely means they could be selling off our treasured Bureau of Land Management lands.
Interior’s plan says the agency will “work to decrease the size of the federal estate.” In other words, it plans to sell our public lands. Its approach is not a narrow, targeted one meant to solve a specific local problem, where transferring a small piece of public land to a local government might make sense from time to time.
Instead, this Department of the Interior appears intent on trying to sell off as much of our public land as it can. There’s no acreage limit, no ceiling on how much public land could be sold, and no endpoint for the sell-off.
The plan calls for public lands to be sold to state and local governments, but those governments are unlikely to be able to afford the long-term costs of land management and will be forced to find a way to make a profit from the land. Ultimately that means many of those formerly-public lands will be privatized, commercialized, or both. Think data center developers aren’t paying attention to this?
At a time when Americans are rightly up in arms about the rapid, irresponsible construction of data centers, it’s hard to understand why the administration would pursue a policy that could allow them to be built even faster by selling BLM lands that may ultimately end up in the hands of data center developers.
Perhaps it’s because many administration officials have been found to have conflicts of interest with the development of data centers.  This, of course, makes the plan to sell public lands even more troubling.
Steve Pearce, a prominent New Mexico Republican and former congressman, addresses the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee on Feb. 25, 2026, as he seeks confirmation as federal Bureau of Land Management director. (Screenshot courtesy U.S. Senate)
And maybe the most disappointing aspect of this is that we were told by BLM Director Steve Pearce during his confirmation hearings that he wouldn’t sell public lands without the approval of Congress. Selling our public lands simply isn’t what senators voted for when they confirmed Director Pearce, and it isn’t what Idahoans want either. Idahoans deserve an answer for why Interior’s new policy doesn’t sync up with statements made during the confirmation hearings.
If Interior follows through with its stated goal of selling our public lands, we’ll no longer have the same freedom to roam the great outdoors that we have today. It’s a freedom that defines who we are as Idahoans. Your favorite chunk of BLM land just might end up on the auction block.
These are the lands where we go to hunt, fish, camp and spend time with our families and friends. There is a land ethic deeply woven into the fabric of our state, and we know that future generations of Idahoans are counting on us to keep the promise of wild public lands for them.
Fortunately, Congressman Simpson, Sen. Risch and Sen. Crapo continue to vocally oppose selling our public lands. In response to the Department of Interior’s plan, Sen. Risch, who helped defeat U.S. Sen. Mike Lee’s previous effort to sell 3 million acres of public lands, said, “If the federal government tries to sell off Idaho’s public lands, I’ll fight to stop it again.”
We’re counting on our Idaho delegation to make clear that the Department of the Interior has no mandate to sell off our public lands. And we’re asking them to use all of the tools at their disposal to make sure that our public lands stay in public hands, including supporting definitive congressional action to prevent such brazen attempts to sell our public lands now and in the future.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota governor ‘exploring’ involvement in ethics panel lawsuit; AG to seek dismissal
description: North Dakota Gov. Kelly Armstrong said Friday his office is looking at whether to become involved in the state Ethics Commission’s lawsuit against Attorney General Drew Wrigley related to a critical opinion the AG issued last year. “We’re exploring it,” Armstrong said in an interview with the North Dakota Monitor. “I mean, I am not […]
text:
Attorney General Drew Wrigley, right, and Gov. Kelly Armstrong listen to a presentation during a meeting of the North Dakota Industrial Commission on Oct. 30, 2026. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota Gov. Kelly Armstrong said Friday his office is looking at whether to become involved in the state Ethics Commission’s lawsuit against Attorney General Drew Wrigley related to a critical opinion the AG issued last year.
“We’re exploring it,” Armstrong said in an interview with the North Dakota Monitor. “I mean, I am not going to step on the attorney general’s toes … but I think the protection of AG’s opinions is pretty important to the overall function of government.”
Wrigley said Friday he will seek to have the Ethics Commission’s lawsuit dismissed, and if not dismissed, “to address what we believe to be the clearly constitutional and legal meritorious side of this discussion.”
The lawsuit relates to a June 2025 advisory opinion by the Ethics Commission that said campaign funds can be used for caregiving and security expenses in certain instances. Secretary of State Michael Howe subsequently asked Wrigley for an opinion on the Ethics Commission’s related authority. 
North Dakota Ethics Commission sues Attorney General Wrigley over ‘void’ advisory opinion

Wrigley issued his opinion late last year in which he said the ethics panel “made unauthorized and expansive legal conclusions” in its opinion “without legal authority to do so.” He also said the ethics advisory opinion is “void” and “has no legal effect.”
“We make very clear that they’ve taken on for themselves the role of Legislature and executive branch and the whole thing, and if they’re in charge of everything, that’s news to us,” Wrigley said. 
Howe said the attorney general is his legal counsel and when members of his office have legal questions, they go to the AG for advice and guidance. 
The lawsuit asks the court, in part, to declare the attorney general lacks legal authority to nullify or void an action of the Ethics Commission.
Armstrong, an attorney and former state lawmaker, reiterated his concerns from last year that the Ethics Commission is trying to write policy through advisory opinions. 
Governor questions scope of Ethics Commission authority

“Policy is in the Legislature’s purview. Enforcement of election and campaign finance law is in the secretary of state’s purview,” the governor said. “And the only way you can look at this opinion is that the Ethics Commission now sits over both the Legislature and the secretary of state. I disagree with that premise.”
In a statement, the Ethics Commission said it respects the authority of the Legislature and secretary of state and applies statutes, “as written by the Legislature,” to the hypothetical facts or prospective conduct presented for advisory opinions.
“The Legislature always retains the constitutional authority to clarify or amend statutes if it disagrees with the Commission’s interpretation or the guidance provided,” as the advisory opinion last year noted, the panel said.
Howe had every right to ask for an attorney general opinion, the governor said. He noted his own office seeking one last year regarding a line-item veto.
“If somebody doesn’t like the attorney general’s opinion, they can go to court,” Armstrong said. “That’s what the Ethics Commission is doing.”
Reach North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Democrat Dan Wilson flipped Winona House seat with a focus on housing and childcare
description: Dan Wilson, a 38-year-old farmer and volunteer firefighter, beat an incumbent Republican by 10 percentage points in a mostly rural House district by running on a platform of abundant housing, affordable childcare and a healthy planet. Wilson’s victory marks a reversal of Democrats’ fortune in Greater Minnesota. He ousted Republican Rep. Aaron Repinski, who w[...]
text:
Dan Wilson beat an incumbent Republican in 2026 to represent state House District 26A, covering much of Winona County. (Courtesy photo)Dan Wilson, a 38-year-old farmer and volunteer firefighter, beat an incumbent Republican by 10 percentage points in a mostly rural House district by running on a platform of abundant housing, affordable childcare and a healthy planet.
Wilson’s victory marks a reversal of Democrats’ fortune in Greater Minnesota. He ousted Republican Rep. Aaron Repinski, who won an open race for House District 26A covering much of Winona County two years ago following the retirement of one of the few rural Democrats left in the Legislature.
Wilson moved to the Winona area about 20 years ago for college at Winona State University. After graduation, he worked at a homeless shelter called Bethany House. He also lived there alongside the guests he served, in keeping with the shelter’s Catholic Worker tradition. He planned to be there just a year while applying to medical school but instead stayed six.
It was a transformative period of his life that he said set him on a path of trying to tackle big systemic issues. He also wanted to do something about climate change, so he started farming rotationally grazed cattle, which sequesters carbon; he’s been at it with his wife and two kids for 10 years.
He made the dragonfly the emblem of his campaign. It appeared darting across yard signs, his website and a pin on his shirt.
Why?
Dragonflies are a signal of a healthy environment, and they are one of the most effective killers in the animal world.
“It was a great encapsulation of our campaign’s ethos,” Wilson said. “We are good, we are positive … and we need to be incredibly effective.”
This interview is the first in a series on rookie state legislators. It has been edited for length and clarity.
Why did you run for office?
I was a stay-at-home dad for the first year and a half of my daughter’s life and — this was in ’22 — listening to the radio and just hearing how Democrats were squandering this opportunity to do really significant change on climate change and preserving our democracy. This was when Biden had a trifecta at the federal level and just hearing the ways in which nothing was moving. So I ran for state sSenate in 2022 and lost.
Then I kind of put my nose to the grindstone and figured out other ways that I could show up, which meant working at a small nonprofit training folks that had previously been homeless on how to advocate for better housing policy. That’s what really got me very passionate about housing policy in Greater Minnesota. Then 2026 came around, and I saw an absence of leadership in our area around housing, so I wanted to run a campaign focused on how to create more housing in Winona County.
Why try and do that at the state level rather than, say, City Council, which has direct control over the zoning?
At the end of the day, a lot of it does come down to budgets and funding, right? And I do think that some zoning reforms at a state level are appropriate and needed because Winona County is not unique.
There really is a very metro-focused conversation that happens around housing that a lot of times forgets Greater Minnesota. It is harder to find a place to rent in the city of Winona than it is in Manhattan, New York. People want to live in small city centers like Winona, and the reason why our communities are shrinking and not growing is because of housing.
I’m also incredibly passionate about climate change and ag policy and healthcare and childcare.
Why do you think you won?
Well, I knocked a lot of doors. That’s always a part of it.
We had a 16 point swing from 2024. When you have a 16 point swing, it’s about more than just a candidate. That kind of enthusiasm, the kind of energy that we saw was not because people are just very excited for me in particular. It is because we were talking about issues people were feeling directly.
I had so many conversations with such a wide variety of people, being like, “I can’t afford to move out of this apartment” or “I can’t afford to own a home” or “I have a son who’s still living with me.” Everyone has a housing story.
I ran on very specific promises of wanting to use a bonding bill to build affordable housing in Winona. So I think it was this kind of politics that we’ve seen across the country with candidates painting a vision of the specific ways in which state government can make your life better and not just talk in vague platitudes of, like, we’re against Trump. I didn’t really talk about Trump at all.
Can you get into the nuts and bolts of specific legislation that you’d like to work on when you get to the capital?
I’ve been a part of the Yes to Homes Coalition. The starter home package that didn’t pass last year — that’s a series of bills I really want to work on. The manufactured home bill of rights. We have three mobile home parks in 26A that have been bought out by private equity within the past couple years. I had a lot of conversations in those communities … heartbreaking conversations about how private equity is ruining people’s lives. Building 100 units of deeply affordable senior housing as a bonding project.
Childcare — working with state leaders and school leaders of how do we create a childcare center in our public school system to start alleviating this deficit of 500 slots of childcare.
And then for soil health and climate change stuff, I think we can do amazing things with just making all of these programs easier to access. In my experience of applying for soil health grants, it took me three years before I finally was able to receive one. This process is often very complicated and slow and requires a farmer to be in an office talking with an agent when often it’s really hard to get off the farm. The Olmsted County water nitrate program, where they have a lot of the application process starting online, is a great way to find efficiencies in the system and not have the government be a barrier.
This could be a tough budget session ahead, and I want to ask what is an area where the state government could spend less.
Tax cuts have the same impact on a budget that spending does, and so when we think about data centers and the fact that the state gives millions of dollars in tax cuts to the richest companies in history … I think that is something the state should look at.
What issues do you think you might disagree with the rest of your party on? 
There’s a move to try to push a year-round session, which I don’t think is a good idea. The legislative session was made for farmers — farmers being able to farm during the summer and come back and legislate during the winters. I really love this idea of citizen legislatures.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Black candidates make gains in Arkansas, but haven’t broken barrier for top offices
description: Chris Jones came the closest any Democrat has to winning federal office in Arkansas in 16 years when he lost his bid for a U.S. House seat by less than a percentage point. He also nearly ended Arkansas’ status as the only former Confederate state that hasn’t elected a Black candidate to Congress. Black candidates […]
text:
Democratic congressional nominee Chris Jones voting with his daughters Janelle (13, left) and Jasmine (10, right) at the Pulaski County early voting site in downtown Little Rock on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. Jones is running against Republican U.S. Rep. French Hill in the 2nd Congressional District (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)Chris Jones came the closest any Democrat has to winning federal office in Arkansas in 16 years when he lost his bid for a U.S. House seat by less than a percentage point.
He also nearly ended Arkansas’ status as the only former Confederate state that hasn’t elected a Black candidate to Congress.
Black candidates made gains in Arkansas’ midterm election with victories that included the race to run the state’s most populous county and flipping a Republican-held legislative seat in the Little Rock suburbs.
In an election where history was made by Black candidates in states like Mississippi, Florida and Georgia, the racial barrier to Arkansas’ federal and top statewide offices remains. But candidates and observers say they see hopeful signs that achieving that milestone is within reach.
“Do I see progress? Absolutely,” Jones said last week. “And let me be clear: it’s not progress for the sake of electing a Black person. I think it is progress for the sake of seeing that no matter what color you are, there is tremendous value you can bring in the work.”
Jones, an ordained pastor and nuclear engineer who ran for governor two years ago, faced an uphill climb challenging Republican U.S. Rep. French Hill in central Arkansas’ 2nd Congressional District.
GOP US Rep. French Hill wins seventh term to central Arkansas seat

The district, which includes Little Rock, was widely seen as more favorable to Republicans after the GOP-led Legislature redrew its boundaries. Hill won reelection to his seat by nearly 18 percentage points two years ago, and President Donald Trump won the district by more than 15 percentage points that year.
Jones and supporters point to him coming closer than any other Democrat has to unseating Hill as a sign of how flippable the seat is. The Democratic Congressional Committee identified the district as a key target ahead of the November election, and Jones had drawn the support of national party figures like former Vice President Kamala Harris, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttiegieg and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker.
“He could have broken it if they didn’t gerrymander Pulaski County and turn it into three different congressional districts,” said Barry Jefferson, president of the NAACP Arkansas State Conference. 
Jones narrowly lost the election as Democratic state Sen. Fred Love, a Black lawmaker from the Little Rock area, unsuccessfully challenged Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders. Love lost to Sanders by double digits.
Senator Fred Love shakes hands with visitors at the Hope Watermelon Festival in Hope, Arkansas on Saturday, August 8, 2026. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)
Love noted he received more votes statewide than any Black candidate previously in Arkansas, but said a lack of national investment in his campaign hurt his bid.
“If leaders would have been more supportive and offered resources, we could have seen more headway than we saw this election cycle, and I believe you have heard this message in other Southern states,” Love wrote in a text message to the Arkansas Advocate.
“Arkansas is ready for change and hopefully leadership will make the investment so that we can see real change in the next election cycle,” he wrote. “In addition, in the future, we can hopefully draw maps that do not intentionally disenfranchise voters so they can truly choose the candidate that best represents them, regardless of race.”
Arkansas is one of a handful of states that hasn’t elected a Black candidate to statewide, nonjudicial office since Reconstruction.
Nationally, the midterms led to historic advances for Black officeholders. Six Black governors will serve at the same time in Florida, Georgia, Maryland, Wisconsin, Virginia and the Virgin Islands. The incoming U.S. Senate will include a record seven Black senators and nine Black lawmakers are set to serve as state House speakers next year. 
Black leaders in Arkansas say the lack of representation at the state or federal level is a distinction they’re eager to end in a state known for the 1957 desegregation battle at Little Rock Central High School.
One of the hurdles has been the lack of congressional districts where African-Americans make up a majority of the voting population. Arkansas has never had a majority-Black U.S. House district, unlike other Southern states like Alabama, Georgia and Mississippi.
About 15% of Arkansas’ population is Black, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. The 2nd Congressional District has the highest percentage of Black residents, with about 21%.
Arkansas has had a history of racialized voting patterns, with white voters tending to support white candidates, said Jay Barth, professor emeritus of politics at Hendrix College. Exit polling showed more than two-thirds of white voters in Arkansas chose Republican John McCain in the 2008 presidential election he lost to Barack Obama.
But Jones’ surprisingly close loss to Hill after the 2021 redistricting moved thousands of Black voters to other districts indicates that pattern may be breaking.
“Now we have a generation that has come of age in which race is kind of less of a divider in politics than historically,” Barth said. “You know, party is the more important divider.”
There were signs of progress at the local level as well. Democrat Wendell Griffen, a former circuit and appeals court judge, became the first Black person elected to the top administrative job in Pulaski County. It’s the latest barrier broken in a county that elected its first Black sheriff and clerk in 2018.
Frank Scott, the first popularly elected Black mayor of Little Rock, easily won a third term in the November election.
Little Rock Mayor Frank Scott prepares to present Kamala Harris a key to the city at the Fisher-Shackleford Dinner, held at the Statehouse Convention Center in Little Rock, on Saturday, April 25, 2026. (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)
Another gain was in the race for a Maumelle-area House seat, where Democrat Cassandra Mayes defeated Republican Stephen Bright. The race was one of 10 House seats Democrats flipped, stripping Republicans of the 75-vote supermajority needed to pass most budget items.
In east Arkansas, Democrat Dexter Miller unseated Republican Rep. Mark McElroy.
Jefferson said building on those gains will require more work in boosting voter turnout, an area where Arkansas has ranked at or near the bottom of the country for years. But that will require state officials working to make it easier for people to register to vote rather than placing obstacles, he said.
“Do you really care about the diversity of the state of Arkansas and want to have people represented?” Jefferson said. “We have work to do.”
Jones isn’t shutting the door on trying again to make history. Days after his loss to Hill, Jones posted on Facebook that “2028 is just around the corner.”
“I have every reason to stay in the game and I have every reason to continue to fight,” he said.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: West Tennessee Megasite Authority to consider creating ‘guiding principles’ for data centers
description: As local governments throughout Tennessee are taking action to regulate where data centers can be built, the state-appointed board that governs the 4,100-acre Memphis Regional Megasite is considering drafting its own “guiding principles” for such resource-intensive projects. “It would be helpful if we had some guiding principles that we believe as an authori[...]
text:
The Megasite Authority of West Tennessee board meets at TCAT Stanton on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. The board is considering creating "guiding principles" around data centers and other resource-intensive development on the megasite's remaining available acreage. (Photo by Cassandra Stephenson/Tennessee Lookout)As local governments throughout Tennessee are taking action to regulate where data centers can be built, the state-appointed board that governs the 4,100-acre Memphis Regional Megasite is considering drafting its own “guiding principles” for such resource-intensive projects.
“It would be helpful if we had some guiding principles that we believe as an authority … that may address the environment and may address other issues that the community cares deeply about,” Deputy Governor and Tennessee Department of Economic and Community Development Stuart McWhorter said during a Megasite Authority of West Tennessee’s board meeting Thursday. McWhorter serves as an ex-officio member of the 11-person board.
“It’s good practice for us to be talking about this,” McWhorter said. “There will be conversations in the future about property that this body controls or presides over.”
Ford Motor Company’s BlueOval City and a battery plant now owned and operated by SK On Tennessee make up about 3,600 acres of the state-owned Megasite. A 45-acre Tennessee Valley Authority substation and a proposed 100-acre gas turbine peaking power plant leave about 300 acres available for future industrial use. 
The Megasite Authority of West Tennessee has exclusive authority to regulate land use within the Megasite, which follows its own zoning regulations. The most recent zoning code published on the authority’s website states that data centers are permitted “by right” in the general industrial zoning district, meaning they do not require a special use permit or additional site plan review. 
But the authority can also have discretion over which leases it approves.
“At the end of the day, it falls under our control as far as zoning, tenants and anything like that,” said board member Michael Banks, an attorney for nearby Stanton and Brownsville who was appointed to the board by outgoing Lt. Gov. Randy McNally. 
McWhorter said Thursday that he has no particular proposal in mind, but believes a set of guiding principles for supercomputing, data centers and advanced manufacturing would help the authority “set the tone.”
“We will hear more and more about this, and we’ll just be better prepared as a governing body,” McWhorter said.
The authority board must adhere to Tennessee’s sunshine laws, which require governing bodies of public entities to publicly conduct meetings and decisions.
Board Chairman Charlie Tuggle said he planned to form a subcommittee to begin discussing proposed guidelines.
The Megasite Authority of West Tennessee’s board will next meet on Jan. 13 at 10 a.m. at the Tennessee College of Applied Technology extension campus in Stanton.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Newly elected county attorney is not yet an Iowa-licensed lawyer
description: With only six weeks remaining before she’s scheduled to be sworn in, Worth County’s newly elected prosecutor doesn’t yet meet all the legal requirements to take office. In the 2026 race for Worth County attorney, challenger Dexter Banks, a Democrat, narrowly defeated the Republican incumbent, Jeffrey H. Greve. The unofficial results had Banks, who practices [...]
text:
(Photo by Peter Dazeley/Getty Images)With only six weeks remaining before she’s scheduled to be sworn in, Worth County’s newly elected prosecutor doesn’t yet meet all the legal requirements to take office.
In the 2026 race for Worth County attorney, challenger Dexter Banks, a Democrat, narrowly defeated the Republican incumbent, Jeffrey H. Greve. The unofficial results had Banks, who practices law in Minnesota, collecting 1,688 votes to Greve’s 1,658 votes.
Banks is scheduled to be sworn in as county attorney on Jan. 1, 2027 — but she doesn’t currently meet the legal requirements to take office.
Under Iowa law, an individual cannot be sworn in as county attorney if they are not licensed to practice law in Iowa. Banks is not yet a member of the Iowa bar and, until she is, she cannot act as Worth County’s legal counsel in civil matters or act as the county’s top prosecutor in criminal matters.
Banks said she submitted the necessary bar application to the Iowa Judicial Branch’s Office of Professional Regulation in June or July, and on Oct. 15, 2026, received confirmation the paperwork had been received and was being worked on.
Asked whether her application is likely to be approved by Jan. 1, 2027, she said, “That’s a good question. Obviously, I’d love to control that timeline … I will be meeting with the board of supervisors this coming Monday during their regular weekly meeting, along with the Winnebago County attorney, who has kind of taken me under her wing and is helping me. But this is really up to the bar association … I’m trying to be patient and just put some faith in the process and we’ll go from there.”



Quotation







My understanding is that she has to have her license by the first of January -- otherwise there will be a vacancy, and the supervisors of Worth County will appoint the next county attorney.


– Worth County Attorney Jeffrey Greve


Banks said she looked at the licensing requirements prior to launching her campaign and saw that it does not require an individual to be an Iowa-licensed attorney to seek election as county attorney, but it does require someone to be licensed before taking that office. Her eligibility was not an issue during the campaign, she said, adding she met the residency requirement by living in the county even while practicing law near Albert Lea, Minnesota, which is about 15 miles north of the Iowa-Minnesota border.
Iowa enables attorneys licensed in other states to gain admission to the Iowa bar without sitting for the bar exam through a process called “admission on motion.” That process is open to lawyers who have practiced law for five full years within the seven years immediately preceding the date of their Iowa application and who meet the character and fitness requirements spelled out in Iowa court rules.
It’s not entirely clear what will happen if Banks’ application is not approved by the time she’s scheduled to take office and Greve vacates the position.
Ashley Hunt Esquivel, director of communications for the Iowa Secretary of State’s Office, said the office has looked into the situation but that the Iowa Attorney General Office’s prosecuting attorneys training coordinator might be best suited to answer questions on the matter. The Iowa Capital Dispatch was unable to reach anyone in the coordinator’s office last week or this week.
Worth County Auditor Jacki A. Backhaus declined to speak to Banks’ eligibility to hold office and referred all questions on the matter to Greve, Banks’ opponent in the election.
“No one has asked me to look into this,” Greve said. “My understanding is that she has to have her license by the first of January — otherwise there will be a vacancy, and the supervisors of Worth County will appoint the next county attorney.”
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach the spokesperson for the Iowa Judicial Branch’s Office of Professional Regulation on Friday.

title: NC immigrants challenge ICE policy allowing re-detention after release
description: Livinton Sosa Martinez, a 41-year-old Nicaraguan man living in Greensboro, fled political persecution in his home country in 2022. Earlier this year, he was detained during a routine ICE check-in in Charlotte. His case is among hundreds of re-detentions in North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia since the Department of Homeland Security reversed a longsta[...]
text:
An ACLU lawsuit  challenges the Department of Homeland Security for re-detaining immigrants who are awaiting the outcome of their immigration cases. The case is being heard in Georgia where immigrants are held at the Stewart Detention Center, a facility run by the private prison company CoreCivic. (Photo by Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder)Livinton Sosa Martinez, a 41-year-old Nicaraguan man living in Greensboro, fled political persecution in his home country in 2022. Earlier this year, he was detained during a routine ICE check-in in Charlotte.
His case is among hundreds of re-detentions in North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia since the Department of Homeland Security reversed a longstanding immigration practice in May 2025, according to a lawsuit filed by the ACLU last week.
Under the previous policy, ICE generally did not re-detain immigrants who had been released from custody while awaiting the outcome of their immigration cases, provided they complied with release conditions, including attending scheduled check-ins and court hearings. 
Officers had to show that a person’s circumstances had changed in a major way, like a new criminal charge, before arresting them again. 
The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Georgia, challenges DHS’ decision to abandon the policy, which had been followed by the ICE Atlanta office for more than four decades.
The ACLU alleges that DHS abandoned the policy without explanation and adopted a new approach that allows immigration officers to re-arrest previously released immigrants without determining whether their circumstances have materially changed.
Sosa Martinez is one of four plaintiffs in the lawsuit, which also names Raquel Mariona Ebora, a 39-year-old Honduran woman in Dunn, along with two residents of Georgia.
According to the lawsuit, Sosa Martinez had attended his annual ICE check-ins and had no criminal history before he was detained March 19. He was transferred to Stewart Detention Center in Georgia, where he remained for several weeks before a federal judge ordered a bond hearing. He was subsequently released on a $10,000 bond.
He remains under ICE supervision and is required to report for in-person appointments every four weeks in Charlotte, according to the lawsuit.
“When I have to go to work, especially in Raleigh or Charlotte, my children cry because they are worried I will be re-detained again,” Sosa Martinez said in a statement provided by the ACLU. “I will continue to pursue my asylum case, but my life has a lot more uncertainty now. I know that I could be detained by ICE at any time even though I follow all the rules.”
Raquel Mariona Ebora was not detained, but her husband, Kelvin Lopez, was arrested during a routine ICE check-in in Charlotte on April 28. The couple, who fled Honduras in 2022, live in Dunn with their 3-year-old U.S. citizen son, who has autism. Lopez was released on bond a few weeks later after a federal judge ordered a hearing, but his arrest disrupted the family’s routine and made it harder to care for their son, according to the lawsuit. 
Both families were taken into immigration custody after crossing the border illegally in 2022 and later released on humanitarian parole, according to the lawsuit.
Jacqueline Landry, a legal fellow at the ACLU of North Carolina, said the policy shift has created constant fear and uncertainty for people who did what they were told.
ICE agents arrested US citizen at gunpoint in Charlotte, NC immigration advocates say

“These are people that have been following all the rules that the government set for them,” Landry said. “They’re going about their lives based on an understanding that as long as they follow the rules, they’ll be able to continue living in the community.”
In their complaint, the plaintiffs argue DHS violated the Administrative Procedure Act by tossing out a decades-old practice without explaining why or considering how the shift would affect people who relied on it. They also contend the arrests violate the Fourth Amendment because ICE is re-detaining people on the same immigration charges without showing anything has changed.
They are asking the judge to put the policy on hold while the case plays out in court. They also filed a motion earlier this week asking the Georgia court to certify the lawsuit as a class action. 
DHS did not respond to Newsline’s request for comment by publication time.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Commentary: Memphis is not progressive… yet. But we can be.
description: One of the conversations that will shape American politics after the 2026 elections is the conflict between so-called centrists and progressives within the Democratic Party. That debate is underway nationally. Some Democrats believe the party’s future rests in moderation and incrementalism. Others argue voters want something more ambitious: universal health [...]
text:
Despite voter registration efforts in Memphis and Shelby County, like the one conducted by The Equity Alliance, pictured here, only 44% of registered voters in Shelby County voted in the midterm election. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)One of the conversations that will shape American politics after the 2026 elections is the conflict between so-called centrists and progressives within the Democratic Party.
That debate is underway nationally. Some Democrats believe the party’s future rests in moderation and incrementalism. Others argue voters want something more ambitious: universal health care, stronger labor protections, higher wages, restraints on corporate power, less militarism and a stronger challenge to concentrated wealth.
Memphis will inevitably be pulled into that conversation. But before we start calling ourselves progressive, we need to be honest.
Memphis is not a progressive city…Yet. We’re still moderate, at best.  
We are a majority-Black city with significant Black political representation. Black women make up the majority on the Memphis City Council, Shelby County Commission and Memphis Shelby County School Board. We have also adopted policies once dismissed as too progressive for this region, including a wage floor above $15 an hour for Shelby County employees.
Those things matter. But representation is not liberation.
A city does not become progressive simply because Black people, women, queer people or other marginalized groups gain access to power. There is nothing inherently progressive about diversifying who administers an unjust system.



State Rep. Justin J. Pearson’s 9th Congressional District campaign also exposed some of our ideological limitations. Several elected leaders hedged their bets. Some appeared to believe Pearson would lose badly. Others seemed reluctant to associate themselves too closely with a candidate identified with a more confrontational, progressive politics. 


Sometimes oppression gets a new face and keeps the same address. That is not progressivism. Nor can progressivism become another ideological culture war where political sophistication is measured by mastering the latest vocabulary, canceling the right target, or disguising personal ambition as social justice.
For a majority-Black city like Memphis, progressivism must mean something deeper. It must mean building the self-determining political power and institutional capacity necessary to move Black people and other marginalized communities closer to genuine freedom. It must challenge economic exploitation, environmental injustice, inadequate health care, generational poverty, political exclusion, militarism and an American political order that too often asks Black people to become more loyal to the empire than the empire has ever been to us.
By that standard, Memphis has made progress. But we are not there yet.
The 2026 election exposed that contradiction.
Shelby County turnout increased. That matters. But only about 44% of registered voters cast ballots, leaving more than 328,000 registered Shelby County voters on the sidelines. Republicans won Tennessee’s 5th, 8th and 9th Congressional Districts by a combined total of fewer than 25,000 votes. The governor’s race was decided by less than 55,000 votes statewide. 
Had Black Memphians gotten 100,000 of those voters who sat out to participate we would’ve decided each Districts 5, 8, and 9 as well as the gubernatorial race right here in Memphis! 
The political power was here. We simply did not fully exercise it.
State Rep. Justin J. Pearson’s 9th Congressional District campaign also exposed some of our ideological limitations. Several elected leaders hedged their bets. Some appeared to believe Pearson would lose badly. Others seemed reluctant to associate themselves too closely with a candidate identified with a more confrontational, progressive politics.
I viewed much of that as political cowardice and miscalculation. But it would be too easy to blame elected officials alone. Their behavior also reflects a broader political culture.
If Memphis were already as progressive as some of us imagine ourselves to be, our electorate would likely look different. Political participation would be deeper. Organizing would be more sustained. Voter education would not be seasonal. People would be more willing to imagine possibilities beyond what consultants, donors and gatekeepers tell us is realistic.
That is the work before us.
Pearson accepts loss in U.S. District 9 race, but says ‘Tennessee politics will never be the same’

A progressive Memphis should mean Black workers earning wages that allow them not merely to survive, but to build wealth and interrupt generational poverty. It should reject the idea that every Black person must become a makeshift entrepreneur just to achieve economic security. Everybody does not need to own a business. Workers deserve dignity, stability, benefits, and a wage sufficient to live and thrive.
A progressive Memphis should mean health care people can reasonably access, clean air, safe water, healthy neighborhoods and protection from environmental hazards that disproportionately burden Black communities. 
It should mean affordable housing without displacement, public education treated as a public good rather than a commodity, strong labor rights, serious investment in public transportation and public safety strategies that do not treat policing as the only legitimate response to social disorder. Politically, it should require enough courage and imagination to stop confusing what is familiar with what is possible.
That is where Memphis has to go next. Not toward performative progressivism, a politics obsessed with labels, or an ideological purity contest. And certainly not toward a politics where ambitious people learn progressive and social justice language because they believe it is the fastest route to personal advancement.
We need something more mature: a political culture rooted in Black freedom, democratic participation, economic justice, community power and self-determination.
That will require massive political education, year-round voter engagement, and a larger civic imagination across our churches, unions, neighborhoods, schools, organizations, and institutions. Most importantly, it will require political courage.
Because progressive politics, if it means anything, must be about more than who gets elected. It must be about what those elections make possible for people whose lives have historically been constrained by systems they did not design.
Memphis is not progressive.
Not yet.
But we have moved closer.
And if we are serious about 2027 — when there will be a Memphis mayor’s race —  2028 and beyond, we have an opportunity to become something more righteous than the labels we casually use.
We have an opportunity to become a city where political representation finally matures into political power. And political power finally moves us toward freedom.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama Power rate cut amounts to about $4 a month
description: Alabama’s largest electric utility said Friday it would propose a cut of about $4 a month in the average household’s power bills. In a filing with the Alabama Public Service Commission, Alabama Power said it could reduce customer rates by about $160 million in total in 2027. The company said in a news release Friday […]
text:
The logo for Alabama Power, as seen on January 24, 2023. Alabama Power said Friday it planned to cut residential customer rates by about $4 a month, or about 2% for the average residential electricity consumer. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)Alabama’s largest electric utility said Friday it would propose a cut of about $4 a month in the average household’s power bills.
In a filing with the Alabama Public Service Commission, Alabama Power said it could reduce customer rates by about $160 million in total in 2027. The company said in a news release Friday that the reduction will save a household about $50 per year, or about $4 per month, in electricity costs for using about 1,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The utility and several Republican elected officials praised the cut Friday afternoon, with some saying it proved the value of data centers, whose construction and potential disruption to communities became a major issue in the state during the 2026 campaign.
Moses Feagin, chief financial officer and treasurer for Alabama Power, said in the filing that the rate reduction “demonstrates the ability of large load data centers to promote positive benefits to all other customers.”
“One such benefit is the fact that these service agreements cover not only the cost of serving the projects, but also include contributions toward the existing power system,” he said in the filing.
Gov.-elect Tommy Tuberville, who attacked data center critics early in the campaign before saying he would allow local communities to decide whether to let them in, said in a social media statement Friday that “the liberal media and the unknown actors trying to stop America’s progress have had the microphone for too long.”
“Under my leadership, the expansion of data centers and the investment in our infrastructure is going to reduce utility cost and today we see that first step,” the statement said.
But critics were skeptical. Alabama residents pay some of the highest residential electricity costs in the South. In August, Alabama residents paid about 16.33 cents per kilowatt-hour, according to EIA. By contrast, Georgia residents paid 15.90 cents per kilowatt-hour; Florida residents paid 14.99 cents per kilowatt-hour, Mississippi residents paid 14.41 cents per kilowatt-hour and Tennessee residents paid 13.42 cents per kilowatt-hour.
Daniel Tait, executive director of Energy Alabama, a nonprofit that advocates for more renewable energy, said in a statement Friday that Alabama Power customers should be wary of the claims made by the company.
“The company credits data centers, but its own numbers show there would be no cut without a roughly $180 million drop in its tax bill, which the company ties to nuclear tax credits from the Inflation Reduction Act,” Tait said. “Even after this action, the company’s own filing shows its return on equity, a marker for its profits, remaining above the national average.”
Senate President Pro Tem Garlan Gudger, R-Cullman, said in a statement Friday that he credits the rate reduction to SB 270, sponsored by Sen. Lance Bell, R-Pell City, that was introduced in the spring.
The bill requires the PSC, the state agency that oversees investor-owned utilities, to consider the impact that large load data centers would have for residents. That includes ensuring that data centers will pay for the additional electricity they will use to operate the facility.
“When the Senate passed SB 270, we made a simple promise to the people of Alabama – if big data centers want to come here, they cover their own costs, and they leave Alabama families better off,” Gudger said. “Today we’re seeing that promise pay off in every family’s power bill.”
Electricity rates became a central issue that drew the attention of lawmakers during the 2026 session as residents complained about their electricity bills. The House this spring passed HB 475, sponsored by Rep. Mack Butler, R-Rainbow City, that originally required the PSC to convene a rate case periodically.
The rate case would have allowed the public to comment on the electricity rates that Alabama Power and other utilities charge customers. However, the legislation was changed dramatically when it arrived in the Senate after it was approved in the House.
The newer version passed by the Legislature expanded the PSC from three to seven. Gov. Kay Ivey appointed four additional members in June who will gradually be replaced by popular election. It also removed the periodic rate case hearing requirement. The bill created a cabinet-level post, the Secretary of Energy, with the authority to decide the PSC agenda and to convene a rate hearing. A supermajority of the PSC, five of the seven members, can also convene a rate case and alter the agenda.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Commentary: Remembering Mark Massa, and all my teachers, with gratitude
description: I hope you had a teacher like Mark Massa. Whenever he gave a lecture at Fordham University, he would prowl around the front of the classroom. In his round glasses and clerical collar or business-casual wardrobe (the preferred habit of Fordham’s Jesuit community), he would gesture with his hands or lean over to drive a […]
text:
Rev. Mark Massa, S.J. is seen in a 2019 photo. (Courtesy Fordham University)I hope you had a teacher like Mark Massa.
Whenever he gave a lecture at Fordham University, he would prowl around the front of the classroom. In his round glasses and clerical collar or business-casual wardrobe (the preferred habit of Fordham’s Jesuit community), he would gesture with his hands or lean over to drive a point home.
Massa used the Socratic method. He often opened a class by asking a randomly chosen student about that day’s assigned readings. It was a powerful incentive to show up prepared. Because the questions were coming, and you might end up being the one expected to provide the answers.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Punctuality was the other red line. A student who arrived after class began could count on a sarcastic “Good morning! How are we today?” as they rushed to their desk. One of my fellow undergraduates told me that she saw Massa ask his class for a quarter, which he took to a pay phone outside the classroom to call a student who had overslept. (That student came running in, breathless, before class ended.)
But within those boundaries, you got to experience an exceptionally gifted professor. Massa’s field of study was American Catholicism, but as befits a priest, he had a deep understanding of theology and church teachings. Nor was he afraid to share his disagreements with them. I once heard him take apart “Humanae Vitae,” the 1968 encyclical that forbade Catholics from taking birth control, saying that the pope’s argument that it interfered with a natural process was also an argument against taking Tylenol to treat a fever.
Heady stuff for a kid from a conservative Catholic household. Like the best instructors, Massa had presence. He could provoke, but never in an insulting way. He could crack funny jokes that also reflected the points he made. Massa cared about what he taught and got us to care, too.
But his most effective motivational tool was treating us like peers. Massa wanted us to do the work because he seemed eager to hear our thoughts about the texts. He treated our opinions, no matter how far off they might have been, with respect and encouragement. You liked interacting with him. You liked watching other students bounce ideas off of him. And his classes often became free-flowing, stimulating discussions. Exactly what you want a course to be.
Nearly all of us who took one of his classes wanted to reciprocate this funny and often sly priest’s interest in our intellectual efforts. Massa in turn could be very generous. When I asked him for one of his prized recommendation letters, he wrote a flattering piece set at a Fordham honors ceremony. When he gave me a copy, I thanked him but also pointed out I hadn’t actually been at the ceremony. “Well, we know that, but they don’t,” he replied.
Massa formed relationships with many of my fellow undergraduates that lasted decades. When he unexpectedly passed away on Nov. 15, there was an outpouring of grief from his colleagues at Fordham and Boston College, and from his former students. It’s hard to lose a great mind; it’s even harder when that mind works with a generous soul.
Teaching is a profession. The ability to teach is a gift. I count myself lucky that in my nearly two decades in school, most of my instructors – even those who taught subjects I struggled to master – were engaged and engaging people.
And it’s hard for me to fully convey my gratitude. Sometimes you see what they’ve done instantly; other times it takes years. For those of us outside the profession, it can be hard to appreciate the challenges a teacher faces. There’s the physical strain of standing and projecting your voice to hold the attention of sometimes disconnected students. There’s the intellectual and often emotional battle to reach a child dealing with issues that impede their education.
That many succeed is a mark of skill and professionalism that needs to be celebrated.
Alabama’s teachers may soon face more struggles. Pay raises don’t appear likely next year, and healthcare costs may go up. We have an incoming governor who has expressed overt hostility toward public school teachers and wants to expand the CHOOSE Act, the state voucher program, that would further reduce what limited resources are available to them.
So this Thanksgiving week, let me say thank you to the teachers who navigate the micro and macro challenges of their jobs every day for my children and yours, quietly making this world better, in the present and the future.
I last saw Mark Massa at a reunion in 2009. As we caught up, he gradually turned the conversation toward Alabama political history. I was many years removed from being a student. But he showed the same interest in my thinking as he had when I was an undergraduate. Like the best teachers, Massa found something worthwhile in each of his students. And I hope he understood we saw something priceless in him.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Department of Reassuring Language: Bringing children home is not same as providing quality care
description: I’m beginning to wonder whether Gov. Patrick Morrisey has established a new office somewhere in Charleston: the Department of Reassuring Language. Its mission? Give government initiatives comforting names emphasizing hope, compassion and opportunity. Make certain the public hears the promises. Consider the Hope Scholarship. Who could object to giving childre[...]
text:
Gov. Patrick Morrisey on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, announces that the Barboursville School, a residential treatment facility for children, will reopen next year. The school closed earlier this year. (West Virginia Office of Gov. Patrick Morrisey video screenshot)I’m beginning to wonder whether Gov. Patrick Morrisey has established a new office somewhere in Charleston: the Department of Reassuring Language.
Its mission? Give government initiatives comforting names emphasizing hope, compassion and opportunity. Make certain the public hears the promises.
Consider the Hope Scholarship. Who could object to giving children hope?
Now comes “Bring Them Home,” an initiative to return West Virginia children receiving residential treatment outside the state to facilities closer to their families. Who could object? Certainly not me.
But bringing children home and providing comprehensive, evidence-based treatment are two very different accomplishments.
Bruce Springsteen’s rendition of Bob Dylan’s “Chimes of Freedom” speaks to those whose suffering too often goes unheard. I think of these children when I hear it.
Many children requiring residential treatment have experienced profound adversity, disrupted attachments and complex psychological and neurodevelopmental difficulties. Some ask a fundamental question: “Where do I belong?”
For nearly 30 years, hundreds of miles from my West Virginia home, I have provided psychological care to children with complex psychological, neurodevelopmental, medical and behavioral conditions across a variety of clinical settings. My concern is whether the children I have spent much of my professional life caring for will receive the treatment, protection and understanding they deserve.
The children at the center of West Virginia’s initiative face many of the same challenges. The difference is that they are West Virginia’s children.
These children need more than a residential bed. Keeping a child near home is a matter of proximity. Helping that child experience belonging, safety and connection requires high-quality psychological care.
The savings are remarkably precise
According to the West Virginia Department of Human Services, average annual out-of-state residential placement costs approximately $250,025, compared with $120,333 in-state. The projected difference is $129,692 per child. For 50 children, the projected annual savings approach $6.48 million, before certain additional expenses.
Impressive calculations. But where is an equally detailed account of the treatment children will receive?
Lower cost is not proof of effective treatment; higher cost is not proof of better care. These statewide averages also do not establish that children in these settings have comparable clinical needs. What explains the difference: staffing, specialized services, treatment intensity, or genuine efficiencies?
We should never establish a financial target and then construct a treatment program around it. First determine what these children need. Then determine what providing that care will cost.
36 beds. But what treatment?
On Nov. 12, Morrisey announced a five-year lease with Utah-based Youth Health Associates to reopen the former Barboursville School, with up to 36 beds and a projected 50 to 60 jobs.
We know the capacity, jobs, and projected savings. Where is the treatment program?
Youth Health Associates publicly describes residential services for a distinct population: adolescent males with histories of sexual misconduct. Reporting identifies eight existing facilities, seven in Utah and one in Texas. That experience warrants consideration, but serving a particular population does not, by itself, demonstrate the clinical competencies needed for every population. 
The governor has described a broader range of complex treatment needs at Barboursville. What qualifications, treatment protocols, and documented outcomes support that expanded role? Which children can this facility appropriately treat, and what safeguards will guide their care? The governor’s announcement suggests that the facility may serve children and adolescents with a broader range of complex, high-acuity needs than those described in the contracted provider’s publicly available services.
Residential supervision, nursing services, social work and daily care are essential. But they cannot, by themselves, substitute for the psychological expertise and medical care required by children with complex conditions.
For children with severe, complex conditions, doctoral-level psychological expertise must be available and integrated into diagnostic assessment, clinical formulation, evidence-based intervention and multidisciplinary care, according to their individual needs.
Who will independently evaluate outcomes? A residential bed is not an intensive treatment protocol.
When children’s voices go unheard
The U.S. Senate Finance Committee’s 2024 report, Warehouses of Neglect, documented serious concerns about staffing, treatment, oversight and child safety across residential facilities. Its findings do not predict what will happen at Barboursville. They do demonstrate why independent oversight matters.
Children with emotional and behavioral difficulties are sometimes labeled manipulative, dishonest or unreliable. When they report mistreatment, those very difficulties can become reasons adults discount their words. For children with histories of maltreatment, the search for attachment and belonging can increase their vulnerability to further exploitation. These children need adults prepared to listen, investigate, and protect them.
The expertise is already here
Marshall University is practically next door. Its American Psychological Association-accredited doctoral psychology program was established in part to prepare doctoral psychologists to serve rural and underserved West Virginia communities. Marshall’s Joan C. Edwards School of Medicine adds medical expertise; West Virginia University also offers substantial psychological and medical expertise.
Were these nationally recognized programs consulted? Could they help develop treatment, provide professional supervision and independently evaluate outcomes? If high quality care is central to this initiative, why isn’t that expertise more visible in the state’s public explanation?
Bringing children home to what?
Family proximity can support attachment and continuity of care. But proximity is not treatment. Clinical needs must determine staffing, resources, and interventions, not projected savings.
The children whose suffering echoes through Chimes of Freedom deserve more than reassuring promises. These children are West Virginia’s children.
Hope is not an educational service. Home is not a treatment protocol.
We should measure success not by how much money we save on our children, but by how much better we care for them.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: More New Jersey parents need help affording childcare, advocates say
description: Advocates want state officials to increase funding for childcare vouchers, saying far too many families can't afford to access care, keeping them out of the economy.
text:
Patricia Velez, the owner and director of Wonder World Nursery School, in Union on Nov. 17, 2026. Velez says parents are struggling to afford childcare at facilities like hers. She's urged the state to expand funding for childcare vouchers. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey has ramped up what it spends to help people afford childcare, but people like Patricia Velez, the longtime owner of Wonder World childcare center in Union, say that too many families are still struggling to get the services they need. 
“Ultimately you want to keep parents in the workforce. And you want to keep kids in programs that will help them,” Velez told the New Jersey Monitor. 
When families can’t get care, “everybody suffers. The economy suffers. The child misses out on the skills they get in child care,” Velez said. 
An advocacy coalition launched earlier this year, Start Strong NJ, wants the state to invest an additional $35 million annually for three years to increase the number of childcare vouchers available to help low-income families pay for licensed programs. 
The additional money would eventually add about 9,000 slots to the program, according to Start Strong, which includes advocates for children, early education groups and multiple business organizations. This year some 77,500 families get help paying for childcare, with the amount each receives based on their income. 
Campaign Director Sharon Levine said New Jersey misses out on some $5 billion a year in lost wages, revenue and productivity as a result of unaffordable childcare. The cost of a licensed program is now nearly $20,000 a year here, she said. 
“I like to say it’s sort of the linchpin. If you don’t have affordable, stable childcare, people can’t show up for their jobs,” Levine said, noting many people can’t work remotely. 
There are also benefits for the child, advocates said. At Wonder World, kids ages 2 ½ to 5 years old do individual and group activities based on their age, learning colors, numbers, even basic science when the leaves change in the fall, Velez said, in addition to gaining social and language skills.
Wonder World Nursery School in Union on Nov. 17, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
“I know some people like to dismiss it as babysitting, but it definitely is not,” Levine said. “It is a time in a child’s life where they are learning so much, their brains are growing the fastest, and they are absorbing just a ton of new information.”  
Gov. Mikie Sherrill budgeted $582 million for childcare subsidies in the current year, budget documents show, up from just under $564 million last year. Her office declined to comment on plans for next year. 
“As a mom of four, Governor Sherrill understands how critical access to affordable childcare is for working parents,” said Maggie Garbarino, her deputy press secretary. “While the Trump Administration continues to drive up everyday costs, New Jersey is laser focused on affordability and easing the strain on our families’ household budgets.”
Velez, at Wonder World, said the affordability crisis is clear when she sees families struggling to cover the cost of care for multiple children. Many earn just above the income limit for the state voucher program, she said, which is now at 200% of the federal poverty level, or $66,000 for a family of four.
“If they’re even a dollar above the eligibility, they don’t get it,” Velez said. 
Velez would also love to pay her staff more, but she said her rising costs make that impossible. Levine, with Start Strong, said the wages — which average less than $15 an hour statewide — make it hard to retain workers, no matter how much they love caring for children. 
Start Strong would like New Jersey to boost wages for these workers and increase the current income limit for the voucher program, Levine said. But the priority is expanding the pool of existing benefits to reach more families, she said, noting other states have done more to make childcare affordable. 
“The state of New Jersey shouldn’t be looking at childcare as an expense. They should be looking at it as an investment in families and an investment in the greater good of the state of New Jersey,” Levine said.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Appalachian advocates urge incoming Congress to bolster flood response after numerous disasters
description: A coalition of environmental and Appalachian advocacy organizations across several states, including Kentucky, is urging the incoming Democratic-controlled U.S. Congress to bolster funding and streamline bureaucracy to better respond to and prepare for flooding disasters. The Appalachian Flood Resilience Coalition published a new report Thursday with recomme[...]
text:
Jackson, the Breathitt County seat, on July 29, 2022. (Photo by Michael Swensen/Getty Images)A coalition of environmental and Appalachian advocacy organizations across several states, including Kentucky, is urging the incoming Democratic-controlled U.S. Congress to bolster funding and streamline bureaucracy to better respond to and prepare for flooding disasters.
The Appalachian Flood Resilience Coalition published a new report Thursday with recommendations for increased funding for flood recovery and adaptation, along with fewer barriers for lower-income communities to access that aid. 
Jessica Arriens, a National Wildlife Federation program director for energy and climate change, told reporters Thursday that “lots of turmoil” at the Federal Emergency Management Agency and other federal agencies and natural disasters, including Hurricane Helene, led the coalition to publish a new policy report aimed at the incoming Congress. 
“I think Helene, in particular, really demonstrated the depth of the challenge facing Appalachia’s rural and mountainous communities that are trying to recover from and build resilience to floods,” Arriens said. “It also put, I think, Appalachia on the national stage as a place that’s particularly flood vulnerable.” 
The Trump administration has sought to cut FEMA staff and shift more responsibility for disaster response to state and local governments, offering sweeping changes earlier this year that could reduce the number of disasters the federal government approves funding for. Meanwhile, Appalachian communities across the region, including in Kentucky this summer, have faced repeated instances of destructive and deadly flooding. 
The report was co-authored by the regional policy group ReImagine Appalachia, the National Wildlife Foundation, the North Carolina-based environmental group Appalachian Voices, the Virginia-based environmental group Wetlands Watch and the Kentucky-based nonprofit legal group Appalachian Citizens’ Law Center. 
Many of the broad recommendations in the report remain similar to another flood policy report published by the coalition in 2024, including: 

Increasing flood mitigation funding through grant programs such as the Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities (BRIC) and reducing the fund matching requirements for “economically distressed” communities across FEMA’s recovery and adaptation programs.
Move forward with reforms, including some offered in the bipartisan FEMA Act of 2025, to simplify disaster aid applications, increase the available disaster case managers and extend the timeframe for when temporary housing is available to flood survivors. 
Provide proper funding to federal agencies such as the United States Geological Survey and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration to better forecast flooding in Appalachian watersheds.
Invest in “nature-based” hazard mitigation and ensure coal mine sites are properly reclaimed to “restore natural hydrologic functions as well as the land’s ecological health.”

Brendan Muckian-Bates, a policy & advocacy associate at the Appalachian Citizens’ Law Center in Letcher County, said he believes the policy platform can gain traction with new members of Congress beyond Appalachia, with the coalition working to hear how flooding and related issues have impacted different Congressional districts across the country. 
“I think there’s certainly a lot of different ways that we can take the information here, that is certainly very Appalachian-specific, but highlighting those common issues, whether it is private roads and bridges, increased flood insurance costs,” Muckian-Bates said.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Commentary: A veteran’s most formidable opponent? A proposed fracking operation in his neighborhood.
description: My wife and I are retired Army veterans who continued service for 10 years as government civilians on a base overseas. Last summer, after 35 years of moving, we decided to plant roots in Colorado. Shortly after, we learned Verdad Resources had proposed a large-scale fracking operation 7,400 feet from our front door. Now, opposing […]
text:
(Photo by Andy Bosselman for Colorado Newsline)My wife and I are retired Army veterans who continued service for 10 years as government civilians on a base overseas. Last summer, after 35 years of moving, we decided to plant roots in Colorado.
Shortly after, we learned Verdad Resources had proposed a large-scale fracking operation 7,400 feet from our front door. Now, opposing the Century Oil and Gas Development plan has become my unpaid job. Why? I can’t unlearn what I have about how unequivocally disruptive and harmful fracking is to our public health and environment.
Notably, I’ve learned that folks informed about residential fracking are against it. Those who don’t know about it but learn become against it, too.
Weld County is known as oil and gas friendly, yet all I’ve spoken to agree that this operation doesn’t belong among neighborhoods. Even the Windsor Town Board shared its opposition with Weld County before the Weld County Oil and Gas Energy Department approved this ill-conceived oil and gas development plan.
Why?
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
We’re scared after learning of the link between childhood leukemia and fracking sites. A 13-year UCHealth Anschutz study, published nationally last year by the American Association of Cancer Research, showed adverse effects up to eight miles away but even more directly impacting children within three miles. Weld RE-4 has six schools and Poudre School District has 2 schools within three miles of the Century Pad.
We’re scared of other chronic effects correlated to fracking operations: birth defects, asthma, heart disease, etc. Colorado’s 2,000-foot setback means nothing when it comes to health. Emissions go with the wind, across towns and county lines and surprisingly long distances. We are still learning about the dangers.
We’re scared of the potential for a truck accident while hauling toxic wastewater on our local roads. As a truck company commander, I’ve seen an overturned fuel truck, but that pales in comparison to an accident with hazardous material in terms of air and ground water contamination. The interruptions to commerce and residents are unthinkable yet plausible in light of major oil and gas accidents in the area: Chevron’s Bishop Well disaster in Galeton, the 2017 Stromberger well pad site explosion in Windsor, and the PDC Energy well failure in 2013 near the proposed site.
Fearful Windsor families are selling their homes, and I know another that decided against moving to Timnath. A friend learned of it two weeks after moving into her first home. Neither of us can afford to move away.
I was a career soldier. I don’t inject hyperbole into such matters. I use factual descriptions and data and trends to arrive at my conclusions. Anything I relate here is without exaggeration and, accordingly, I believe the fear is justified, especially with Verdad’s poor record of safety.
According to the Energy and Carbon Management Commission’s data, Verdad had 35 failures in eight years — 16 of those 35 in the last three years. In the last 15 years, Windsor’s population grew by 2.5 times. We can’t trust Verdad to operate such a large operation near tens of thousands. Everyday, homes are built closer to this site.
I’m not alone in feeling this is too big an endeavor with so many so close. More residents are writing to elected leaders and not just in Windsor. Folks in Timnath, and Severance are also taking action. They’re educating themselves, speaking out at town board meetings, talking to their neighbors, and contacting media outlets. The “what ifs” just don’t seem close to worth it.
In my profession, we considered the most likely and dangerous outcomes and planned accordingly. If we determined the benefits don’t outweigh the risks, we told our commanders that and sought alternate courses of action.
It’s time to do that now.
