name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Immigrant workers fight widespread wage theft in Wisconsin construction industry
description: On a bright October afternoon, David Oritz-Whittingham, 25, walked into a construction contractor’s office in an industrial park in Middleton, accompanied by two women from Mexico, Maria, 54, and Ana, 53. Ortiz-Whittingham, an organizer with Worker Justice Wisconsin, an interfaith group that fights for workers’ rights, was bringing the women to the office of[...]
text:
Robert Christl, executive director of Wisconsin Worker Justice, speaks at a protest outside the Monona Terrace Convention Center in downtown Madison on Nov. 18. "We are here because exploitation is happening on construction sites across our state, including sites that receives loans and tax credits from the Wisconsin Housing and Economic Development Authority," Christl said. (Ruth Conniff/Wisconsin Examiner)On a bright October afternoon, David Oritz-Whittingham, 25, walked into a construction contractor’s office in an industrial park in Middleton, accompanied by two women from Mexico, Maria, 54, and Ana, 53. Ortiz-Whittingham, an organizer with Worker Justice Wisconsin, an interfaith group that fights for workers’ rights, was bringing the women to the office of the NCH Construction company to confront their employer and demand thousands of dollars in unpaid wages.
Not only had NCH failed to pay them for six weeks of work they did as painters on a new apartment complex in Pleasant Prairie, Maria and Ana told the Examiner, their employer kicked them out of the house he had been providing near their worksite, threatening to call the local sheriff if they didn’t leave. (The Examiner is not publishing the women’s last names because of the threat of immigration enforcement actions against them.) 
Maria and Ana crossed the border from Mexico together two years ago to earn money in the U.S. and send it home to their families. In May, they traveled to Wisconsin from a different job on a construction site in Texas, after they were hired over the phone by a man who said he was a subcontractor to work on the Inspire Prairie Springs apartments built by Stevens Construction, one of the five largest construction firms in the state. They didn’t have any friends or family in the area. When they were kicked off the job without pay and facing eviction, they became desperate. They saw a post on TikTok from Worker Justice Wisconsin, describing the group’s work helping victims of wage theft, and reached out to Ortiz-Whittingham,.
“It’s good we connected with David,” Maria told the Examiner in Spanish. “Any advance is because of him. Because with us, we couldn’t even get them to answer a message.”
Maria and Ana’s experience is typical of the cases he sees, Ortiz-Whittingham told the Examiner. Almost all of the workers who come to Worker Justice Wisconsin for help are Hispanic immigrants, many of whom have traveled long distances for a job and don’t have anywhere to turn for support in the local community. Often they have been misclassified as independent contractors instead of as regular employees, giving employers an excuse for withholding their wages, he said. 
David Ortiz-Whittingham, construction organizer for Worker Justice Wisconsin (photo courtesy WJW)
“We don’t know how big the problem is with this company,” Oritz-Whittingham said of NCH. “What we do know is that the story of these women is representative. It’s a perfect example of misclassification, wage theft, possibly labor trafficking, which are the most common problems we see in construction.” 
A 2021 study by the Midwest Economic Policy Institute found that one in five construction workers in the Upper Midwest was illegally misclassified as an independent contractor or paid off the books. 
“It’s pervasive,” Burt Johnson, an attorney for the Northern Midwest Carpenters Regional Council, told the Examiner. Johnson’s union covers Wisconsin, Michigan, Minnesota and the Dakotas.
Especially in Wisconsin, he said, there’s “a race among contractors to see how skilled they are at exploiting a vulnerable workforce. There’s essentially no bottom to it. The way the workers are treated is abysmal. It’s a problem we see every day.”
Confronting the construction contractors
When Ortiz-Whittingham arrived at the NCH office with Maria and Ana, an older man greeted them at the door and told them that his son, Geoffrey Hartnell, the owner of NCH, was not in the office. He dialed his phone and held it up so they could hear the call going to his son’s voicemail. “He’s out on a job,” the man said. Ortiz-Whittingham asked to leave a message, explaining that “it’s becoming very urgent” that the workers get paid. Maria and Ana had nowhere to stay and could not afford a hotel that night. Ortiz-Whittingham later reached out to Project RESPECT, a nonprofit that helps victims of human trafficking, to try to find them shelter space. Walking back to his car through the parking lot at NCH, he apologized.
But his efforts were not entirely unsuccessful. He received an email from Hartnell on Oct. 12, the same day as his surprise visit to NCH, which he shared with the Examiner, confirming that Maria and Ana were each owed more than $7,000. That was less than the $9,539 and $10,194 Ortiz-Whittingham had calculated the women were owed, but Maria and Ana were relieved and prepared to accept what NCH seemed ready to offer. In the same email, Hartnell acknowledged that five of Maria and Ana’s coworkers, also represented by Worker Justice Wisconsin, were owed thousands of dollars each for work at Inspire Prairie Springs and another Stevens project, the NOVA apartments in Green Bay. After the email, however, there was silence.
Ortiz-Whittingham made good on his promise to find temporary housing for Maria and Ana in Madison. He also took them to visit the corporate headquarters of Stevens Construction. When they arrived unannounced, the construction firm’s general counsel, David Bohl, met with them and listened to their story, they said. Bohl gave them two checks for $500 each, calling it a “donation” to help cover the cost of a hotel through the weekend. He expressed optimism that Stevens and NCH would work things out and that the workers would be paid by Monday, possibly through a joint check that Stevens and NCH would issue together out of the money Stevens was paying NCH on its contract.
But on Monday, Ortiz-Whittingham said, Bohl revised the plan. NCH was “so far in the hole as far as the work they were doing that there wouldn’t be any more money going to NCH,” he said Bohl told him over the phone. “He couldn’t write joint checks after all.”
Bohl and Stevens Construction did not respond to multiple voicemail messages and emails requesting comment for this story over a two-week period.
Stevens Construction offices in Madison (Photo by Ruth Conniff/Wisconsin Examiner)
‘I don’t really feel bad for the folks’
In a phone interview with the Examiner, Hartnell, the owner of NCH Construction, acknowledged that he had calculated Maria and Ana were owed $7,245 and $7,647. But, he said, “Stevens is the crux of the problem. They haven’t paid me since July.” 
Hartnell said he recently resolved his own dispute with Stevens, after the larger company alleged that NCH hadn’t completed the work outlined in its contract and that NCH owed Stevens money. “Frankly, it’s pretty messy,” Hartnell told the Examiner. “And they also billed me for a lot of stuff that’s not even in my contract. So it’s like, what the hell, guys? So we just kind of agreed to put the guns down. Let’s just kind of figure out what we can actually prove and pay for. So they’re letting me walk away without litigating the sh-t out of it, because I don’t have pockets that are that deep, frankly.”
As Hartnell explained it, he came up short and doesn’t have the money to pay Maria and Ana. “It’s up to Stevens,” he said. “A lot of folks are not getting paid. They are owning that process. … There’s a lot of people that are hurting because of them.”
After the phone interview, Hartnell sent a follow-up email to the Examiner clarifying that Stevens does not plan to pay the workers either. He copied Bohl, Stevens’ general counsel, on the message. 
“Stevens is not taking responsibility for any employees directly employed by NCH regarding the Inspire Prairie Springs job site,” Hartnell wrote. “Stevens and NCH have resolved any peripheral contractual disagreements to our satisfaction.” 
As for the workers, “A lot of them didn’t show up at all. So, I mean, I don’t really feel bad for the folks,” Hartnell told the Examiner. 
Hartnell denied that he was the workers’ employer or that he provided them housing. He said he provided the housing to a man he sometimes works with (who was copied on Hartnell’s emails at an NCH email address). “… he’s the one that brought them on. [He] and I have been working together for a while, but that’s just kind of how that is,” Hartnell said.
Asked if he gave the man money to pay Maria and Ana, Hartnell said, “That’s what we were, yeah, supposed to be doing. But at the same time, too, sometimes I just gave it to them directly. And I mean, they overbilled quite a bit in June and July.” 
Hartnell confirmed that he’d calculated unpaid wages owed to all of the NCH workers, including Maria and Ana, totalling more than $50,000 in his Oct. 12 email to Worker Justice Wisconsin and Stevens. But in his phone interview with the Examiner he said he wasn’t sure the workers were really owed that money after all. 
“I tried to assert that to Stevens, so that they could try and get some of that money, because at the base level I do care about people,” Hartnell said. “But at the same time, Stevens is probably correct that they were not on site a lot. A lot of those hours are probably bogus.”
Maria and Ana tell a different story 
Maria and Ana said they sent text messages to their supervisor at the start and end of every shift and took pictures to show the work they had completed.
At first, after they were hired over the phone and moved up to Wisconsin, things went smoothly, they said. In May they moved in with the other workers in the house NCH provided. For the first few weeks, they said, they were paid a good wage, $23 an hour, in weekly installments. But in June their supervisor told them NCH was low on funds and wouldn’t be able to pay them until July. Since they had free housing, they were able to continue working. But July came and they were still not paid.
In mid-July, inspectors arrived at the work site, Maria said. The workers didn’t know who they were or where they were from. “They asked us if we were doing OK at work, if they were forcing us to work, if we suffered any problems,” she said. “So they got to the point where they asked me how we were being paid. And I said well, we don’t know because they are not paying us. And there were people there from Stevens and people from NCH. So they were made aware around the 15th of July that we were not being paid.”
“The person who 100% knew that we were not being paid was the foreman from Stevens,” said Ana. “Because at that moment the foreman spoke with [our NCH supervisor], and he said, ‘Listen, your workers are complaining that they aren’t being paid.’ So from that moment on, [the supervisor] started treating us poorly, because we opened our mouths.”
On July 15, Hartnell got in touch with the women directly, they said, and gave them partial back payments and a promise to pay the rest of their wages going forward. But they worked through the month of August and the first two weeks of September without any pay.
“Things got worse and worse. People left,” Maria said.
“They were yelling at us: ‘Run up to this room and that room, hurry up and clean up, hurry up and tape,’” Ana said. “We had to do it all ourselves because there were so few people.”
Screenshot of an online ad for apartments at the new Inspire Prairie Spring development
“We were the last ones there – two women, all alone. We papered all 48 apartments on each floor, three floors. We did it all. Painting, papering, making sure the alarms didn’t get paint on them. And they never paid us,” said Maria.
“We should have known,” Ana said. She and Maria didn’t want to stop working, she said, because if they left they might lose all their back wages. Even before the other workers left, their supervisor had stopped showing up on the site. He “didn’t want to show his face. Some of the young men were angry. He was afraid,” Ana said.
“Dummies that we didn’t realize,” she added, her voice cracking with emotion. “We were all ‘new people’ from far away.”
“On Sept. 15, [NCH] sent us a text saying now you are no longer part of Stevens, you can’t work here, you have to leave the house,” Maria said. “With no money, no place to live, nothing.”
‘Gray area’ of the law
Whether or not he is responsible for paying the workers as employees, or whether they are subcontractors, is “a gray area,” Hartnell told the Examiner. “That’s a question for their attorney.”
“Paid when paid. That’s very, very common in the construction industry, almost every commercial job is paid when paid,” he added. “So if you aren’t paid, you don’t get paid.”
Kurt Kobelt, a retired labor attorney and board president of Worker Justice Wisconsin, acknowledged that stiffing subcontractors is common in the construction industry. But worker misclassification — treating employees as if they were subcontractors — is not a gray area of the law, he told the Examiner. “The issue is not so much that the law is gray. The issue is that people don’t necessarily have the resources or the time to go through the legal system to correct it,” Kobelt said.
“There’s lots of different legal tests to determine if you’re a genuine independent contractor or an employee,” Kobelt said. “You have to be able to show, if you’re an independent contractor, that you have a business that’s outside of your immediate job you’re doing, and most importantly that you control the way you do your work and how you do your work. You don’t take orders like a conventional employee.”
In Wisconsin, misclassification is a matter of case law, Kobelt explained. Court precedent, rather than a single piece of legislation, governs the distinction between independent contractors and employees. He hopes that the incoming state Legislature will pass a law imposing a standard called the ABC test on employers to determine whether workers are really independent contractors, which the Economic Policy Institute calls the strongest protection against misclassification.
“The employer has a considerable economic incentive to say that they’re not my employee; they’re an independent contractor. Therefore, I don’t owe any workers’ compensation coverage. I don’t owe federal taxes, FICA taxes, and a whole array of benefits,” Kobelt said. Part of the problem with worker misclassification, he said, is the cost in lost tax revenue to local and state governments. In addition, Worker Justice Wisconsin has been drawing attention to wage theft on construction sites that receive both local and state tax subsidies.
Workers march outside the Monona Terrace Convention Center in Madison on Nov. 18 to protest wage theft on publicly subsidized construction sites during a meeting of the Wisconsin Housing and Economic Development Agency (WHEDA) (Ruth Conniff/Wisconsin Examiner)
“Hispanic workers are constantly preyed upon by unscrupulous contractors who steal their wages and expose them to dangerous working conditions, and it’s happening on sites backed by tax credits. This is unacceptable,” Robert Cristl, executive director of Worker Justice Wisconsin said during a Nov. 18 protest in downtown Madison outside  a meeting of the Wisconsin Housing and Economic Development Authority (WHEDA). Recently, he added, “workers from three different WHEDA sites have approached us, alleging tens of thousands of dollars in back wages, misclassification, a lack of workers’ comp, and retaliation.”
Strengthening worker protections
Earlier this year, state Rep. Angelina Cruz, a labor advocate and former president of the Racine teachers’ union, hosted a listening session in her office with immigrant workers who were victims of wage theft and misclassification. “It was pretty breathtaking,” she said. “It’s dehumanizing exploitation that they’re experiencing.”
Cruz is currently drafting legislation based on Minnesota’s Construction Workers Protection Act, which holds general contractors responsible for employee wages if a subcontractor doesn’t pay.
Restoring Wisconsin’s prevailing wage laws, eliminated a decade ago, which set minimum wages for publicly subsidized projects, and increasing funding for enforcement through the Department of Workforce Development are other proposals Cruz hopes to advance.
Detail of a mural inside the Madison Labor Temple building celebrating unions, worker rights and the fight for an eight-hour day. (Mural begun by artist Marcus Nickel and completed by artist Sharon Kilfoy. Wisconsin Examiner photo)
Before Wisconsin repealed prevailing wage, in multifamily housing developments, “exploitation was virtually nonexistent,” said Johnson, the carpenters’ union lawyer. 
“There are great developers in Wisconsin who don’t have issues like this,” he added, but they are at a competitive disadvantage in the current climate.
“Walk on the job and the vibe is very different where workers are trained and paid middle-class wages and where workers are paid off the books,” Johnson said. “If it’s obvious to you, imagine how obvious it should be to a general contractor. They’re hiring the subs and it’s really on them to prevent it.”
What’s next for the unpaid workers
Maria and Ana’s coworkers from Inspire Prairie Springs have scattered to other job sites in different states. One of them, José Lopez, from Venezuela, moved to Florida, where he is working in construction again.
“It’s bad not to get paid. You have to support your family,” he told the Examiner in a phone interview. “It has really weighed on me. It’s very hard.” He has two little boys to support, a 13-year-old and an 18-months old, he said, and he sends money to his parents back in Venezuela. 
“I figure the money is lost. It’s stolen money and it’s gone. That’s how I look at it, for my own mental health,” he said. “It’s bad, but what are you going to do? They don’t pay you and they never respond to your messages.”
But Maria and Ana, who are now working in Illinois, have not given up. “We have to try,” Ana said. 
Ortiz-Whittingham says Worker Justice Wisconsin has successfully clawed back hundreds of thousands of dollars in unpaid wages the group helped workers pursue over the last several years, sometimes by pressuring general contractors — including Stevens — to make good on wages their subcontractors failed to pay. That’s only “the tip of the iceberg” he says. In March, the group organized 13 construction workers on an affordable housing project on East Washington Avenue in Madison. The workers filed liens on the property and ultimately recovered $75,331 in unpaid wages.
Worker Justice Wisconsin is currently helping Maria, Ana and their coworkers file liens on the Stevens Construction property where they worked. 
“Stevens may not have a legal responsibility for these things,” Ortiz-Whittingham said. “But there are legal and then moral responsibilities. They should take responsibility.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: Put American democracy on the road to Oz following Kansas’ landmark midterm election
description: I spent some of my journalism career covering politics on the East Coast — Maryland, Pennsylvania and Vermont. When I told the locals that I was from Kansas, I would usually get a perplexed, blank-stare look, as they struggled to find some connection to the state. A typical response was, “Yes, Dorothy of Oz,” or, […]
text:
Inside the Wizard of Oz Museum in Wamego, a larger-than-life Tin Man with an illuminated heart greets visitors. (Photo by Clay Wirestone/Kansas Reflector)I spent some of my journalism career covering politics on the East Coast — Maryland, Pennsylvania and Vermont. When I told the locals that I was from Kansas, I would usually get a perplexed, blank-stare look, as they struggled to find some connection to the state.
A typical response was, “Yes, Dorothy of Oz,” or, “ Yes, Jayhawks basketball,” or, “Good God, yes, that boring, forever drive on Interstate 70 across Kansas to Denver.”
That rather drab image of Kansas as just another flyover politically red state took a major hit during the recent midterm election that saw Kansas Democrats sweep most of the most important offices. The result was unprecedented, most notably Adam Hamilton’s election to the U.S. Senate, the first Kansas Democrat to win the race since 1932.
Indeed, the U.S. Senate race between Hamilton and incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall was so compelling it made the front pages of several of the world’s foremost newspapers. In the last few weeks of the campaign, the New York Times, Wall Street Journal, Le Monde in Paris and The Times of London all sent reporters to Kansas to cover the contest.
Perhaps Democrats’ Kansas success was not all that surprising, given the state’s political genetics. Hamilton ran as an economic populist and cultural moderate. That resonates with the late 19th century Kansas populists — “Sockless” Jerry Simpson, William Peffer and Mary Elizabeth Lease, who urged Kansas farmers to “raise less corn and more hell.”
Similarly, Hamilton reflects many Kansans’ view on social issues — pro-choice on abortion but opposed to biological men participating in women’s sports and other excesses of the progressive left.
A Methodist pastor, Hamilton has a unique opportunity to confront the most damaging aspect of current American politics: the hatred, the acrimony, the brutal cruelty and character assassinations that characterize so much of the national political dialogue.
Fortunately, in post-election interviews Hamilton stressed he would not lead a highly partisan chorus to demean and insult the political opposition. As many congressional Democrats prepare for an all-out assault on all things Republican and Trumpian, Hamilton and other newly elected moderate Democrats need to lead the party in a different direction.
One of the most notable results from the 2026 midterms is how the vast majority of Americans are disgusted by both parties. Entering the midterms, according to the Real Clear Politics polling average, only 38% of respondents had a favorable view of the Republican Party, while the Democrats barely scored better — with a 39% favorable rating.
A political reporter and commentator for more than 40 years, I always asked office-seekers why they came to their political views. Invariably, they had — for them — a compelling answer: I loved JFK, and so I became a Democrat; or Ronald Reagan understood the communist threat, so I’m a Republican. To me, those and other such responses meant most people take their civic responsibility seriously.
Sadly, agreeing to disagree while respecting one another is perhaps a lost skill in American politics.
In an historical echo of today, late-19th century Kansas populists captured the national imagination. In 1900, a South Dakota newspaperman, L. Frank Baum, published “The Wonderful Wizard of Oz,” which quickly became an icon of popular American culture. According to some literary scholars, the book can serve as an allegory for populism: Dorothy of Kansas is the typical all-American girl; the Scarecrow represents Kansas farmers oppressed by railroads; the Tin Woodman is the factory worker who has been made robotic by industrial capitalism; the Cowardly Lion is William Jennings Bryan, the Populist/Democratic 1896 presidential candidate; the Wizard is the robber baron who manipulates the denizens of Oz (average Americans) with smoke and mirrors.
In his recently published book, “American Odyssey,” Notre Dame University political scientist Patrick J. Deneen wrote that “ ‘The Wizard of Oz’ is for Americans what the ‘Odyssey’ was for the Greeks: a tale that provides a mythic revelation of our deeper inner selves.”
Dorothy, in Deneen’s view, seeks to escape from gray, mundane Kansas. But her fantastic journey — like that of Homer’s ancient hero seeking Ithaca — is actually a quest to return to Kansas. “There’s no place like home” is her prayer to get there.
The combination of “Oz” and “Odyssey” suggests how core Kansas is to American identity. Perhaps stored among the master film reels of “Oz” and other archives in the salt mines in Hutchinson are the traditional American political values of compromise and faith in the good judgment of the American people.
Are Hamilton and the other newly elected Kansas Democrats up to the challenge of reinvigorating American democracy?
David S. Awbrey is a former editorial page editor of The Wichita Eagle. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Audit finds Wisconsin Department of Public Instruction lacks written policies on test scores
description: The Wisconsin Legislative Audit Bureau reported Friday that the Department of Public Instruction does not have written policies for establishing student performance cut scores or changing school accountability thresholds. It also found the agency adjusted student achievement scores downward in 2023-24. The 146-page report is the result of an audit launched b[...]
text:
Underly speaks at a press conference in November 2025. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)The Wisconsin Legislative Audit Bureau reported Friday that the Department of Public Instruction does not have written policies for establishing student performance cut scores or changing school accountability thresholds. It also found the agency adjusted student achievement scores downward in 2023-24.
The 146-page report is the result of an audit launched by the Wisconsin Legislative Joint Audit Committee in February 2025 amid criticism of the state education department for adjusting the cut scores and names used for achievement levels. Republican lawmakers and conservative advocacy groups accused the agency of lowering standards and making the changes without being transparent. DPI maintains that it made the changes in a transparent way and the changes were made to better align testing standards with Wisconsin educational standards as opposed to a national test. 
Joint Audit Committee co-chair Sen. Eric Wimberger (R-Oconto) said in a statement about the audit results that DPI had turned state report cards into an “untrustworthy sham.”
“Accountability is not optional,” co-chair Rep. Robert Wittke (R-Caledonia) said. “The Department of Public Instruction must demonstrate that it is putting Wisconsin students, families, and schools ahead of politics and bureaucracy.”
The audit made 13 recommendations to the agency including establishing written policies and complying with state statute. The Legislative Audit Bureau also suggested that the agency report to the Joint Legislative Audit Committee by March 30, 2027 on its efforts to implement all of the recommendations. 
In its response Friday, DPI noted that the audit was released the same week the agency issued this year’s school and district report cards. According to the agency, the Legislative Audit Bureau hadn’t contacted DPI since April 2026 and the report follows “months of silence.” 
This week, DPI released its annual school and district report cards, which found that 95% of the state’s 377 public school districts receiving report cards met or exceeded expectations. 
Superintendent Jill Underly said in a statement that the audit “offers nothing new” and that the agency had been transparent throughout the process including participating in legislative hearings. 
“Let’s be clear: Our job at the DPI is to do what’s best for Wisconsin’s kids and families. The Legislative Audit Bureau’s job is to conduct objective, fact-based audits, and not play politics,” Underly said. 
“Instead of providing meaningful new information and recommendations, the audit makes factually incorrect assertions, goes beyond the scope of its review, and reads like a continuation of last legislative session’s partisan political theater rather than a review conducted in good faith,” Underly said.
DPI started the process of reviewing Wisconsin’s academic standards in 2023, and according to the audit, the agency met with administrators from the state’s largest school districts, got feedback from parents, educators and administrators and considered information from other states. However, there were no written policies guiding the changes to student performance level categories. It also did not have written policies to guide communication related to the changes. 
DPI said in its response to the audit that it does have written guidance for making changes to cut scores and producing school district report cards, but said that it would improve those and would develop a policy document governing school and district report card threshold changes. 
DPI changed its cut scores by dropping the National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP) — also known as the “nation’s report card” — as a reference point and instead using the Wisconsin Forward Exam and other similar exams in Minnesota, Michigan and Illinois. 
The report found that DPI adjusted school year 2023-2024 achievement scores downward to align them with the distribution of achievement scores in Wisconsin from the previous year.
According to the audit, the agency decided that a student achievement score should not be lower than the previous year. 
“If a school or school district’s adjusted student achievement score for school year 2023-2024 would have been lower than its score for school year 2022-2023, DPI instead used the school or school district’s student achievement score for school year 2022-2023,” the audit states. “As a result, no school or school district’s student achievement score for school year 2023-2024 decreased from the previous year, regardless of performance.” 
DPI said in its response to the audit that the “one-time adjustment: to achievement scoring for 2023-24 report cards was made to maintain comparability across report card years, while incorporating the 2024 results.
“Applying this one-time adjustment universally to all schools and districts was the best way to include the updated Forward Exam results in 2023-24 report cards until the DPI could conduct a report card standard setting in 2025,” the agency said. 
The agency said it made the adjustments in consultation with “national experts in assessment and accountability systems.”
In 2025, DPI implemented new school performance thresholds. State statutes do not prescribe a method for DPI to implement those and the agency, similar to setting cut scores, did not have a written policy for the process. 
The audit states that “developing and implementing written policies can improve transparency and accountability, help ensure that processes are conducted consistently and appropriately, and preserve institutional knowledge.” 
The report suggests that the Legislature could modify state statute to specify the process that DPI must use to change assessment cut scores or it said lawmakers could leave statutes as they are to give the agency flexibility to pursue changes at its discretion. 
“Statutes do not prescribe a process for DPI to use to establish or change assessment cut scores,” the audit states. “In the future, DPI could choose to modify assessment cut scores or modify the processes it will use to determine assessment cut scores, which again may make academic assessment results not comparable over time.”
As lawmakers ordered an audit over the achievement issues in 2025, Republican lawmakers also passed a bill that would have reversed the changes made by DPI and tied future changes back to previous standards. 
The bill was vetoed by Gov. Tony Evers, who had publicly disagreed with DPI over the changes, but wrote that the bill would “essentially strip control over school scoring and standard metrics” from the state superintendent and give lawmakers that power. He said it would have been an “untenable result” for students and schools. 
“Metrics for school scores and standards should be based on science, data, doing what is best for kids, and improving student outcomes, not the whims of legislative party control or what is politically palatable for lawmakers in the Legislature,” Evers wrote then. 
The audit also found DPI did not comply with statutes by producing school accountability reports containing all the required information and did not comply with statute on producing school performance reports. 
One instance of agency noncompliance identified by the audit was that the agency did not include information about “gap closure” in student achievement in reading and mathematics. The DPI said that it is required to define that measure and it redesigned the measure in 2020 to focus on target groups of the lowest-performing students in schools. It said the prior measure “suffered from severe score volatility in small schools, widespread confusion, and frequent exclusions of demographic subgroups due to small group size.” 
“The DPI strongly asserts that it meets statutory requirements pertaining to school and district report cards. The DPI will work with the Legislature to update unfeasible statutes to reflect current operational practice,” the agency said.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Democrats demand answers from Oz after delay in $50B rural health awards
authors: Sarah Jane Tribble | KFF Health News
description: Congressional Democrats are demanding answers and more transparency from the Trump administration after a nine-day delay of annual awards from a $50 billion fund meant to improve healthcare for rural Americans. Saying rural care is “in an acute state of crisis,” 18 members of Congress sent a letter to Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services […]
text:
Dr. Mehmet Oz is administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. In this photo, Oz speaks at a March 15, 2022 press conference in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Pennsylvania Capital-Star).Congressional Democrats are demanding answers and more transparency from the Trump administration after a nine-day delay of annual awards from a $50 billion fund meant to improve healthcare for rural Americans.
Saying rural care is “in an acute state of crisis,” 18 members of Congress sent a letter to Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz late Thursday. The letter pointed to what it called “an alarming lack of public transparency” and said the fund “lacks sufficient guardrails to protect rural hospitals at greatest risk of closure.”
Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski said her state “got no explanation from CMS as to why” it got $3 million less in its second-year Rural Health Transformation Program allocation. It was a roughly 1.5% reduction from its $193.4 million first-year award. State leaders have not received information about an appeals process, she said.
Any delay in knowing how much they received and any reduction in their base funding is significant, Budzinski said, because states need to plan for an “acute impact” from the loss of other federal funding.
In the first year, states competed for their initial share of the $50 billion, which is handed out at $10 billion a year for five years. They won awards ranging from $147 million to $281 million. Most of the lawmakers who signed the letter were from states that lost funding this year. Rep. Terri Sewell of Alabama, which got $4.1 million less, along with Sen. Michael Bennet of Colorado, which saw a nearly $3 million drop, also spearheaded the letter along with Budzinski.

One concern, Budzinski said, is “making sure that the money isn’t going to consultants, that it’s actually getting to the rural providers that it is supposed to be getting to.” The lawmakers asked Oz for a response to detailed questions by Nov. 25. They also requested a briefing about the delays to the funding announcement, which was first reported by KFF Health News, and the impact on states.
The second-year awards were due to be announced by Oct. 31, but an Oct. 30 letter from CMS stated officials “discovered an additional administrative process requirement.” Instead, second-year funding was announced Nov. 9.
“Those kind of delays prevent a state to fully prepare for what’s to come,” Budzinski said.
CMS oversees the fund and its newly formed Office of Rural Health Transformation. Agency officials did not respond to questions for this article before the given deadline.
Republicans passed the Rural Health Transformation Program last summer as a last-minute sweetener to offset other ramifications of President Donald Trump’s signature budget law, including an estimated $137 billion in Medicaid spending cuts for rural America over 10 years.
That rural money is “retail therapy for Congress,” said Cara James, president and chief executive of Grantmakers in Health, while speaking at a Milken Institute event this month.
Because the same tax law cut Medicaid spending, which rural hospitals and people disproportionately use, as well as supplemental food assistance and other government grants, the short-term money would not “help sustain people” in rural America, James said.
Then, she posed a persistent fear about the fund: “If it’s even getting to the communities.”
Five rural hospitals have closed or been converted into lower-level facilities since the rural fund was created, including one in Michigan that shuttered beds and switched to providing only emergency services to survive, according to a list curated by the Cecil G. Sheps Center for Health Services Research at the University of North Carolina.
The letter stated lawmakers’ concerns that too much of the rural fund “could flow to large consulting and technology firms rather than supporting providers and communities on the ground.”
After the law passed last year, state leaders had just over seven weeks to write applications as they competed for the first-year funds. All 50 states won funding with allocations determined by a federal scoring process. Each year, officials are to revisit the funding allotments.
Most states saw their funding change by less than 2%. North Dakota and Iowa won the largest gains; New Jersey, Florida, and Vermont saw the biggest reductions.
Although federal officials have created state data maps, released a slew of press announcements, and led sessions on the complicated scoring of state applications, it’s not enough, said Alan Morgan, CEO of the National Rural Health Association.
The association, which represents hospitals and community clinics nationwide, sent its own letter to federal officials Nov. 9. Morgan said that the way states win money needs “to be articulated in a way that success can be replicated by all states going forward.”
Morgan said his association’s analysis found that state leaders are sending the federal money to local hospitals and clinics because communities and individuals are “relying on rural hospitals to be there to deliver care.” But it’s unclear, he said, how much of the overall rural fund local hospitals are actually receiving versus how much is benefiting other entities, such as consultants.
In their letter, Budzinski and the other Democrats asked if CMS would establish a searchable database that tracks spending. They also asked for an explanation of how federal officials will evaluate state performance and allocate awards.
It was just the latest congressional letter to federal health officials on this issue.
In August 2025, a month after the law passed, Democrats sent a letter about the program’s rollout to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. And last November, Budzinski reached out to Oz on behalf of Illinois. Bennet, along with Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine and others, signed a letter in June asking that the funds be targeted to rescue rural hospitals and clinics.
“We haven’t gotten full responses to any of these inquiries,” said Budzinski, who will become chair of the House’s largest Democratic caucus, the New Democrat Coalition, as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress.
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF—an independent source of health policy research, polling, and journalism. Learn more about KFF.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Georgia Democrats intend to look for ‘pathway’ to target state’s six-week abortion ban
description: It was the biggest applause line of the biggest event in Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms’ campaign, a rally featuring former President Barack Obama less than a week ahead of the Nov. 3 election. “I believe in a woman’s right to make decisions –” Bottoms said, then paused for more than 20 seconds of cheers and […]
text:
Protesters on both sides of the abortion issue clash outside the Georgia Capitol in 2022. A newly elected Democratic majority in the Georgia House could mean changes to the state's six-week abortion ban, but that wouldn't be easy.  Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderIt was the biggest applause line of the biggest event in Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms’ campaign, a rally featuring former President Barack Obama less than a week ahead of the Nov. 3 election.
Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms speaks at the state Capitol about her transition into office on Nov. 6, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
“I believe in a woman’s right to make decisions –” Bottoms said, then paused for more than 20 seconds of cheers and chants of “Keisha, Keisha.”
“ — a woman’s right to make decisions about her own body and her future,” she continued. “And as governor, I will fight to restore that right.”
Georgia has banned most abortions since a 2022 U.S. Supreme Court decision overturned the federal right to an abortion and left the issue to the states. With some exceptions, Georgia bans abortions once embryonic cardiac activity is detectable, typically around the sixth week of pregnancy. The ban remains in place while a challenge against it moves through court. Before Roe v. Wade was overturned, Georgia allowed abortions up to about 20 weeks of pregnancy.
Bottoms’ health platform included repealing that law and returning to “the Roe-era standard.”
Speaking to reporters at the Capitol the Friday after Election Day, Bottoms appeared to acknowledge obstacles to making that happen.
“If we see a pathway to do something about it this session, then we’re going to take that opportunity,” she said, referring to the annual lawmaking session set to begin in January. “And it may not be this session. If it’s not this session, then we’re going to take it at the first opportunity that we have.”
All pathways run through the Senate
Senate Majority Leader Jason Anavitarte speaks to members of the press. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Georgia Democrats outperformed expectations in this year’s midterm election, sweeping all statewide offices on the ballot and narrowly gaining control of the state House. But any pathway for Bottoms to change the abortion law, known as the LIFE Act, would need to run through the state Senate, which is set to remain under slim Republican control.
Republicans will have a two-seat majority in the chamber, which means GOP leadership will likely have final say over which bills are assigned to committee, a required first step toward becoming law.
And once a bill makes it to the full Senate, Democrats will need the support of at least two Senate Republicans to move legislation through the chamber.
Speaking on a recent episode of the Atlanta Journal-Constitution’s “Politically Georgia” podcast, Senate Majority Leader Jason Anavitarte indicated that the Senate’s Republican majority would not have much appetite to shift its priorities on issues like abortion.
State Sen. Josh McLaurin, who is set to become the next lieutenant governor. Jill Nolin/Georgia Recorder
“Georgia elected a majority state Senate of Republicans,” the Dallas Republican said. “I mean, those are the electoral results, whether it was 29 or 31 or 32, they elected 29. So we’re going to stand by what we believe is the right thing to do, whether it’s on abortion or gun rights or the economy or taxes or whatever. We’re gonna have a deliberative conversation, and then we’ll make decisions.”
While the Senate will be under a Republican majority, a Democrat is set to preside over it. Sandy Springs Democratic state Sen. Josh McLaurin is set to become the state’s next lieutenant governor in January after winning the majority of votes in the midterm.
McLaurin said a majority is not the same thing as a mandate.
“Those 29 seats are gerrymandered,” he said. “If we had fair maps, Democrats would already have a majority. It’s a testament to the size of voters’ mandate this year that we flipped four Senate seats that were previously considered unwinnable because of gerrymandering. The majority leader should keep that in mind as he performs his moral calculus.”
Room for compromise?
Sen. Sally Harrell. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Some Democrats hope a full repeal is possible but believe a compromise is more likely.
“The compromise is going to have to happen in the Senate because that’s where you still have a narrow margin of Republicans,” said state Sen. Sally Harrell, an Atlanta Democrat who previously sought to overturn the abortion ban. “That’s where they have the majority, but there’s so much public support for being able to access abortions and support of reproductive freedom that you might find some Republicans who feel that pressure and who might be willing to enter into a dialogue about making some changes around the edges.”
Harrell said those changes might include reexamining the legal ramifications of fetal personhood, the idea that a fetus ought to be treated as a distinct legal person, or protecting doctors’ right to perform procedures on pregnant women that may harm the fetus.
Georgia’s abortion law seeks to provide these protections, including specifying that doctors are clear to act in cases of “medical emergency,” defined as “a condition in which an abortion is necessary in order to prevent the death of the pregnant woman or the substantial and irreversible physical impairment of a major bodily function of the pregnant woman.”
Some doctors and medical organizations say the language of the law isn’t compatible with the actual practice of medicine.
Rep. Michelle Au. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
State Rep. Michelle Au, a Johns Creek Democrat and a physician, said a prime example is the case of Amber Thurman, a 28-year-old medical assistant who died in 2022.
Thurman experienced a rare complication after undergoing a medication abortion. She went to the hospital with a severe infection, but doctors delayed treatment for 20 hours, and by then it was too late to save her life. Georgia’s maternal mortality review committee deemed her death preventable and found the delay largely responsible, ProPublica reported.
Au said all kinds of healthcare providers are regularly tasked with caring for pregnant women, not just obstetricians, and there are no bright lines establishing when a medical emergency exists. She said the law makes treating pregnant women more difficult, even when the consequences are not fatal.
“The law, which is not a clinical mechanism, it’s not a clinical recommendation, interjects itself in a way that does not harmonize with the way medicine is practiced, and it interferes with the way that medicine is practiced,” she said. “And that’s what we’re seeing, not just in these cases with catastrophic outcomes, but across the spectrum. Anytime that you are tasked with taking the best care of a patient the way you were trained to do and you hesitate because you’re like, ‘I’m not sure if I can do this now because of this legal regime,’ that impedes patient care.
Democrats and abortion rights advocates held a press conference in 2023 to unveil a proposal to repeal Georgia’s six-week abortion ban and protect access to the procedure. Jill Nolin/Georgia Recorder
“That makes patient care worse,” she added. “It creates worse outcomes, even if the patient doesn’t ultimately end up dying.”
Au said lawmakers will be hearing from doctors and medical organizations about what changes they would like to see.
“The most important thing moving forward is we cannot have a law, we cannot have it written into statute that healthcare providers are criminalized for providing what we have been taught to be the best standard of care for certain clinical situations,” she said.
Elizabeth Edmonds, executive director of the Georgia Life Alliance, a nonprofit that advocates against abortion, said she thinks the law protects doctors as-is, but legislation to spell that out more clearly could be more palatable for conservative senators than an outright repeal.
“I don’t think it’s out of the question to maybe put together a piece of legislation that just spells that out but doesn’t touch any of the restrictions or other things established in the LIFE Act,” she said.
Other states have passed similar legislation. In Texas, it was called the “Life of the Mother Act.”
“They called it a ‘cleanup bill,’ even though it wasn’t really cleaning anything up, it was really more of a public education thing, letting people know doctors are allowed to provide these services and treatments, that a woman doesn’t have to be on the doorstep of death to receive life-saving care and things like that,” Edmonds said. “So I don’t think that that would be out of the question, and we would certainly work with anybody on either side if it helps to clear up that public confusion.”
Pressure from both sides
Cole Muzio stumps for Georgia religious liberty at the state Capitol in 2025. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
If Georgia’s new Democratic leadership decides that kind of compromise will be a goal for next year’s session, they can expect resistance.
Cole Muzio is founder and president of Frontline Policy Action, an influential rightwing evangelical lobbying group that has successfully pushed for culturally conservative legislation, including Georgia’s abortion law.
Muzio said the current law provides protections for doctors and he would resist changes to it.
“I don’t see a problem with the language of the law,” he said. “I think we’ve just got political narratives that have been pushed, and it would take a lot of convincing for me to see anything beyond the politics aiming to increase abortion.”
Muzio said he is hopeful Democrats will not exceed what he views as a narrow mandate from voters and that his organization is ready to work with them on legislation focused on bipartisan issues like boosting support for special education and children in foster care.
But he said Frontline is ready to defend outgoing Gov. Brian Kemp’s legacy, including the abortion ban.
“Our voters will not look kindly on any senator that participates actively in undoing what the governor achieved,” Muzio said. “I don’t believe or expect that will happen, but the unity of the caucus and a unified front behind caucus leadership will serve these individual members well as they go back to their districts.”
But legislators are likely to receive pushback not only from the anti-abortion side.
Kwajelyn Jackson, executive director of the Feminist Center for Reproductive Liberation, a health clinic in Atlanta providing abortions within the current law, said reproductive rights advocates will be lobbying for change as well.
“We will ensure that, whether or not there is waffling or hesitation, that it is made clear to everyone who is holding public office that we are demanding real change and that we are not willing to wait and see, that we actually want to see action being taken as quickly and as definitively as possible,” she said.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio had more than 130 intimate partner-related fatalities in one-year span, according to new report
description: If you are experiencing relationship abuse, call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 800-799-SAFE (7233) or text START to 88788.  Ohio had the second-highest number of intimate partner-related fatalities, according to a new report.  There were 134 intimate partner relationship fatalities in 101 cases from July 1, 2025 to June 30, according to a new […]
text:
A domestic violence awareness ribbon. (Stock photo from Getty Images.)If you are experiencing relationship abuse, call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 800-799-SAFE (7233) or text START to 88788. 
Ohio had the second-highest number of intimate partner-related fatalities, according to a new report. 
There were 134 intimate partner relationship fatalities in 101 cases from July 1, 2025 to June 30, according to a new report from the Ohio Domestic Violence Network. There were 157 fatalities in last year’s report. 
“Domestic violence is very prevalent in Ohio and ultimately very deadly,” said Maria York, Ohio Domestic Violence Network’s director of policy and communications. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“There’s people behind the numbers, and so we always want to make sure that we remember that there’s people with lives and futures behind the data.”
This is the eleventh year of the report, which the Ohio Domestic Violence Network compiles using statistics from media reports of intimate partner relationship fatalities. 
Of this year’s fatalities, 89 were victims and 45 were perpetrators. There were 73 female fatalities and 61 male fatalities. 
The youngest person who died was seven months old and the oldest person was 88 years old, according to the report. 
There were 20 murder/suicides and four multiple murder/suicides. 
In nearly half of all the cases, the relationship was ending or had recently ended. 
More than 19,000 survivors reached out for emergency shelter last year, but not all can be taken in, York said. 
“Over half of the survivors who reached out for shelter were turned away just because we don’t have the capacity or the resources,” she said. 
“It’s probably very safe to say that there are survivors who are seeking help and are not getting served just because we can’t begin to meet the need.”
Ohio has 76 domestic violence programs. 
“There’s not a shelter in every county or a program in every county,” York said. 
“A lot of the neighboring counties are doing outreach to counties that don’t have a program. But southeast Ohio, like Gallia County, that area is pretty sparse.”
Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine’s recently announced new initiatives designed to help domestic violence survivors including an additional $1 million will be directed toward the state’s domestic violence shelters recognized by the Office of Criminal Justice Services, among others. 
“Ohio must continue to be innovative in its work to protect both domestic violence survivors and the law enforcement officers who respond to calls for help,” DeWine said in a statement.
Three-fourths of domestic violence deaths were a result of gun violence, according to the Ohio Domestic Violence Network report. 108 people were shot in these cases, and only seven people survived. 
Nearly all of the other deaths were strangulations, traumatic brain injury, or stabbing, according to the report. One woman was beaten to death with a handmade wooden club while she was sleeping, according to the report. 
Five children were murdered, either by a parent or a stepparent. 
“These are children who are murdered by a parent, specifically in an effort to get back at the other parents about power and control,” York said. 
“So they’re using their kids as a message to say, ‘This is against you’ is why they’re killing the kids.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Wisconsin DOA projects $4 billion budget surplus and $2 billion rainy day fund
description: The Wisconsin Department of Administration is projecting the state will end the 2026-27 fiscal year with $4.18 billion — over $1.8 billion higher than previously estimated — marking the sixth year of a state budget surplus.  The agency’s report released Friday stated that fiscally Wisconsin is “well-positioned for the future,” as Democrats prepare to write [[...]
text:
Wisconsin State Capitol (Baylor Spears | Wisconsin Examiner)The Wisconsin Department of Administration is projecting the state will end the 2026-27 fiscal year with $4.18 billion — over $1.8 billion higher than previously estimated — marking the sixth year of a state budget surplus. 
The agency’s report released Friday stated that fiscally Wisconsin is “well-positioned for the future,” as Democrats prepare to write the next state budget, but also said there are some factors that could change the projection. 
The state’s stabilization fund — also known as the rainy day fund — is nearly $2.1 billion, the largest in state history and over six times the balance at the end of fiscal year 2017-18. 
Gov. Tony Evers said in a statement that the report is proof of his administration’s work to “be good stewards of Wisconsinites’ tax dollars while still making smart, strategic investments in needs that were long neglected before I took office.” 
“We have one of the largest budget surpluses in state history, the highest ‘rainy day’ fund balance in state history, and some of the best, record-breaking years Wisconsin has ever seen for tourism, apprenticeship, unemployment, and much more,” Evers said. “Wisconsin’s in darn good shape, and it’s in large part due to the hard work of so many across our administration these last eight years.”
The report is the last before Democratic Gov.-elect David Crowley and state lawmakers take office in January. Democrats will lead the state budget process for the first time since 2009. During the session that produced the 2009-2011 budget, Gov. Jim Doyle and lawmakers were dealing with the Great Recession and a $6 billion budget deficit. Under the resulting budget, most state programs had cuts of at least 1%, but many had cuts of 5% or more.
The DOA report projected the state’s finances in the future considering agencies’ requests for the next state budget. If all were approved, the state would have a $435.7 million surplus at the end of 2027-28 fiscal year and a $4 billion budget deficit at the end of the 2028-29 fiscal year. 
Most agencies were directed by Evers not to increase state spending, but exceptions were made in a few areas including K-12 schools aid, the University of Wisconsin system and Medical Assistance. 
Of all the agencies, the Department of Public Instruction is requesting the largest investment from the state, putting in a request totaling an additional $2.75 billion. State Superintendent Jill Underly is calling for the overhaul of the funding formula and investments to stop public schools’ reliance on local property tax increases to keep up with costs.
The University of Wisconsin system is seeking an additional $730 million from the state over the two-year period. The Department of Health Services is requesting an additional $1.8 billion in state funds in the 2027-29 budget to continue Medicaid services. 
“It is not uncommon for agency requests to exceed available projected revenues,” the report stated. “Again, this imbalance assumes that all state agency requests are approved, which is quite unlikely.”
Democratic lawmakers have said they will address high costs including for education, healthcare and local government. They’ll consider agency requests as well as input from across the state and from the incoming governor as they write the budget. 
The incoming chairs of the Joint Finance Committee Rep. Tip McGuire (D-Kenosha) and Sen. LaTonya Johnson (D-Milwaukee) said in a statement about the report that Wisconsinites “spoke loud and clear in November.”
“We are looking forward to crafting a budget that prioritizes working families and puts affordability first,” the lawmakers said. 
The report also identifies factors that could change the projections in the future including the war in Iran and artificial intelligence. It states that the conflict in Iran “poses a significant risk” to the economic forecast as there are higher energy prices, weakening consumer demand and the potential for higher inflation. 
Investments in AI, meanwhile, could go one of two ways. 
“Given the proportion of current economic growth and stability tied to investment in AI, an AI bust would heighten the risk of a recession or at least a sharp slowdown in growth,” the report states. “However, if AI investment proves to be substantially more additive than projected to productivity gains, growth could accelerate from its current trajectory.”
